chapters.title: Scaling from Zero to Millions of Users
chapters.fullTitle: Chapter 1: Scaling from Zero to Millions of Users
keyPoints: Scaling is iterative: observe, find the bottleneck, add one layer of capability, then verify. Don't scale a layer that isn't the bottleneck.
Vertical scaling is simple but capped and still a single point. Horizontal scaling offers more capacity, but move sessions out of the web nodes first.
Read replicas share reads, not write locks. Replication lags, so get read-your-writes from the primary or a version number; don't bet on fast replicas.
A cache trades possibly stale reads for speed: update the database first, then delete the cache entry, and retry or compensate if the delete fails.
Queues redeliver, so consumers must be idempotent: commit the dedup record and the business change in one transaction, then ack.
The shard key decides data placement. Adding shards won't split a celebrity hotspot; handle reads, writes, and fan-out separately.

lessons.title: Single to Tiered
lessons.summary: One server first: when to split the DB, how to scale

exercises.explanation: Scaling is an iteration: observe, find the bottleneck, add one layer of capability, then verify. Sharding or splitting services while the CPU is still idle just brings the complexity forward, and buying a bigger machine without knowing the bottleneck may leave the problem in place.
options: Upgrade to the biggest server available and see what happens
Split everything into microservices to prepare for the future
Shard the database right away and be done with it
Check the metrics and find the resource that runs out first
exercises.prompt: A system has been getting slower since launch, and the team is about to scale it. Following this chapter's approach, what should they do first?

exercises.explanation: On one machine, the CPU, memory, disk, and database all compete: a slow query that saturates the disk slows the API too, and deploying the app can even restart the database. The machine going down takes the whole site with it, but that is only one of the failure modes.
exercises.prompt: On a single server, the web app and the database each use their own resources, so as long as the machine stays up, one being busy won't slow down the other.

exercises.explanation: DNS first turns the domain into an IP address, so the client knows which machine to send the HTTP request to. After processing, the server returns HTML to web pages and JSON to mobile apps.
items: The user visits the domain api.mysite.com
DNS resolves the domain to an IP address
The client sends an HTTP request to that IP
The web server returns HTML or JSON
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of handling one request on a single-server setup in order

exercises.explanation: Once separated, the two tiers no longer fight over one machine, and each can scale to match its own bottleneck. The database is still a single point of failure and the network adds a hop, so check connection pools, timeouts, backups, and a rollback plan before migrating.
options: It clears the way to switch to NoSQL
The web tier and database tier can scale independently
The same SQL queries automatically run faster
The database is no longer a single point of failure
exercises.prompt: As users grow, you move the database off the web server onto a dedicated server. What is the main benefit?

exercises.explanation: Pick a database starting from queries: access keys, transactions and JOINs, consistency needs, and what the team can operate. Stock deduction needs multi-table atomic transactions, where mature SQL is usually safer. Benchmarks alone miss that need, and dual-writing two stores breaks atomicity and adds sync and ops work.
options: Keep MySQL for transactions and dual-write inventory to NoSQL
List query and transaction needs first; for strong transactions SQL is often safer
Load-test the inventory table; if NoSQL is faster, switch everything
The data is still small, so either choice is fine; don't agonize
exercises.prompt: Deducting inventory for an order needs an atomic multi-table transaction, and the team knows MySQL well. Someone proposes switching to NoSQL for lower latency. Following this chapter, what is the most sensible response?

exercises.explanation: Ultra-low latency, schema-less data, and massive storage are classic NoSQL use cases. Multi-table JOINs and transactions are exactly what SQL does best, and moving to NoSQL when the team only knows how to run MySQL just adds risk.
options: You need multi-table JOINs with atomic transactions
The data has no fixed structure and no relationships to maintain
The application needs extremely low latency
You need to store massive amounts of data
The team only has experience operating MySQL
exercises.prompt: In which situations might a non-relational database be a better fit?

exercises.explanation: Every new capability brings a new cost. Separating the database adds network overhead; vertical scaling (a bigger pot) is simple but capped and still a single point; horizontal scaling (many pots cooking together) must solve routing and sessions; before switching to NoSQL, confirm you don't need transactions or JOINs.
pairs: Extra network hop; connection pools to manage
A bigger machine, but with a hardware ceiling
Needs a load balancer and shared sessions
May lose transactions and multi-table JOINs
exercises.prompt: Match each scaling move with its main cost

exercises.explanation: A bigger machine is the smallest change and works fastest, but it has a hardware ceiling and is still a single point. A pool of servers behind a load balancer removes the single point and lets traffic fail over.
exercises.prompt: Complete the scaling template for interviews
exercises.text: When the bottleneck is single-machine capacity, use [[vertical scaling]] first for a bigger machine as a quick fix, then [[horizontal scaling]] for a server pool that removes the single point and allows failover.

exercises.explanation: When you need to validate the business quickly, one machine is enough. What matters is recording total request time and database time as a baseline. Split by bottleneck once some resource actually runs out first, instead of starting with a distributed architecture.
exercises.prompt: For an internal tool or low-traffic MVP, starting with one server that runs the web app, database, and cache together is a reasonable choice.

lessons.title: Load and Replicas
lessons.summary: Spreading traffic, read/write split, replication lag

exercises.explanation: A load balancer only distributes requests; the lock wait happens inside the shared database. More web servers start more concurrent transactions, which can lengthen the lock queue. First find the lock holder and the transaction duration, then shorten transactions and add indexes instead of adding web servers.
options: The load balancer becomes the new bottleneck
Latency drops to about a tenth
The lock waits get spread across the web servers
Little improvement, and possibly a longer lock queue
exercises.prompt: At peak, an API slows down, and traces show the time is all spent waiting on locks in one database. What is the most likely result of adding 10 more web servers behind the load balancer?

exercises.explanation: With serial lock holding, the ceiling is about 1 / 0.05 = 20 per second, and real systems lose some to other overhead. Whether there are 2 or 20 web servers in front, the database holds only this one inventory row.
options: About 20
About 200
Depends on the number of web servers
About 50
exercises.prompt: Every order updates the same inventory row, and each transaction holds the lock on that row for 50 ms, one after another. At best, how many updates per second can that row complete?

exercises.explanation: Read replicas only share reads. Writes must still go to the primary, so write locks on the same row still run one after another. Fix hot writes by shortening transactions, using atomic conditional updates, or splitting inventory along business lines.
exercises.prompt: When every order updates the same inventory row, adding a few read replicas to the database noticeably eases lock waits on the primary.

exercises.explanation: Reads can fall back to the primary temporarily or move to other replicas, and when the primary fails, you promote one replica. Letting several replicas accept writes causes conflicts, and multi-primary or ring replication doesn't automatically remove data loss, conflict, or split-brain risk.
options: Switch to ring replication, and failover can no longer lose data
When the only replica goes down, send reads to the primary for now
With several replicas, route reads to healthy ones and build a new replica
When the primary goes down, let all replicas accept writes at once
When the primary goes down, promote one replica to be the new primary
exercises.prompt: In a primary-replica setup, which of these failure-handling practices are reasonable?

exercises.explanation: In production the chosen replica may lag behind the old primary and need a recovery script to catch up. You also need a quorum mechanism and must fence off the old primary; otherwise, if it comes back and keeps accepting writes, you get a split brain.
exercises.prompt: After the primary goes down, the replica that gets promoted may not be fully up to date, so confirm the replication position before switching and fill in missing data with a recovery script.

exercises.explanation: Lag is usually small but can exceed 1 second at peak or during failures, and the user would still see the old value; don't bet on replicas being fast enough. A stricter approach returns a version number with the write response, requires the replica to reach it on read, and otherwise waits or reads from the primary.
options: All reads now go to the primary for good, leaving the replicas idle
The primary only handles writes and cannot serve reads
No problem; replication lag is usually far below 1 second
Replication lag can exceed 1 second, so it isn't a strict guarantee
exercises.prompt: A user changes their nickname and refreshes right away, but still sees the old one. The team's fix is “for 1 second after a write, send reads to the primary.” What is the main problem with this fix?

exercises.explanation: Write down the version, check it on read, and wait or switch paths if the replica isn't there yet. The version token must be issued by a trusted service; a position claimed by the client can't simply be believed. That way, even when replication lag exceeds expectations, the user never reads a value from before their own write.
items: Write to the primary; version goes from 41 to 42
The write response returns version 42 to the client
A later read request carries min_version=42
The read router checks whether a replica has reached 42
If the replica is still at 41, wait or read the primary
exercises.prompt: Use version numbers to guarantee read-your-writes: put the reads that follow a nickname change in order

exercises.explanation: A replica takes time to catch up with the primary, and reads during that window return old values. Read-your-writes only guarantees that users see their own writes; it doesn't mean every user sees the latest global state.
exercises.prompt: Complete the consistency problem that replication causes
exercises.text: Reading from a replica right after writing to the primary may miss the new data; this is [[replication lag]]. When you need [[read-your-writes]], read the primary for a short window or carry a version number.

exercises.explanation: Read-your-writes depends on the whole read path. Routing only covers the database leg; if the cache still holds the version-41 nickname, the request returns the old value at the cache layer. So after a write, the related cache entries must be invalidated too.
exercises.prompt: Even if a read request is correctly routed to the primary, the user still sees the old nickname when the request first hits a cache holding an old version.

lessons.title: Caching and CDN
lessons.summary: Cache reads and writes, hit rate, CDN, stateless web

exercises.explanation: The database has committed and is the source of truth, so rolling back makes no sense. A failed deletion leaves the old value in the cache, and the next read will hit it rather than correct it, so retry or compensate with a message.
options: Roll back the database update that was just committed
Retry the deletion, or compensate asynchronously through a message
Ignore it; the next read will correct it automatically
Change this key to never expire
exercises.prompt: On a write you update the database first, then delete the cache entry. This time the database commit succeeded but the cache deletion failed. What should you do?

exercises.explanation: Only misses go to the database: from 10,000×2%=200 per second to 10,000×20%=2,000 per second, which is 10 times, not just 18% more. The hit rate looks like it fell only a little, yet database load grew by an order of magnitude.
options: About 1.2 times
Basically unchanged
About 10 times
About 18 times
exercises.prompt: There are 10,000 cacheable reads per second, and the hit rate drops from 98% to 80%. Roughly how many times more origin requests does the database now take?

exercises.explanation: Many evictions with full memory mean too little capacity; clustered expirations may come from a uniform TTL or a deployment flush; cache timeouts counted as misses also drag the rate down. Cumulative values dilute recent changes and a blended ratio hides who is missing, so compare per-endpoint increments in the same window.
options: The overall hit rate with all endpoints mixed together
Timeout and error rates of cache requests
The cumulative hit rate since the process started
Eviction counts, and whether memory has hit its limit
Expiration counts, and whether TTLs cluster at the same moment
exercises.prompt: The cache hit rate suddenly drops. Which of the following are worth checking first to find the cause?

exercises.explanation: Applications often log “cache timed out, fell back to the database” as a miss. Then look at cache latency, error rate, and connection-pool waits to tell “not found” from “couldn't be reached.” A single percentage can't explain the cause.
exercises.prompt: If the application treats a cache query timeout as a miss, a falling hit rate doesn't necessarily mean the data isn't in the cache.

exercises.explanation: Caches suit data that is read often and changed rarely. Data that changes every time almost always misses and still goes to the database, with an extra layer to maintain and a risk of stale reads. A cache trades “slow” for “possibly stale”; it is not free speed.
exercises.prompt: For an endpoint whose data changes on every read and whose hit rate is very low, adding a cache still reliably reduces database load.

exercises.explanation: Expiration handles “leave when time is up,” eviction handles “who leaves first when full.” Writing the database and cache separately inevitably leaves an inconsistency window, and a single cache server is a potential single point of failure, so deploy several across data centers.
pairs: Drops entries at expiry to free memory
Frees space when full; LRU is common
Database and cache aren't written atomically
Avoids a single point of failure at the cache
exercises.prompt: Match each cache design point with the problem it addresses

exercises.explanation: With a content hash in the file name (such as app.8f3c.js), the URL changes whenever the content does, so stale cache entries are never hit. A longer expiry keeps old files around longer, manual purges are easy to miss, and turning off the CDN loses nearby acceleration.
options: Set the CDN expiry as long as possible
Turn off the CDN and send every request to the origin
Manually purge every node on each release
Put a content hash in the file name so an update changes the URL
exercises.prompt: After a front-end release, some users still get the old app.js from the CDN. What is the most reliable and least laborious way to prevent this long term?

exercises.explanation: A CDN is only an acceleration layer; the origin still holds the original files. If clients can fall back to the origin, a CDN failure just makes pages slower instead of making resources completely unreachable.
exercises.prompt: When the CDN has a temporary outage, clients should be able to detect the problem and request resources directly from the origin server.

exercises.explanation: Once sessions live in shared storage, any web server can handle any user's request, so scaling and failover are unaffected. Sticky sessions are only a temporary workaround and reduce failover flexibility.
options: Only in the load balancer's memory
A copy in each web server's local memory, synced periodically
In shared storage, so web nodes are stateless
Enable sticky sessions to pin users to one machine long term
exercises.prompt: You want web servers to scale in and out automatically with traffic. What is the best way to store users' login state?

exercises.explanation: Stateless means request handling doesn't depend on the local memory of one web machine. Session data still exists; it has just moved to shared storage, tokens, or a user database, and those stores are themselves state.
exercises.prompt: A “stateless” web tier means the whole system no longer stores any session data.

lessons.title: Queues and Shards
lessons.summary: Multi-data center, queues, monitoring, and sharding

exercises.explanation: GeoDNS only routes users to the nearest site; data sync needs its own design. Multi-region writes must resolve conflicts, and synchronous cross-region replication adds a round trip to every write. So decide first: one write region with read-only copies elsewhere, or writes everywhere.
options: Making cross-region replication synchronous removes the latency problem
First decide between writes in one region or in several, then design replication
GeoDNS sends users to the nearest site, so data sync is handled too
Letting both sites accept writes is easiest; the database resolves conflicts itself
exercises.prompt: You are deploying across two data centers. Which statement is most accurate?

exercises.explanation: Keeping messages only in memory doesn't guarantee they survive a restart or power loss. When you need durability, the queue must rely on disk logs, replication, and acknowledgements, so check the specific configuration when choosing one.
exercises.prompt: As long as you use a message queue, messages won't be lost after a process restart or power failure, even if they exist only in memory.

exercises.explanation: Tasks that can finish later, need traffic smoothing, or should be decoupled from the main request suit a queue. Login checks and reading prices on a detail page are synchronous paths where the user is waiting for the result, so queueing them only makes the user wait for nothing.
options: Generating image thumbnails
Reading the price when opening a product detail page
Sending notification emails
Exporting reports
Verifying the password at login and returning the result
exercises.prompt: Which of these tasks suit asynchronous processing through a message queue?

exercises.explanation: When the queue gets no ack, it redelivers a message that was already processed; this is the classic window for duplicate execution. Acking first and then crashing, or messages expiring, cause message loss rather than duplicates.
options: Acking first, then the process crashes
The backlog grows so long that messages expire and are dropped
The business change is committed, then the process crashes before sending the ack
exercises.prompt: A consumer takes messages from a queue and processes them. Which situation causes the same message to be **executed twice**?

exercises.explanation: Registering the event and changing the account in one transaction means a redelivered E7 hits the unique constraint and adds no points. Doing them separately leaves a crash window: record first and the points are lost forever, add first and they may be added twice. Acking first can lose the message.
options: In one transaction, insert E7 (unique constraint) and add the points
Ack the message on receipt, then add the points
Add the points first, then record E7 as processed separately
Record E7 as processed first, then add the points separately
exercises.prompt: Event E7 means “award 10 points for an order,” and the queue may redeliver it. Which approach guarantees the points are added only once?

exercises.explanation: The same shard key always lands on the same shard; more baskets won't split one big watermelon. Split by hotspot type: caches absorb repeated reads, a push-pull mix handles fan-out, and independent writes can use a bucket suffix.
options: The celebrity's traffic is spread across 100 shards
Ordinary users are spread thinner, but the celebrity's traffic still lands on one shard
Every shard's load drops to a tenth
Consistent hashing automatically splits up the celebrity hotspot
exercises.prompt: Sharded by user_id: 1,000 ordinary users at 100 QPS each, plus one celebrity alone at 100,000 QPS. What is the effect of going from 10 shards to 100?

exercises.explanation: Read hotspots can be replicated, fan-out hotspots can switch to a push-pull mix, and independent writes can be bucketed. But a single balance must keep atomic semantics: copying stale values or random bucketing breaks correctness, so you can only serialize or redefine the business operation.
pairs: CDN and multiple caches share the reads
Push for ordinary users, pull for celebrities
Add a bucket suffix to split into sub-shards
exercises.prompt: Match each type of celebrity hotspot with a suitable remedy

exercises.explanation: A dedicated shard fixes the collateral damage to others, but all of the celebrity's traffic still lands on that one shard. If it can't cope, you still need caching, a push-pull mix, or bucketing to split the workload.
exercises.prompt: Moving the celebrity to a dedicated shard isolates the impact on other users, but it doesn't remove that shard's own capacity limit.

exercises.explanation: The shard key decides where data lands, and a poor choice creates hotspots. When shards fill up, reshard and migrate data; consistent hashing narrows the migration. Replicas copy the same data and can't fix a full shard. Cross-shard JOINs are costly, so denormalization duplicates fields together; normalization does the opposite.
exercises.prompt: Complete the key ideas of sharding
exercises.text: A shard key should spread data [[evenly]]; when distribution is uneven and some shards fill first, you must [[reshard]]; when cross-shard JOINs are hard, [[denormalization]] keeps the fields a query needs together.

exercises.explanation: “The service is up” doesn't mean “the service meets its targets.” To locate a bottleneck you need at least request volume, P50/P95/P99 latency, database connections, cache hit rate, and queue backlog; without those numbers you can't tell which layer is slow.
exercises.prompt: If health checks are always green and the error rate is zero, you can conclude the system has no performance bottleneck.

chapters.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
keyPoints: Write “people × actions ÷ time” first, then multiply by a peak factor. Give every number a unit, and write assumptions down so they are easy to swap.
2^10≈10^3 and 2^30≈a billion. GB is decimal and GiB is base 1024; for exact capacity, go back to the exact value.
Memory takes hundreds of nanoseconds, SSD hundreds of microseconds, an HDD seek ten milliseconds: seek less, cache more, batch, compress first.
Each extra 9 cuts the downtime budget by ten times. Independent dependencies in series multiply, so three 99.9% components leave about 99.7%.
Size capacity for the peak, not the average, and state how you count headroom. If measurements disagree, align definitions and units before blaming code.

lessons.title: Powers and Latency
lessons.summary: Binary magnitudes and a feel for latency numbers

exercises.explanation: 1024≈1000, and every 10 extra bits multiplies the value by about 1,000, so 2^30≈(10^3)^3. The exact value, 1,073,741,824, is about 7.4% above a billion, which is still the same order of magnitude. Each extra bit only multiplies the value by 2, not by 10.
options: Each extra binary bit multiplies the value by ten
2^30 is exactly equal to 1 billion
30 binary bits can represent at most 3 billion values
2^10≈10^3, so cubing both sides gives about 1 billion
exercises.prompt: Back-of-the-envelope estimates often treat 2^30 as “about a billion.” What is the basis for that?

exercises.explanation: 1 GiB is 2^30 bytes; divided by 8 that is 2^27=134,217,728 records. 1 billion ÷ 8 uses the decimal GB convention, and “a billion records” mistakes the number of bytes for the number of records. Real systems also lose space to indexes and object headers, so they fit fewer.
options: About 8 billion records
About 134 million records (2^27)
About 125 million records (1 billion ÷ 8)
About 1 billion records
exercises.prompt: Each record is a fixed 8 bytes, with no overhead at all. In theory, how many records fit in 1 GiB?

exercises.explanation: Decimal 1 GB is 1 billion bytes, about 0.931 GiB; 1 GiB is 2^30 bytes, about 1.074 GB. In an interview it is enough to state which convention you use, but for exact capacities or field limits, use the exact value.
exercises.prompt: A vendor’s decimal 1 GB is slightly smaller than 1 GiB.

exercises.explanation: Every 10 binary bits multiplies the value by about 1,000: 2^10 is thousands, 2^20 millions, 2^30 billions, 2^40 trillions (TB), and 2^50 quadrillions (PB).
exercises.prompt: Complete the link between powers of 2 and magnitudes
exercises.text: [[2^20]] is about a million; [[2^40]] is about a trillion, which corresponds to the TB scale.

exercises.explanation: 0.5 ns → 100 ns → 150 µs → 500 µs → 10 ms → 150 ms. Memory is thousands of times faster than an SSD, and an HDD seek is more than sixty times slower than an SSD random read. That is the basis for “memory is fast, disk is slow, avoid seeks.”
items: L1 cache access
Main memory access
SSD random read
Round trip within a data center
HDD random seek
Cross-region data center round trip
exercises.prompt: Put these operations in order from fastest to slowest, using 2020 reference latencies
exercises.refAnchor: d2/程序员应该知道的延迟数字latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know
exercises.refTitle: Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know

exercises.explanation: 100×10 ms=1 s, and 100×150 µs=15,000 µs=15 ms. For the same number of accesses, the medium alone makes a difference of nearly 70 times, so avoid disk seeks where you can and keep hot data in memory.
options: About 100 ms / about 1.5 ms
About 1 s / about 150 ms
About 10 s / about 15 ms
About 1 s / about 15 ms
exercises.prompt: A request randomly reads 100 records. By the reference latencies, an HDD seek takes about 10 ms and an SSD random read about 150 µs. Roughly how long does this part alone take on each?
exercises.refAnchor: d2/程序员应该知道的延迟数字latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know
exercises.refTitle: Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know

exercises.explanation: 150 ms=150,000 µs, and dividing by 500 µs gives 300. If an endpoint makes a few serial calls to cross-region services, the network alone costs hundreds of milliseconds. That is why multi-data center systems route users to the nearest site.
options: About 3,000
About 3
About 300
About 30
exercises.prompt: By the reference latencies, one cross-region data center round trip (about 150 ms) equals roughly how many round trips within a data center (about 500 µs)?
exercises.refAnchor: d2/程序员应该知道的延迟数字latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know
exercises.refTitle: Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know

exercises.explanation: Memory is fast, disk is slow, and crossing the network is expensive, so cache, avoid seeks, and compress before sending. An SSD random read takes about 150 µs, still thousands of times slower than memory, so SSDs cannot replace a cache. Splitting a batch into single items multiplies the network round trips.
options: After switching to SSDs, hot data no longer needs to live in memory
Keep hot data in an in-memory cache
Avoid random disk seeks where possible
Split one batch request into many single-item requests
Compress data before sending it over the internet
exercises.prompt: Given the latency numbers, which of these optimizations make sense?
exercises.refAnchor: d2/程序员应该知道的延迟数字latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know
exercises.refTitle: Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know

exercises.explanation: They are orders of magnitude for reference, not any vendor’s SLA. SSD model, network, indexes, and concurrency all change the measured values. Use the table to judge direction, and verify real capacity with load tests or monitoring.
exercises.prompt: The numbers in the latency table can be used directly as your cloud provider’s performance guarantee for capacity planning.
exercises.refAnchor: d2/程序员应该知道的延迟数字latency-numbers-every-programmer-should-know

lessons.title: Availability Math
lessons.summary: Nines to downtime; chained dependencies multiply

exercises.explanation: 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime per year, well inside “under a day.” Every extra 9 costs redundancy, multi-region setups, and operations effort, so work out the downtime budget before deciding. 3.65 days corresponds to 99%, so dropping to 99% would exceed the budget.
options: Drop to 99% to save money; it is still within budget
Worth it, because 99.9% means 3.65 days of downtime a year
The current level is within budget, so this is not a priority
Worth it, because higher availability is always better
exercises.prompt: An internal reporting system is 99.9% available today, and the business says up to a day of downtime per year is acceptable. Someone proposes multi-region deployment to reach 99.999%. How do you assess that?

exercises.explanation: A year has about 525,600 minutes; multiply by the unavailable fraction. 1% is about 5,256 minutes (3.65 days), 0.1% is about 526 minutes (8.8 hours), and each extra 9 divides it by ten. Remember the formula rather than memorizing the numbers.
exercises.prompt: Match each availability target with its allowed downtime per year

exercises.explanation: 99.9% means 0.1% unavailable and 99.99% means 0.01%, exactly a factor of ten apart. Multiply “1 − availability” by the roughly 525,600 minutes in a year and you can compute the downtime budget for any target on the spot.
exercises.prompt: Complete the availability conversion rule
exercises.text: Yearly downtime ≈ total time in a year × [[unavailable fraction]]; each extra 9 shrinks the downtime budget to about [[one tenth]] of what it was.

exercises.explanation: All three must be up at once, and for independent events you multiply the success rates: 0.999³≈0.997, about 99.7%. That is lower than any single component, so it does not inherit the “three nines” label of the weakest one. 97% comes from mistaking 0.1% for 1%.
options: About 99.97%
About 97%
About 99.7%
exercises.prompt: A payment must succeed through the API, the database, and the payment gateway in turn. Each is 99.9% available, and failures are independent. What is the end-to-end availability?

exercises.explanation: The unavailable fraction is about 0.3%, and 8,760 hours × 0.002997 ≈ 26.25 hours, about three times a single 99.9% component (8.76 hours). The more dependencies, the faster the failure budget adds up.
options: About 26 hours
About 3.65 days
About 8.8 hours
About 52 minutes
exercises.prompt: Three required dependencies in series, each 99.9% available with independent failures, give about 99.7% end to end. Roughly how much downtime per year does that chain have?

exercises.explanation: The exact calculation 1 − 0.999³ subtracts the overlap where failures coincide, but at 0.1% the chance of two failing at once is around one in a million, so you can ignore it. When failure rates are large, simple addition clearly overestimates.
options: Availability adds up by nature; it does not multiply
Components in series never fail at the same time, so nothing overlaps
When failure rates are small, the overlap of simultaneous failures is negligible
Adding is more precise than multiplying, so it should be preferred
exercises.prompt: For a quick estimate, you add up the unavailability of three components, about 0.1% each, and get about 0.3%. Why does this approximation work?

exercises.explanation: If any dependency in series fails, the request fails. For independent failures, availability multiplies, and three 99.9% components leave only about 99.7%; more dependencies mean lower still. The path would be exactly 99.9% only in the extreme case where the components always fail at the same moments.
exercises.prompt: Every required component on a request path is 99.9% available, so the whole path is 99.9% available too.

exercises.explanation: Multiplication assumes independent failures. If all three always fail together, their downtime windows coincide completely and the chain is still 99.9%, which is higher than 99.7%. Shared failure domains such as a common data center or power supply call for re-analysis based on the real joint events.
exercises.prompt: If the failures of three 99.9% components always happen at the same moments, directly multiplying to 99.7% underestimates the availability of the chain.

exercises.explanation: Multiplication applies only to a series where everything must be up and failures are independent. Shared failure domains break independence; degradation and redundancy change the success condition, so redraw it before writing the formula. Different availabilities still multiply, e.g. 0.999×0.99.
options: A dependency can degrade and return cached results when it fails
A critical dependency is deployed with redundant replicas
Components share a data center, power supply, or DNS
The three components have different availabilities
All three components must be up, and their failures are independent
exercises.prompt: Which of these make “multiply the availability of each component” no longer apply?

lessons.title: Twitter Estimate
lessons.summary: From MAU to QPS, peak load, and storage

exercises.explanation: Write “people × actions” first, then divide by time, then apply the peak factor, and finally convert to servers using the load-test capacity. Each step depends on the one before it. With the assumptions written first, an interviewer can change one parameter and you can recompute down the chain.
items: List assumptions: MAU, DAU ratio, actions per user
DAU = MAU × daily-active ratio
Average QPS = DAU × actions ÷ 86,400
Peak QPS = average QPS × peak factor
Instances = peak ÷ per-server load-test capacity
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a QPS and server-count estimate in order

exercises.explanation: DAU is 150 million, so 300 million tweets a day; divided by 86,400 seconds that is ≈3,472, about 3,500 tweets/s. 7,000 is the peak after a 2× peak factor. For mental math, round 86,400 to 100,000 to judge the order of magnitude.
options: About 7,000
About 3,500
About 35,000
About 1,700
exercises.prompt: 300 million MAU, 50% of them daily active, and each active user posts 2 tweets a day on average. What is the average tweet QPS?

exercises.explanation: A day has 86,400 seconds, which is the “time” in “people × actions ÷ time.” Apply the peak factor only after you have the average; using MAU instead of DAU counts inactive users too.
exercises.prompt: Complete the formula for average QPS
exercises.text: Average QPS = DAU × [[actions per user per day]] ÷ [[86,400 seconds]]

exercises.explanation: 150 million × 2 × 10% = 30 million media items at 1 MB each, about 30 TB/day; keeping them for 5 years is about 30 TB × 365 × 5 ≈ 55 PB. 300 TB forgets the 10% media share. Carrying units through every step makes such mistakes less likely.
options: About 30 TB
About 3 TB
About 300 TB
About 30 GB
exercises.prompt: 150 million DAU, 2 tweets per person per day, and 10% of tweets carry 1 MB of media. How much new media storage is added per day?

exercises.explanation: The ratio of actions is 10÷2=5. QPS follows requests and storage follows new bytes, so both become 5 times. Each person adds 8 actions, but the total is 5 times the original, an increase of 400%, not “8 times more.”
options: QPS is unchanged; storage becomes 5 times
Both become 5 times
QPS becomes 5 times; storage is unchanged
Both increase by 8 times
exercises.prompt: DAU stays the same, but each person’s daily actions go from 2 to 10. The distribution of active hours, the data written per action, and the retention period all stay the same. What happens to average QPS and new storage?

exercises.explanation: 7,000 is the peak for tweet writes. Real systems usually read far more than they write, so estimate read QPS separately: how many times each DAU refreshes per day and how many items each refresh pulls.
exercises.prompt: The estimated peak of about 7,000 QPS can be used directly to plan the read capacity of the home feed.

exercises.explanation: The 55 PB figure counts only the 1 MB media items, and 64 bytes versus 8 bytes is negligible next to 1 MB. In an estimate, focus on the largest term. For real capacity planning, still measure the actual serialized format.
options: It must be recomputed together with QPS
Almost unchanged, since media dwarfs the ID
It drops to one eighth
It grows to 8 times
exercises.prompt: The chapter sizes tweet_id at 64 bytes, while a common 64-bit integer ID takes only 8 bytes. After correcting to the real size, what happens to the conclusion of about 55 PB of media over 5 years?

exercises.explanation: 55 PB is raw media data only. Replicas, thumbnails, metadata, indexes, and backups are counted separately. For capacity planning you can multiply by a redundancy factor of 2 to 4, and list average media size and peak upload bandwidth on their own.
options: The original media files of tweets with media
Replicas and backups
Thumbnails
The media added each day over 5 years
Object storage metadata and indexes
exercises.prompt: Which of these are **not** included in the 5-year result of about 55 PB?

exercises.explanation: Tens of terabytes of large files per day suit object storage for holding and a CDN for delivery, with the database keeping only metadata and references. Relational storage or memory is too costly and hard to scale. Local web disks make the web tier stateful, lose files when a machine dies, and block free scaling in and out.
options: Keep all media in Redis memory for the lowest read latency
Store media on the web servers’ local disks and read it from nearby
Put media in object storage behind a CDN; the database holds only metadata
Store media in relational BLOB columns and shard by user
exercises.prompt: You have estimated about 30 TB of new media per day and a write peak of about 7,000 per second. What is the most reasonable architectural conclusion?
exercises.refAnchor: d2/面试可直接套用的-90-秒模板

lessons.title: Estimation Tips
lessons.summary: Rounding, units, peak headroom, and calibration

exercises.explanation: The exact value is about 10,988, and the approximation stays in the same order of magnitude. System design estimates care about “10 servers or 100,” so the process and assumptions matter more than decimals. Return to exact math only when you need exact capacity.
exercises.prompt: In an estimate, rounding 99987 / 9.1 to 100,000 / 10 = 10,000 is off by about a tenth, which is perfectly acceptable when you only need the order of magnitude.

exercises.explanation: 10 million × 10% × 50% = 500,000 people, and × 20 KB = 10 million KB ≈ 10 GB. 20 GB forgets the 50% coverage ratio. A real deployment also adds replicas and protocol overhead.
options: About 100 GB
About 1 GB
About 20 GB
About 10 GB
exercises.prompt: 10 million users, 10% of them daily active, about 20 KB of hot data per user, and a cache target covering 50% of daily active users. Ignoring replicas, roughly how much memory does the cache need?

exercises.explanation: 7,000 / 350 = 20 is the theoretical minimum with no headroom at all, so losing one machine or a small traffic rise causes overload. With 30% headroom, take 26 to 30, and say that this is an estimate to be calibrated with load-test results.
options: About 10
Exactly 20
About 70
About 26 to 30
exercises.prompt: Peak load is 7,000 QPS, and one instance sustains 350 QPS in load tests. With about 30% headroom, what is a reasonable instance count?

exercises.explanation: Count each server at only 500×70%=350 QPS: 5,000/350≈14.3, rounded up to 15. 10 leaves no headroom. 13 is “10 servers plus 30%,” a different convention from a 70% target utilization. 16 would also require meeting the target with 1 server down.
options: 10 servers
15 servers
13 servers
16 servers
exercises.prompt: At the evening peak of 5,000 QPS, one instance steadily handles 500 QPS at the target P99. If each server may be used at only 70% of its load-tested capacity, how many servers are needed at minimum?

exercises.explanation: The backlog grows by arrivals minus processing: 2,000 tasks/s × 60 s = 120,000 tasks. A queue can absorb a spike, but the backlog does not vanish by itself, so plan time to drain it after the peak. Online requests certainly cannot queue forever.
options: 180,000 tasks
300,000 tasks
2,000 tasks
120,000 tasks
exercises.prompt: At peak, tasks arrive at 5,000 per second, and the backend can process only 3,000 per second. This lasts for 60 seconds. How much does the backlog grow?

exercises.explanation: An average flattens busy and quiet periods, but servers face the arrival rate within a particular time window. When arrivals outpace processing, queueing and timeouts grow fast. Do the accounting with the average, and protect the service with the peak.
exercises.prompt: If the all-day average QPS works out as sufficient, the evening peak and the start of a promotion will not be a problem either.

exercises.explanation: 1,000 × 5 × 1.2 = 6,000. The gap comes from “API requests” and “SQL statements” being different quantities. Retries add only a factor of 1.2, so the database is not doing six times the work, and the DAU assumption stands. Compare the same quantity first, then suspect code or assumptions.
options: The database does six times the business work; the code has a bug
The estimate’s assumptions are wrong; re-estimate DAU
Different units of count plus amplification explain the gap
Retries amplified requests 6 times; turn retries off first
exercises.prompt: The estimate says the application sees 1,000 QPS, but database monitoring shows 6,000 queries/s. Tracing shows each API call runs 5 SQL statements on average, and failure retries add 20% more attempts. What is the most reasonable conclusion?

exercises.explanation: First confirm you are comparing the same quantity, over the same window, in the same unit; this is cheapest. Then check the estimate’s inputs. Only if a large gap remains should you look for N+1 queries, duplicate consumption, and similar issues. Finally, record the correction so nobody guesses again.
items: Align metric definitions, windows, and units
Check assumptions such as DAU and read/write ratio
Trace requests and load-test to find implementation cost
Record the corrected formula and the evidence
exercises.prompt: When an estimate and the monitored reality differ widely, put the troubleshooting steps in order

exercises.explanation: MB means bytes and Mbit means bits, and 100 MB/s × 8 = 800 Mbit/s. Bits and bytes differ by a factor of 8, and milliseconds and seconds by a factor of 1,000. Labeling units exists so that one quantity is not mistaken for a discrepancy.
exercises.prompt: Complete the unit conversion
exercises.text: The estimate says 100 MB/s of uploads, and network monitoring shows 800 Mbit/s. In decimal terms, the two are [[equal]], because 1 byte = [[8 bits]].

exercises.explanation: With assumptions clearly recorded, checking and adjusting touches only one input, and nobody has to argue over the whole design again. If you cannot compute something, stating your assumption also gives the interviewer a chance to correct it.
exercises.prompt: One benefit of writing down assumptions is that when the interviewer changes the peak factor from 2 to 5, you only replace that one parameter and recompute.

chapters.title: System Design Interview Framework
chapters.fullTitle: Chapter 3: A Framework for System Design Interviews
keyPoints: Four steps: clarify scope, agree on a high-level design, deep dive, wrap up. In 45 minutes, spend about 3–10, 10–15, 10–25, and 3–5 minutes on them.
Ask only questions that change the design. With no numbers, propose assumptions, write them down, and invite the interviewer to correct them.
Draw the data flow first (who writes, who reads, where it rests), then add technologies. Get buy-in while the diagram is cheap to change.
A component deep dive quantifies workload, the first resource to run out, how failures spread, and recovery cost. “Add machines” is not enough.
Wrap up with what you covered, why you chose it, where it breaks, and when to upgrade. Admit any correctness gap on the spot.

labs.title: Interview Pacing Drill: 45 Minutes, Last 5 Minutes, 90 Seconds
News Feed: How Requirement Answers Change the Architecture

lessons.title: Clarify Scope
lessons.summary: Ask design-changing questions, then write assumptions

exercises.explanation: Step 1 is to understand the problem and set the scope, so you don't jump to solutions too early. If you pile on components or design tables first, and the question turns out to need only a friends' feed sorted by time, that detail work is wasted. Estimation belongs to step 2 and only makes sense once the scope is clear.
options: Work out the exact five-year storage need first
Draw Kafka, Redis, and microservices right away
Ask clarifying questions about features, scale, and ranking
Design the post table's columns and indexes first
exercises.prompt: An interviewer says only, “Design a news feed system.” What is the best first step?
exercises.refAnchor: d3/第-1-步理解问题并确定设计范围understand-the-problem-and-establish-design-scope
exercises.refTitle: Step 1: Understand the Problem and Establish Design Scope

exercises.explanation: Ranking decides between reading a materialized list and needing candidate retrieval plus ranking. The follower distribution decides the fan-out strategy. The media type decides whether you need object storage, a CDN, and transcoding. Field naming and front-end framework change none of these paths; asking just looks busy.
options: Whether the web front end uses React or Vue
Whether API fields use camelCase or snake_case
Whether the feed includes images and videos
The average and maximum number of followers
Whether the feed is newest first or personalized
exercises.prompt: When designing a news feed, which of these clarifying questions have answers that substantially change the architecture?

exercises.explanation: For each question, say how the answer changes the design: how you rank affects the read path, how many people affects fan-out, and what kind of content affects the media path. Remember: how to rank, how many people, what content.
pairs: Read a materialized list by time + ID cursor
Needs candidate retrieval, features, and ranking
Pull on read, or hybrid fan-out
Object storage, CDN, and async transcoding
exercises.prompt: Match each requirement answer with the design change it brings

exercises.explanation: 100 × 200 = 20,000 writes per second. But this is only an average: one post from a celebrity with a million followers causes a million writes, and an average must not hide the instantaneous load from the top users, so ask about the follower distribution.
options: About 2,000
About 200,000
About 300
About 20,000
exercises.prompt: A feed system has 100 posts per second, and each post has 200 recipients on average. With fan-out on write, about how many inbox writes per second is that?

exercises.explanation: Without numbers, propose reasonable starting values yourself, write them on the whiteboard, and invite the interviewer to correct them. Written assumptions can be revisited with every later change. Waiting passively only wastes time and shows no judgment.
exercises.prompt: When the interviewer gives no scale numbers, you should wait for them and not offer assumptions, to avoid being wrong.

exercises.explanation: Good questions can change the design: whether duplicate publishing is allowed affects idempotency, whether offline access is needed affects caching and sync, and peak QPS affects sharding and queues. Don't ask questions that won't change the design just to look professional.
exercises.prompt: “Is duplicate publishing allowed?” is worth asking while clarifying, because the answer affects whether you need an idempotent design.
exercises.refTitle: Example: Designing a News Feed System

exercises.explanation: This is the classic failure of step 1: piling on components before confirming requirements. The components themselves may be fine, but they solve problems the question doesn't have, so the time goes to the wrong place.
options: The microservices aren't fine-grained enough, so responsibilities are unclear
The scope was never locked down, so more detail just means more drift
The diagram isn't detailed enough for the interviewer to follow
The chosen middleware is too slow to handle feed traffic
exercises.prompt: A candidate immediately draws Kafka, Redis, and ten microservices, then halfway through realizes the question only needs a friends' feed sorted by time. What is the root problem?
exercises.refTitle: Example: Designing a News Feed System

exercises.explanation: Once an assumption is written down, if the interviewer says “peak is 5 times, not 2,” you only change one parameter. Inviting corrections turns the interview into collaboration instead of guessing the answer.
exercises.prompt: Complete the step 1 practice
exercises.text: With no numbers, propose a reasonable [[starting assumption]] and write it on the whiteboard, then invite the interviewer to [[correct]] it.

exercises.explanation: Video must be transcoded into several resolutions, usually asynchronously, so there is a gap between “immediately visible” and “processing finished,” and you must define the visibility semantics first. Large media belongs in object storage served by a CDN, and the post record stores only a media reference.
options: Whether to turn the CDN off to keep videos real time
Whether to show a placeholder or wait until transcoding is done
Whether videos go straight into the business database
Which video encoding format is the most popular
exercises.prompt: The feed must support video, and product also wants “visible immediately after upload.” What must you pin down with the interviewer before designing?

lessons.title: High-Level Design
lessons.summary: Draw the blueprint, estimate, walk use cases, align

exercises.explanation: Buy-in confirms the scope, the success criteria, and the main data flows. Database details matter only if they serve those goals. Agreeing early corrects course while the diagram is cheap. It doesn't mean the design is frozen: if a deep dive reveals a problem, feed it back and adjust.
options: Database details never need to be discussed in an interview
Once you reach agreement, the design can no longer change
Interviewers usually don't care about databases
If a basic assumption is wrong, deeper detail means more rework
exercises.prompt: In the high-level design phase, why get the interviewer's buy-in first instead of diving straight into the database design?

exercises.explanation: Write to the authoritative store first, then reliably create the fan-out task after the commit succeeds, so that “published” has a clear meaning. If you fan out before writing, a failed write leaves followers seeing a post that doesn't exist.
items: The client submits the post
Post text and media references go into the database
After the commit, a fan-out task is created
The post ID is pushed into followers’ inboxes
exercises.prompt: Put the main path of the feed publishing flow in order

exercises.explanation: Buy-in means agreeing on the scope, the main path, and the key assumptions. It is not box-by-box approval, and it doesn't mean the design can't change later. Confirm direction as you draw, and treat the interviewer as a teammate instead of handing over the decision.
exercises.prompt: Getting buy-in means pausing after every box you draw and waiting for the interviewer's approval before continuing.

exercises.explanation: The data flow is the skeleton of the design and the technology choices are the parts that fill it. You need to discuss both, just in that order. If you draw the arrows first, then when the interviewer asks “could we use a different database?”, you can say which paths stay the same and which constraints to re-check.
options: So that you can skip the capacity estimation
Technology names don't matter, so you can leave them out
The design logic still holds if the tech stack changes
Interviewers only look at data flow and ignore technology choices
exercises.prompt: Why is it recommended to mark “who writes, who reads, and where the data rests” before choosing a database or queue in the high-level design?

exercises.explanation: The publish flow writes the post to the database and fills the friends' feeds. The fetch flow takes IDs from the inbox, then aggregates the post text, and media goes through object storage and the CDN. Each component is a stop on the data flow.
pairs: Sends the post ID to followers after publishing
Stores each person's list of post IDs to read
Stores images and videos, serves them nearby
exercises.prompt: Match each component in the feed's high-level design with its responsibility

exercises.explanation: This is over-engineering: a few hundred thousand users are nowhere near a single database's limit, so sharding only brings migration, cross-shard queries, and operational cost early. The shard count isn't the issue. Switching to NoSQL or splitting into microservices would also solve a scale problem the question doesn't have.
options: It adds needless migration, cross-shard queries, and operational burden
It should use NoSQL, which scales horizontally by nature
The shard count is too low, so resharding will be needed later
It should split into microservices first, then shard
exercises.prompt: The requirements turn out to be an internal activity feed for only a few hundred thousand users, yet the candidate starts sharding the database right away. What is the main problem?

exercises.explanation: Labeled assumptions let the reasoning continue and let the interviewer correct you at any time. Stating the sensitivity shows you know what needs validating. But silence must not be taken to mean that the assumptions have all been confirmed.
exercises.prompt: When the interviewer doesn't give numbers yet, you can state labeled working assumptions, keep reasoning, and say which conclusion is most sensitive to them.

exercises.explanation: Estimation checks scale and use cases check logic: walking through the core flows and edge cases reveals paths the blueprint missed. Both belong in the high-level design phase, not something to patch in during the deep dive.
exercises.prompt: Complete the step 2 method
exercises.refAnchor: d3/第-2-步提出高层设计并取得共识propose-high-level-design-and-get-buy-in
exercises.refTitle: Step 2: Propose High-Level Design and Get Buy-In
exercises.text: After drawing the blueprint, do a [[back-of-the-envelope]] estimate to check that request volume, storage, and bandwidth hold up, then [[walk through use cases]] to validate the design's assumptions.

exercises.explanation: It gives its own judgment and assumptions first, says how it will adjust if conditions change, and finally asks the interviewer to confirm the scope. That is getting buy-in. The candidate still leads the design instead of pushing the judgment onto the interviewer.
options: To stall for time until the interviewer gives hints
To hand the decision to the interviewer and avoid making a call
To prove they memorized the standard feed answer
To state assumptions so the interviewer can correct course early
exercises.prompt: A candidate says: “I'll design for 10 million users, read-heavy, sorted by time. If you care more about real time, I'll adjust. Is this scope OK?” What is the main purpose of this?

lessons.title: Deep Dive
lessons.summary: Pick key components; quantify bottlenecks, failures

exercises.explanation: A deep dive should focus on the components most relevant to the question: for a short URL it is short code generation, for chat it is latency and online status, and for a feed it is the publish and read flows. A payment system can't copy the feed's “seconds-level propagation is fine.” Its focus is correctness.
exercises.prompt: Match each question with the focus most worth a deep dive

exercises.explanation: The backlog grows at arrival rate minus processing rate, which is 10,000 per second, and multiplying by 60 seconds gives 600,000. 1,800,000 is the total that arrived and 1,200,000 is the total processed. What matters is the difference.
options: 1,200,000 messages
10,000 messages
1,800,000 messages
600,000 messages
exercises.prompt: A feed worker can process 20,000 inbox updates per second, but for one minute 30,000 per second arrive. How much does the backlog grow?

exercises.explanation: Add capacity where the resource runs out first. The API only accepts requests, while the backlog builds up in the workers and the hot shard. Unless you raise worker capacity or switch celebrities to merging on read, the backlog keeps growing.
options: The backlog grows half as fast but still can't be stopped
Workers automatically scale along with the API
The backlog keeps growing; the bottleneck is the workers or a hot shard
The API absorbs some traffic, so the backlog gradually shrinks
exercises.prompt: When fan-out workers can't keep up and the backlog keeps growing, what happens if you only add stateless API servers?

exercises.explanation: How much traffic comes in, how much resource is left, what happens when it breaks, and how long recovery takes decide whether the component holds up. Spending the time on class names and framework lists is exactly the failure mode the chapter calls out.
options: Which resource runs out first: CPU, connections, or locks
How it degrades and recovers under overload or failure
How its classes and packages are organized
Which popular frameworks exist in the same category
How much work reaches it at peak
exercises.prompt: When deep-diving a hotspot component, which of these questions must you answer?

exercises.explanation: A throughput-only best result is often reached when latency is already bad. If you size machines by it, P99 will exceed the target in production. Also check whether a single key, shard, or serial critical section can scale horizontally.
exercises.prompt: When calculating how many instances you need, use the load-test capacity at the target latency, not a best result measured on throughput alone.

exercises.explanation: A deep dive should prioritize key components, discuss bottlenecks, and keep detail under control. Listing every technology crowds out time for the core flows and doesn't explain why you chose them or what they cost. Depth comes from quantifying and weighing trade-offs on the critical path.
exercises.prompt: In the deep dive, covering every technology you might use shows the most depth.

exercises.explanation: A cache shields hot reads, but when it is invalidated it exposes the backend's limit: once the hit rate drops, database load can multiply. Every measure has a cost: replicas bring replication lag, sharding brings migration cost, and caching brings fall-through bursts.
options: Can the cache replace the database as durable storage?
After a cache hit, must the database still be queried again?
Should the cache be switched to disk-based storage?
If the whole cache is invalidated, can the database handle the load that falls through?
exercises.prompt: After adding a cache to a hot read endpoint, which failure question must you still answer in the deep dive?

exercises.explanation: The four deep-dive questions: the primary key and access pattern, the capacity limit and failure modes, the consequences of lost, duplicated, or delayed data, and when to upgrade plus the migration path. They force you to state boundaries instead of stopping at table columns and class names.
exercises.prompt: Complete two of the four deep-dive questions
exercises.text: What are this component's [[capacity limit]] and failure modes? When must the design be upgraded, and what is the [[migration path]]?

exercises.explanation: The oldest message's age is how long the slowest message has already waited, which maps directly to the propagation-delay promise. A large backlog doesn't always mean long waits if processing is fast. The enqueue rate only says how much arrives, and the consumer count is just a means. Read it with P95/P99 and the error rate.
options: Average message size
Age of the oldest message
Number of consumer processes
New messages enqueued per second
exercises.prompt: When monitoring the feed fan-out queue, besides the backlog size, which metric most directly shows how long followers wait to see a new post?

lessons.title: Wrap-Up and Pacing
lessons.summary: Time budget, the 5-minute close, the 90-second answer

exercises.explanation: The wrap-up gets only 3–5 minutes, so you should stop adding components before minute 40. Mention the new idea in one sentence as a “next step.” A redo can't be finished in time, and silence violates the principle of communicating continuously.
options: Say nothing and perfect it on paper first
Scrap the current design and redo it around the new component
Draw the new component immediately and explain it in detail
Stop adding components and start reviewing failures and trade-offs
exercises.prompt: At minute 40 of a 45-minute interview, you suddenly think of a new component that would improve performance. What is the best move?

exercises.explanation: Restate the goal first so the interviewer knows what you covered. Then walk the diagram to prove the design works. Then explain why you chose it and where it can break. Only then say when to upgrade, leaving room for follow-ups. A wrap-up is not a list of technology names, nor “we'll optimize the rest later.”
items: Restate the goal and core assumptions
Walk the key write and read paths on the diagram
Summarize trade-offs, top bottleneck, failure safeguards
Give upgrade triggers and a validation plan
exercises.prompt: Only 5 minutes are left. Put the wrap-up content in the recommended order

exercises.explanation: Correctness gaps such as losing money, overselling, or leaking permissions must be admitted on the spot, and the success criteria must be fixed. Only performance enhancements that don't affect the main path can be listed for later. Important errors belong in the current conclusion.
exercises.prompt: You only notice at the end that the design could oversell, but to wrap up neatly on time you can skip it and list it as a later optimization.

exercises.explanation: It makes clear when you can return success: once the post is written to the main store, fan-out runs asynchronously, and a brief propagation delay is allowed. This is not strong consistency, nor does it mean fan-out can be ignored: async tasks must still be retryable and deduplicated, and inboxes still get written.
options: It means follower inboxes never need to be written
It says fan-out failures never need to be retried
It says the system uses strongly consistent replication
It defines when a write succeeds and that propagation is async
exercises.prompt: In the 90-second answer you say, “Publishing succeeds when the post is saved; it doesn't guarantee every follower has received it.” What does this sentence do?

exercises.explanation: Asking, communicating, and iterating are all things to do. Silence and giving a design too early are on the “don't” list: the former leaves the interviewer unable to assess your thinking, and the latter often goes off track before the requirements are clear.
options: Think out loud continuously
Clarify ambiguity before moving to the design
The earlier you give a full design, the more skilled you look
Treat the interviewer as a collaborator and iterate together
Stay silent when stuck so you don't say something wrong
exercises.prompt: Which of these should you do in a system design interview?

exercises.explanation: Saying clearly what you don't know beats covering the gap with unverified jargon. Interviewers evaluate your reasoning and trade-offs, and clearly marking what is uncertain makes the design more credible.
exercises.prompt: When you don't know a piece of middleware well, stating your assumptions, the interface semantics, failure handling, and how you'd verify them is also a skill.

exercises.explanation: The wrap-up should prove the design works, make the trade-offs explicit, put boundaries on failures, and name a conditional next step. Adding components now can't be explained in time, “optimize later” carries no information, and a pile of names doesn't show why the design holds.
options: Say what you covered, why you chose it, where it breaks, when to upgrade
Rattle off a string of technology names to show broad knowledge
Add search and recommendation services to make the design look complete
Say “the rest can be optimized later” and end there
exercises.prompt: In the last 5 minutes, which way of wrapping up is best?

exercises.explanation: State trade-offs in pairs: what you gain and what you pay. Fan-out on write moves the computation to publish time, and reading just takes a ready-made list, so reads are fast. The cost is many inbox writes per post, and followers may see it a little later.
exercises.prompt: Complete the sample sentence that summarizes a trade-off
exercises.text: Precomputing the feed buys [[low read latency]] at the cost of extra [[fan-out writes]] and a brief propagation delay.

exercises.explanation: The storyline “requirements, path, bottleneck, trade-off, evolution” is universal, but every step must answer this question's constraints. Payments can't copy the feed's seconds-level propagation and fan-out, and an idempotency key alone isn't enough: success conditions and ordering must follow payment's correctness needs.
options: Yes, copy it verbatim, including seconds-level propagation
Add an idempotency key and keep the rest of the feed design
No structure carries over; payments must be explained from zero
The storyline carries over; swap in payment's correctness needs
exercises.prompt: If the question changes to a payment system, can you reuse the feed's 90-second answer as is?

chapters.title: Rate Limiter
keyPoints: Answer three questions first: who to limit, how much, and what happens on overflow. Decide in advance whether a failing limiter allows or rejects.
A frontend limit is only a UX hint. The gate must sit on the server or gateway, and counting keys must use a verified identity.
Token bucket capacity governs bursts; the rate governs the long-term average. A leaking bucket smooths output but needs a queue limit and a maximum wait.
A fixed window has boundary bursts, a sliding log is exact but memory-hungry, and a sliding window counter saves memory but has approximation error.
With multiple gateways, run read, refill, check, and deduct in one atomic script on the same Redis. Async sync across regions can briefly oversell.
Return 429 with Retry-After; clients use backoff plus jitter. Keep monitoring allows, rejects, latency, and false positives.

labs.title: Five Rate Limiting Algorithms Side by Side
Two Gateways Race for the Last Slot

lessons.title: Needs & Placement
lessons.summary: Who to limit, how much, what on excess, where

exercises.explanation: Who to limit decides what you count by, how much decides the time window and quota, and what happens on overflow decides whether you return 429, queue, or degrade. Until all three are settled, no algorithm choice has a basis; storage and deployment location are implementation choices that come later.
exercises.prompt: Complete what each of the three rate-limiting questions decides
exercises.text: Who to limit decides the [[counting key]] (user, IP, or API key), how much decides the [[window and quota]], and what happens on overflow decides the [[overflow action]] (reject, queue, or degrade).

exercises.explanation: Users control the browser and scripts: they can edit JavaScript, clear localStorage, or skip the page and call the API directly. A frontend limit only improves the experience for well-behaved users. The button is a hint; the server is the gate.
options: The browser periodically clears the countdown automatically
Users can skip the page and call the API directly with a script
localStorage is too small to hold the count
Graying out the button hurts legitimate users
exercises.prompt: A web page allows at most 10 requests per minute: the button is grayed out, a countdown is shown, and the count is stored in localStorage. Why does this not stop someone from hammering the API?

exercises.explanation: Client parameters can be forged freely, so changing the userId bypasses the limit. Only a verified identity (an authenticated account, an API key, and so on) makes a trustworthy counting key.
exercises.prompt: When a gateway limits by userId, it can use the userId that the client sends in the request parameters as the counting key.

exercises.explanation: With per-IP counting, all employees share one quota; when a few use a lot, everyone else gets rejected. Company and campus networks often look like this, so choose the counting dimension together with a verified account or API key.
options: Legitimate users behind the same egress get blocked together
The gateway automatically splits the count per employee
IPs cannot be spoofed, so this is the most precise dimension
Each employee is counted separately and none affects the others
exercises.prompt: Thousands of employees at one company reach your service through the same egress IP. If you limit only by IP, what is the most likely problem?

exercises.explanation: Whether to allow (fail-open) or reject (fail-closed) depends on the business. Letting a few extra ordinary queries through does little harm, so availability can come first. For a paid or risk-control API, losing control is costly, so protecting the resource comes first. Agree on this during the requirements stage.
options: Lean toward allowing queries and toward rejecting on the risk-control API
Reject both, to be safe
Allow both, to stay available
Lean toward rejecting queries and toward allowing on the risk-control API
exercises.prompt: The Redis behind your rate limiter goes down. For an ordinary product query and a paid risk-control API, which policies make the most sense, respectively?

exercises.explanation: The client is in the user's hands, so it can only give hints for the user experience. The server has the strongest control. A microservice architecture can use an API gateway to limit centrally. If the team has no capacity to build its own, consider a commercial solution.
pairs: Can be modified or bypassed, so unreliable
Checked inside the service, strongest control
One central entry point for microservices
Option when team resources are limited
exercises.prompt: Match each way of implementing rate limiting with its characteristic

exercises.explanation: By the time a request reaches the application layer, the bandwidth is already used up. Application-layer limiting can stop excessive calls and protect the database and billable services, but it is only one layer of defense and cannot handle a bandwidth-exhaustion attack alone.
exercises.prompt: With application-layer rate limiting in place, you can defend on its own against an attack that exhausts network bandwidth.

exercises.explanation: The per-user rule stops a single user from hammering the endpoint, and the site-wide rule protects overall capacity. They target different risks, and a request must satisfy both to pass. This is what “support multiple throttling rules” means in the requirements.
exercises.prompt: The same endpoint can have two rules at once: “10 requests per user per minute” and “1,000 requests per second site-wide.”

exercises.explanation: Multiple rules, the failure policy, and the limiting identifier (plus allowlists and hot rule updates) all change the design directly. Key prefixes and variable names are implementation details you settle while coding; you do not need to clarify them with the interviewer in the requirements stage.
options: Variable names inside the Lua script
Whether to combine per-user and site-wide rules
Whether to allow or reject when the limiter fails
What identifies callers before and after authentication
Prefix naming for Redis counter keys
exercises.prompt: When designing a rate limiter, which of the following should you clarify early as requirements?

lessons.title: Bucket Algorithms
lessons.summary: Burst capacity, average rate, steady queueing

exercises.explanation: Extra tokens stop accumulating once the bucket is full: an empty bucket refills 20 tokens in about 4 seconds, and no matter how long it then idles, it holds only 20, not 5×60=300. The rate r governs the long-term average; the capacity B caps the instantaneous burst.
options: 5 requests
300 requests
20 requests
100 requests
exercises.prompt: A token bucket has B=20 and r=5 per second. After the bucket is emptied, it sits idle for a full minute, and then 100 requests arrive at the same instant. How many can be allowed immediately?

exercises.explanation: 20 tokens ÷ 5 per second = 4 seconds; with continuous refill, one token is added every 0.2 seconds. 0.2 seconds is only the gap between two tokens, and 20 seconds comes from wrongly assuming just 1 token per second.
options: About 0.2 seconds
About 1 second
About 4 seconds
About 20 seconds
exercises.prompt: A token bucket has B=20 and r=5 per second, with continuous refill. About how long does it take to go from empty to full?

exercises.explanation: A full bucket can release B requests in an instant. Over a period of length Δt, you can use at most about B + r×Δt tokens. The rate r only bounds the long-term average and does not promise at most 5 per second, which is exactly what “allows short bursts” means for a token bucket.
exercises.prompt: Setting a token bucket to r=5 per second guarantees that no one-second period ever lets through more than 5 requests.

exercises.explanation: Multiply the elapsed time by the rate r to get the refill, then cap it at the bucket capacity B; once the bucket is full, the surplus is not saved. This lazy calculation means each key stores only a token count and the last timestamp, so memory use is tiny.
exercises.prompt: Complete the formula for refilling tokens based on request arrival time
exercises.text: When a request arrives, compute tokens = min([[B]], tokens + [[r × elapsed]]); there is no need to start a timer every 0.2 seconds.

exercises.explanation: The long-term allow rate is set by r: r=80 exceeds the downstream’s sustained 50 per second, so as long as traffic stays above the limit, the downstream stays overloaded. B only affects how big one burst can be, but it must not be so large that a single burst overwhelms the downstream either.
options: B=50, r=45 per second
B=100, r=40 per second
B=10, r=20 per second
B=100, r=80 per second
exercises.prompt: A downstream service can sustain 50 requests per second. If upstream traffic keeps exceeding that, which token bucket settings would leave the downstream overloaded for a long time?

exercises.explanation: A leaking bucket drains a FIFO queue at a fixed rate, so its output is the smoothest. A token bucket allows bursts, a fixed window has boundary bursts, and a sliding window counter only smooths the counting; none of them guarantees a steady output. The price of a leaking bucket is that new requests queue during a burst.
options: Sliding window counter
Fixed window counter
Token bucket
Leaking bucket
exercises.prompt: The downstream is an old payment API that can only process requests at a steady pace. The rate hitting it should be as smooth as possible, and queueing is acceptable. Which algorithm fits best?

exercises.explanation: The essence of a leaking bucket is a constant output rate. An implementation can block the caller until the next point in time instead of queueing explicitly. Either way, you must cap the maximum wait time rather than queue forever.
exercises.prompt: Some rate limiting libraries implement a leaking-bucket-style smooth rate with a blocking call, without necessarily maintaining a real request queue.

exercises.explanation: “The size of the bucket decides how hard you can sprint; the flow rate decides how long you can keep running.” A leaking bucket drains at a fixed rate and makes requests queue during a burst, so you must limit both the queue length and the maximum wait time. It is not an unbounded queue.
pairs: Most requests allowed in one instant
How fast it allows on long-term average
Most requests allowed to wait in line
Reject after waiting too long, not forever
exercises.prompt: Match each bucket parameter with what it controls

exercises.explanation: A token bucket is capped, allows bursts, and needs atomic deduction in a distributed setting. “Long queueing during bursts” is a drawback of the leaking bucket; the token bucket’s drawback is precisely that its parameters need careful tuning.
options: New requests wait in a queue for a long time during bursts
No tuning is needed; the defaults are fine
Refill, check, and deduct must run atomically
Extra tokens stop accumulating once the bucket is full
It allows a limited short burst
exercises.prompt: Which of the following statements about a token bucket are correct?

lessons.title: Window Algorithms
lessons.summary: Fixed window, sliding log, and sliding counter

exercises.explanation: The two batches fall in two different fixed minutes, and neither exceeds its quota, so about 200 requests pass within roughly 0.2 seconds. A fixed window limits calendar-aligned windows, not any continuous 60 seconds: at the moment of reset, two quotas can pile up together.
options: The window slides automatically, so only 100 are allowed
Both batches pass: about 200 requests in roughly 0.2 seconds
Each batch gets 50 requests
The second batch is rejected entirely because 100 were just allowed
exercises.prompt: A fixed window allows 100 requests per calendar minute. A user sends 100 requests at 12:00:59.9 and another 100 at 12:01:00.1. What happens?

exercises.explanation: The counter is not miscounting. The algorithm only ever promised “100 per fixed minute,” not “at most 100 in any continuous 60 seconds.” If you need the latter, switch to an algorithm such as the sliding window log.
exercises.prompt: A fixed window letting through twice the quota near a boundary means the counter has a bug.

exercises.explanation: The rolling 60 seconds still covers 75% of the previous minute: 30 + 80 × 75% = 90, which is below 100, so the request is allowed. 110 counts the whole previous minute. The formula assumes the previous minute’s traffic was uniform, so it is only an approximation.
options: 110 requests
90 requests
30 requests
50 requests
exercises.prompt: A sliding window counter allows 100 requests per minute. The previous minute had 80 requests, the current minute has 30 so far, and you are 25% into the current minute. About how many requests does the estimate say are in the rolling window?
