exercises.explanation: The formula scales the previous window’s count proportionally. If all of that window’s requests were bunched at its start or end, the scaled result is too high or too low. That is why it saves memory and is fairly smooth, but may not satisfy a strictly exact quota.
exercises.prompt: A sliding window counter assumes traffic in the previous window was evenly distributed, so it can be off when traffic is extremely clustered.

exercises.explanation: Remove expired timestamps first, so the count reflects the current rolling window. If the steps are not atomic, concurrent requests may all think a slot is still free. You also need to define up front whether rejected requests are recorded in the log.
exercises.prompt: Complete the decision steps for a sliding window log
exercises.text: On each request, first [[purge old entries]], then [[count what remains]], and finally decide whether to record this timestamp; these steps must run atomically.

exercises.explanation: No algorithm is free: a token bucket’s bursts must be survivable downstream; a leaking bucket buys smoothness with queueing; a fixed window is cheap but has boundary bursts; a sliding log is exact but uses memory per request; a sliding window counter saves memory but is only approximate.
pairs: Capacity must match what downstream can absorb
Queueing delay and a queue limit
exercises.prompt: Match each rate limiting algorithm with its main cost
exercises.refAnchor: d4/批注选择算法的速记表

exercises.explanation: Only the sliding log counts any rolling window exactly; the cost is memory proportional to the number of requests, which is fine when volume is small. A fixed window has boundary bursts, a sliding window counter is approximate, and a token bucket allows controlled bursts, so none of them equals an exact rolling window.
options: Sliding window counter
Sliding window log
Token bucket
Fixed window counter
exercises.prompt: The business strictly requires “at most 100 requests in any continuous 60 seconds,” and each user’s request volume is small. Which algorithm fits best?

exercises.explanation: Resetting per day is itself fixed-window semantics: one counter plus an expiry is the cheapest implementation. A sliding log stores a timestamp per call; a token bucket refills continuously and does not reset at midnight; a leaking bucket shapes the output rate, so it does not suit a quota such as a daily total.
options: Leaking bucket
Sliding window log
Fixed window counter
Token bucket
exercises.prompt: An open platform gives each API key 1,000 calls per day, reset at midnight on the calendar day, and can tolerate a burst across midnight. Which algorithm is the least effort?

exercises.explanation: The more requests in the window, the more timestamps to keep. That is the price of an exact rolling window. A sliding window counter stores only two counters, for the current and previous windows, so it saves memory.
exercises.prompt: A sliding window log’s memory use grows with the number of requests, because it stores a timestamp for every request in the window.

lessons.title: Distributed Counts
lessons.summary: Atomic checks, regions, 429, and monitoring

exercises.explanation: The read and the write run separately, so both gateways decide based on the same stale value, both allow the request, and both write back 0, spending the quota twice. Redis does not detect this kind of read-modify-write conflict for you; make the whole check one atomic operation.
options: Redis detects the conflict and rolls one of them back
Both requests are rejected
Both are allowed, spending one more unit of quota than exists
Only the one that writes back first is allowed
exercises.prompt: Only 1 token is left for a key. Gateways A and B both read it with GET at nearly the same time and see 1, each decides to allow the request, and each writes back 0. What is the result?

exercises.explanation: A Lua script runs atomically on Redis: A finishes and deducts to 0 before B starts checking, so B is rejected. Locking only the deduct step still lets the check use a stale value, and independent regional counts each allow requests, so the global total can be exceeded.
options: Put it in one Lua script on the same Redis instance
Add a distributed lock around the deduct step only
Each gateway runs GET to read the balance, then SET to write it back
Each region counts independently in its own Redis
exercises.prompt: Which approach guarantees that “refill, check, deduct” on the same key across multiple gateways never oversells?

exercises.explanation: One side supplies the time, so gateway A’s fast clock does not refill early and B’s slow clock does not double-count; elapsed=max(0, now−last) guards against clock rollback. Refill, check, deduct, and write must all happen in one atomic script.
items: The side that owns the key reads the current time
Compute elapsed time; a clock rollback counts as 0
Refill tokens, capped at capacity B
Check there are enough tokens, then deduct
Write back tokens and time, return the result
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of an atomic distributed token bucket script in order

exercises.explanation: A sorted set is just a data structure that makes it convenient to store and purge by time. Each command still runs separately, and other gateways can slip in between commands. The whole flow has to go into an atomic operation such as a Lua script.
exercises.prompt: Storing timestamps in a Redis sorted set automatically makes the whole “purge, count, check, write” flow atomic.

exercises.explanation: The script runs serially on a single instance. When several regions each have their own Redis, they sync through replication, and a stale count after asynchronous replication can allow requests again. A strict global quota needs a single coordinating authority or non-overlapping regional quotas.
exercises.prompt: A Lua script’s atomicity covers only the Redis instance it runs on and does not automatically make counts across regions strongly consistent.

exercises.explanation: Split the 1,000 among regions (such as 600+400); each decides locally and the sum never exceeds the total. The cost is utilization: a region that runs out rejects requests even while another has quota left. Async syncing briefly oversells, and independent counts let every region allow 1,000.
options: Pre-assign each region a non-overlapping share of the quota
Count only on the client to skip cross-region calls
Each region counts independently up to 1,000
Count locally in each region and sync totals asynchronously
exercises.prompt: A global service must keep each user strictly within 1,000 requests per day, while every region should decide locally for low latency. Which approach meets the requirement?

exercises.explanation: 429 means too many requests, and Retry-After tells the client how long to wait before trying again. If all clients retry at the same moment, they create a second wave of congestion, so backoff needs random jitter to spread the retries out.
exercises.prompt: Complete the response and retry convention for rate-limited requests
exercises.text: When over the limit, the server often returns HTTP [[429]] Too Many Requests and may include [[Retry-After]]; clients retry with backoff plus [[random jitter]].

exercises.explanation: Allowed and rejected counts show whether the rules are too loose or too tight, extra latency maps to the low-latency requirement, and false positives (such as a shared IP) show whether the counting dimension is right. A frontend countdown is only a hint, and test coverage measures code quality, not rule fit.
options: Extra latency added by the limiting check
Allowed and rejected request counts
Whether the frontend countdown displays accurately
Legitimate users who get rate limited by mistake
Unit test coverage of the limiter code
exercises.prompt: After a rate limiter goes live, which of the following metrics should you keep monitoring to tune the rules?

exercises.explanation: Each region first decides on its local count without waiting for cross-region sync, so it is fast; but until the sync arrives, every region thinks there is still quota left and they allow requests together. To be strict, you need central coordination or pre-allocated quotas, which cost latency or utilization.
exercises.prompt: Syncing counts between data centers with eventual consistency lowers latency, at the cost of possibly overshooting the global quota for a while.

chapters.title: Consistent Hashing
keyPoints: When N changes, `hash % N` moves most keys to other machines. The cache misses en masse, and scaling out can crush the database first.
Consistent hashing puts keys and nodes in one hash space; a key walks clockwise to the first node. The ring is a sorted table, not a network cable.
A new node takes over only the range after its predecessor, up to itself. A removed node hands its whole range to its clockwise successor.
Virtual nodes cut a big territory into many small pieces: less skew, and the count can follow capacity. Too many raise routing upkeep.
Even data placement is not even traffic: one hot key still lives on one machine. Use replication, request coalescing, or splitting.
The ring only says which keys should move. A real migration still needs copying, throttling, and verification, plus one node-table version everywhere.

labs.title: Hash Ring: Who Moves When a Server Joins or Leaves
Virtual Nodes: Even Keys, Same Hot Key

lessons.title: The Cost of Modulo
lessons.summary: Why hash % N breaks on every resize

exercises.explanation: `17 % 4 = 1` and `17 % 5 = 2`. A key’s remainder depends only on N, so when N changes most remainders change, whether or not the old machine is healthy. Expecting keys to move only to the new machine applies a property of consistent hashing to modulo.
options: It moves to server 4, the new one, which takes it over
It stays on server 1, because server 1 never failed
It moves to server 2, even though server 1 is still healthy
It moves only if server 1 goes offline
exercises.prompt: Requests are routed with `hash(key) % N`, and a key has `hash(key)=17`. The pool grows from 4 to 5 servers (numbered from 0). What happens to this key?

exercises.explanation: When N changes, most keys get a new remainder and land on other old servers, not just on the new one. Moving only a fraction of the keys is exactly what consistent hashing sets out to achieve.
exercises.prompt: With `hash(key) % N` cache sharding, adding one server invalidates only the keys that get assigned to the new server.

exercises.explanation: Changing N reroutes most keys, and their new cache locations are empty, so a flood of misses goes straight to the database. The modulo operation costs almost nothing and the cache needs no bulk preload. The problem is the wholesale reshuffle of routes.
options: The new cache server must bulk-load its data from the database before going live
A larger N makes every routing decision cost a heavier modulo operation
Every client must restart to pick up the new N when the cluster scales
Most keys changed machines, so they miss the cache and hit the database
exercises.prompt: A cache cluster shards with modulo hashing. After adding a cache server to handle more traffic, the database shows a load spike first. What is the most likely cause?

exercises.explanation: The root cause is that changing N reshuffles the routes. Cache invalidation is the result, and database load is the final knock-on effect. So scaling out, normally a good thing, can hit you with a shock first.
items: Server count N goes from 4 to 5
Most keys get a new remainder and route elsewhere
New locations lack these keys: mass cache misses
Requests fall through to the database, causing a spike
exercises.prompt: Put in order how a modulo-hash resize causes a database load spike

exercises.explanation: The remainder depends only on N: adding a machine, removing a failed one, or scaling in all change N and cause a large-scale remapping. A hardware upgrade or restart that leaves the count unchanged does not change any key’s route. Losing cached contents on restart is a separate problem.
options: Servers restart one by one, with the pool size always unchanged
One server crashes and is removed from the pool
Two servers are taken offline to scale in
One server gets a CPU upgrade and stays in the pool
One server is added to scale out
exercises.prompt: With `hash(key) % N` routing, which changes make most keys move to a different server?

exercises.explanation: By definition, consistent hashing remaps only some of the keys when nodes come and go, which limits the disruption. It does not guarantee a perfectly even spread (virtual nodes improve that), does not move data on its own, and cannot split up a single hot key.
options: It automatically moves data to the new node when nodes change
It gives every server exactly the same number of keys
It spreads the requests of a hot key evenly across all nodes
When servers are added or removed, only some keys change owner
exercises.prompt: What is the core improvement of consistent hashing over modulo hashing?

exercises.explanation: The ring is a numbering space, not a network cable. In practice you usually need just one table of nodes sorted by hash value: look up the successor position and send the request straight to it. “Walking around the ring” is only a picture of the routing rule.
exercises.prompt: A hash ring requires servers to be connected in a ring topology, with a request forwarded server by server around the ring until it reaches the responsible one.

exercises.explanation: Once nodes are sorted by hash value, you only need to find the successor, and past the maximum you wrap around to the smallest node. “Numerically nearest” is a common misconception, since the rule cares only about the clockwise direction. Taking the modulo of the node count brings back the original problem.
options: Compute the numeric distance from the key to each server and take the nearest
Start at any server and forward step by step until the owner is found
Look up the successor in the sorted node table, wrapping to the start past the end
Take the key’s hash modulo the node count to get a node index
exercises.prompt: In code, how do you usually find the first server clockwise from a key’s hash position?

exercises.explanation: Nodes and keys must be compared within one space for a “successor” to be defined. The direction is a clockwise convention; if implementations disagreed on it, the same key would be sent to different machines.
exercises.prompt: Complete the routing rule of consistent hashing
exercises.text: Keys and servers are mapped into [[the same hash space]]; the server responsible for a key is the first one found [[clockwise]] from its position.

exercises.explanation: With N fixed, the same key always yields the same remainder, so routing is stable. The trouble with modulo hashing only shows up when servers are added or removed and N changes.
exercises.prompt: When the server pool size never changes, `hash(key) % N` by itself assigns keys to servers stably.

lessons.title: Owners on the Ring
lessons.summary: Clockwise lookup, node changes, affected ranges

exercises.explanation: No server lies after 90, so the search goes clockwise past 99 back to 0 and meets S1=20 first. S3 is only the numerically nearest, but the rule cares about the clockwise direction alone. So S1 owns the range (80,20], which crosses zero.
options: S3
No server is at a position ≥ 90, so the write fails
S1
S2
exercises.prompt: On a ring 0…99 running clockwise (99 wraps to 0), servers are S1=20, S2=50, S3=80, and a key belongs to the first server at a position ≥ its hash. Who owns a key with hash 90?

exercises.explanation: The rule is “greater than or equal,” so 50 belongs to S2, which sits at position 50. S2 owns (20,50]. Giving it to S3 gets the range endpoint backwards; the endpoint convention must match the lookup implementation.
options: S2
S3
S1
exercises.prompt: On a ring 0…99 with S1=20, S2=50, S3=80, a key belongs to the first server at a position ≥ its hash. Who owns a key whose hash is exactly 50?

exercises.explanation: The counterclockwise predecessor of S4 is S2=50, so it takes over only (50,65], which used to belong to S3. Of the four keys, only 60 falls inside; 10, 35, and 90 keep their owners. “Recompute everything” is the modulo-hash way of thinking.
options: Only 60, from S3 to S4
60 and 90, both to S4
35 and 60, with S2 and S3 each giving up one
All four keys must be recomputed for the new node count
exercises.prompt: On a ring 0…99 with S1=20, S2=50, S3=80 (a key belongs to the first server at a position ≥ its hash) and four keys with hashes 10, 35, 60, 90, S4=65 is added. Which keys change servers?

exercises.explanation: Adding a node: find its predecessor counterclockwise, and (predecessor, new node] moves from the old owner to the new node. Removing a node: its whole range goes to its clockwise successor, and the successor of S3, wrapping past zero, is S1.
exercises.prompt: On the ring S1=20, S2=50, S3=80, perform each operation (always starting from the original ring) and match it to the one range that changes owner

exercises.explanation: The counterclockwise predecessor of S4=5 is S3=80, so the affected range must be written across zero as (80,5]. Cutting off only 0…5 forgets that 81…99 also lies after the predecessor. A small number does not mean there is no range.
options: None, since 5 is lower than every node position and takes no keys
[0,5], that is 0…5, moving from S1 to S4
(80,5], crossing zero, moving from S1 to S4
(5,20], that is 6…20, moving from S1 to S4
exercises.prompt: On a ring 0…99 with S1=20, S2=50, S3=80 (a key belongs to the first server at a position ≥ its hash), S4=5 is added. Which range changes owner?

exercises.explanation: The removed server hands only its own range, as a whole, to its clockwise successor; the other servers are unaffected. This also means the successor’s load can suddenly double, an imbalance that virtual nodes are meant to ease.
exercises.prompt: On a basic ring with no virtual nodes, when a server is removed, its keys are split evenly among all the remaining servers.

exercises.explanation: The new node cuts off only the stretch after its predecessor, up to itself. That stretch used to belong to its clockwise successor, and no other range changes hands. Only when one physical machine joins with several virtual nodes at once do multiple small ranges change.
exercises.prompt: On a basic ring, when one ordinary node is added at a time, only the keys between the new node and its counterclockwise predecessor change primary owner.

exercises.explanation: Rule of thumb: “find the owner clockwise, find the range by looking at the predecessor.” Keys after the predecessor used to walk clockwise to the old successor first; now they meet the new node first.
exercises.prompt: Complete the rule for the range a new node takes over
exercises.text: A new node takes over the keys from its counterclockwise [[predecessor]] up to itself, and these keys used to belong to its clockwise [[successor]].

exercises.explanation: S2’s whole range goes to its clockwise successor S3, so S3’s range grows to (20,80] and S1 is not affected at all. Splitting it between the two neighbors, or recomputing everything, is not how the basic ring behaves.
options: S1 and S3 each take half of S2’s range
The range S3 owns becomes (20,80]
The keys S1 owns are unaffected
The keys in (20,50] are handed to S3
All keys must be recomputed and migrated
exercises.prompt: On the basic ring S1=20, S2=50, S3=80, S2 is removed. Which statements are correct?

exercises.explanation: With strictly greater, a key whose hash equals a node’s position goes to the next node: a node’s own position is not its own, while its predecessor’s position is, so the range becomes [predecessor, node). The endpoint convention must match the lookup implementation.
options: (node, successor]
(predecessor, node], unchanged
[node, successor)
[predecessor, node)
exercises.prompt: If the lookup is changed to “find the first node at a position strictly greater than the key’s hash,” how should each node’s range be written?

lessons.title: Virtual Nodes
lessons.summary: Skew, virtual nodes, hot keys, and migration

exercises.explanation: The basic approach has two issues, uneven partition sizes and uneven key distribution: server positions are decided by the hash, so the gaps can differ a lot, and an unlucky machine gets a big territory. Lookup efficiency and migration scope are not the problem.
options: Gaps differ, so some servers get much larger ranges
Every key must migrate whenever a server is added or removed
The same key is mapped to two servers
Looking up a key requires scanning all servers
exercises.prompt: 3 servers each take a single position on the ring. What problem is most likely?

exercises.explanation: Think of opening branches in many neighborhoods: owning one big block can leave you much better or worse off, while owning many small pieces lets the deviations cancel and shrinks the standard deviation of the distribution. It does no data replication, and the routing table gets bigger, not smaller.
options: They make the hash function’s output more random
One machine owns many scattered small ranges, so deviations cancel out more easily
They shrink the routing table, so lookups are faster
Each key is stored on several machines and reads pick any one
exercises.prompt: Why do virtual nodes make the key distribution more even?

exercises.explanation: The number of virtual nodes can follow capacity: a machine with more nodes covers more of the ring in total and gets more keys. The length of a single position’s range is decided by the hash and cannot be set precisely, and the direction rule is the same for every node.
options: Give A about twice as many virtual nodes
Place A earlier on the ring
Give A one position, but make its range twice as long
Let A receive keys both clockwise and counterclockwise
exercises.prompt: Machine A has twice the capacity of machine B. How do virtual nodes reflect that?

exercises.explanation: Too few virtual nodes is still uneven, while too many increases the routing table and maintenance cost, and more small ranges are involved whenever a machine joins or leaves. The count is a parameter to trade off, not something to raise without limit.
exercises.prompt: The more virtual nodes the better; adding more costs nothing except a more even distribution.

exercises.explanation: Virtual nodes improve the statistical balance of many keys across machines. Every lookup still locates `product:hot` at the same primary owner, so all 500,000 QPS land on one machine. Even data is not even traffic.
options: Close to 0, since the hot key is split across all machines
About 1/10, since virtual nodes spread the requests
Still at least half, since this key is located on one machine only
It depends on whether the number of keys is spread evenly enough
exercises.prompt: 10 million keys are spread evenly over 10 machines. `product:hot` takes 500,000 QPS, and all other keys together take another 500,000 QPS. After greatly increasing each machine’s virtual nodes, what is the least load on the machine holding `product:hot`?

exercises.explanation: Hotspots need application-level fixes matched to the operation: replication spreads reads, request coalescing blocks the stampede to the origin, and sub-counters spread writes. Adding virtual nodes only changes how other keys are assigned, and switching hash functions just moves this key to another machine.
options: Coalesce requests on a cache miss so they do not all hit the origin
Switch the hash function from MD5 to SHA-1
Replicate read-only hot data to several caches to spread the reads
Split a hot counter into sub-counters and sum them on read
Add virtual nodes to the machine that holds the key
exercises.prompt: Which measures really relieve the pressure from a single hot key?

exercises.explanation: Each machine deducts without seeing the others’ deductions, so the total can oversell. Replication suits read-only hot data; a write hotspot still needs coordination, pre-allocated quotas, or a redesign around the business logic.
exercises.prompt: For inventory deduction that must never oversell, replicating a hot key to several machines that each deduct on their own breaks the inventory constraint.

exercises.explanation: Virtual nodes cut a machine’s territory into many small pieces, so the fluctuation of per-machine load shrinks, while the average stays the same. They are not replicas: a key still has a single primary owner.
exercises.prompt: Complete the role of virtual nodes
exercises.text: One physical server maps to several [[virtual nodes]] on the ring; usually, the more there are, the smaller the [[standard deviation]] of the key distribution.

exercises.explanation: The two node tables name different owners for the affected range: one side writes to the new node while the other reads from the old one, so reads return stale values or nothing. Migration therefore has to manage node-view versions; the ring itself will not detect this for you.
options: The hash ring detects and rejects requests from the old table
The same key goes to different machines, and fresh writes may not be found
Only some requests get slower; reads and writes stay correct
Every key is remapped and the whole cache is invalidated
exercises.prompt: During a scale-out, half the clients have the new node table and the other half still use the old one. What goes wrong?

exercises.explanation: The hash ring only tells you which keys should move; it never moves the data itself. Copy and verify first, then switch routing, and delete old data last. Switching or deleting too early sends requests where the data does not exist yet.
items: Determine the range the new node takes over
Copy that range from its current owner, throttled
Confirm the new node’s data is complete and readable
Publish the new routing version and switch traffic
Delete the migrated data from the old node
exercises.prompt: After adding a new node to the ring, put the steps of a real migration in order

chapters.title: Key-Value Store
keyPoints: In a network partition you can’t have both linearizability and availability; P is a given, so decide per operation: reject, or allow stale reads.
Partitioning splits data for capacity; replication copies it to survive failures, and replicas must span machines and failure domains.
`W+R>N` only guarantees that read and write sets overlap; linearizability also needs version comparison, write-back on reads, and handling of failed writes.
A vector clock only tells ordered from concurrent; siblings are merged by business rules or the user, never by picking the larger sum.
Handle failures in layers: gossip only suspects a failure, sloppy quorum with hinted handoff covers temporary ones, and Merkle trees do anti-entropy.
Writes go through the commit log, memtable, and SSTable; reads use a Bloom filter to skip files, and “possibly present” still needs an exact lookup.

labs.title: Quorum Reads and Writes: Does Overlap Guarantee the Latest Value?
Vector Clocks: Who Is the Ancestor, Who Conflicts
Bloom Filter: Why Read the Disk After “Possibly Present”

lessons.title: CAP and Trade-offs
lessons.summary: API semantics, single-node limits, partition choices

exercises.explanation: It works like a huge Map spread across machines: overwrite versus multiple versions, deletes and expiration, and conditional updates all shape the rest of the design. It does not provide SQL joins, foreign keys, or multi-row transactions, so those are not part of this interface.
options: Which join algorithm multi-table queries use
Whether deletes and expiration are needed
How foreign key constraints cascade deletes
Whether putting the same key again overwrites or keeps versions
Whether conditional updates are needed
exercises.prompt: Before designing a distributed key-value store, which interface semantics should you clarify with the interviewer?

exercises.explanation: Compression and spilling cold data to disk buy time, but one machine’s capacity is capped, so larger data sets must be spread across servers. A hash table can resize and lookups stay close to constant time, and data on disk can still be read by key; the bottleneck is single-machine capacity.
options: One server’s capacity has a ceiling, so optimizations only delay the problem
Once cold data is on disk, it can no longer be read by key
With more data, hash table lookups degrade into scanning one by one
A hash table has fixed slots and can’t insert new keys once full
exercises.prompt: An in-memory hash table on one machine already compresses its data and moves cold data to disk. Why still go distributed?

exercises.explanation: In CAP, A requires that a request to a non-failed node eventually gets a non-error response. Returning 503 gives up availability to protect consistency. Treating “it responds” as available, or mixing consistency into the definition of availability, are common misreadings.
options: Yes: the node is up and responds, so it is available
No: availability requires all nodes to hold consistent data
Yes: the client can keep retrying and will eventually succeed
No: a non-failed node must eventually return a non-error response
exercises.prompt: During a network partition, a healthy node returns 503 for every request. By the CAP definition of availability, does it count as available?

exercises.explanation: P is the environment, not a feature switch: the network can break. Real network failures are unavoidable, and once a partition happens you can only trade between C and A; a CA assumption guarantees nothing about behavior during a partition.
exercises.prompt: A distributed system deployed across a network can choose CA and still guarantee both consistency and availability when a network partition happens.

exercises.explanation: CAP is about the trade-off during a partition: either reject some requests to stay consistent, or keep responding and risk inconsistency. Without a partition, a system can be both consistent and available, so don’t recite “pick two of three” mechanically.
exercises.prompt: A more accurate reading of “pick two of three” is: when a network partition happens, you can’t guarantee both linearizability and CAP-style availability.

exercises.explanation: CP doesn’t have to stop everything: n1/n2 are still a majority and can keep reading and writing safely, while the minority n3 can’t confirm the latest state and must refuse. Which side gets blocked depends on the protocol; the textbook example of blocking writes on n1/n2 is only a simplification.
options: n3 keeps accepting writes and overwrites n1/n2 after recovery
All three nodes stop reads and writes until the network recovers
The n1/n2 majority keeps serving reads and writes, and n3 refuses service
Reads are allowed only on n3, and all writes are blocked
exercises.prompt: Three replicas n1, n2, n3, and n3 is cut off from n1/n2. The system coordinates by majority and favors consistency for this operation. What most likely happens during the partition?

exercises.explanation: AP keeps serving during a partition: n3 may return stale values, and the new writes on both sides are synced after the network recovers, with conflicts resolved by versions and merge rules. Rejecting requests is what CP does; queueing without responding doesn’t meet availability either.
options: All writes queue up and run after the network recovers
All requests to n3 are rejected to avoid returning stale values
Both sides keep reading and writing, may return stale values, and merge afterward
The system automatically picks the one correct value, so no conflicts occur
exercises.prompt: Three replicas n1, n2, n3, and n3 is cut off from n1/n2. If this operation favors availability, what happens during the partition?

exercises.explanation: Linearizability requires operations to appear to take effect instantaneously, in real-time order; availability concerns non-failed nodes, and a crashed node is outside the requirement. Reading A as “every node must respond” is a common misreading.
exercises.prompt: Complete the exact meanings of C and A in CAP
exercises.text: C usually means operations appear to take effect instantaneously in [[real-time order]]; A requires that requests to [[non-failed nodes]] eventually get a non-error response.

exercises.explanation: You can’t call a whole system CP just because the business is “banking.” In an interview, state for each operation what is allowed during a partition: a debit should be rejected rather than overdrawn, while display data that is briefly stale is usually acceptable.
exercises.prompt: One system can choose its trade-off per operation: a balance deduction demands stricter consistency, while display data tolerates briefly stale reads.

lessons.title: Replicas & Quorums
lessons.summary: Partitioning, replica placement, and N/W/R trade-offs

exercises.explanation: Replication stores the same data several times, so each machine still holds the full 3 TB. To make it fit, you must partition first; replication solves “the data survives a machine failure.” Fitting the data and surviving failures are two separate problems.
options: It fits: replication automatically splits the data into three pieces
It doesn’t fit: each machine still has to hold the full 3 TB
It fits, but writes must sync three copies, so latency is high
It fits: 3 machines together have 3 TB of space
exercises.prompt: 3 TB of logical data, and one machine can safely store only 1 TB. You store 3 copies of the full 3 TB on 3 machines. What happens?

exercises.explanation: Each partition is 1 TB, and 3 replicas make 3 TB; the three partitions total about 9 TB. 27 TB multiplies the full data’s 3 copies by 3 again; 3 TB is just the logical size, without replicas.
options: About 3 TB
About 27 TB
About 1 TB
About 9 TB
exercises.prompt: 3 TB of logical data is split into 3 partitions, each stored as 3 replicas. Ignoring indexes and headroom, roughly how much physical space does it use?

exercises.explanation: Adjacent virtual nodes may belong to the same physical machine, so one failure could take several replicas with it; pick distinct physical servers and, where possible, different data centers. A shared rack saves latency but loses all replicas together when the rack loses power.
options: Skip virtual nodes on the same machine and spread across data centers
Put replicas in the same rack to lower write latency
The N positions must be adjacent so replicas can sync quickly
The more virtual nodes, the larger N has to be
exercises.prompt: With virtual nodes, you take the first N positions clockwise on the ring as replicas. What else should you watch for?

exercises.explanation: Spreading replicas across machines only survives single-machine failures; a data center power outage makes all three unavailable. To withstand a data center failure, replicate across multiple data centers and plan for traffic switching, DNS, and spare capacity.
exercises.prompt: Three replicas on three different machines in the same data center can also survive a power outage of the whole data center.

exercises.explanation: The more replicas a side waits for, the slower that side is: with R=1 reads are fast but writes wait for all N copies, and W=1 is the reverse. N=3, W=R=2 makes both wait for a majority, a common compromise. When W+R≤N, the read and write sets may not overlap.
pairs: Both wait for a majority; a common compromise
A read may miss the latest acknowledged write
exercises.prompt: Match each quorum configuration with its characteristic

exercises.explanation: The two sets have 2+2=4 slots but there are only 3 replicas, so they overlap in at least `2+2−3=1`. The reader therefore touches at least one node that holds the completed write, but it must still identify which version is newer.
options: 0 replicas
3 replicas
1 replica
2 replicas
exercises.prompt: N=3, W=2, R=2. For any write-acknowledgement set and any read set, how many replicas do they share at minimum?

exercises.explanation: The inequality only guarantees that the read and write sets overlap. Linearizability also needs correct version comparison, ordering of concurrent writes, handling of failed writes, read repair, and membership changes; without them you can still read a new value and then read the old one back.
exercises.prompt: As long as `W+R>N` holds, every read is guaranteed to return the latest, linearizable result.

exercises.explanation: Both reads satisfy R=2, yet after seeing 1 the system goes back to 0, which violates linearizability. Some protocols have a read write the chosen version back to a majority before returning, closing this regression. R=1 would only make it worse, and there was no partition or corruption in the process.
options: A network partition caused this, and it won’t happen after the partition heals
Replica A is corrupted and should be restored from B and C
R was set wrong; with R=1 you would read the new value
Overlap isn’t enough; linearizability also needs steps like write-back on reads
exercises.prompt: Initially A/B/C all hold x=0. The write x=1 reaches only A and has not gathered W=2. Read 1 queries A and B, returns 1, and does not write it back; then read 2 queries B and C and returns 0. What does this show?

exercises.explanation: Like and view counts being briefly off doesn’t affect correctness, so eventual consistency is fine and buys lower latency. Order status must be readable right after the write, and a balance deduction can’t overdraw, so both need stronger read/write semantics.
options: Like counts shown on a post
View counts shown on a product page
Account balance deduction that prevents overdrafts
Order status that must be visible right after placing the order
exercises.prompt: Which of these data can usually accept eventual consistency?

exercises.explanation: Choosing W, R, and N is a trade-off between latency and consistency: waiting for more is safer but slower, and when some replicas fail you can’t gather enough responses, so requests fail.
exercises.prompt: Complete the cost of raising R and W
exercises.text: Raising R and W means waiting for [[more replicas]]: consistency is stronger, but [[latency]] is higher, and requests fail more easily when nodes are down.

lessons.title: Conflict & Failure
lessons.summary: Vector clocks, failure detection, temporary failures

exercises.explanation: A version is an ancestor only when every entry is ≤ the other’s and at least one is <; all equal means the same version; one larger and one smaller means concurrent. (2,1) and (1,2) have equal sums, but each has an update the other lacks, so the sum can’t decide the winner.
pairs: The first is an ancestor of the second
The second is an ancestor of the first
exercises.prompt: Vectors are written as (A’s count, B’s count). Decide the relationship between each pair of versions

exercises.explanation: A vector clock only judges causality: (2,1) and (1,2) don’t dominate each other, so they are siblings. Which name is correct is a business question for the user or an explicit rule; summing, comparing strings, or splicing characters are not valid merges.
options: Pick the version with the larger vector sum as the correct name
Take one character from each and merge them into “Li Ming”
Detect the concurrent conflict and hand it to business rules or the user
Compare the strings and pick the newer one
exercises.prompt: A name was originally “Zhang Min” with vector (A:1,B:1). While disconnected, A changes it to “Zhang Ming” (2,1) and B concurrently changes it to “Li Min” (1,2). What can the vector clock do?

exercises.explanation: First take the entry-wise maximum of the two branches to get (2,2), showing that both sides’ updates were seen; then A, the node doing the write, increments its own count to get (3,2). (2,2) misses the “whoever writes increments” step.
exercises.prompt: Vectors are written as (A’s count, B’s count). A and B concurrently write two conflicting versions, (2,1) and (1,2). The user picks the value of (2,1), and A performs the merge write. What is the new version’s vector?

exercises.explanation: Vectors grow as more participants appear, so a pruning policy is needed to limit their size. After entries are dropped, orderings that could once be determined may become ambiguous; that is the price of bounding the size.
exercises.prompt: Pruning entries to cap a vector clock’s length can lose causal information.

exercises.explanation: Each node periodically increments its own heartbeat counter and sends it to a random set of nodes; only when a member’s counter stays flat for a long time is it considered offline. Counter values aren’t comparable across nodes, and a single report isn’t enough to conclude.
options: Its heartbeat messages weren’t sent to all nodes
Its heartbeat counter has stopped increasing for a preset period
Its heartbeat counter is much smaller than the other members’
A single node reported losing contact with it more than once
exercises.prompt: In gossip-based failure detection, what makes a node conclude that a member is offline?

exercises.explanation: Slow machines, network congestion, and GC pauses can all drop heartbeats, so a timeout is a suspicion, not proof. Multi-source confirmation, retries, and damping flapping reduce false positives; removing a node on a single report turns brief stalls into frequent membership changes.
options: Treat a timeout as a suspicion first, and confirm with retries
Add measures to stop nodes from flapping online and offline
Confirm with at least two independent sources before marking a failure
Treat timeouts caused by GC pauses as a crash outright
Remove a node immediately when one node reports losing contact
exercises.prompt: Which practices help avoid mistaking a slow node for a failed one?

exercises.explanation: Dynamo skips the down node and sends the request to the first N healthy nodes on the preference list; the write returns once W acks arrive, and the coordinator’s local write counts as one. Saying the write goes to the first W healthy nodes is a simplification.
options: Send it to the first 3 healthy nodes on the preference list and collect W acks
Send it to every healthy node on the ring and succeed only after all ack
Write only to the 2 remaining original replicas, and fail if 3 can’t be reached
Wait for the down node to recover so only the original replicas are written
exercises.prompt: N=3, and the 2nd node on a key’s preference list is down. Under the Dynamo paper’s sloppy quorum, how is a write handled?

exercises.explanation: A stand-in node may not be one of the original N replicas: if the write lands on a stand-in and the read goes to the original replicas, the two sets can miss each other. The overlap proof relies on a fixed set of N replicas, and no longer applies directly once that is relaxed.
exercises.prompt: With sloppy quorum enabled, as long as `W+R>N` still holds, the read and write sets always overlap.

exercises.explanation: Hinted handoff has the stand-in record “who this data belongs to” and hand the changes back when the original node recovers, restoring consistency gradually. It relies on hints being stored reliably and returned promptly, and is no substitute for full replica repair.
options: D pushes the changes back to C based on its saved hints
D permanently replaces C as the key’s replica
D’s data is discarded, and clients retry the write to C
C copies all of D’s data in full
exercises.prompt: While node C is down, stand-in node D accepted writes that belong to C. What happens when C recovers?

exercises.explanation: Different roots mean a difference exists somewhere: compare downward level by level, skip subtrees with equal hashes, and finally transfer only the differing buckets. A full copy is exactly what a Merkle tree avoids; it only locates differences and doesn’t decide which version is correct.
options: Declare a hash collision and recompute the root hash
Overwrite the whole tree with the side that has the newer version
Compare child nodes level by level and sync only the differing buckets
Give up comparing and copy the entire replica
exercises.prompt: Two replicas use a Merkle tree for anti-entropy repair and find different root hashes. What should happen next?

lessons.title: Repair & I/O Paths
lessons.summary: Merkle repair, the write path, and Bloom filter reads

exercises.explanation: If only keys are hashed and both sides have the same key set, the fingerprints are identical. Real systems hash a canonical encoding of key, value, version, and so on together, and every replica must use the same bucket boundaries.
options: It is detected, as long as both sides use the same bucket boundaries
The root hashes differ, but the specific bucket can’t be located
The difference is found at the matching leaf and synced
It isn’t detected: the value never enters the fingerprint
exercises.prompt: An implementation builds its Merkle tree by hashing only keys. The same key has different values on two replicas. What does the comparison show?

exercises.explanation: Without matching buckets you can’t compare bucket by bucket; equal hashes mean only a very low collision probability, not mathematically no difference; and the tree suits continuous anti-entropy. Deciding which version is correct takes versions and conflict rules, and when the roots differ you sync only the differing buckets.
options: It can tell which of two versions is correct
Equal root hashes are a judgment based on a very low collision probability
All replicas must use the same bucket boundaries
When root hashes differ, a full sync is required
It can also serve routine anti-entropy, not just permanent failures
exercises.prompt: Which statements about using Merkle trees for replica repair are correct?

exercises.explanation: Log first, so the write can be recovered after a crash; then memory, for speed; when memory fills, flush to a sorted, immutable SSTable; compaction later merges and cleans up old versions.
items: Append the write to the commit log
Write it to the in-memory memtable
The memtable reaches its threshold
Flush it to an immutable SSTable on disk
Background compaction merges old versions
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of handling one write on a single storage node in order

exercises.explanation: After a crash the log can be replayed to recover writes that were only in memory; the memtable lets a write land in memory and finish quickly. Persistence comes from the log and the SSTables flushed later, not from the memtable.
options: The log stores indexes, and the memtable stores Bloom filters
Both handle persistence and back each other up
The log speeds up reads, and the memtable handles persistence
The log is for crash recovery, and the memtable is for fast writes
exercises.prompt: In the write path, what are the commit log and the memtable each responsible for?

exercises.explanation: Whether the log has really been flushed to disk before the write is acknowledged depends on the durability settings; if it is still in a buffer when the power goes out, the write is lost. You can’t conclude anything just from “it uses a log.”
exercises.prompt: Appending to the commit log first guarantees that an acknowledged write is never lost on power failure.

exercises.explanation: Bits 1 and 6 were already set to 1 by other keys, so gamma happens to hit every checked bit, a false positive: the only answer is “possibly present,” and only reading the SSTable reveals that gamma is missing. The filter records bits, not who set them; only seeing a 0 proves absence.
options: Definitely absent, so this SSTable can be skipped
Possibly present, and you must check the SSTable to learn it isn’t there
Bits 1 and 6 belong to different keys, so it counts as absent
Definitely present, so the value can be returned directly
exercises.prompt: An 8-bit Bloom filter: inserting alpha sets bits 1 and 4, and inserting beta sets bits 4 and 6. gamma, never inserted, maps to bits 1 and 6. What does the query return?

exercises.explanation: Several keys share bits, so a key that was never inserted may hit all of its bits by chance, a false positive; every bit of an inserted key is always 1, so it is never missed. The filter only helps rule out files and doesn’t locate the exact record.
exercises.prompt: Complete how a Bloom filter answers
exercises.text: A Bloom filter answers only “definitely absent” or “[[possibly present]]”; it can give [[false positives]], but when maintained correctly it never misses a key that was inserted.

exercises.explanation: Those bits may also have been set to 1 by other keys; clearing them makes those keys look “definitely absent,” causing false negatives. For an immutable SSTable, build a matching filter when the table is created.
exercises.prompt: When deleting a key, you can clear its bits in an ordinary Bloom filter.

exercises.explanation: Updates and deletes both write new records, so old versions and tombstones are scattered across SSTables until compaction cleans them up. A read has to merge versions and recognize deletions to return the right result.
exercises.prompt: In an LSM structure, one key can appear in several SSTables, so a read must apply version and tombstone rules instead of returning at the first file it hits.

exercises.explanation: Peer design only avoids a fixed single point among data nodes; bootstrap addresses, the config service, the network, or credential services may still be shared by all nodes, so check the real dependency graph. Calling the coordinator “always” a single point is also wrong: the design stresses equal roles.
options: Yes: nodes are peers, so there is no single point at all
Yes: any data with N≥3 replicas has no single point
No: the coordinator sits on one machine, so it is always a single point
No: config services, bootstrap addresses, and the like may still be shared dependencies
exercises.prompt: In the final architecture, data nodes have equal responsibilities and are decentralized. Can you conclude that the whole deployment has no single point of failure?

chapters.title: Distributed Unique ID Generator
chapters.fullTitle: Chapter 7: Design a Unique ID Generator in Distributed Systems
keyPoints: Unique, consecutive, and ordered are three independent properties; this problem needs 64 bits, unique, and roughly time-ordered, not consecutive.
Multi-primary step is hard to resize and not time-increasing; UUID exceeds 64 bits (v7 is also 128); a ticket server is a central single point.
Snowflake: 1 sign bit, 41 millisecond bits, 5 data center, 5 machine, 12 sequence bits; any differing field means a different ID.
One machine issues 4096 IDs per millisecond, in theory about 4.096 million per second; 41 bits last about 69.7 years. Bits are a fixed budget.
Machine IDs must be exclusive and not reused until the old instance is confirmed stopped; taking a sequence number must be synchronized across threads.
When the sequence runs out, wait for the next millisecond or reject; on rollback, wait or reject and alert. NTP cuts drift but isn’t rollback protection.

labs.title: Snowflake ID Generator: Bit Budget, Sequence Exhaustion, and Clock Rollback

lessons.title: ID Properties
lessons.summary: Unique, consecutive, ordered, and the 64-bit limit

exercises.explanation: Unique prevents collisions, consecutive means no gaps, and ordered tells you what came first; the three are independent. 10, 12, 15 has gaps yet is perfectly valid. This problem needs only unique IDs that roughly increase with time, not consecutive ones.
pairs: Unique and increasing, but not consecutive
Unique, but not increasing in issue order
Has a duplicate, so it can’t be a unique key
exercises.prompt: These ID sequences are listed in the order they were issued. Match each one to the property it shows

exercises.explanation: A single database issues auto-increment values serially. With several machines issuing at once, you must either coordinate or partition the number space, or they will collide. Auto-increment values fit in 64 bits and sort fine; gaps come from rollbacks or preallocation, not from distribution itself.
options: Machines increment independently and will issue the same number unless synchronized
Auto-increment IDs inevitably have gaps in a distributed setup
Auto-increment IDs can’t be sorted by size
Auto-increment IDs don’t fit in a 64-bit integer
exercises.prompt: Why does the traditional database auto-increment primary key run into trouble when several machines issue IDs?

exercises.explanation: Clocks differ across machines. Snowflake delivers “roughly ordered,” but a global, strictly increasing order that respects real-time ordering needs extra coordination and a completely different design. The other points are implementation details that don’t change which design you pick.
options: Whether sorting happens in the database or the application
Whether time is shown in UTC or local time
Whether IDs are stored as strings or 64-bit integers
Whether roughly ordered is enough, or globally strictly increasing
exercises.prompt: An interviewer says, “IDs should be sorted by time.” If you don’t ask a follow-up, where are you most likely to end up disagreeing?

exercises.explanation: When one database meets the scale, auto-increment is still a great fit. This chapter covers distributed ID generation because issuing has to scale across nodes; adding a new service before you need it only adds complexity and failure points.
options: Switch to multi-primary step to prepare for more data centers
Switch to UUIDs to rule out collisions for good
Switch to Snowflake now to avoid migrating later
Keep using database auto-increment and skip an ID service
exercises.prompt: The business has a single database whose auto-increment key easily handles the traffic, and there is no multi-data-center requirement. What is the better choice?

exercises.explanation: Transaction rollbacks and preallocated ID ranges both make auto-increment skip numbers, so a gap doesn’t mean an order was lost. “Consecutive” is a separate requirement; if you truly need gap-free voucher numbers for accounting, you may need a separate business numbering scheme.
exercises.prompt: A gap in the order number sequence means some orders were lost.

exercises.explanation: Issue order is not commit order: the transaction holding 101 may commit first. When you say “ordered,” specify whether you mean issue order, physical time, or commit order; ID size reflects only one of them.
exercises.prompt: One transaction gets ID 100 and another gets 101 afterward, so in the database 100 must have committed before 101.

exercises.explanation: The bit width rules out 128-bit UUIDs; the throughput requirement means the design must scale horizontally. These two numbers drive the trade-offs of every approach that follows.
exercises.prompt: Complete the basic requirements
exercises.text: IDs must fit in [[64]] bits, be generated at more than [[10,000]] per second, and sort by date.

exercises.explanation: Ordered means comparing sizes reflects some notion of “before,” which can be issue order, physical time, or commit order, and these don’t always agree. No gaps is “consecutive” and no duplicates is “unique”: two other independent properties that don’t belong under “ordered.”
options: Arranged by physical time
Arranged by issue order
No two IDs are ever the same
Arranged by transaction commit order
No gaps between adjacent IDs
exercises.prompt: The interviewer requires “ordered IDs.” Which of these might “ordered” mean and should be confirmed on the spot?

exercises.explanation: When a new millisecond starts, the time field goes up by 1 and the value jumps by about 4 million. Within a millisecond, usually only part of the sequence is used and the rest stays empty forever. This problem only requires IDs to increase with time, not to go up by exactly 1 each time, so gaps are not a defect.
exercises.prompt: Even with a single machine issuing IDs, Snowflake IDs are not guaranteed to be consecutive.

lessons.title: Alternatives
lessons.summary: Where multi-primary, UUID, ticket server fall short

exercises.explanation: A issues only odd numbers and B only even numbers, so they never collide; but the machines issue at different speeds, so the numbers decouple from real time, and B lagging doesn’t mean a misconfiguration. So the step approach gives uniqueness but not IDs that increase with time.
options: 20 must have been generated before 101
B will eventually collide with A if it keeps going
B lags so far behind that its start was misconfigured
You can’t judge real order from ID size
exercises.prompt: Two databases issue 1,3,5… and 2,4,6… respectively. Machine A has issued up to 101 while machine B has just issued 20. What follows?

exercises.explanation: For example, if B has reached 20 and then steps by 3, it will issue 23 and 29, odd numbers that A has long since issued, so B runs into historical IDs. When adding or removing machines, start values, steps, and existing ranges all need replanning.
exercises.prompt: When growing the multi-primary step approach from two machines to three, you can change the step from 2 to 3 and let each machine continue from its current value.

exercises.explanation: Each server can generate on its own, so it scales with the web servers. But a UUID is 128 bits, and random versions don’t sort by time; uniqueness comes from a huge random space that makes collisions extremely unlikely, not from a central guarantee.
options: It takes only 64 bits, saving storage
IDs are naturally sorted by time
Each server generates IDs independently, with no coordination
A central server guarantees they never repeat
exercises.prompt: What is the most prominent advantage of the UUID approach?

exercises.explanation: v7 fixes the time layout, but `48+4+2+12+62=128` bits, so the width is unchanged; 74 of those bits are available for randomness or counters, so it doesn’t lack uniqueness. It can also be stored as 16-byte binary instead of a string. It is ruled out because the constraint doesn’t match, not because the design is outdated.
options: It needs a central server to assign the random bits
It has too few random bits, so same-millisecond IDs collide easily
It is still 128 bits and doesn’t fit in 64
It can only be stored as a hyphenated string
exercises.prompt: The high 48 bits of a UUIDv7 are Unix milliseconds, so it already sorts by time. Why does it still fail this problem’s requirements?

exercises.explanation: A binary UUID is 16 bytes, which is 128 bits: you only save the text overhead, and it is still twice as wide as a 64-bit ID. Changing the storage format can’t change the bit count.
exercises.prompt: Storing a UUID as binary instead of 36-character text meets this problem’s 64-bit requirement.

exercises.explanation: The first 64 bits are 48 bits of time, 4 version bits, and 12 random bits, so only 12 bits tell apart IDs from the same millisecond. The version bits are fixed and don’t affect time comparison; taking the second half is what loses time ordering. In general, 128 bits can’t be mapped to 64 bits without collisions.
options: The time part is dropped, so it no longer sorts by time
With the version bits added, it still exceeds 64 bits
Few random bits separate same-millisecond IDs, so collisions are likely
Version bits sit inside the first 64 bits, so values can’t be compared by time
exercises.prompt: Someone proposes “just take the first 64 bits of a UUIDv7 as the ID.” What is the main problem?

exercises.explanation: Random generation always carries a tiny collision probability, and it also depends on a good random source and implementation. So you can’t treat every UUID implementation as absolutely duplicate-free.
exercises.prompt: A random UUID’s uniqueness comes from a huge random space that makes collisions extremely unlikely, not from a mathematical guarantee that duplicates never occur.

exercises.explanation: It works like a central ticket dispenser: easy to understand and control, but if it breaks, nobody can get a number. It does generate numeric IDs, and a single incrementing point doesn’t repeat; going to several servers brings back synchronization and conflicts to solve.
options: Each server needs a different step configured
The IDs it generates aren’t numbers
The IDs it generates may repeat
The central server can become a single point of failure
exercises.prompt: What is the main risk of a ticket server (a central database that issues incrementing IDs)?

exercises.explanation: After batch allocation, the application uses up a range locally before coming back, which cuts visits to the central server. If a primary-standby failover hands out the same range again, IDs collide. Range allocation is an add-on direction, not part of the original design.
exercises.prompt: Complete one optimization for a ticket server
exercises.text: A ticket server can hand an application a whole [[ID range]] at a time to cut the cost of each call; when it fails over for high availability, the ranges must be [[non-overlapping]].

exercises.explanation: Multi-primary step is also hard to extend across data centers, and its IDs don’t increase with time; UUID exceeds the bit width; a ticket server is a single point. Snowflake has prerequisites too: machine IDs must be exclusive and the clock must not move backward, which is its failure boundary.
pairs: Step and ranges are hard to adjust when scaling
Centralized issuing makes it a single point
Depends on the clock and unique machine IDs
exercises.prompt: Match each approach to its main weakness in this problem

lessons.title: Bit Layout
lessons.summary: What each Snowflake field does, and capacity math

exercises.explanation: `1+41+5+5+12=64`. Time sits in the high bits so IDs sort by time; data center and machine tell generators apart; the sequence tells apart multiple IDs from the same machine in the same millisecond.
exercises.prompt: Complete Snowflake’s 64-bit layout
exercises.text: 1 sign bit, [[41]] bits of millisecond timestamp, 5 bits of data center, 5 bits of machine, and [[12]] bits of sequence number.

exercises.explanation: Think of an ID as “issue time + window position + this millisecond’s ticket number.” As long as machine identities are unique and the clock and sequence are maintained by the rules, any two IDs differ in at least one field.
exercises.prompt: In each case, which field guarantees that two IDs differ? (DC = data center)
exercises.refAnchor: d7/批注为什么组合后不重复
exercises.refTitle: Note: Why the Combination Never Repeats

exercises.explanation: Comparing integers starts with the high bits, so with time in the most significant bits, an earlier ID has a smaller value. Where a field sits affects neither read speed nor how many bits each field gets.
options: Time determines integer size, so IDs sort roughly by time
It leaves more usable bits for the sequence number
High bits are read faster, which raises issuing throughput
A sequence overflow can’t spill into the sign bit
exercises.prompt: Why does Snowflake put the timestamp in the highest bits, right after the sign bit?

exercises.explanation: Each millisecond allows `2^12 = 4096`, and a second has 1000 milliseconds, so `4096×1000 = 4,096,000`. This is a theoretical ceiling; real throughput is limited by the implementation and runtime. 4096 is only one millisecond’s worth.
exercises.prompt: With a 12-bit sequence, what is the theoretical maximum number of IDs one machine can generate per second?
exercises.refAnchor: d7/批注为什么组合后不重复
exercises.refTitle: Note: Why the Combination Never Repeats

exercises.explanation: `2^41 / 1000 / 60 / 60 / 24 / 365 ≈ 69.7`. 34.9 years is the result for 40 bits and 139 years for 42 bits. Before it runs out you need to migrate the epoch or the bit layout; this layout can’t be used forever.
options: About 69.7 years
About 34.9 years
About 139 years
About 41 years
exercises.prompt: About how many years can a 41-bit millisecond timestamp cover?
exercises.refAnchor: d7/批注为什么组合后不重复
exercises.refTitle: Note: Why the Combination Never Repeats

exercises.explanation: The timestamp is milliseconds since a custom epoch; counting about 69.7 years from late 2010 runs out around 2080. If you wrongly count from 1970, you get around 2039.
options: About 2080
About 2039
About 2149
About 2059
exercises.prompt: The chapter counts from Twitter’s epoch (2010-11-04 UTC). Given a 41-bit millisecond span, around which year does the time field run out?

exercises.explanation: 5 bits distinguish only 32 machines. The bits are a fixed 64-bit budget: with one data center, you can give the data center field’s bits to the machine field; for example, 8 bits distinguish 256 machines. Reusing IDs by wrapping around makes machine IDs repeat and collide right away.
options: No change; the 5-bit machine field is enough
Reuse machine IDs by wrapping around after 31
Extend the total ID width to 72 bits
Borrow bits from the data center field for the machine field
exercises.prompt: The business has one data center but needs 200 machines issuing IDs at once. How should the Snowflake fields be adjusted?

exercises.explanation: The total is fixed at 64 bits, so 1 more time bit means 1 fewer machine or sequence bit, which lowers the number of machines you can tell apart or the per-millisecond throughput. You also need to consider parsing and sort compatibility with existing IDs.
exercises.prompt: To make IDs last more years, you can add bits to the timestamp without affecting the other fields.

exercises.explanation: Number is a double-precision float and can’t hold every 64-bit integer, so a large ID may lose its last few digits once parsed. Inside services you can use a 64-bit integer type or BigInt; sending a decimal string externally is the safest.
exercises.prompt: A JavaScript Number can’t represent every 64-bit integer exactly, so JSON APIs often pass such IDs as decimal strings.

lessons.title: Failure Boundaries
lessons.summary: Duplicate machine IDs, sequence overflow, rollback

exercises.explanation: Time, data center, machine, and sequence are all identical, so the formula necessarily produces the same output; this isn’t a rare hash collision. The IP isn’t part of the calculation, and each instance maintains its own sequence, so they don’t stagger.
options: There is a very small chance of collision, which can be ignored
They generate identical IDs: a deterministic duplicate
No duplicates, because the two machines have different IPs
The sequence numbers stagger automatically, so no duplicates
exercises.prompt: Two cloned instances are both configured with dc=3, machine=7, and each issues its first ID in the same millisecond. What happens?

exercises.explanation: Machine IDs only need to be exclusive within one data center; the data center fields differ, so the combinations differ. The real danger is the same dc and machine pair being used by two active instances at once.
exercises.prompt: A machine=7 instance in data center 1 and one in data center 2 issue IDs at the same time, and this causes no ID conflict.

exercises.explanation: Losing contact doesn’t mean it stopped issuing; the old instance may still be issuing IDs to other clients. Use a lease or similar mechanism to revoke its right to issue, or use identities or time ranges that don’t overlap, before reusing the machine ID.
options: Wait for the new instance to finish NTP clock sync first
Confirm the old instance can no longer issue IDs, e.g. its lease expired
A failed ping to the old instance proves it has stopped
The new instance starts its sequence from 0 at startup
exercises.prompt: An old instance lost its network connection, and ops want to give its machine ID to a new instance. What must be true for that to be safe?

exercises.explanation: A 12-bit sequence has only 0…4095, so at most 4096 values per millisecond; the 4097th request must wait for the next millisecond, queue, or be rejected explicitly. Wrapping to 0 duplicates IDs already issued in this millisecond; borrowing other fields or machine IDs may collide with other generators.
options: Wait for the next millisecond, then reset the sequence to 0
Borrow an idle machine ID and keep issuing
Borrow data center bits as extra sequence bits
Wrap the sequence to 0 and keep issuing at 1000ms
exercises.prompt: lastTimestamp=1000ms, and this machine has just issued seq=4095 while the clock still reads 1000ms. How should the next request be handled?

exercises.explanation: NTP only reduces drift; a clock can still move backward because of time adjustments, VM resume, and so on. The code must compare the current time with the last issue time, and on seeing it go backward, wait, reject, or use a deliberately designed logical time.
exercises.prompt: If servers run NTP time sync, the ID generator code no longer needs to detect clock rollback.

exercises.explanation: Waiting, rejecting with an alert, and a deliberately designed logical time all work; logical time drifts from real time and must still handle sequence exhaustion and restart state. Issuing again at 998ms may repeat IDs already issued at 998ms.
options: Keep using 1000ms and increment the unused sequence
Ignore the rollback; NTP will fix it later
Reject issuing and raise an alert on a large rollback
Wait a bounded time to catch up on a small rollback
Reset the sequence to zero and issue at 998ms
exercises.prompt: The last issue time was 1000ms, but the clock rolled back to 998ms. Which responses are acceptable?

exercises.explanation: Comparing time, updating the sequence, and saving state must happen as one synchronized step: first block rollbacks, then update the sequence depending on whether it is the same millisecond, wait for the next millisecond on overflow, and finally record the time and assemble the ID from the fields.
items: Read the current time now
If now < last time, apply the rollback policy
Same ms: sequence +1; new ms: sequence to 0
If the sequence overflows, wait for the next millisecond
Save this time and assemble the ID
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of one ID issue, run under synchronization, in order

exercises.explanation: Both threads may read seq=5 and each add one to get 6; with the same time and machine, they issue the same ID. So incrementing the sequence on one machine must also be synchronized across threads; making machine IDs exclusive only solves the cross-instance part.
options: They get the same sequence number and generate duplicate IDs
The two threads’ timestamps stagger by 1 millisecond automatically
The machine ID field is overwritten by the other thread
Only the ID order is reversed; no duplicates occur
exercises.prompt: In the generator, comparing the time and updating the sequence are not synchronized, and two threads take IDs at the same time. What can happen?

exercises.explanation: Machine clocks always differ a little, so an ID issued earlier by A can be larger than one issued later by B; Snowflake is only roughly ordered by time. Strictly respecting real-time order across nodes needs extra coordination, not local clocks.
exercises.prompt: As long as machine IDs are exclusive and the clock never rolls back, Snowflake guarantees globally strictly increasing IDs across machines.
exercises.refAnchor: d7/批注为什么组合后不重复
exercises.refTitle: Note: Why the Combination Never Repeats

exercises.explanation: A restart wipes the last time and sequence held in memory; if the clock lands in a millisecond that already issued IDs, (time, machine, sequence) coincides with historical IDs. Persist the last issue time and, at startup, wait for the current clock to pass it before issuing.
exercises.prompt: After a generator restarts, if the clock falls back into a millisecond already used, a sequence starting at 0 may repeat historical IDs.

chapters.title: URL Shortener
keyPoints: 100 million a day for 10 years is 365 billion records, about 365 TB at 1 KB each. Average writes are about 1,157/s; reads are about 10 times that.
A 301 lets browsers remember the redirect, cutting load. To count every click, use 302 with cache headers; request count is not click count.
Unique ID + Base62: 7 characters give about 3.5 trillion codes. A unique ID never collides, but short codes from sequential IDs are easy to enumerate.
The first 7 hex characters of a hash give only about 268 million codes, far too few. Hash schemes must handle collisions; a Bloom filter only pre-filters.
Creation relies on a unique constraint for concurrency; redirects check the cache, then the database. Keep the web tier stateless; replicate and shard.
A short code is an address, not a credential. Private content needs auth at the target service; plan for abuse, enumeration, and cache hotspots.

labs.title: Truncated Hash vs. Base62 for Short Codes
301 or 302: How Many Clicks Can the Server Count

lessons.title: Scale Estimation
lessons.summary: Converting records, storage, and QPS

exercises.explanation: `100 million × 365 × 10 = 365 billion`. This number sets how large the short code space must be, and the code length is chosen to cover it. 36.5 billion counts only one year, which is off by a factor of 10.
options: 365 million
365 billion
36.5 trillion
36.5 billion
exercises.prompt: A service generates 100 million short URLs per day. At 365 days a year for 10 years, about how many records is that?
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注把规模换成-crud-能理解的数字

exercises.explanation: 365 TB ÷ 365 billion ≈ 1 KB. This is only a rough size for the mapping record itself; indexes, replication, backups, and database overhead are not counted yet.
options: About 10 KB
About 1 KB
About 100 B
About 1 MB
exercises.prompt: The book estimates that 365 billion records need about 365 TB. What average record size does this imply?
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注把规模换成-crud-能理解的数字

exercises.explanation: 365 TB is only the raw data: 365 billion records × about 1 KB each. Indexes, replication, backups, and database overhead all add to it, so real usage is noticeably larger.
exercises.prompt: The 365 TB estimate already includes the space needed for indexes, replicas, and backups.
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注把规模换成-crud-能理解的数字

exercises.explanation: The record count is the daily volume times days times years; storage multiplies that by the size per record; average write QPS spreads the daily volume over 86,400 seconds; with a 10:1 read-to-write ratio, average redirect QPS is about 10 times the write QPS.
exercises.prompt: Match each estimate with the calculation it comes from
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注把规模换成-crud-能理解的数字

exercises.explanation: Traffic is not evenly spread across the day, so sizing for the average leaves you short at peak. Estimate the average first, then add a peak assumption based on the business.
exercises.prompt: About 1,157 writes per second is only an average, so planning write capacity also needs a separate peak assumption.
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注把规模换成-crud-能理解的数字

exercises.explanation: Redirect requests are about 10 times as frequent as creations, so reads are the main load: the redirect path should check the cache first and query the database only on a miss. A 301 affects whether the browser asks for the redirect again, not how many writes happen.
options: Optimize link creation first, for example with batch writes
Optimize redirect reads first, for example by caching mappings
Reads and writes matter equally, so there is no need to separate the two paths
Always use 301 to reduce the number of writes
exercises.prompt: A read-to-write ratio of about 10:1 means what for the design?

exercises.explanation: The record count scales linearly with the retention period: `100 million × 365 × 5 = 182.5 billion`, and at about 1 KB each that is about 182.5 TB. Every step of an estimate should let you change an input and recompute.
options: About 182.5 TB
About 365 TB
About 73 TB
About 730 TB
exercises.prompt: All else equal, if the retention period drops from 10 years to 5 years, what is the raw storage estimate?
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注把规模换成-crud-能理解的数字

exercises.explanation: The server only looks up the mapping from short code to long URL and returns a redirect, so the browser visits the long URL itself. Hashes are generally not reversible; “mapping back” works through a database lookup.
options: Generate a brand-new short code for this one
Look up the longURL by short code and return a redirect
Fetch the long URL’s page for the browser and return its content
Invert the hash of the short code to compute the long URL
exercises.prompt: For the redirect endpoint `GET api/v1/shortUrl`, what is the server’s core action?

exercises.explanation: n positions with k possible values each give only `k^n` short codes, and that count cannot be smaller than the number of records. 6 Base62 characters give only `62^6 ≈ 56.8 billion`, which is not enough; you need 7 (about 3.5 trillion). So look for the shortest combination of alphabet size and length.
options: Code length affects only looks, not capacity
The shorter the code, the fewer combinations are available
With Base62, a 6-character code can hold 365 billion records
With k symbols per position and n positions, `k^n` must reach at least 365 billion
The larger the alphabet, the more codes a given length can represent
exercises.prompt: A short code should be as short as possible yet cover 365 billion records. Which statements about this trade-off are correct?

lessons.title: Redirects & Stats
lessons.summary: 301/302, caching, and click counting

exercises.explanation: A 301 says the resource has moved permanently, so after caching it the browser goes straight to the long URL and the service skips those requests. The cost is that later clicks cannot be counted; 302 suits cases that need counting.
options: 302: a temporary redirect, so every click comes back to the service
Neither: they differ only in the status code number
Neither: the server should proxy the long URL’s content
301: browsers can cache it, so later requests may skip the service
exercises.prompt: A short URL service does not need click counts and wants to cut redirect load as much as possible. Which redirect fits best?

exercises.explanation: A 302 is not absolutely uncacheable: whether each click reaches the server also depends on cache headers and caching policy. Even if every click does, bots, prefetching, and repeated requests make the request count differ from real clicks.
exercises.prompt: As long as you switch to a 302 redirect, the server’s request count accurately reflects every click.
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注先定统计目标再定状态码
exercises.refTitle: Decide What to Measure, Then the Status Code

exercises.explanation: Bots, prefetching, and repeated requests create requests that match no real click; conversely, a browser-cached 301 lets real clicks produce no request at all. A server-side cache hit or spreading requests over several servers changes nothing: the requests still reach the service, and totaling them leaves the count unchanged.
options: The server checks the cache first and skips the database on a hit
The same user may send repeated requests
Requests are spread across several web servers
Browsers may prefetch links
Preview bots may fetch links
exercises.prompt: Why can’t the server treat the number of redirect requests it receives as the number of user clicks?
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注先定统计目标再定状态码
exercises.refTitle: Decide What to Measure, Then the Status Code

exercises.explanation: A 301 makes the browser treat the redirect as permanent. Once cached, later requests may never reach the service, so it cannot see that the mapping changed. If you need to change targets or count clicks at any time, use 302 with suitable cache headers.
options: Goes straight to the new address: the service tells the browser to update
