Goes to the old address first, then is redirected to the new one
Gets an error: the browser notices the code and long URL no longer match
Still goes to the old address: the browser cached the permanent redirect
exercises.prompt: A short URL has always returned 301, and then operations repoint it to a new long URL. What most likely happens when a user who clicked it before clicks again?

exercises.explanation: Reads dominate writes, so the redirect path checks the cache first and reaches the database only on a miss. The server only returns a redirect; the browser fetches the actual page from the long URL.
items: The user clicks the shortURL
Look up the short code’s long URL in the cache first
On a cache miss, query the database
Return a redirect; the browser visits the longURL
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of one short URL redirect in order

exercises.explanation: Hashes are generally not reversible, and truncating throws away information, so you cannot compute the long URL from the short value. Every hashValue maps back to its longURL because the pair is stored in the database and looked up.
exercises.prompt: A short code maps back to the long URL because the database stores the pair, not because anyone inverts the hash value.
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注映射回去靠数据库不靠逆哈希
exercises.refTitle: The Mapping Comes from the Database, Not an “Inverse Hash”

exercises.explanation: Uniqueness requires that one short code maps to only one long URL; it does not forbid one long URL having several short codes. Checking whether the long URL already exists and reusing its code is just one policy; if different users need separate stats, issue each one a code.
options: Yes: a hash function gives the same output for the same input
Not necessarily: it is a product decision, and each can get their own code
Yes: otherwise it breaks “a short URL must be unique”
Never: the same code would cause a hash collision
exercises.prompt: Two users shorten the same long URL separately. Must the system return the same short code to both?
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注映射回去靠数据库不靠逆哈希
exercises.refTitle: The Mapping Comes from the Database, Not an “Inverse Hash”

exercises.explanation: A 302 is a temporary redirect and suits counting, but it does not absolutely forbid caching either; cache headers decide whether browsers and intermediate caches come back to the server each time. Changing only the status code and ignoring cache headers can still miss clicks.
exercises.prompt: Complete the approach for counting clicks one by one
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注先定统计目标再定状态码
exercises.refTitle: Decide What to Measure, Then the Status Code
exercises.text: To observe every redirect request, the status code is usually [[302]], together with correct [[cache headers]].

exercises.explanation: Creation is a low-frequency write that must produce a unique code, backed by a unique constraint; redirection is a high-frequency read that checks the cache first and queries the database on a miss. Both paths use one mapping table; they are designed separately because their concerns and scaling differ, not their HTTP methods.
options: They use different HTTP methods, so they must be separate services
The two paths access different tables
Creation goes through the cache; redirects must hit the database directly
Creation must guarantee unique codes; read-heavy redirects must check the cache first
exercises.prompt: Why design “create a short URL” and “redirect” as two different paths?
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注最短面试回答模板
exercises.refTitle: A Short Template for the Interview Answer

lessons.title: Short Codes
lessons.summary: Base62, truncated hashes, collisions, enumeration

exercises.explanation: 10 digits plus 52 upper- and lowercase letters make 62 symbols, and `62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208`, about 3.5 trillion, which covers 365 billion records. Digits plus lowercase letters only give 36^7, about 78.4 billion, which is not enough.
options: 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion
36^7 ≈ 78.4 billion
10^7 = 10 million
16^7 ≈ 268 million
exercises.prompt: Encoding with `[0-9, a-z, A-Z]`, how many values can a 7-character short code represent at most?

exercises.explanation: Each hex position has only 16 values, so `16^7 ≈ 268 million`, less than a thousandth of 365 billion; codes run out long before the table fills. The 3.5 trillion figure is the 7-character Base62 space, and a truncated hash will certainly collide.
options: There is enough space; it is just slower to compute than Base62
There are only about 268 million codes, far fewer than 365 billion records
There are about 3.5 trillion codes, enough but with occasional collisions
No collisions, because MD5 gives different outputs for different inputs
exercises.prompt: You take the first 7 characters of an MD5 hex digest as the short code. What happens at this problem’s scale?
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注截取十六进制前-7-位空间不够
exercises.refTitle: Truncating to 7 Hex Characters Is Not Enough Space

exercises.explanation: A collision depends on any two records colliding, and the number of pairs grows with the square of the record count. In a space of about 268 million, the collision probability is already past one half at roughly 20,000 records, long before the space fills up.
exercises.prompt: In the space of 7 truncated hex characters, the birthday problem says the chance of a collision passes 50% after about 20,000 records.
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注截取十六进制前-7-位空间不够
exercises.refTitle: Truncating to 7 Hex Characters Is Not Enough Space

exercises.explanation: `62^7` is about 2^41.7, so you need at least 42 bits of hash information converted to Base62 to fill 7 characters. 9 hex characters give only about 68.7 billion and are longer; changing the hash function or hashing again cannot change the size of the 16^7 space.
options: Run MD5 again on the first 7 hex characters
Take the first 9 hex characters for a larger space
Swap MD5 for SHA-1 and still take the first 7 hex characters
Take at least 42 bits of the hash, convert to Base62, and keep 7 characters
exercises.prompt: If you insist on hashing yet want a 7-character code space of about 3.5 trillion, how should you derive the code?
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注截取十六进制前-7-位空间不够
exercises.refTitle: Truncating to 7 Hex Characters Is Not Enough Space

exercises.explanation: 365 billion is about 10% of a 3.5 trillion space, so each randomly drawn code has roughly a one-in-ten chance of hitting an occupied one, and new writes keep colliding and retrying. Concurrent writes still need a unique constraint as the backstop.
exercises.prompt: Once the space reaches about 3.5 trillion, new writes almost never collide even after 365 billion records are stored.
exercises.refAnchor: d8/批注截取十六进制前-7-位空间不够
exercises.refTitle: Truncating to 7 Hex Characters Is Not Enough Space

exercises.explanation: Both generation schemes have a cost: Base62 depends on an ID generator, and hashing must handle collisions. A Bloom filter can only confirm “definitely not present”; “maybe present” still needs an exact lookup. What truly guarantees uniqueness is an atomic mechanism such as a database unique constraint.
pairs: Needs a unique ID; a unique ID never collides
Fixed length, but must handle collisions
Quickly rules out codes that are definitely free
exercises.prompt: Match each approach or component with its role in short code generation

exercises.explanation: Two requests may both see “absent” at the same time and then each write the same short code. Concurrent creation needs an atomic backstop such as a unique constraint; a Bloom filter is only a sieve that speeds up existence checks.
exercises.prompt: Once a Bloom filter says a candidate short code is “definitely absent”, you can write it directly without relying on a database unique constraint.
exercises.refTitle: A Bloom Filter Only Helps Filter

exercises.explanation: With sequential IDs, one short code lets you work out the codes before and after it, so they can be enumerated in bulk. Unique IDs encoded correctly never collide; the length grows with the ID, and you can pad with zeros for a fixed width.
options: Different IDs may encode to the same short code
A short code cannot be decoded back to the original ID
The code length cannot be controlled at all
Adjacent codes are easy to predict and can be enumerated
exercises.prompt: You generate short codes by encoding an auto-increment ID as Base62. What is the main new risk?

exercises.explanation: Check for duplicates first to decide whether to reuse an existing code; then issue an ID, encode it, and write it to the database. A unique ID guarantees a unique short code, and the database unique index remains the last line of defense for concurrent creation.
items: Check whether the longURL already exists
If not, get an ID from the distributed ID generator
Convert the ID to a Base62 short code
Save the id, shortURL, and longURL mapping
exercises.prompt: Put the “unique ID + Base62” link-creation flow in order

exercises.explanation: Base62 just writes the same number in a different base, so it can be undone one-to-one, and distinct IDs give distinct codes. A hash squeezes arbitrarily long input into a limited space, and truncating it makes collisions even more likely.
exercises.prompt: Complete the essential difference between the two code schemes
exercises.text: Base62 is an [[encoding]], so a unique ID gives a unique short code; a truncated hash value can [[collide]], so you must detect and retry.

lessons.title: Scaling and Risks
lessons.summary: Rate limits, hot keys, tiers, auth boundaries

exercises.explanation: The code space can be enumerated and links leak when forwarded, and a short URL service does not manage permissions. Private content must be protected by auth at the target service; longer codes or a different generator only make guessing harder, which is not authorization.
options: A short code is only an address; private content still needs auth at the target service
It should switch to 301 so browsers remember the access permission
The code is too short; making it 10 characters would make it safe
Generating codes with MD5 instead would make them unguessable
exercises.prompt: A team treats the short URL of a private document as an access credential: anyone who knows the code can view the document. What is wrong with that?

exercises.explanation: A stateless web tier lets you simply add machines, the cache absorbs most redirect reads, and the database scales by replication and sharding. The book deliberately stores the mappings in a relational database; hashes are not reversible, so a redirect can only look up the mapping.
options: Keep mappings only in memory, never in the database
Recompute the hash on every redirect to find the long URL
Keep the web tier stateless and add or remove servers with load
Replicate and shard the database
Check the cache first on redirects, then the database on a miss
exercises.prompt: For read-heavy redirect traffic, which scaling approaches make sense?

exercises.explanation: Rate limiting caps the request rate per IP or similar dimension, which blocks the abuse directly. The long URLs are all different, so duplicate checks and reuse do not stop it; a cache speeds up redirect reads; and code length does not affect creation frequency.
options: Lengthen the short code to 10 characters
Rate limit by IP and similar dimensions
Check whether the longURL already exists before creating
Add a cache layer to the redirect path
exercises.prompt: Someone uses a script to call the create endpoint, submitting huge numbers of distinct long URLs to mass-produce short links. What is the most direct defense?

exercises.explanation: Start small: make uniqueness and correctness hold first, then add components where the real bottleneck is. A cache exists for redirect reads; adding it before the pressure appears just means one more component to maintain.
exercises.prompt: A first version can use just a relational database with a unique index, and add a cache once redirect reads are actually what strain the database.

exercises.explanation: Reads concentrated on one key are a cache hotspot, and you must keep it from overwhelming a single cache node or falling through to the database. Going viral brings reads, not writes; ID issuing and code length only matter for creation.
options: Write overload on the database shard holding that code
Base62 length overflow, running out of short codes
The ID generator running out of sequence numbers within one millisecond
A cache hotspot: reads concentrate on a single key
exercises.prompt: One short URL suddenly goes viral and redirect requests pile onto a single code. Which failure mode needs the most attention?

exercises.explanation: It is the opposite: a stateless web tier, where any server can handle any request, is what lets you add or remove servers freely. Data that must be shared belongs in storage tiers such as the database and cache.
exercises.prompt: The web tier should keep each user’s session state, which makes it easier to scale by adding or removing servers.

exercises.explanation: Rate limiting slows enumeration, unpredictable codes make neighboring guesses useless, and auth at the target service means a leaked link still cannot show private content. Enumeration requests ask for new codes, so both 301 and 302 reach the service first; a cache only speeds up redirects and cannot stop enumeration.
options: Cache the redirect path to raise the hit rate
Switch to 302 so every redirect comes back to the service
Make short codes unpredictable so neighbors cannot be guessed
Have the target service authenticate private content
Rate limit by IP and similar dimensions to slow enumeration
exercises.prompt: Someone enumerates Base62 short codes in sequence to bulk-scrape other people’s links. Which measures reduce this risk?

exercises.explanation: Statelessness lets the load balancer send a request to any web server; replication shares reads and adds fault tolerance, and sharding spreads the 365 billion mappings across many databases.
exercises.prompt: Complete how each tier scales
exercises.text: Keep the web tier [[stateless]] so you can add or remove servers directly; the database tier scales through replication and [[sharding]].

exercises.explanation: High availability comes from database replication and fault-tolerant design: a replica takes over from the failed node, and popular mappings in the cache keep being served. Adding web servers cannot fix a database outage; a Bloom filter and rate limiting only reduce load, and data on the failed node still cannot be read.
options: Adding web servers to share the redirect requests
Database replication, so a replica takes over on failure
Rate limiting, to reduce requests that hit the database
A Bloom filter that blocks nonexistent short codes
exercises.prompt: A database node goes down. What mainly keeps short URL redirects working with as little interruption as possible?

exercises.explanation: Analysis cares about click-through rate, source, timestamps, and other user behavior; filter out the noise from bots and prefetches, and remember that once a 301 is cached, some clicks never reach the server at all. Database QPS, cache hit rate, and creation details say nothing about click behavior.
options: Periodically crawled and stored page content of the long URLs
Database queries per second and the cache hit rate
Click time, source, and similar data, with bots and prefetches filtered out
The creation time, creator, and long URL of each short code
exercises.prompt: To evaluate how well short URL campaigns perform, what data is worth collecting on the redirect path?

chapters.title: Web Crawler
keyPoints: A crawler is a loop: the Frontier hands out a URL, then download and parse, content dedup, extract links, filter and URL dedup, and back to the Frontier.
URL dedup saves repeat downloads; content dedup saves repeat storage. If recrawling is allowed, the “seen” record must carry the last fetch time.
Front queues handle priority; back queues handle politeness per host. Even top priority can’t skip a site’s rate limit.
Use BFS rather than DFS to avoid sinking into very deep branches, but BFS ignores importance, so layer priority and freshness on top.
Crawler traps need a combination of crawl budgets, depth limits, parameter normalization, and per-site quotas, not just a URL length cap.
Judge a crawler by useful new-content throughput, error rate, and load on sites; more threads don’t mean more pages fetched.

labs.title: The URL Frontier Decides What to Crawl, When, and What to Skip

lessons.title: Requirements
lessons.summary: Crawler uses, design challenges, and scale

exercises.explanation: A month is about 30×24×3600 ≈ 2.6 million seconds, and 1 billion ÷ 2.6 million ≈ 385, which rounds to about 400 pages/s. The 800 QPS in the requirements is the peak, not the average.
options: About 4,000 pages/s
About 40 pages/s
About 400 pages/s
About 800 pages/s
exercises.prompt: The requirement is to crawl 1 billion web pages per month. Assuming a 30-day month, roughly what is the average download rate?

exercises.explanation: An average hides the peaks. The stated peak is about 800 QPS, 2 times the average. Sizing for the average means crawling can’t keep up at peak, the Frontier backs up, recrawls slip, and there is no headroom for failure retries.
exercises.prompt: The average is about 400 pages/s, so a download cluster sized for 400 pages/s is enough.

exercises.explanation: 1 billion × 500 KB = 500 TB per month, and × 12 × 5 gives about 30 PB. Without stating the average page size, this number means nothing.
exercises.prompt: Complete the two assumptions in the storage estimate
exercises.refAnchor: d9/批注估算必须说明平均页面大小
exercises.refTitle: Estimates Need an Average Page Size
exercises.text: If each page is about [[500 KB]], then 1 billion pages × 12 months × [[5 years]] ≈ 30 PB.

exercises.explanation: Storage scales with average page size: 100 KB is 1/5 of 500 KB, so 30 PB ÷ 5 = 6 PB. This is still only the raw page volume; replicas and indexes are counted separately.
options: About 6 PB
About 600 TB
About 30 PB
About 150 PB
exercises.prompt: Keep the 30 PB estimate. If pages average only 100 KB after compression and all other assumptions stay the same, about how much raw storage is needed over 5 years?
exercises.refAnchor: d9/批注估算必须说明平均页面大小
exercises.refTitle: Estimates Need an Average Page Size

exercises.explanation: The 30 PB figure excludes replication and indexing. With 3 replicas, for example, the disk need approaches 90 PB, so state what the number covers whenever you quote it.
exercises.prompt: 30 PB is only the size of the raw pages; replication and indexing must be counted separately.
exercises.refAnchor: d9/批注估算必须说明平均页面大小
exercises.refTitle: Estimates Need an Average Page Size

exercises.explanation: Compression, actual page size, duplication rate, and recrawl policy all change the result, because they decide how many bytes you store. Thread count and DNS cache only affect how fast you crawl, not how much data must be kept.
options: The share of duplicate content
The number of download worker threads
Whether pages are stored compressed
The recrawl policy (how many versions of a page are kept)
The DNS cache hit rate
exercises.prompt: Which factors would noticeably change the “about 30 PB over 5 years” storage estimate?
exercises.refAnchor: d9/批注估算必须说明平均页面大小
exercises.refTitle: Estimates Need an Average Page Size

exercises.explanation: Scalability is a problem of size, while extensibility is about adding features, so they are easy to mix up. Robustness is about bad input and failures; politeness is about the impact on other people’s websites.
pairs: Processing billions of pages in parallel
Surviving bad HTML, crashes, and malicious links
Not overwhelming target sites with requests
Supporting new content types with few changes
exercises.prompt: Match each design challenge to the problem it addresses

exercises.explanation: Web archiving preserves pages for future viewing, as in the US Library of Congress’s archiving work. Search indexing serves retrieval of current content, mining extracts knowledge from pages, and monitoring detects problems such as copyright infringement.
options: Search engine indexing
Web archiving
Web mining
Web monitoring
exercises.prompt: An organization wants to periodically save government web pages so they can still see how the pages looked ten years later. What kind of crawler application is this?

exercises.explanation: Extensibility means new content types plug in as independent modules, such as a PNG downloader or a web monitor, while the main crawl loop stays unchanged. “HTML only” is a scope constraint, not an architectural limit.
exercises.prompt: To crawl images later, you can add a separate download module without changing the main collection flow.

lessons.title: The Crawl Loop
lessons.summary: How components form a loop, and why two dedups

exercises.explanation: Download first, then parse, then check whether the content is a duplicate; only new content is worth extracting links from. Links go back to the Frontier only after filtering and URL dedup, which closes the loop.
items: Seed URLs are put into the Frontier
The downloader takes a URL, resolves DNS, and downloads
The parser validates and parses the page
Content dedup: check whether the page has been seen
Extract links from new content and filter them
URLs not seen before go back into the Frontier
exercises.prompt: Put in order how a URL is processed, from entering the system to producing new URLs

exercises.explanation: The two “seen” checks are the easiest to mix up: URL-seen looks at the address and blocks before download; content-seen looks at the page hash and blocks after download. The filter excludes blacklisted and bad URLs by rule, whether or not they were seen.
pairs: Resolves host names to IP addresses
Records visited URLs to avoid recrawling
Compares page hashes to spot duplicate content
exercises.prompt: Match each component to its responsibility

exercises.explanation: Tracking parameters and mirror sites give different addresses with identical content; URL dedup can’t see that, but page hashes can. One URL linked from many places is a single address that URL dedup blocks. Pagination is different content, and an updated URL is a recrawl question.
options: The URLs carry different tracking parameters
The same URL is updated with new content the next day
The same URL appears in links on two different pages
A mirror site copies the same content
A long article is split into page 1 and page 2 with two URLs
exercises.prompt: In which cases do two different URLs return the same page?
exercises.refAnchor: d9/批注为什么需要两道去重

exercises.explanation: URL dedup looks only at the address. Once it is sealed off permanently, the URL is never downloaded again and every update is missed. When recrawling is allowed, the seen record must store the last fetch time and release the URL again when its freshness interval expires.
options: Nothing, because BFS will visit it again
Content dedup will automatically fetch the updates
Later updates will never be fetched
The URL filter will let it through again
exercises.prompt: A news homepage keeps the same URL, but its content changes every hour. What happens if the URL-seen record marks it as “crawled” forever?
exercises.refAnchor: d9/批注为什么需要两道去重

exercises.explanation: Computing the page hash requires downloading the page first. So saving downloads is the job of URL dedup (blocking before enqueue), while content dedup stops repeated storage, repeated link extraction, and other follow-up work.
exercises.prompt: Content dedup happens after download, so it can’t save this download’s traffic; what it saves is repeated storage and later processing.
exercises.refAnchor: d9/批注为什么需要两道去重

exercises.explanation: Identical content has an identical hash, so duplicates can be spotted across URLs. If URL-seen only records whether a URL was seen, it seals the URL off forever; storing the last fetch time lets you tell when a recrawl is due.
exercises.prompt: Complete what each of the two dedups depends on
exercises.refAnchor: d9/批注为什么需要两道去重
exercises.text: Content dedup compares the page’s [[hash]]; if recrawling is allowed, the URL-seen record must also store the [[last fetch time]].

exercises.explanation: Seeds are the starting points of the traversal and should reach as many sites as possible through links. Organizing them by region or topic (such as popular local sites, sports, or health) gives more balanced coverage. A single portal or random picks leave large blind spots.
options: Use only the single biggest portal as the sole seed
Pick only the most frequently updated news pages, for freshness
Pick link-rich entry sites by region or topic
Pick any batch of pages, as long as there are enough
exercises.prompt: When choosing seed URLs, which approach is most sensible?

exercises.explanation: Same content means same links, and they were already extracted the first time this content was processed. The branch for duplicate content can simply end, which is exactly the follow-up work content dedup saves.
exercises.prompt: When content dedup finds a duplicate page, it should still extract the page’s links so no new URLs are missed.

exercises.explanation: If an already-crawled address is blocked before enqueue, it never occupies the Frontier, DNS resolution, download, or parsing. The later you block it, the more cost you waste.
options: When a URL is taken from the Frontier and given to the downloader
After the page is downloaded and its hash is computed
Before a new URL enters the Frontier
After DNS resolution, before the download starts
exercises.prompt: At which step is the “has this URL been seen” check cheapest?

lessons.title: Scheduling
lessons.summary: BFS, politeness, priority, and freshness together

exercises.explanation: Page links can keep going down forever, and DFS sinks deeper and deeper into one branch. BFS advances level by level and is more balanced, but it ignores importance and won’t deduplicate for you; DFS with a visited record can also handle cyclic graphs.
options: Link chains can be extremely deep, so DFS can get stuck in one branch
BFS goes level by level, so it automatically crawls important pages first
BFS never revisits a page, so no dedup is needed
DFS can’t traverse a link graph that contains cycles
exercises.prompt: Viewing the web as a directed graph, why does a crawler usually use BFS rather than DFS?

exercises.explanation: Standard BFS queues URLs only in discovery order and doesn’t distinguish quality or importance. That is why the Frontier also ranks URLs by signals such as PageRank, page importance, and update frequency.
exercises.prompt: Standard BFS traverses level by level, which already lets important pages be crawled first.

exercises.explanation: Priority decides “who goes first”; politeness decides “when it may be fetched”. A host normally gets only one request at a time, with a gap between downloads, and top priority can’t skip the target site’s rate limit.
exercises.prompt: Even if all 1,000 URLs of a site have top priority, they must still be downloaded one at a time under that host’s rate limit.
exercises.refAnchor: d9/批注调度器像医院挂号处
exercises.refTitle: The Scheduler as a Hospital Front Desk

exercises.explanation: Front queues handle priority and back queues handle politeness: URLs are first picked by importance, then queued by host in their own back queues for download. The mapping table makes sure URLs from one host always go to the same queue.
pairs: One per priority; high ones picked more often
Each holds URLs from one host only
Records which back queue each host uses
Downloads one host’s pages in order, with a gap
exercises.prompt: Match each Frontier part to its role

exercises.explanation: Weights make high-priority queues more likely to be picked without starving low-priority ones; if it always took the top queue, other pages would never get a turn while important URLs keep arriving. Politeness is handled per host by the back queues, not by random selection in the front queues.
options: To favor important pages without starving low-priority queues
To cut the cost of the Prioritizer re-sorting repeatedly
To spread out requests to one host and enforce rate limits
To give every queue the same chance of being picked, for fairness
exercises.prompt: Why does the front-queue selector use weighted random choice instead of always taking the highest-priority queue?

exercises.explanation: Politeness means not overwhelming the target site: only one request to a host is in flight at a time, and a gap is left between downloads. A timeout limits how long a single request waits, not the gap between downloads.
exercises.prompt: Complete the two politeness scheduling rules
exercises.text: A host normally gets only [[one]] request at a time, with a [[delay]] between downloads.

exercises.explanation: Freshness sets recrawl timing from a page’s update history and importance: a news homepage updated hourly needs frequent visits, while a page unchanged for years is revisited rarely. A uniform schedule wastes crawl capacity and still misses updates.
exercises.prompt: A freshness policy should recrawl all pages on the same schedule, which is the fairest and most economical.

exercises.explanation: Retrying immediately or adding concurrency adds pressure while the site is struggling and causes a retry storm. Backing off, recording the next allowed time, and a shorter timeout protect the site and keep workers from being held up by a slow one.
options: Add more concurrent connections to the host to finish sooner
Back off for a while, then retry
Immediately put the failed URL back at the head of the queue
Record the next time the host may be crawled
Use a shorter timeout so a slow site doesn’t hold a worker for long
exercises.prompt: A host has been timing out frequently. Which responses are sensible?
exercises.refAnchor: d9/批注调度器像医院挂号处
exercises.refTitle: The Scheduler as a Hospital Front Desk

lessons.title: Robust Downloading
lessons.summary: Download tuning, fault tolerance, traps, scale-out

exercises.explanation: A DNS cache skips repeated resolution, geographic proximity shortens network round trips, and a short timeout keeps slow sites from holding resources. Content dedup happens after the download, and robots.txt is a crawling rule, not a speedup.
options: Obeying robots.txt
A DNS cache
Placing download servers close to target sites
Content dedup
Setting a shorter timeout
exercises.prompt: Which practices directly reduce the HTML downloader’s waiting on the network?

exercises.explanation: The value of consistent hashing is that adding or removing a node moves only a few mappings, while the other hosts stay with their original servers. It doesn’t guarantee perfect balance or remove hotspots, and spreading one host across servers would break politeness.
options: Every server ends up with exactly the same load
One host can be spread across several servers and crawled in parallel
Hotspots caused by popular sites are removed automatically
Only a small fraction of hosts have to move to the new server
exercises.prompt: You grow the download servers from 10 to 11 and use consistent hashing to assign hosts to servers. What is the benefit?

exercises.explanation: A trap such as an infinite calendar can have short URLs and still never end. A length limit is only one rule; you also need a crawl budget, a depth limit, parameter normalization, and per-site quotas.
exercises.prompt: Capping the maximum URL length is enough to stop crawler traps.
exercises.refAnchor: d9/批注规则不能只靠一条长度限制
exercises.refTitle: A Length Limit Alone Is Not Enough

exercises.explanation: Depth limits and per-site budgets put a cap on endless paths. Parameter normalization needs care: some parameters really do change the page, so stripping them all would hurt normal pages. More workers just fall into the trap faster.
options: Set a crawl budget or quota for each site
Strip all URL parameters before dedup, no exceptions
Add more download workers
Limit the crawl depth
exercises.prompt: Which measures are sensible against crawler traps such as an “infinite calendar”?
exercises.refAnchor: d9/批注规则不能只靠一条长度限制
exercises.refTitle: A Length Limit Alone Is Not Enough

exercises.explanation: An exact hash only recognizes identical content; a one-byte difference gives a different hash. The URLs differ, so URL dedup can’t block it either. Catching near-duplicates like this needs other techniques, which is a known limit of exact hashing.
options: URL dedup blocks the second copy first
The hashes match, so the second copy is dropped
The parser drops it as a malformed page
The hashes differ, so both are stored as new content
exercises.prompt: Two different URLs have the same page body except for one line of advertising. What happens with content dedup based on an exact hash?
exercises.refAnchor: d9/批注规则不能只靠一条长度限制
exercises.refTitle: A Length Limit Alone Is Not Enough

exercises.explanation: Workers must be stateless so you can add or remove them freely. But which URLs are pending and which have been seen is global state; if it lives only in one machine’s memory, scaling out or a crash causes repeated or missed crawling.
exercises.prompt: When scaling out horizontally, crawl workers can be stateless, but the Frontier and the dedup state still need to be shared or persisted.

exercises.explanation: The content is generated only after a browser runs the script, so the raw HTML the server returns is an empty shell, and no amount of waiting will produce it. The chapter lists this item as server-side rendering; what actually needs solving is crawling with browser rendering or another approach that suits the site.
options: The HTML lacks the content, so you need browser rendering or a similar approach
The server waits for the script to finish and returns the complete HTML
robots.txt usually forbids crawling such pages
A longer timeout is enough to wait for the content to load
exercises.prompt: A site’s main content only appears after JavaScript loads it. What happens if you download only the raw HTML?

exercises.explanation: A single host is limited by politeness, so extra threads just queue up, and duplicate pages, errors, and traps aren’t useful output either. Judge a crawler by useful new-content throughput, error rate, and load on sites, not by thread count alone.
exercises.prompt: Doubling the number of download threads also doubles the useful crawl throughput.

exercises.explanation: Error handling and data validation belong to robustness: bad pages and crashes must not drag down the whole system. An independent new module shows extensibility, and obeying robots.txt is the downloader’s basic courtesy to a site.
pairs: Isolates faults so the system doesn’t crash
Ensures the crawled content is complete
Adds a content type without changing the loop
Follows the crawling rules a site publishes
exercises.prompt: Match each measure to its purpose

chapters.title: Notification System
keyPoints: Ask about channels, platforms, daily volume, timeliness, and opt-out first: say 10 million push, 1 million SMS, and 5 million email per day.
Persist and enqueue business events; per-channel workers call the third parties. Separate queues keep one provider’s outage from hurting other channels.
A queue smooths short spikes but doesn’t raise a third party’s long-term capacity; for a lasting backlog, check channel quota, worker throughput, expiry.
A third-party timeout means “state unknown”; retry with an atomic claim and a stable idempotency key: promise at-least-once plus dedup, not exactly-once.
“Accepted,” “delivered,” and “opened” are different states; expired verification codes need no resend, and opt-outs are checked before sending.

lessons.title: Needs and Channels
lessons.summary: Channels, scale, timeliness, and contact info

exercises.explanation: Push goes through the platform’s official channel: Apple’s APNS for iOS, Firebase’s FCM for Android. SMS and email are handed to third-party providers. The source notes these are only example implementations; the real choice depends on your platform.
exercises.prompt: Match each notification type to the delivery channel the source gives as an example

exercises.explanation: 16 million ÷ 86,400 seconds ≈ 185 per second. The average isn’t large; the hard parts are traffic spikes, slow third-party responses, and retries after failures, which is why a queue comes next.
options: About 1,850 per second
About 185 per second
About 16,000 per second
About 20 per second
exercises.prompt: Push, SMS, and email add up to about 16 million messages a day. Roughly how many per second is that on average?

exercises.explanation: This contact info is collected at app install or sign-up and stored: device tokens in the Device Tokens table, phone numbers and email addresses in the User table. An IP address changes and can’t locate a user; an event ID is the identifier used for deduplication.
exercises.prompt: Fill in the contact info each channel needs in order to send
exercises.text: Push needs a [[device token]], SMS needs a phone number, and email needs an [[email address]].

exercises.explanation: Soft real-time means “as fast as possible,” and being slow once in a while is acceptable; only in hard real-time does a missed deadline count as a system failure. So a notification system focuses on low latency and reliability, not on a hard deadline for every message.
exercises.prompt: Soft real-time tolerates occasional delays: arriving late now and then is not a system failure, unlike hard real-time.
exercises.refAnchor: d10/批注软实时不等于永远立即到达
exercises.refTitle: Soft Real-Time Is Not Always Instant

exercises.explanation: Verification codes have a validity period. Sending an expired one only annoys the user, wastes quota, and delays the new codes behind it. Define a validity period per notification type and discard whatever has expired: that is the right trade-off under soft real-time.
options: Drop the expired codes and don’t resend them
Resend the backlogged codes first, then handle new requests
Resend the backlogged codes by email instead
Resend all of them in order so none is lost
exercises.prompt: The SMS provider was down for 2 hours and has just recovered. The queue holds a backlog of login verification codes. What is the most sensible handling?
exercises.refAnchor: d10/批注软实时不等于永远立即到达
exercises.refTitle: Soft Real-Time Is Not Always Instant

exercises.explanation: The device token is collected at install or sign-up and stored in the Device Tokens table, ready to use when sending; asking for it at send time would be far too late. The push platform handles delivery, but your backend must supply the token that says whom to push to.
options: Only APNS/FCM keep it; your backend doesn’t need to
Requested from the user just before each send
Kept only on the client; the server doesn’t store it
Collected at install or sign-up and stored in the device token table
exercises.prompt: The device token needed for push: when is it usually collected, and where is it stored?

exercises.explanation: Opt-out is part of the requirements: the notification settings table records each user’s opt-in/opt-out per channel, and it must be checked before sending. Sending anyway annoys the user and burns third-party quota for nothing.
exercises.prompt: When a user turns off a type of notification, it is only a front-end display issue, so the server can keep sending as usual.

exercises.explanation: A bill reminder is triggered in batches by a scheduled job such as cron, according to the date and regardless of what any user is doing right now. The other three are all caused by a user’s action, so they are client-triggered.
options: A user taps “Resend verification code”
A user likes a friend’s post in the app, and the friend is notified
A bill reminder is sent automatically on the 1st of every month
A user gets a welcome email after signing up
exercises.prompt: The requirements say notifications can be triggered by “client actions” or by “server-side scheduled jobs.” Which one is triggered by a server-side scheduled job?

lessons.title: From Sync to Queue
lessons.summary: Problems in the first design and decoupling

exercises.explanation: The trigger service only says “time to send”; the notification server validates and prepares the content; the queue buffers; workers talk to each channel; and the third party does the final delivery. Each stage can scale independently.
pairs: Emits events: bill reminders, shipping updates
Exposes the API; validates, fetches render data
Pulls events and calls the matching third party
Actually delivers the notification to the device
exercises.prompt: Match each role in the notification pipeline to its responsibility

exercises.explanation: The key change is in the middle: once the notification server has validated the request, it puts the event on the queue, and the slow, failure-prone work of calling the third party is left to workers, asynchronously.
items: Trigger service calls the notification API
Notification server validates it and fetches metadata
Notification event is put on the message queue
Worker takes the event and calls the third party
Third party delivers the notification to the user
exercises.prompt: Put the steps a notification takes through the improved architecture in order

exercises.explanation: Moving storage out removes coupling, multiple servers remove the single point, and the queue decouples and buffers. A shared worker would let one failing channel drag down all the others, and waiting synchronously on the third party was the original design’s bottleneck.
options: All channels share one worker to simplify deployment
Moved the database and cache out of the notification server
Notification server waits for the third party’s reply before responding
Deployed multiple notification servers to scale horizontally
Added a message queue to decouple and buffer notifications
exercises.prompt: Compared with the original single-server synchronous design, what did the improved design change?

exercises.explanation: This is a single point of failure (SPOF): when the only server dies, the whole pipeline stops, and the database becomes unavailable with it. The improved design scales the notification servers horizontally and moves the database and cache out to scale on their own.
options: Notifications on every channel stop going out
The third-party services automatically take over sending
The database holds requests and resends them automatically later
Only push is affected; SMS and email carry on
exercises.prompt: The first design has one notification server hosting the database, cache, and sending logic. What happens when it goes down?

exercises.explanation: The business service hands the “parcel” to a reliable shipping dock and leaves, rather than waiting for the courier to deliver it. The third party itself isn’t any faster; slowness and failures are absorbed by workers asynchronously.
options: The notification server no longer validates requests
The queue makes the third party send faster
It can return once the event is enqueued, without waiting for delivery
The queue merges duplicate notifications, so fewer are sent
exercises.prompt: Why does the trigger service’s call to the notification API return faster once a message queue is added?
exercises.refAnchor: d10/批注队列像快递站的待发货区
exercises.refTitle: The Queue as a Shipping Dock

exercises.explanation: Extra notifications during a spike wait in the queue and drain slowly in the quiet periods. But if they arrive faster than the third party can handle for a long time, the backlog just keeps growing.
exercises.prompt: Fill in the limits of what a message queue can do
exercises.refAnchor: d10/批注队列像快递站的待发货区
exercises.refTitle: The Queue as a Shipping Dock
exercises.text: A queue can smooth out short-term [[spikes]], but it does not raise the third party’s long-term [[processing capacity]].

exercises.explanation: A steadily growing backlog means consumers can’t keep up, usually due to channel quota or worker throughput. Extra notification servers and faster templates sit upstream of the queue and only speed up enqueuing; a bigger queue just stores the backlog longer. Discard expired notifications so they don’t hold quota.
options: Template rendering time; optimize the templates first
The queue’s capacity limit; raise it so the backlog can’t overflow
The SMS channel quota, worker throughput, and expiry policy
The number of notification servers; add a few first
exercises.prompt: The SMS queue’s backlog has kept growing for several hours. What should you check first?
exercises.refAnchor: d10/批注队列像快递站的待发货区
exercises.refTitle: The Queue as a Shipping Dock

exercises.explanation: The average hides spikes and third-party jitter. The queue’s value is decoupling and buffering: when traffic bursts or the third party slows down or fails, notifications aren’t lost and the business service isn’t held up.
exercises.prompt: 16 million notifications a day is under 200 per second on average, so there is no need for a message queue.

exercises.explanation: Per-channel queues confine a failure to one pipeline, while push and email keep being consumed as usual. If all channels shared one queue, stuck SMS tasks would slow the other channels down.
exercises.prompt: If iOS, Android, SMS, and email each have their own queue and worker, an SMS provider outage backs up only the SMS pipeline.

lessons.title: Reliable Delivery
lessons.summary: Notification log, retries, idempotent dedup

exercises.explanation: A timeout only means no reply arrived. The third party may have accepted and sent the message while the response was lost on the network, and blindly resending would then create a duplicate. That is why retries rely on an idempotency key and state records.
options: It definitely wasn’t sent, so it’s safe to resend
It was definitely delivered, so mark it successful
Its state is unknown; the third party may already have sent it
The user definitely hasn’t seen it, so resend on another channel
exercises.prompt: A worker’s call to the SMS service timed out with no response at all. What is the right conclusion about that message?
exercises.refAnchor: d10/批注为什么简单先查后发不够

exercises.explanation: A notification is persisted before it is sent, and the log records which state each one is in; after a crash or a third-party failure it supports retries and troubleshooting, and the data doesn’t vanish with memory. Open rates, templates, and opt-outs each have their own components.
options: Record each notification’s state, for retries and troubleshooting
Store notification templates to standardize formats
Store users’ opt-out settings for each channel
Track users’ open and click rates
exercises.prompt: What is the main role of the notification log database in a reliable design?

exercises.explanation: The idempotency key must be stable: every retry of the same event carries the same key, which is how the third party recognizes “already handled.” With a new key each time, it sees a brand-new notification.
exercises.prompt: If each retry uses a new idempotency key, the third party can recognize the request as a duplicate.
exercises.refAnchor: d10/批注为什么简单先查后发不够

exercises.explanation: The three cases share one thing: a gap between “already sent” and “recorded as sent” (concurrent checks, a lost response, a crash before writing state). Two orders are two events, so one notification each is correct; if the first call wasn’t accepted, nothing was sent, so the user gets just one after the retry.
options: The third party accepted the request, but the response was lost and the worker retried
Two workers both check and see “not seen before”
The first call wasn’t accepted by the third party and only the retry succeeded
A worker crashes after sending successfully but before writing the state
A user places two orders and gets one order notification for each
exercises.prompt: Even with a “check, then send” step based on the event ID, in which cases can the user still receive duplicate notifications?
exercises.refAnchor: d10/批注为什么简单先查后发不够

exercises.explanation: In “check, then send,” the check and the write are two steps, and the window between them lets two workers both pass. An atomic claim merges “check and mark as in progress” into one step, so only one worker wins. Checking more times or staggering randomly only lowers the odds of a collision; it doesn’t close the window.
options: Use an atomic claim that makes “check + mark” a single step
Write the event ID record only after sending succeeds
Have each worker wait a random time to stagger the checks
Check the event ID record several times before sending
exercises.prompt: To stop two workers from processing the same event at the same time, what is the key improvement?
exercises.refAnchor: d10/批注为什么简单先查后发不够

exercises.explanation: The third party may have accepted a request while the response was lost, so no system can guarantee exactly-once under every failure. What you can do is guarantee at least one send, then deduplicate as far as possible with atomic claims, stable idempotency keys, and the third party’s own idempotency support.
exercises.prompt: “At-least-once delivery plus deduplication” describes a notification system’s reliability more accurately than promising exactly-once.
exercises.refAnchor: d10/批注为什么简单先查后发不够

exercises.explanation: A transactional outbox writes the pending event and the business data in the same database transaction, so both succeed or both fail, and a background process then delivers the event to the queue. Swapping the order only trades one inconsistency for another.
options: Have the third-party service look up whether the order exists
Use a transactional outbox, committing the order and the event in one transaction
Enqueue right after the write; that step rarely fails
Enqueue first, then write; if the write fails, so be it
exercises.prompt: After the order service writes to the database successfully, it must send an “order placed” notification, but the write and the enqueue might succeed or fail independently. What does the chapter recommend?
exercises.refAnchor: d10/批注为什么简单先查后发不够

exercises.explanation: Accepted, delivered, displayed, and opened are different states. Even after acceptance, a notification can fail to arrive because the device is offline, the token is invalid, and so on; whether the user opened it must be counted separately through event tracking.
exercises.prompt: When the third party returns “accepted,” it means the user has already seen the notification.

lessons.title: Support & Tracking
lessons.summary: Rate limiting, retry, monitoring, tracking, security

exercises.explanation: The rate limiting component caps how often notifications go to a single user, blocking a burst in a short time. Retries would only send more; queue monitoring and event tracking are for observation and don’t block anything.
options: Rate limiting: cap how often one user is sent notifications
Retry: redeliver after a failure
Event tracking: measure open rates
Queue monitoring: adjust workers based on backlog
exercises.prompt: A promotion sends the same user 20 push notifications in one hour. Which component should prevent this bombardment?

exercises.explanation: The source uses AppKey/AppSecret as an example, but real providers may use certificates, tokens, or service accounts, so integrate according to each platform’s requirements. Either way, keep the secrets safe on the server, never in the client.
exercises.prompt: Using AppKey/AppSecret, as the source does, is enough to authenticate with every push platform such as APNS and FCM.

exercises.explanation: Campaign impact depends on whether users opened and clicked, which event tracking measures. “Accepted” only says the third party took the request; queue backlog and retry counts reflect system health, not user engagement.
options: The retry count in the notification log
The number of “accepted” responses from the third party
Open and click rates counted by event tracking
The message queue’s backlog length
exercises.prompt: Operations wants to evaluate how well a push campaign worked. Which data matters most?

exercises.explanation: A growing backlog means consumers can’t keep up, so you can add workers for that channel; a backlog that stays at zero lets you scale in. Adding notification servers doesn’t help: they sit upstream of the queue and would just stuff it faster.
exercises.prompt: Fill in what queue monitoring does
exercises.text: Queue monitoring tracks each queue’s [[backlog]] and uses it to adjust the number of [[workers]] dynamically.

exercises.explanation: Caching hot data and regional delivery optimization are both among the chapter’s key optimizations, with horizontal scaling and queues. The source mistakenly wrote the regional one as Distributed Crawling; no crawler is needed here. One shared provider amplifies single-point risk, and no retries loses notifications.
options: Turn off retries to reduce load on the third party
Cache frequently used data to cut latency
Add a distributed crawler component
Use the same third-party service for every channel
Optimize message delivery by region
exercises.prompt: One item under the source’s “key optimizations” is written as Distributed Crawling. In context, which are sensible optimizations for a notification system?

exercises.explanation: The same “99%” means very different things under different definitions: third-party acceptance may be very high while real user opens are very low. Define the states first, and only then does the number mean anything for comparison.
options: What programming language the workers use
Which SMS and push providers are used
How it is measured: accepted, delivered, or opened
Whether the message queue delivers strictly in FIFO order
exercises.prompt: In an interview someone says, “Our notification delivery rate is 99%.” What should you ask first?

exercises.explanation: Notifications of the same kind share a format, and only a few variables such as the user name or order number are swapped in. Predefined templates avoid assembling content from scratch each time and give notifications from different businesses a consistent style.
exercises.prompt: Predefining notification templates with a fixed format and filling in only variables at send time both unifies formats and makes rendering more efficient.

exercises.explanation: Backoff gives the third party time to recover, the same idempotency key lets it recognize duplicates, and a retry cap plus an expiry check end notifications that are doomed or no longer meaningful. Immediate, endless retries pile on during an outage.
options: Give up after one failure and never retry
Back off, reuse the key, stop at cap or expiry
Use a new idempotency key on each retry
Retry at once, endlessly, until it succeeds
exercises.prompt: When a third party has a temporary outage, how can the retry mechanism avoid making things worse?

chapters.title: News Feed
chapters.fullTitle: Chapter 11: Design a News Feed System
keyPoints: The feed has two paths, publishing and reading. Newest-first is a simplifying assumption; ranking is a separate requirement.
Fan-out on write reads fast but amplifies writes; fan-out on read writes light but reads slowly. Hybrid: push for regular users, pull celebrities.
The feed cache stores only (post_id, user_id) with a capped length; bodies are cached separately, never copied into each feed.
Fan-out on write depends on follower count, reader activity, and posting frequency, not just a “celebrity” label.
A cache hit doesn’t mean still visible: filter by current permissions on read, clean old IDs asynchronously, and page with a stable cursor, not offset.

labs.title: Fan-out on write, fan-out on read, and hybrid when a celebrity posts
The feed cache holds only IDs; assemble and filter on read

lessons.title: Scope and Flows
lessons.summary: Requirements, APIs, and the publish and read flows

exercises.explanation: Newest-first is a simplifying assumption: merge posts from all sources by time. Ranking is a separate requirement. IDs written by fan-out on write can be sorted by time too, and a precomputed feed cache exists precisely to avoid scanning every friend on each read.
options: You must build a ranking model before you can return a feed
Only fan-out on read works; fan-out on write can’t keep time order
Merge posts by publish time; layer ranking on later
Every read must scan all friends’ posts in real time
exercises.prompt: The interviewer says, “Sort by time, newest first.” What does that mean for the design?

exercises.explanation: Authenticate and rate-limit first to block invalid requests and spam. Save the post before fanning out, so the IDs in friends’ feeds point to a post that exists. The notification service that alerts friends runs in parallel as a side step.
items: The user calls POST /v1/me/feed
The load balancer routes the request to a web server
The web server authenticates and rate-limits
The post service writes to the database and cache
The fan-out service pushes the ID into friends’ feeds
exercises.prompt: Put the steps for publishing a post in order

exercises.explanation: On the publishing path the jobs split into authentication and rate limiting, storing the post, fan-out, and notification. The news feed service handles reading: it gets the ID list first, then fills in details from the content cache or database.
pairs: Stores the post in the DB and cache
Pushes post IDs into friends’ feed caches
Alerts friends to a new post
Fetches feed IDs, then fills in posts
exercises.prompt: Match each service to its job in the news feed

exercises.explanation: Writing feeds is the fan-out service’s job; the notification service only alerts friends that there is a new post. Both run after the post is saved, but their roles differ, so don’t mix them up.
exercises.prompt: Writing a post ID into friends’ feed caches is the notification service’s job.

exercises.explanation: Fan-out on write pushes the post_id into every friend’s feed at publish time. With at most 5,000 friends, that is at most 5,000 writes (fewer after settings filters). The 10 million is the DAU, not one person’s friend count.
options: 1 feed
10 million feeds
It isn’t known until friends open the app
5,000 feeds
exercises.prompt: Each person has at most 5,000 friends. A regular user publishes one post. At most how many friends’ feeds does fan-out on write update?

exercises.explanation: Publishing creates a new resource, so use POST; reading changes no state, so use GET. The `me` in the path means the current user, who is identified by the auth_token.
exercises.prompt: Complete the two news feed APIs
exercises.text: Publish a post with [[POST]] /v1/me/feed and retrieve the feed with [[GET]] /v1/me/feed; both take an auth_token.

exercises.explanation: The retrieval API has a single parameter, auth_token, and `me` in the path stands for the logged-in user. That keeps the interface simple and stops anyone from forging another user’s ID to read their feed.
exercises.prompt: A request to retrieve the feed doesn’t need a user ID; the server identifies the current user from the auth_token.

exercises.explanation: The web server guards the entry point: it authenticates the user, rate-limits against flooding, and then forwards the request to the backend. Fetching the friend list and writing feed caches are fan-out service steps.
options: Rate-limits to block spam and flooding
Writes the post ID into friends’ feed caches
Reads the friend list from the graph database
Verifies the user’s identity with the auth_token
exercises.prompt: In the publishing flow, what does the web server do?

lessons.title: Fan-out Strategies
lessons.summary: Fan-out on write, on read, and the hybrid trade-offs

exercises.explanation: Each post is written into 1 million feeds, so 10 posts mean 10 million writes. That is write amplification: writes grow with the reader count, and the more active a celebrity is, the worse it gets.
options: 10 writes
10 million writes
1 million writes
100 million writes
exercises.prompt: An author has 1 million readers and you use pure fan-out on write. They publish 10 posts a day. How many feed writes does the fan-out service do for them each day?
exercises.refAnchor: d11/批注像提前准备目录而非复印整本书
exercises.refTitle: Fan-out Is a Table of Contents, Not a Photocopy

exercises.explanation: Fan-out on write only prepares a list of post IDs to read for each reader. The feed cache stores (post_id, user_id) pairs, and the body is shared in a single copy. Write amplification means many list updates, not many copies of the body.
exercises.prompt: Fan-out on write copies the whole post into every friend’s feed.
exercises.refAnchor: d11/批注像提前准备目录而非复印整本书
exercises.refTitle: Fan-out Is a Table of Contents, Not a Photocopy

exercises.explanation: Fan-out on read aggregates only when the reader opens the app, so inactive users cost nothing. Fan-out on write writes their feeds on every post; shorter lists save memory but not write count.
options: Fan-out on write, with shorter feed lists
All approaches cost the same
Fan-out on write
Fan-out on read
exercises.prompt: Many registered users in a community log in only once every few months. Which approach avoids doing work for them in advance?

exercises.explanation: In the hybrid approach, regular authors use fan-out on write while celebrities don’t push to all their followers. A read must merge and sort the cached IDs with the celebrities’ recent posts. That is the cost of its more complex merge logic.
options: Read only the feed cache; celebrity posts were pushed in too
Scan every friend’s full post history in real time, then sort
Read IDs from the cache, then pull celebrities’ recent posts and merge
Fetch only friends’ recent posts and skip the cache
exercises.prompt: With the hybrid approach, what happens when a user opens the feed?

exercises.explanation: Write amplification depends on the reader count and posting frequency, and pushing to inactive readers is wasted work. An account with many followers that almost never posts may be cheap to fan out on write.
exercises.prompt: Whether to fan out on write for an author depends on follower count, reader activity, and posting frequency, not just on a “celebrity” label.
exercises.refAnchor: d11/批注像提前准备目录而非复印整本书
exercises.refTitle: Fan-out Is a Table of Contents, Not a Photocopy

exercises.explanation: The trade-off is when the work happens: fan-out on write moves it to publish time, fan-out on read defers it to read time. The more friends, the heavier fan-out on write; the more sources to aggregate on each open, the slower fan-out on read.
exercises.prompt: Complete the cost of each fan-out approach
exercises.text: Fan-out on write makes reads fast, at the cost of [[write amplification]]; fan-out on read keeps writes light, at the cost of slower [[reads]].

exercises.explanation: Fan-out on write pushes IDs to all friends at publish time, so reads are fast, but writes grow with the friend count and also go to people who never open the app. Aggregating after the reader opens the app describes fan-out on read; celebrities are exactly where fan-out on write creates hotspots.
options: The more friends an author has, the more writes one post causes
Inactive readers get written to as well
Aggregation starts only after a reader opens the app
The feed is already prepared when the reader opens it, so reads are fast
It removes the hotspots caused by celebrities
exercises.prompt: Which statements about pure fan-out on write are correct?

exercises.explanation: A lower threshold turns more authors from push to pull: fewer writes at publish time, but readers must pull and merge more authors when they open the feed. Writes and reads trade off against each other; no threshold is free.
options: Both writes and reads drop, saving on both sides
Neither is affected; the threshold only affects storage
Site-wide writes drop, but reads must merge more authors
Writes go up, and reads merge fewer authors
exercises.prompt: In the hybrid approach, authors whose follower count exceeds a threshold switch to pull at read time. What happens if you lower the threshold from 1 million to 10,000?

lessons.title: Fan-out Service
lessons.summary: Fetch friends, filter, enqueue, and bounded ID lists

exercises.explanation: First decide who gets the post, then exclude people who shouldn’t see it, then hand off to the queue for asynchronous processing, and finally a fan-out worker writes the caches. Filtering before enqueueing avoids writing feeds for friends who can’t see the post.
items: Fetch friend IDs from the graph database
Check settings cache; filter out muted or blocked friends
Hand the friend list and post_id to the message queue
A worker writes to friends’ feed caches
exercises.prompt: Put the fan-out service’s steps for a new post in order

exercises.explanation: Not every friend should receive the post: those who muted or blocked the author, or who are outside the sharing scope, are excluded first. The login check already happened at the web server, and a feed holds only the post_id, never the body.
options: To recheck the poster’s login state and permissions again
To exclude friends who muted or blocked the author or are outside the sharing scope
To fetch the post body so it can be written into friends’ feeds as well
To decide whether the post is ordered by time or by recommendation
exercises.prompt: Why query the user settings cache before fanning out?

exercises.explanation: 10 million × 500 = 5 billion entries; × 16 bytes = 80 billion bytes ≈ 80 GB. Copying a full post of about 2 KB into every entry would take about 10 TB, which is why the cache stores only IDs and caps the list length.
options: About 8 GB
About 80 GB
About 800 GB
About 8 TB
exercises.prompt: Suppose you keep the latest 500 feed entries for each of 10 million DAU, at about 16 bytes per (post_id, user_id). About how much memory does the feed cache need?

exercises.explanation: Users rarely scroll back to very old posts, so caching everyone’s full history isn’t worth it. Capping the length keeps the memory cost under control; time order has nothing to do with list length.
options: Only short lists can keep time order
The system deletes old posts after a certain age
Users mostly read the newest content, so this caps memory
Cache systems can’t store long lists
exercises.prompt: The feed cache keeps only the most recent post IDs (the length is configurable). What is the rationale?

exercises.explanation: Writing 5,000 friends’ feeds synchronously would make publishing slow. With a queue, workers consume tasks asynchronously, the publish request returns quickly, and the queue buffers fan-out tasks at peak.
exercises.prompt: The fan-out service hands work to a message queue and fan-out workers, so the publish request doesn’t wait for every friend’s feed to be written.

exercises.explanation: Friend relationships form a graph, so they are read from the graph database. The feed cache only records who should see which post; bodies, author profiles, and counts live in their own caches and are assembled at read time.
exercises.prompt: Complete the data source and what gets written
exercises.text: The friend list comes from the [[graph database]]; the worker writes only the mapping between [[post_id]] and user_id into the feed cache.

exercises.explanation: Fan-out tasks may be consumed more than once, so writes must be idempotent: a given post_id appears only once per feed. A new ID creates duplicates, clearing the feed loses other posts, and giving up on retries leaves friends without the post.
options: Write idempotently by post_id, and skip it if it already exists
Give up retrying; friends who weren’t reached don’t see the post
Generate a new post_id on each retry
Clear the friend’s entire feed before retrying
exercises.prompt: A fan-out worker crashes midway; when the task is redelivered, it rewrites some friends’ feeds. How do you keep the same post from appearing twice in a feed?

exercises.explanation: A queue provides decoupling and buffering, but reliability depends on configuration: whether messages are persisted, whether you ack only after successful processing, and whether failures are retried. Misconfigured, tasks are still lost when the queue goes down or a worker crashes.
exercises.prompt: Once a fan-out task is in a message queue, it can never be lost.

lessons.title: Reads and Caching
lessons.summary: Five caches, visibility filters, paging, and scaling

exercises.explanation: The feed cache holds only IDs, so a read still fetches the bodies from the content cache. “Did I like this?” goes to the action cache and “how many likes in total?” to the counter cache; these two are the easiest to confuse.
pairs: Each user’s post IDs to read
Post details; popular posts go to a hot cache
Whether I liked, replied to, or shared
exercises.prompt: Match each cache to the data it holds

exercises.explanation: An ID in the cache doesn’t mean the content is still visible. When assembling a page, filter by the latest delete, block, and privacy state, and let a background job clean up stale IDs. Cleaning every friend’s feed synchronously is expensive and would slow the delete itself.
options: Show it as usual and let the cache expire on its own
Delete the ID from every friend’s feed synchronously before reporting success
Filter it out by current status and permissions, and clean up old IDs asynchronously
Clear every friend’s feed cache
exercises.prompt: User A deletes a post, but its ID is still in friends’ feed caches. What should a read do?
exercises.refAnchor: d11/批注缓存命中也不代表内容仍可见
exercises.refTitle: A Cache Hit Doesn’t Mean Still Visible

exercises.explanation: New posts are inserted at the front, so older posts shift back by 3 positions: items 18–20 become 21–23 and show up again at the start of page 2. Using the last item you saw as a stable cursor is unaffected by insertions.
options: The first 3 items on page 2 repeat ones you already saw
The request errors out; you must go back to page 1 and refresh
The result is exactly right; new posts only affect page 1
Page 2 skips 3 older posts
exercises.prompt: You finish page 1 (20 items), then friends publish 3 new posts. What happens when you fetch page 2 with offset=20?
exercises.refAnchor: d11/批注缓存命中也不代表内容仍可见
exercises.refTitle: A Cache Hit Doesn’t Mean Still Visible

exercises.explanation: When nodes are added or removed, consistent hashing moves only a few keys. But if one celebrity’s data is extremely hot, whichever node it lands on stays busy; hotspots call for caching, replication, or splitting.
exercises.prompt: Complete the limits of consistent hashing
exercises.text: Consistent hashing mainly reduces [[key remapping]] when nodes change; it cannot remove a [[hotspot]] caused by one key being accessed too often.

exercises.explanation: Sharding and read replicas share the database’s own load, while layered caches and the hot cache keep most reads from reaching it at all. Hitting the database on every read, or sending all reads to the primary, pushes the pressure back onto it and makes the read replicas pointless.
options: Layered caching of frequently accessed data
Send all reads to the primary and use read replicas only as backups
Shard, and use read replicas to absorb high-traffic queries
Put popular posts in a hot cache
Fall through to the database on every read to guarantee freshness
exercises.prompt: Which practices reduce the load on the news feed database?

exercises.explanation: A falling hit rate means many reads are falling through to the database, possibly because of too little capacity, lists that are too short, or too-frequent invalidation. A common recommendation is to track QPS, latency, and cache hit rate and tune accordingly.
exercises.prompt: Monitoring the cache hit rate helps you decide whether cache capacity and policies need adjusting.

exercises.explanation: If a session lives on one machine, requests must return to that machine, and adding or removing servers loses sessions. Keep the web tier stateless and put state in shared storage so you can scale out freely.
exercises.prompt: Keeping user sessions in a web server’s local memory makes the news feed easier to scale horizontally.

exercises.explanation: The feed cache stores only IDs, so the news feed service fetches bodies from the content cache (falling through to the database on a miss), adds author and count information, and returns the assembled page. Letting the client query item by item would cause many round trips.
options: Return the IDs as they are and let the client query each one
Fetch post details from the content cache or database and assemble the page
Write the IDs back into the fan-out queue
Re-query all friends’ posts and aggregate again
exercises.prompt: After the news feed service gets 20 post IDs from the feed cache, what does it usually do next?

chapters.title: Chat System
keyPoints: 50 million DAU does not mean 50 million concurrent connections; concurrency depends on peak hours, devices per user, and connection-keeping policy.
Polling wastes empty requests, and long polling must hold requests and reconnect. A WebSocket is two-way once open, but the channel alone is not reliable.
Chat servers are stateful because they hold long connections. Write to KV first, then deliver; push to offline users, who catch up by cursor.
Unique does not mean ordered: Snowflake IDs only roughly follow time, so strict order within a conversation needs a per-conversation sequence number.
Keep cursors per device and per conversation (or use a monotonic sync sequence), and advance one only after all earlier messages are confirmed received.
Heartbeat every 5 s, offline after 30 s without one. Presence is approximate; with many friends, subscribe only to visible contacts.

labs.title: How a Message Reaches Every Device
Does a Network Blip Count as Offline?

lessons.title: Needs & Protocols
lessons.summary: Sizing chat and three ways to receive

exercises.explanation: DAU counts people active at some point during a day, and they are not all online together. Concurrent connections depend on the peak-hour distribution, devices per person, and the connection-keeping policy. With several devices per person, connections can even outnumber online users.
exercises.prompt: 50 million DAU means the chat servers must hold 50 million WebSocket connections at the same time.
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注dau-不能直接当连接数
exercises.refTitle: Note: DAU Is Not Concurrent Connections

exercises.explanation: Concurrent connections count the devices connected at the same moment: the activity pattern decides how many people are online together, device count multiplies connections, and the keeping policy decides how long idle ones linger. Message length and group size affect storage and fan-out, not connection count.
options: The connection-keeping policy (how long idle connections stay open)
Group chats hold at most 100 members
A single message is at most 100,000 characters
How users’ activity is distributed across the day
How many devices each user has online on average
exercises.prompt: To estimate how many concurrent connections the chat servers must carry, what else do you need to know?
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注dau-不能直接当连接数
exercises.refTitle: Note: DAU Is Not Concurrent Connections

exercises.explanation: Polling and long polling are both client-initiated and differ only in how they wait. HTTP keep-alive saves repeated handshakes, but the server still cannot send on its own. Only once a WebSocket is open can the server push at any time.
pairs: Holds until message or timeout, then reconnects
exercises.prompt: Match each communication method with its trait

exercises.explanation: Long polling must end and reconnect after every message or timeout, and the server has to keep the held requests. A WebSocket is set up once and stays two-way. It runs on TCP, not UDP, and it does not guarantee delivery. It also needs the server to keep connection state, which is exactly why chat servers are stateful.
options: WebSocket runs on UDP, so latency is lower
WebSocket needs no connection state on the server
WebSocket guarantees messages are never lost
Once open, both sides send any time, no hold-and-reconnect
exercises.prompt: The receiver needs the server to push new messages. Why does this design choose WebSocket over long polling?

exercises.explanation: Keep-alive only reuses the connection and cuts handshake cost; the request/response pattern is still started by the client. For the server to push on its own, you need a two-way channel such as a WebSocket.
exercises.prompt: If the sender uses HTTP keep-alive persistent connections, the server can push new messages to the client at any time.
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注http-keep-alive-不等于服务器可随时推消息
exercises.refTitle: Note: Keep-Alive Does Not Let Servers Push

exercises.explanation: A live channel does not make messages reliable: messages sent during a disconnect must be fetched from persisted history, and reconnects and retries can create duplicates, which you remove by a stable message ID.
exercises.prompt: Even with an established WebSocket connection, you still need catch-up after disconnects and deduplication to avoid lost or duplicate messages.
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注http-keep-alive-不等于服务器可随时推消息
exercises.refTitle: Note: Keep-Alive Does Not Let Servers Push

exercises.explanation: Polling asks whether or not there is a message, so when messages are rare it mostly spins for nothing. Long polling holds the request until a message arrives, which cuts empty replies; a WebSocket lets the server push the moment one arrives.
options: Most requests return empty, wasting resources
The server cannot tell which user is asking
Messages arrive out of order and must be re-sorted
Messages sent between polls are always lost
exercises.prompt: A client polls for new messages every 2 seconds, but a user receives one only every few minutes on average. What is the main problem?

exercises.explanation: Long polling returns only when a message arrives or the request times out, so there are fewer empty replies. The cost is that the server holds many requests at once, even for inactive users, and the client must send a new one after every round.
exercises.prompt: Complete the benefit and cost of long polling
exercises.text: Long polling reduces [[empty responses]], but the server must keep [[held requests]], and the client reconnects after each one ends.

exercises.explanation: Recent messages are read often and old ones rarely. Keeping hot data in fast storage and moving cold data to cheaper storage keeps history permanent while controlling cost. Holding everything in memory is neither necessary nor realistic.
options: For low latency, all history must be kept in memory
A single message is capped at 100,000 characters, so storage volume is negligible
Permanent storage does not mean all in memory; tier hot and cold history
Permanent storage can only be done with a relational database
exercises.prompt: The requirements call for storing chat history permanently. Which understanding of history storage is most reasonable?
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注dau-不能直接当连接数
exercises.refTitle: Note: DAU Is Not Concurrent Connections

lessons.title: Components & Data
lessons.summary: Stateful servers, KV storage, and message IDs

exercises.explanation: Only the chat server holds long-lived connections, so it is the stateful service; API servers handle ordinary requests and can scale out statelessly. Offline users cannot receive WebSocket messages, so the notification server pushes to them.
pairs: Holds WebSockets, sends and receives messages
