exercises.prompt: Match each chat system component with its responsibility

exercises.explanation: Messages for a client must be relayed through whichever chat server it is connected to, so this connection state is bound to a specific machine. History lives in the KV store, and an API server keeps no state after a request, so you can add machines freely.
options: The chat server holds the client’s long-lived connection
The chat server stores chat history permanently
The API server cannot scale horizontally and must be a single machine
The chat server stores users’ login passwords
exercises.prompt: Why is the chat server stateful while the API server can be stateless?

exercises.explanation: That is just the chapter’s choice, based on scalability and latency. The point is to pick the database by access pattern: chat history is mostly read in conversation order, so what matters is a good partition key and sort key, and a well-designed relational database works too.
exercises.prompt: The chapter picks a KV store, which shows that a relational database cannot be used for chat records.
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注按访问模式选数据库
exercises.refTitle: Note: Choose a Database by Access Pattern

exercises.explanation: channel_id keeps one group’s messages together and message_id orders them within the group. That matches the most common read: open a group chat and scroll up through its history.
options: Sorting all groups’ messages globally by time
Fetching one group’s messages and paging back through them in order
Looking up which groups a user has joined
Looking up all messages sent by a given sender
exercises.prompt: The group message table uses (channel_id, message_id) as a composite key. Which access does this mainly support?

exercises.explanation: Uniqueness and ordering are separate problems. Clock drift, concurrency across nodes, and late messages can make Snowflake order differ from the real order. Strict order within a conversation needs rules for assigning and persisting a per-conversation sequence number.
exercises.prompt: Snowflake IDs are globally unique and roughly increasing with time, so they guarantee strict order of messages within a conversation.
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注唯一性与顺序是两件事
exercises.refTitle: Note: Uniqueness and Ordering Are Separate Problems

exercises.explanation: Users care about order within one conversation, not whether group A or group B came first. A per-conversation number narrows ordering to one conversation. The cost: it is unique only there and cannot be compared across conversations, so identifying a message still takes the conversation ID or a separate global ID.
options: Order is needed only within a conversation, so no global ordering to coordinate
Local numbers are globally unique, so they can be used directly for deduplication
Local numbers can be compared across conversations to see which came first
Local numbers need no persistence, so they save storage
exercises.prompt: The chapter suggests a local sequence number for each conversation. Compared with relying on a global sequence, what is its advantage?

exercises.explanation: Easy scaling, low latency, and avoiding the cost of random access on large relational indexes are the chapter’s three reasons. KV is actually weak at JOINs, and order comes from key design and sequence rules, not automatically.
options: Random access on large indexes can be expensive in a relational database
KV automatically guarantees strict message order
KV natively supports cross-table JOINs
Easy to scale horizontally
Low access latency
exercises.prompt: The chapter chooses a KV store for chat history. Which reasons does it give?

exercises.explanation: Connection state lives only in the old machine’s memory and vanishes when it fails; ZooKeeper stores registration data and does not migrate connections. The client reconnects and service discovery recommends a new node. History is safe in KV and caught up by cursor. API servers use request/response and cannot push.
options: An API server pushes messages to the client over HTTP instead
ZooKeeper moves the connections from the old machine’s memory to a new one
The client reconnects, and service discovery assigns a new chat server
The chat history on that server is lost with it
exercises.prompt: The chat server a user is connected to goes down. What is most likely to happen next?
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注zookeeper-保存信息不替你决定业务策略
exercises.refTitle: Note: ZooKeeper Stores Information, Not Decisions

exercises.explanation: Assigning by proximity lowers latency, and assigning by capacity keeps individual servers from overloading. ZooKeeper only stores registration and coordination data; which server to pick is usually decided by routing logic in the application.
exercises.prompt: Complete the basis and the tool for service discovery
exercises.text: Service discovery recommends a chat server based on [[geographic location]], server capacity, and similar factors, and the chapter uses [[ZooKeeper]] to manage coordination data.

exercises.explanation: Each ID has its own job: the global ID identifies and deduplicates a message, and the per-conversation sequence number defines order. You don’t need one ID to meet both needs.
exercises.prompt: A globally unique ID can still identify a message, with per-conversation order guaranteed by a separate sequence rule.
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注唯一性与顺序是两件事
exercises.refTitle: Note: Uniqueness and Ordering Are Separate Problems

lessons.title: Messages & Sync
lessons.summary: 1:1 delivery, group inbox, multi-device cursors

exercises.explanation: Assign the ID and persist first, then deliver in real time: even if delivery fails or B drops, the message is already saved and B can catch up after reconnecting. If B is offline, it is not forwarded to server 2; a push notification is sent instead.
items: A sends the message to chat server 1
Server 1 assigns a unique message ID
The message is written to the KV store
It is forwarded to server 2, which holds B’s connection
Server 2 pushes it to B over WebSocket
exercises.prompt: B is online. Put the delivery of a one-on-one message in order

exercises.explanation: The message is persisted first, whether or not B is online. An offline B has no WebSocket to push on, so the notification server sends a push alert; B catches up from KV by cursor once online. Memory-only data is lost on restart, and a push is just an alert with no delivery guarantee, so it cannot replace persistence.
options: Write it to KV as usual and alert B with a push notification
Keep it only in server 1’s memory and send it when B connects
Skip KV and put the full text in a push notification to B
Drop the message and have A resend it when B comes online
exercises.prompt: B is offline. How does chat server 1 handle the message from A?

exercises.explanation: An inbox is a sync queue organized by recipient: whoever sends in the group, a copy (or index entry) goes to every member’s inbox. So one person’s inbox naturally holds messages from many senders, and the client only has to sync its own inbox.
exercises.prompt: With the inbox approach to group chat, one user’s inbox can contain messages from several senders.

exercises.explanation: The message or its index is copied to every member’s inbox, so a 100-member group needs about 100 records. Offline members need one too, or they would have nothing to sync when they return. The larger the group, the worse the write amplification.
options: Only for online members, depending on how many are online
About 100
About 10,000
exercises.prompt: With the chapter’s inbox approach, how many inbox records are written when someone sends one message in a 100-member group?
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注小群可用写扩散大群需重新估算
exercises.refTitle: Note: Fan-out on Write for Small Groups Only

exercises.explanation: About 100 inbox writes per message is fine for a small group, but a 10,000-member group needs 10,000, and that write amplification is unacceptable. Share one copy of the body, keep the sync index light, and use a stable message ID to deduplicate retries.
exercises.prompt: Fan-out on write should not be copied to 10,000-member groups; better to store the body once and keep a sync index per member or conversation.
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注小群可用写扩散大群需重新估算
exercises.refTitle: Note: Fan-out on Write for Small Groups Only

exercises.explanation: A phone and a laptop have different sync progress, so the cursor must be stored per device; with one cursor per user, once one device reads, the other would miss messages. A message is new if the recipient is me and its ID is greater than my local maximum.
exercises.prompt: Complete the rule for multi-device sync
exercises.text: Each [[device]] keeps its own cur_max_message_id; a message addressed to the current user whose message_id is [[greater than]] it is new.

exercises.explanation: Message 500 in group A and message 3 in group B are not comparable: once the cursor sits at 500, messages 4 to 500 in group B are wrongly treated as already synced. That means missed messages, not extra pulls. Keep a cursor per conversation, or give the user’s inbox its own monotonic sync sequence.
options: You only pull some old messages again, and the client can deduplicate
Sync just becomes a little slower
Numbers from different conversations are not comparable, so new messages are missed
Nothing wrong; a larger ID is always newer
exercises.prompt: Message IDs increase only within each conversation, but a single user-level cur_max_message_id is used to sync all conversations. What happens?
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注原文两种-id-方案不能直接混用
exercises.refTitle: Note: Don’t Mix the Two ID Schemes

exercises.explanation: Messages can arrive out of order: when 105 arrives, 103 and 104 may still be in flight. If you advance straight to 105, the late 103 and 104 are skipped. Advance the cursor only after confirming that all earlier messages have arrived.
exercises.prompt: When a client receives any new message, it can advance its cursor to that message’s ID.
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注原文两种-id-方案不能直接混用
exercises.refTitle: Note: Don’t Mix the Two ID Schemes

exercises.explanation: A stable message ID is what makes deduplication possible: a retry with the same ID lets the server and client recognize the same message. A new ID creates a new message, and rebuilding the connection has nothing to do with deduplication.
options: The sender reuses the same message ID when retrying
The receiver deduplicates by message ID before displaying
Tear down and rebuild the WebSocket before retrying
Generate a new message ID on retry to tell attempts apart
exercises.prompt: Network flapping causes the same message to be resent. Which practices keep users from seeing it twice?
exercises.refAnchor: d12/批注小群可用写扩散大群需重新估算
exercises.refTitle: Note: Fan-out on Write for Small Groups Only

lessons.title: Online Presence
lessons.summary: Heartbeat timeout, status fan-out, failures

exercises.explanation: Offline is decided by how long it has been since the last heartbeat: 30 seconds with no new one after 12:00:00 is 12:00:30. At 12:00:05 only one heartbeat has been missed, which is still within tolerance.
options: Immediately when the network drops
exercises.prompt: A client sends a heartbeat every 5 seconds, and the server marks it offline after 30 seconds without one. A user sends the last heartbeat at 12:00:00 and loses the network. When is the earliest they are marked offline?

exercises.explanation: In an elevator or when switching networks, connections often drop briefly and recover. Marking offline on disconnect makes status flicker and causes heavy fan-out; a heartbeat gives a tolerance window, and recovering within it is not offline. The cost: a real departure is noticed only after the timeout, so it is less prompt.
options: Heartbeats guarantee messages are never lost
A heartbeat timeout is detected sooner than a disconnect
With heartbeats you no longer need a WebSocket connection
A brief network blip would make status flip online/offline constantly
exercises.prompt: Why not mark a user offline the moment the connection drops, instead of using a heartbeat timeout?

exercises.explanation: The threshold trades stability against speed: a short one reacts quickly to real departures but mistakes weak networks and sleeping devices for offline; a long one is steadier, but it takes longer to show that a user really left.
exercises.prompt: Complete the trade-off in the heartbeat timeout threshold
exercises.text: A shorter timeout detects departures faster, but on weak networks [[false offline marks]] increase; a longer one makes [[departure detection]] slower.

exercises.explanation: Each pair of friends has a publish/subscribe channel, A’s status change is published to the channel for each friend, and the friends receive it in real time by subscribing. Cost grows with the number of friends, so the chapter says it suits smaller groups of relationships.
options: Write it to KV and let friends read it the next time they log in
B, C, and D each poll A’s status every second
Broadcast to one site-wide shared status channel
Publish to three channels: A-B, A-C, and A-D
exercises.prompt: User A has friends B, C, and D. When A’s status changes, how does the fan-out model notify the friends?

exercises.explanation: Only a few contacts are visible on screen, so subscribing to just those is enough, cutting fan-out from all friends to those watching. Shortening the heartbeat or switching to polling would only cost more. Pushing only online events would leave friends seeing “online” forever.
options: Shorten the heartbeat interval to 1 second
Have each friend pull his status every second
Subscribe to status only for the contacts currently open on screen
Notify friends only when he comes online, not when he goes offline
exercises.prompt: A user has 5,000 friends, and fanning every status change out to all of them is too costly. What does the note suggest?

exercises.explanation: Online status means “recently reachable.” If the phone loses its network but the laptop is still connected, messages can still be delivered in real time, so showing online is reasonable.
exercises.prompt: If either the phone or the laptop of the same user still has a valid connection, the user can be shown as online.

exercises.explanation: A timeout can also come from a weak network or a sleeping device. A heartbeat expresses “recently reachable,” not exact proof, so online status is only an approximation.
exercises.prompt: A heartbeat timeout means the user has deliberately quit the app.

exercises.explanation: Scaling means adding machines horizontally, load balancing, and caching; fault tolerance means queueing and retrying failed deliveries, and service discovery assigning a new server. Old connections exist only in the failed machine’s memory and cannot be migrated, so clients reconnect; forbidding it cuts users off.
options: Forbid clients from reconnecting after a server failure, to avoid an avalanche
Use caching to reduce database load and latency
Queue and retry when message delivery fails
Add servers horizontally and spread connections with a load balancer
Have ZooKeeper migrate the existing connections when a server fails
exercises.prompt: For growth and failures, which practices does the chapter mention under “Additional Considerations”?

exercises.explanation: Media files are large, so compress them and put them in cloud storage rather than the message store; end-to-end encryption protects privacy; a client-side cache means content already on the device need not be downloaded again; a geo-distributed cache puts data on nodes closer to users in each region.
pairs: Compress images/video, store in the cloud
exercises.prompt: Match each future extension with the problem it solves

chapters.title: Search Autocomplete
chapters.fullTitle: Chapter 13: Design a Search Autocomplete System
keyPoints: Separate query real-time from data real-time: suggestions should return within 100 ms, while rankings can update periodically.
A naive Trie must traverse a subtree and sort; caching top-k on each prefix node trades storage for query speed.
Append logs, aggregate into a frequency table, build a new Trie on a schedule; validate, warm up, switch whole versions, keep the old for rollback.
Remove harmful suggestions instantly with a filter layer on the query path; do physical deletion later in the background.
Prefix-range sharding hits short-prefix hotspots; pre-aggregate a global top-k, or query all shards in parallel and merge.

labs.title: Top-K on a Trie: Compute Now or Precompute?

lessons.title: Scope and Numbers
lessons.summary: Requirements, request volume, two kinds of real-time

exercises.explanation: 10 million × 10 × 20 = 2 billion requests/day, ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 23,000 QPS. The 48,000 QPS in the requirements is the peak, about 2 times the average. Every character triggers a request, so request volume is far higher than the number of searches.
options: About 2,300
About 230,000
About 23,000
About 48,000
exercises.prompt: 10 million DAU, each user searches 10 times a day, each query averages 20 characters, and every character typed sends one request. What is the average QPS?

exercises.explanation: Both numbers are the chapter’s design assumptions, not derived figures. If user behavior changes (say, each person searches only 3 times a day), QPS and storage growth change with it, so say your assumptions out loud in an interview.
exercises.prompt: The requirements’ 48,000 QPS and 0.4 GB of new data per day are both design assumptions; a real estimate also needs the number of searches, characters per query, and the share of new queries.

exercises.explanation: The two kinds of real-time have very different costs. Query real-time comes from precomputation and caching; data real-time means changing the index on every search. This chapter lets rankings update periodically, in exchange for simple, stable online queries.
exercises.prompt: Complete the difference between the two kinds of “real-time”
exercises.text: Seeing suggestions right after typing is [[query real-time]]; having every search immediately change the ranking is [[data real-time]]. This chapter prioritizes the former.

exercises.explanation: This confuses the two kinds of real-time. Users want results right after they type; they don’t need rankings to change every second. Updating the Trie per search is expensive, and popular suggestions rarely change much from one second to the next.
exercises.prompt: To make suggestions “real-time”, the ranking in the Trie must be updated immediately every time someone searches.

exercises.explanation: Move heavy work like sorting to the background and compute it ahead of time; online, you only walk to the prefix node and read the result, which keeps latency stable under 100 ms. Scanning on demand or rewriting on every search makes the online path heavy.
options: Prebuild a Trie with top-k in the background, then look it up online
Scan all historical queries and sort them on every request
Rewrite the frequencies in the Trie on every search
Send all query logs to the browser and compute locally
exercises.prompt: Suggestions must return within 100 ms, at most 5 of them, ranked by popularity. Which approach fits best?
exercises.refAnchor: d13/批注先做工作再把答案贴在节点上
exercises.refTitle: Do the Work Once, Then Attach the Answer to the Node

exercises.explanation: The system splits into an offline half and an online half: the gathering service aggregates logs into a frequency table and builds the Trie, while the query service only fetches results from the Trie by prefix. Keeping them separate lets each scale on its own.
pairs: Answers user input, returns top-k suggestions
Stores how often each query was searched
Layers by character, shares common prefixes
exercises.prompt: Match each autocomplete component with its role

exercises.explanation: The chapter narrows the scope to 5 suggestions, ranked by popularity, lowercase English only, returned within 100 ms. Spelling correction and personalization are common extensions but not part of these requirements; clarify first, then decide whether to build them.
options: Personalized ranking from each user’s history
Automatic spelling correction
Ranking by query frequency
Lowercase English characters only
Returning at most 5 suggestions
exercises.prompt: Which of these are in scope for this chapter’s autocomplete?

exercises.explanation: Look only at queries starting with tw and take the top 5 by frequency: twitter 35, twitch 29, twilight 25, tweet 15, twin 10. tree has the highest frequency but doesn’t start with tw; twist (9) ranks sixth; alphabetical order doesn’t satisfy the popularity requirement.
options: twitter, twitch, twilight, tweet, twist
tree, twitter, twitch, twilight, tweet
tweet, twilight, twin, twist, twitch
twitter, twitch, twilight, tweet, twin
exercises.prompt: The frequency table has tree 50, twitter 35, twitch 29, twilight 25, tweet 15, twin 10, twist 9. The user types tw. Which 5 suggestions should be returned?

lessons.title: Trie Queries
lessons.summary: Prefix lookup, cached top-k per node, and its cost

exercises.explanation: The naive approach spends its time in two steps: traversing the subtree and sorting. The shorter the prefix, the bigger the subtree, and the more words to collect and sort. Caching top-k on each node moves exactly those two steps into background precomputation.
items: Walk from the root to the prefix node
Traverse its subtree and collect all complete queries
Sort by frequency
Return the first k
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a naive Trie prefix top-k lookup in order

exercises.explanation: With caching, you only walk the prefix character by character to the node and read the k ready-made results; no matter how large the subtree, you don’t traverse it. Add a prefix length cap (say, 50 characters) and the cost of a single query has an upper bound.
options: The average character length of candidate words
The prefix length (steps to reach the node)
The total number of words under the prefix node
The total number of queries in the frequency table
exercises.prompt: Once every prefix node caches its top-k, what does the cost of one query mainly depend on?
exercises.refAnchor: d13/批注先做工作再把答案贴在节点上
exercises.refTitle: Do the Work Once, Then Attach the Answer to the Node

exercises.explanation: Each node now stores an extra candidate list, so storage clearly grows. This is the classic trade of space for time: extra storage saves the online traversal and sorting.
exercises.prompt: Caching top-k on every node speeds up queries without increasing storage.
exercises.refAnchor: d13/批注先做工作再把答案贴在节点上
exercises.refTitle: Do the Work Once, Then Attach the Answer to the Node

exercises.explanation: Almost nobody types a very long prefix and waits for suggestions. With a cap, the steps to reach a node have an upper bound, and you don’t build nodes and caches for overlong prefixes. It’s a deliberate engineering limit, not a limit of word length, browsers, or the Trie itself.
options: To keep extremely long inputs from blowing up lookup and caching costs
English words are at most 50 letters long
Queries longer than 50 characters can’t be stored in a Trie
Browsers can send at most 50 characters
exercises.prompt: Why limit the query prefix length to something like 50 characters?

exercises.explanation: These are different data. The end node answers “how many times was this word searched”; a prefix node’s top-k answers “which few words starting with this prefix are most popular”, and the latter is aggregated from the former.
exercises.prompt: The frequency of an individual query is usually stored on that query’s end node, while prefix nodes cache an aggregated candidate list.
exercises.refAnchor: d13/批注先做工作再把答案贴在节点上
exercises.refTitle: Do the Work Once, Then Attach the Answer to the Node

exercises.explanation: bee appears only in the candidate lists of its own prefixes (root, b, be, bee), so those nodes’ top-k may change. Nodes below bee, such as beef, count only words starting with beef, which doesn’t include bee; other branches like ca are unaffected too.
options: The bee node and every node in the subtree below it
The prefix nodes on the path from the root to bee
Only bee’s end node
Every node in the whole Trie
exercises.prompt: This week bee’s search count rises from 20 to 40; all other words are unchanged. On rebuild, whose cached top-k might change?
exercises.refAnchor: d13/批注先做工作再把答案贴在节点上
exercises.refTitle: Do the Work Once, Then Attach the Answer to the Node

exercises.explanation: The shorter the prefix, the bigger the subtree and the slower the naive approach. The optimized version uses the node’s cache in the “top-k sort” step of query processing, skipping traversal and sorting; only the walk to the node and building the response remain.
exercises.prompt: Complete the difference between naive and optimized queries
exercises.text: A naive query traverses the whole [[subtree]] under the prefix node and then sorts; the optimized one reads the cached [[top-k]] list on the node directly.

exercises.explanation: A Trie is organized by prefix: it excels at “starts with” lookups and doesn’t help with “contains a substring”. The node count equals the number of distinct prefixes, so longer words with less shared prefix mean more nodes.
options: A Trie can directly find queries that contain an arbitrary substring
Caching top-k on nodes trades space for time
Querying ca takes two steps from the root, c then a, to reach the prefix node
It layers by character, so a common prefix is stored once
The number of nodes depends only on the number of query words, not their length
exercises.prompt: Which statements about a Trie are correct?

lessons.title: Build and Update
lessons.summary: Log aggregation, rebuilds, filtering, version switch

exercises.explanation: On one side is cost: every query would update frequencies and top-k along its path. On the other is benefit: rankings rarely swing every second, and users can’t tell if they update in real time. Logs are still the raw material for the next build, and a Trie can be modified.
options: Popular suggestions rarely change much every second
There may be billions of queries a day, so updating the Trie per query is expensive
A Trie can’t accept new nodes at all
After a batch build, query logs no longer need to be kept
exercises.prompt: Why does the chapter replace “update on every query” with periodic batch builds of the Trie?

exercises.explanation: The log is append-only, aggregation runs in batches per time window, and the build finishes asynchronously in the background. The new version is validated and warmed up before a whole-version switch, and the old version is kept for rollback, so online queries are never affected by the build.
items: Queries are appended to the analytics log
The aggregator builds a frequency table per time window
Workers build the new Trie asynchronously
Validate and warm up the new version
The query service switches to the new version
exercises.prompt: Put the improved data gathering and build flow in order

exercises.explanation: The log’s reader is the aggregator, which scans whole batches by time window and needs no random lookups. Skipping indexes keeps writes cheap; online queries go through the Trie, not the log.
exercises.prompt: The analytics log is append-only and has no query index, because it only feeds later batch aggregation and doesn’t serve online queries.

exercises.explanation: The chapter notes that a platform like Twitter, which stresses instant trends, can shorten the time window, while other scenarios may be fine with weekly. The window is an adjustable knob; you needn’t go to the extreme of rebuilding on every search.
options: Shorten the aggregation window and update more often
Keep it weekly; trends don’t matter
Skip aggregation and sort the raw logs directly
Rebuild the whole Trie on every search
exercises.prompt: A social platform that stresses instant trends builds autocomplete. How should the aggregation step change?

exercises.explanation: The three stores have different jobs: the in-memory cache serves online reads, the document store keeps snapshots of the whole tree, and the KV store splits the tree into “prefix → node data” so you can fetch by prefix directly. The aggregator sits upstream and produces the raw material for building the Trie.
pairs: Distributed cache; Trie in memory for fast reads
Periodic snapshots of the whole serialized Trie
Each prefix is a key, node data is the value
Turns raw logs into a frequency table
exercises.prompt: Match each pipeline component with its role

exercises.explanation: The filter layer removes harmful suggestions by rule before returning them, so a rule change takes effect immediately without waiting for a rebuild; physical deletion happens asynchronously in the background. Waiting a week is too slow, and a shutdown rebuild hurts the service.
options: Shut down, rebuild the whole Trie, then relaunch
Wait for next week’s routine build to remove it
Hide it only on the client; do nothing on the server
Block it in the filter layer, delete it physically later
exercises.prompt: A suggestion containing hate speech is found, and you want it gone as soon as possible. What is the best approach?

exercises.explanation: While overwriting and serving at the same time, a query can read a half-new, half-old mix. Build the new version first, validate and warm it up, then switch over as a whole, keeping the old version for rollback.
exercises.prompt: Once the new Trie is built, you can simply overwrite the old Trie’s nodes in place without affecting queries in flight.

exercises.explanation: The whole Trie is still rebuilt periodically; only a few sudden trends go into a lightweight real-time layer, and queries merge results from both. You keep the stability of batch processing and still keep up with breaking events.
exercises.prompt: Complete the fix for sudden trending terms
exercises.text: Periodic builds mean a new trend appears only in the next version; add a small [[real-time delta layer]], and [[merge]] it with the periodically built Trie before returning.

lessons.title: Sharding & Client
lessons.summary: Prefix shards, hotspots, front end, languages

exercises.explanation: The first-letter distribution of English words is naturally uneven, so an even split by letter will always be skewed. The chapter’s fix is to keep splitting oversized ranges, with a shard map manager recording the mapping and routing queries. A bigger machine is only vertical scaling and hits a ceiling as data keeps growing.
options: Give the first server a machine with more memory
Shard by the length of the query word instead
Reject some queries that start with a-m
Keep splitting oversized ranges, such as aa-ag
exercises.prompt: After splitting by first letter into a-m and n-z on two servers, the first holds far more data and load than the second. Sticking with prefix-range sharding, what is the best adjustment?

exercises.explanation: Even letter ranges don’t mean even traffic: queries starting with s or c far outnumber those starting with x or z, and short prefixes concentrate lots of requests. Monitor the prefix access distribution first, then decide the shard boundaries.
exercises.prompt: If prefixes are split evenly by letter range across shards, traffic across the shards will also be roughly even.

exercises.explanation: A single sub-shard knows only its own words, so its top-k is not the global top-k. Either pre-aggregate the global result for short prefixes offline, or query all shards in parallel, merge, and take the top k again by frequency; plain concatenation exceeds 5 and the order is wrong.
options: Take 5 from each shard and return them all concatenated
Return an empty result and wait for more characters
Query just one sub-shard and return its result
Pre-aggregate the global top-k, or query all shards and merge
exercises.prompt: The user has typed only a, and the data starting with a is spread across several sub-shards. How do you return the correct top-k?

exercises.explanation: The shard map manager answers “which server to ask”; AJAX and the browser cache improve the front-end experience; the filter layer guards content safety; and per-country Tries serve multiple languages and regional differences.
pairs: Maps prefixes to shards and routes queries
Fetches suggestions while typing, no page reload
Reuses results for common prefixes locally
Fit each region’s language and popular queries
exercises.prompt: Match each optimization with its role

exercises.explanation: Async requests go out concurrently, each with its own processing and network time, so the return order isn’t guaranteed to match the send order; the late ca response would overwrite cat’s results. Have responses carry the prefix or a request ID, and let the client show only the one that matches the current input.
options: The server handles them in arrival order, so responses never arrive out of order
The suggestions jump back to ca’s results, so stale responses should be discarded
The server automatically rejects the stale ca request
Nothing, the browser sorts responses into the order they were sent
exercises.prompt: The user types c, ca, cat quickly, but the response for ca arrives later than the one for cat. What happens if you don’t handle it?

exercises.explanation: A suggestion newly blocked by the filter layer may still sit in a user’s browser cache. The TTL limits how long stale results can live, a trade-off between the benefit of browser caching and how quickly server rules take effect.
exercises.prompt: When the browser caches results for common prefixes, it needs a sensible TTL; otherwise old suggestions can still appear after the server’s filter rules are updated.

exercises.explanation: Unicode handles character representation and per-region Tries fit different languages and trending terms, but you also need normalization and each language’s product rules; changing the encoding alone is far from enough. The top-k cache is language-independent, and a Trie per user is unaffordable.
options: Normalize text and follow each language’s product rules
Remove the top-k cache on each node
Represent non-English characters in Unicode
Build different Tries per country or region
Build a separate Trie for each user
exercises.prompt: To extend autocomplete to multiple languages, which pieces of work are needed?

exercises.explanation: With prefix-range sharding, all data for a prefix lands on one shard, so a query touches just one shard (short prefixes are the exception). The shard map manager stores the mapping, and uneven ranges can be split further.
exercises.prompt: Complete how prefix sharding works
exercises.text: The Trie is split across servers by [[prefix range]], for example a-m and n-z; a query first consults the shard map, then is [[routed]] to the right shard.

exercises.explanation: The chapter suggests updating the relevant nodes dynamically, or weighting recent queries more heavily, to react to live events; you can also add a small real-time delta layer for trending terms and merge it with the periodically built Trie.
exercises.prompt: A sudden trend can only show up after the next periodic Trie build.

chapters.title: YouTube
keyPoints: The API handles only auth, upload control, and metadata; video bytes go straight to object storage via pre-signed URLs and play from the CDN.
Upload the original once; a DAG transcodes it into many resolutions, bitrates, and formats. Independent tasks run in parallel; GOP splits enable retries.
Publish ready only after the required outputs and manifest are persisted and verified, or users see “playable” and get a 404. HD can follow later.
The player fetches the manifest, then downloads segments; ABR switches bitrate by throughput and buffer. MP4 is a container; H.264 and VP9 are codecs.
CDN traffic is the biggest cost. Serving cold videos from the origin and transcoding on demand saves money but adds latency and waits; check watch data.
Retry temporary failures in uploads, transcoding, and allocation; stop on unrecoverable errors such as corrupt formats and return a clear error code.

labs.title: Transcoding DAG: Parallelism, Retries, and Completion

lessons.title: Scale Estimates
lessons.summary: Design goals, assumptions, and two estimates

exercises.explanation: Fast uploads come from parallel chunks and a nearby entry point; low latency from CDN edge delivery; switchable quality from transcoding into several versions; savings from skipping unwatched transcodes; reliability from retries and similar fault tolerance. The CDN only distributes; the quality versions come from transcoding.
pairs: Parallel chunk upload, nearby upload entry
Stream from a nearby CDN edge node
Transcode into many resolutions and bitrates
exercises.prompt: Match each design goal with the approach that supports it most directly

exercises.explanation: 150 TB ÷ 300 MB = 150 trillion bytes ÷ 300 million bytes ≈ 500,000 videos, which is 1 upload per 10 of the 5 million DAU each day. The chapter’s estimate leaves this ratio unstated; saying it out loud in an interview lets you check whether 150 TB is reasonable.
options: About 500,000, 1 upload per 10 DAU
About 50,000, 1 upload per 100 DAU
About 5 million, 1 upload per DAU
About 150,000, 1 upload per 33 DAU
exercises.prompt: This chapter assumes 5 million DAU, an average video of 300 MB, and 150 TB of new storage per day. Working backward, roughly how many videos are added per day?

exercises.explanation: 5 million × 5 = 25 million views, × 0.3 GB = 7.5 million GB, × $0.02 = $150,000/day. $30,000 forgets to multiply by the 5 views per person. This is only a rough estimate at historical prices, not a current quote.
exercises.prompt: The chapter estimates CDN cost: 5 million DAU, 5 videos per person per day, 0.3 GB each, at $0.02/GB. Roughly how much is that per day?

exercises.explanation: The formula “DAU × views per person × video size × unit price” is linear in every term, so doubling the video size doubles traffic and cost. Cost follows the traffic that is watched, not DAU alone.
options: Still $150,000; cost depends only on DAU
About $600,000, 4 times as much
About $75,000, half as much
About $300,000, double
exercises.prompt: Everything else stays the same, but the average video size goes from 300 MB to 600 MB. Using the chapter’s formula, what is the daily CDN cost?

exercises.explanation: New storage is driven by uploads (about 500,000 videos × 300 MB); CDN cost is driven by views (25 million views × 0.3 GB). The two estimates have different drivers, so to estimate storage you also have to assume how many people upload.
exercises.prompt: Using the chapter’s estimation method, “5 videos watched per person per day” affects only the CDN traffic cost, not the daily new storage.

exercises.explanation: Those are background figures from around 2020, not inputs to the exercise formula. The exercise uses its own assumptions (5 million DAU, 300 MB average, and so on). Mixing the two sets of numbers can throw the estimate off by several orders of magnitude.
exercises.prompt: The chapter lists 2 billion monthly active users and 5 billion views per day; these should be inputs to this exercise’s storage and bandwidth estimates.
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注历史背景与本题假设分开

exercises.explanation: CDN cost depends on the bytes actually sent: how long people watch, which bitrate they get, and whether the edge hits all change the traffic. Titles and descriptions are metadata, and API server CPU is not on the CDN bill.
options: Length of video titles and descriptions
Number of CPU cores on API servers
Bitrate differences between quality versions
CDN cache hit rate and origin traffic
Actual watch time, since many people don’t finish a video
exercises.prompt: The chapter’s CDN cost is only a rough estimate. Which factors should you add to get closer to the real number?

exercises.explanation: The first is the storage estimate, driven by uploads. The second is the traffic estimate, driven by views; multiply it by $0.02/GB and you get $150,000 per day.
exercises.prompt: Complete the two estimates
exercises.text: 150 TB ÷ 300 MB ≈ [[500,000]] videos/day; 5 million DAU × 5 views × 0.3 GB ≈ [[7.5 million GB]] of traffic/day.

exercises.explanation: One reason to transcode is to provide formats that work across devices and browsers. A single MP4 is not enough: the same container does not mean the codec and resolution inside are supported. Splitting systems by device is duplicated effort, and relaying video bytes through the API is exactly what this chapter avoids.
options: Uploads must pass through the API server for unified validation
Transcode into several formats and resolutions for different devices
Deploy a separate upload and storage system for each device type
Store one MP4 original and let each device play it as it can
exercises.prompt: The requirements say the service must support phone apps, web browsers, and smart TVs. Which part of the design does this affect most directly?

lessons.title: Upload & Playback
lessons.summary: Control vs. data plane, completion, adaptive playback

exercises.explanation: The API handles only small requests: auth, upload control, and metadata. Video bytes, often hundreds of MB, flow through object storage and the CDN, and each side scales independently with its own load. Relaying all video bytes through the business API is a common mistake.
options: API servers can’t authenticate, so the CDN has to
Video traffic is huge and would swamp the API’s bandwidth and connections
Object storage can’t hold metadata, so it bypasses the API
A CDN guarantees strong consistency more easily than an API server
exercises.prompt: Why do video bytes go straight to object storage and play from the CDN instead of passing through the API server?

exercises.explanation: The API server handles interactions other than moving video data. Original storage and transcoded storage are both object storage, one for inputs and one for outputs. The CDN delivers the finished videos from the location closest to the user.
pairs: Stores the raw videos users upload
Caches and serves video from nearby
exercises.prompt: Match each component with its responsibility

exercises.explanation: The textbook’s original diagram draws “write to transcoded storage” and “queue the completion event” as parallel branches. But the required outputs and manifest must be written and verified before ready is published; otherwise users see “playable” and get a 404.
items: The client uploads the original to original storage
Transcoders produce several formats and resolutions
Outputs and manifest are written and verified
The completion handler marks the metadata as playable
The user streams from the CDN
exercises.prompt: Put the main steps from upload to playable in order
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注完成通知必须有真正的完成条件

exercises.explanation: Metadata only describes the video (file name, size, format). Whether it can play depends on whether the transcoded outputs and manifest are persisted and verified. Marking ready when the metadata has arrived but the outputs have not gives users a 404.
exercises.prompt: Metadata and the original are uploaded in parallel, so once the metadata write succeeds, the video can be marked playable.

exercises.explanation: In the original design, 3a (write to transcoded storage) and 3b (enqueue the event) are parallel branches, and a queue cannot guarantee the object has landed. When the CDN fetches from the origin, the object does not exist yet, so it returns 404. The system has no “fall back to the original” mechanism.
options: The player falls back to the original
Nothing goes wrong; the completion queue guarantees the order
The CDN waits until the outputs are written
The user sees “playable” but the video request returns 404
exercises.prompt: The completion event enters the completion queue and the handler marks the video playable at once, but the outputs are not yet written to transcoded storage. A user opens the video now. What is the most likely result?
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注完成通知必须有真正的完成条件

exercises.explanation: Once the required outputs are persisted and verified, ready can be published and higher qualities can become available gradually. Waiting for every version delays launch for nothing, and marking an unfinished version available creates 404s.
options: Publish 360p now and add 1080p when it finishes
Substitute the original for the unfinished 1080p version
Wait for every quality level, then publish them together
Mark 1080p available too and retry if it fails
exercises.prompt: A video’s 360p version and its manifest are written and verified, but 1080p is still transcoding. To let users watch as soon as possible, what is a sensible approach?
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注完成通知必须有真正的完成条件

exercises.explanation: A CDN usually caches on demand: the first miss at an edge fetches from the origin and caches it, and later requests hit nearby. Pushing unpopular videos to every edge wastes space and is not a prerequisite for playback.
exercises.prompt: After transcoding finishes, the video must be copied to every CDN edge node before users can play it.
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注完成通知必须有真正的完成条件

exercises.explanation: The player fetches the manifest first, then downloads segment by segment; adaptive bitrate (ABR) switches versions based on throughput and buffer level. ABR only switches among existing versions. On-demand transcoding is a cost optimization for unpopular videos’ first play and can’t keep up with second-by-second swings.
options: Switching between segments of different bitrates by throughput and buffer
Pausing until the whole video has downloaded
Downloading from nearby users over P2P
Asking the server to transcode it again on the spot
exercises.prompt: A user watches on the subway, where the network speed keeps jumping up and down. What mainly lets the player reduce stalling?
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注把视频想成一串小片段
exercises.refTitle: Think of Video as Small Segments

exercises.explanation: The manifest lists which versions exist and where each segment is; segmented download lets the player change bitrate between segments. The completion queue belongs to the post-transcoding notification, the pre-signed URL to upload authorization, and the DAG to transcoding tasks.
exercises.prompt: Complete the streaming playback process
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注把视频想成一串小片段
exercises.refTitle: Think of Video as Small Segments
exercises.text: The player first fetches the [[manifest]], then downloads video segment by segment; [[adaptive bitrate]] switches quality versions based on network throughput and buffer.

lessons.title: Transcode Pipeline
lessons.summary: Containers, codecs, DAG, GOP splits, scheduling

exercises.explanation: MP4 is a container (the box) that wraps video, audio, and metadata; H.264 and VP9 are codecs (the packing method). The same MP4 can hold different codecs, so supporting the container doesn’t mean supporting every codec. Switching to AVI only changes the box, and quality comes from the codec and bitrate, not the container.
options: It doesn’t support the video codec in the file, such as VP9
The MP4 container sets quality, and this file’s quality is too high
MP4 is a compression algorithm and the file uses a newer version
The MP4 must be converted to an AVI container before decoding
exercises.prompt: A player says it “supports MP4” but can’t open a particular MP4 file. What is the most likely cause?
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注mp4-像盒子h264-像打包方法
exercises.refTitle: MP4 Is the Box, H.264 Is the Packing Method

exercises.explanation: When the chapter says transcoding “reduces space,” it means a single compressed version can be smaller than a high-bitrate original. The several quality versions together, plus the original you keep, usually increase total storage; they do not necessarily reduce it.
exercises.prompt: Transcoding compresses video, so after transcoding into several versions, total storage is generally smaller than storing only the original.
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注mp4-像盒子h264-像打包方法
exercises.refTitle: MP4 Is the Box, H.264 Is the Packing Method

exercises.explanation: A DAG lays out tasks such as encoding, thumbnails, and watermarks along with their dependencies, so tasks with no dependency can go to different workers at the same time. Transcoding is slow and compute-heavy, so parallelism is the key to speed.
options: Preprocessing can be skipped and encoding can start directly
They can run in parallel, shortening total processing time
They must run serially so the output order is consistent
Temporary storage can be dropped
exercises.prompt: In the transcoding DAG, “generate thumbnails” and “encode the 1080p version” don’t depend on each other. What is the direct benefit of describing tasks as a DAG?

exercises.explanation: Video frames depend on each other for decoding, so a segment cut at an arbitrary byte offset may not decode on its own. At a GOP (group of pictures) or keyframe boundary, each segment can be encoded alone and retried alone.
options: Object storage only accepts files aligned to GOP boundaries
Quality is highest at GOP boundaries, which suits thumbnails
Frames depend on each other, so only GOP cuts decode independently
Splitting by bytes makes the transcoded files larger overall
exercises.prompt: Why does the preprocessor split video at GOP boundaries instead of every fixed number of bytes?

exercises.explanation: The preprocessor splits the video (including GOP alignment for older clients), generates the DAG from config, and stores intermediate data in temporary storage. Picking workers is the task scheduler’s job in the resource manager, and CDN distribution happens after the outputs exist.
options: Generate the DAG from a config file
Pick an idle worker and tell it to run a task
Distribute finished videos to the CDN
Store GOPs and metadata in temporary storage for failure retries
Split the video at GOP boundaries
exercises.prompt: Which of the following are responsibilities of the preprocessor?

exercises.explanation: Pipeline order: the preprocessor generates the DAG, the scheduler splits it into stages, the resource manager matches tasks to workers, workers run them, and outputs are written to transcoded storage. The completion handler updates metadata only after the outputs exist.
exercises.prompt: Complete the division of labor in the transcoding pipeline
exercises.text: The [[preprocessor]] generates the DAG from config, the [[DAG scheduler]] splits it into stages and puts them in the task queue, and the [[resource manager]] picks a suitable worker for each task.

exercises.explanation: The three queues answer “what needs doing,” “who is free,” and “who is doing what.” From them, the task scheduler assigns the right task to the right worker.
pairs: Picks a task and worker, then starts it
exercises.prompt: Match each resource manager part with its responsibility

exercises.explanation: Use “video, version, segment, parameters” as a stable ID; however many times the task runs, it writes to a fixed location or publishes atomically, so the result is the same. Random file names leave two outputs behind, and starting over wastes a lot of compute.
options: Delete all transcoded output for the video before each retry and start over
Forbid automatic retries and make users re-upload on failure
Give tasks a stable ID so repeated runs write to the same place or publish atomically
Have each run write a random file name and pick either one at playback
exercises.prompt: A segment’s 720p encoding task times out and is retried, but the original task actually finished writing. How do you avoid ending up with two inconsistent outputs?

exercises.explanation: The preprocessor puts GOPs and metadata into temporary storage precisely so a failed encode can be retried from them. When choosing temporary storage, also consider data type, size, access frequency, and lifecycle.
exercises.prompt: Temporary storage holds the split GOPs and metadata, so when one segment’s encoding fails, you can retry just that segment instead of reprocessing the whole video.

lessons.title: Tuning & Errors
lessons.summary: Speed-ups, pre-signed URLs, cost, error types

exercises.explanation: Chunked parallel upload both speeds things up and supports resuming: chunks already acknowledged need not be sent again. A longer timeout can’t save a dropped connection, and transcoding on the phone does nothing about restarting from scratch after an interruption.
options: Split into small chunks, upload in parallel, and record completed chunks
Raise the API server timeout to 1 hour
Transcode to 1080p on the phone before uploading
Upload the whole video into API server memory, then copy it over
exercises.prompt: A user uploads an 800 MB video on a weak network and loses connection halfway. Which design lets them resume without starting over?

exercises.explanation: The closer the upload entry is to the user, the fewer round trips and packet losses a long-distance link suffers. The chapter uses a CDN as a nearby upload hub as an example; in practice, pick a service that offers upload or acceleration features. Compressing to 360p would ruin the original’s quality.
options: Force compression to 360p before upload
Funnel all uploads into one big data center
Connect each user to the upload entry nearest them
Add read-only replicas to the metadata DB
exercises.prompt: Users overseas always upload videos slowly. What is the idea behind the chapter’s “distributed upload centers”?

exercises.explanation: When modules depend on each other directly, one slow module holds up its upstream. With a message queue in between, the upstream puts a task in the queue and moves on, the downstream consumes at its own pace, and modules can work in parallel.
exercises.prompt: After decoupling modules such as upload and transcoding with a message queue, an upstream module can keep accepting new tasks without waiting for downstream processing to finish.

exercises.explanation: The API authenticates first, then issues a short-lived address scoped to one object and one operation; video bytes never pass through the API. The final object must still be verified after upload, because anyone who gets the URL can use it while it is valid.
items: The client asks the API server to upload
The API server authenticates, issues a time-limited URL
The client uploads directly to object storage via the URL
The server verifies object size, type, and completion
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a pre-signed URL upload in order
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注预签名-url-是限时授权

exercises.explanation: A pre-signed URL is itself a time-limited credential, and whoever holds it can use it until it expires. So scope it to one object and operation, give it a short expiry, and verify the object’s size, type, and completion status after upload.
options: The URL is bound to the device, so nobody else can use it
Whoever has the URL can also upload with it
The URL stays valid forever; the only quick fix is deleting the bucket
Object storage asks for an account and password again
exercises.prompt: A user forwards the pre-signed upload URL they received to someone else. What happens during the URL’s validity period?
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注预签名-url-是限时授权

exercises.explanation: DRM, encryption, and watermarks each serve a different goal: controlling authorized playback, protecting content, and marking ownership. None of them means “cannot be copied.” A pre-signed URL authorizes uploads and has nothing to do with playback protection.
options: DRM (such as FairPlay and Widevine) controls who can play
A pre-signed URL is itself a form of DRM
Watermarks overlay identifying information on the picture
Any one of the three guarantees the video can’t be copied
AES encryption stops unauthorized parties from reading the content directly
exercises.prompt: Which of the following statements about protecting video are correct?

exercises.explanation: Bypassing the CDN loses nearby caching: viewers far from the origin see higher latency, and every request hits the origin. So first work out the watch distribution and confirm that unpopular traffic is small enough to make this worthwhile.
options: Higher latency for unpopular videos and more load on the origin
Popular videos are forced to be served from the origin too
Authors must re-upload unpopular videos once
Metadata DB writes double as a result
exercises.prompt: To save CDN cost, you serve unpopular videos directly from high-capacity origin servers. What is the main cost you accept?
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注成本优化有规模门槛
exercises.refTitle: Cost Optimization Has a Scale Threshold

exercises.explanation: Many versions of an unpopular video may never be watched, so on-demand transcoding avoids generating them ahead of time. The price is that the first viewer waits for transcoding to finish. The original must still be kept; without it there is nothing to transcode on demand.
options: Saves original storage, but later transcoding becomes impossible
Saves CDN traffic, but uploads get slower
Saves metadata storage, but thumbnails can’t be generated
Skips versions nobody watches, but the first play may wait
exercises.prompt: For long-tail unpopular videos, you switch to transcoding a version only when someone watches it. What does this save, and what does it cost?
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注成本优化有规模门槛
exercises.refTitle: Cost Optimization Has a Scale Threshold

exercises.explanation: Per-GB price is only part of the bill: building your own also means construction, an operations team, and ISP partnerships, which pay off only at large enough traffic. Check the scale threshold first, then work out the total from actual watch time, cache hit rate, and popularity distribution.
exercises.prompt: As long as the per-GB cost of building your own CDN is lower than a CDN vendor’s quote, you should build your own.
exercises.refAnchor: d14/批注成本优化有规模门槛
exercises.refTitle: Cost Optimization Has a Scale Threshold

exercises.explanation: Temporary failures may succeed on retry. A corrupt input fails the same way however many times you retry, so stop the task and return a clear error code. Telling the two kinds of error apart keeps you from wasting resources on a bad task.
options: The uploaded video’s format is corrupt and can’t be decoded
A transcoding worker is temporarily down
The network drops during an upload
Resource allocation fails temporarily
exercises.prompt: Which of the following should be treated as “recoverable errors” and retried automatically?

chapters.title: Google Drive
keyPoints: A drive = block store + metadata directory + change notifications: blocks go to object storage, the directory to a database, and each scales on its own.
Files are split into blocks of at most 4 MB and identified by hash, which enables resumable uploads, delta sync, and block-level deduplication.
Chunk on the client to save upstream bandwidth: send the block list, then upload only missing blocks. Chunking on a block server saves only the hop to S3.
A successful upload is a state transition: verify blocks and checksums, then atomically publish pending as uploaded. Keep the callback idempotent.
Conflicts are caught by a conditional update on base_version: the first request the server handles wins; the other is kept as a conflicted copy.
A notification only says “changed”; the client then fetches the delta. Notifications can be lost, so add version numbers, a cursor, and full re-sync.

labs.title: Upload Only Changed Blocks, Keep Conflicted Copies

lessons.title: Scope and Sizing
lessons.summary: Requirements, capacity assumptions, two upload modes

exercises.explanation: Delta sync sends only the blocks that changed and, together with compression, cuts unnecessary transfer. Replication and a standby load balancer serve high availability; sharding serves scalability.
options: Upload only the changed blocks (delta sync)
A standby load balancer that takes over
Primary-replica replication of the metadata database
Sharding storage by user_id
exercises.prompt: One non-functional requirement for a cloud drive is bandwidth efficiency. Which design choice serves it most directly?

exercises.explanation: The chapter gives no total users, actual utilization, or version and replica multipliers, so 10 million DAU × 10 GB = 100 PB does not match 500 PB. The programming language and the notification mechanism have no bearing on a capacity estimate.
options: Total registered users, not just DAU
How much of the free space users actually use
Which programming language the API servers use
The multiplier from version history and replicas
Whether notifications use long polling or WebSocket
exercises.prompt: The chapter states 500 PB of total storage, but that number cannot be derived from the other assumptions. Which capacity inputs should you confirm first in an interview?

exercises.explanation: 10 million × 10 GB = 100 PB, and DAU is not the same as total users. The chapter also gives no utilization, version, or replica multiplier, so 500 PB cannot be derived. In an interview, confirm the capacity assumptions first, then estimate daily growth and replica overhead.
options: 10 million × 10 GB is exactly 500 PB
500 PB is derived exactly from 10 million × 10 GB × 5 replicas
500 PB is the amount of new storage added each day
500 PB is a separate assumption; 10 million × 10 GB is only 100 PB
exercises.prompt: The requirements say 10 million DAU, 10 GB of free space per user, and 500 PB of total storage. What is the best way to read these numbers?

exercises.explanation: 10 million × 2 × 500 KB = 10 million × 2 × 500,000 B = 10 trillion B ≈ 10 TB. At that rate it would take over a hundred years to accumulate 500 PB, which shows that 500 PB is a separate capacity assumption.
options: About 1 TB
About 100 TB
About 10 PB
About 10 TB
exercises.prompt: With 10 million DAU, 2 uploaded files per user per day, and an average file size of 500 KB, roughly how much new upload data arrives per day (ignoring versions and replicas)?

exercises.explanation: However big the machine, it is a single point of failure: if it breaks the service is down, and a disk failure loses data, which violates the availability and reliability requirements. That is why the chapter moves to sharding, redundant S3 storage, load balancing, and metadata database replication.
exercises.prompt: The single-server design can already identify every file uniquely, so moving to a big enough machine is enough to serve 10 million DAU.

exercises.explanation: Each namespace holds all the uploaded files of one user, and namespace plus relative path uniquely identifies a file or folder. This single-machine design is only a starting point; it cannot handle large-scale capacity or availability.
options: It maps to one user, and adding the relative path locates a file
It marks which block of a file this is
It marks which data center region stores the file
It distinguishes revisions of the same file
exercises.prompt: In the single-server design, files live under `drive/{namespace}/{relative path}`. What does the namespace do?

exercises.explanation: If a large file is sent in one piece, a failure means starting over. A resumable upload records progress on the server, so you pick up where you left off after a disconnect. Delta sync solves “only a little changed”, not “the transfer broke halfway”.
exercises.prompt: Complete the two upload modes
exercises.text: Small files use a [[simple upload]] that sends everything in one request; large files use a [[resumable upload]]: get an upload URL first, and after an interruption continue from the confirmed position.

exercises.explanation: First initiate the session and get its dedicated URL. Then upload in parts and query how far the server has confirmed. After a disconnect, send only the unconfirmed part.
items: Send the initiation request
Receive the resumable upload URL
Upload the data in parts and check the status
After an interruption, resume from the confirmed position
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a resumable upload in order

exercises.explanation: An implementation should record the upload session, block index, checksum, and expiration time. With a session and a block index, a resent block lands in the same place and never creates an extra file.
exercises.prompt: In a resumable upload, if the client resends the same block after a timeout, the server should recognize it instead of creating a duplicate file.

lessons.title: Distributed Design
lessons.summary: Sharding, block servers, two planes, sync conflicts

exercises.explanation: A single server eventually runs out of space, and sharding by user_id spreads different users' data across several servers. A conflict is a concurrent-edit problem, which sharding does not solve, and deduplication relies on block hashes, not shards.
options: One machine runs out of space, so data is spread across machines by user
The system no longer needs a metadata database to track files
Files with identical content are stored only once across the site
Two devices can no longer conflict when editing the same file
exercises.prompt: When moving from a single server to a distributed design, the chapter shards storage by `user_id`. What main problem does this solve?

exercises.explanation: Metadata records which blocks make up which version of which file, and in what order. If the metadata is lost, the blocks in S3 cannot be reassembled into files. So the chapter shards and replicates the metadata database, and promotes a replica when the primary fails.
exercises.prompt: File blocks are already replicated in S3, so the metadata database only needs sharding and no replication.

exercises.explanation: The hash is computed from the block content, so identical content gives an identical hash. That tells you whether a block exists, whether it changed, and whether it can be shared. Sharding uses user_id, and notification order comes from version numbers or a change cursor.
options: Ordering change notifications
Deciding which shard holds a user's data
Letting multiple files or versions share one block (deduplication)
Telling whether the server already has a block, so the upload can be skipped
Spotting which blocks changed during delta sync
exercises.prompt: Every block has a unique hash. What can the hash be used for?

exercises.explanation: File blocks are large and read and written per block, which suits object storage. Metadata is small and needs queries and updates, which suits a database plus a cache. Think of blocks as boxes in a warehouse and metadata as the directory of which boxes make up which file.
options: Once separated, a notification service is no longer needed to push changes
Object storage has no redundancy, so the metadata database must back it up
The metadata database cannot store file names with special characters
Bulk content and the small directory have different loads, so each scales on its own
exercises.prompt: Why separate file blocks and metadata into two planes instead of storing whole files in the metadata database?

exercises.explanation: The block server handles content, the API server handles every workflow except the upload itself, and the notification service only says “something changed”. The offline backup queue accumulates changes for clients that are not online, and cold storage cuts cost.
pairs: Chunks, compresses, encrypts, stores to cloud
Holds changes for clients that are offline
exercises.prompt: Match each component with its responsibility

exercises.explanation: A notification only says the directory changed. The client then asks the API server for the latest metadata and downloads the changed blocks, so file content travels over the high-volume block storage path.
exercises.prompt: When the notification service pushes a change, it only needs to tell the client which file changed, not carry the file content.

exercises.explanation: The update processed first succeeds, and the later one receives a conflict. The system keeps both copies and lets the user merge or overwrite. This is a conflict policy, not Google Docs-style character-level real-time merging, and silently overwriting or discarding would lose data.
options: Merge both users' edits character by character on the server
Silently discard user 2's edit without any notice
Flag a conflict and keep both user 2's copy and the latest server version
Overwrite with user 2's content; the last writer wins
exercises.prompt: User 1 and user 2 both edit the same file starting from version 5, and the server processes user 1's request first. When user 2's request arrives, what should the system do?

exercises.explanation: Client clocks can be inaccurate or even changed by users. “Processed first” must be defined by the server's version rule, for example a conditional update with base_version: whoever moves the version from 5 to 6 first wins.
exercises.prompt: To decide which of two conflicting edits was “processed first”, you can compare the local clocks of the two clients at submission time.

exercises.explanation: base_version is the version the edit was based on. A conditional update guarantees that only one request can move the version from 5 to 6; the other finds the version has already changed and enters the conflict flow.
exercises.prompt: Complete the conflict detection approach
exercises.text: When submitting an edit, the client includes [[base_version]], and the server performs a [[conditional update]]: it writes only if that value equals the current version, and otherwise reports a conflict.

lessons.title: Upload and Sync
lessons.summary: Upload states, delta sync, and where to chunk

exercises.explanation: File describes the file itself, Block records which blocks rebuild it, and File Version lets users go back to older versions. The block content itself is not in the metadata database; it lives in cloud storage.
pairs: Block info needed to rebuild a file
exercises.prompt: Match each metadata table with what it stores

exercises.explanation: The callback is only a signal that an object was written. The version is published atomically only after the whole block list is verified, and other devices are notified after that. Otherwise they would download an incomplete file.
items: Upload the file blocks; metadata is marked pending
Cloud storage fires the upload-complete callback
Verify the block list, sizes, and checksums
Atomically publish the version; status becomes uploaded
The notification service informs the relevant clients
exercises.prompt: Put one file upload in order, from start until it becomes visible to other devices

exercises.explanation: An object event only proves that one object was written, not that every block of the file has arrived. Verify the block list, sizes, and checksums, then publish the file version atomically.
exercises.prompt: If S3 fires an object-upload-complete callback, all blocks of the whole file have arrived.

exercises.explanation: Callbacks can be duplicated, so the handler must be idempotent: if the version is already published, simply return. Creating a version per callback would add phantom versions to the history, and erroring and deleting could destroy a perfectly good file.
options: Raise an error on a duplicate callback and delete the file
Make it idempotent: a duplicate callback neither republishes nor notifies again
Create a new file version on every callback
Move the file back to pending on the second callback
exercises.prompt: The upload-complete callback is delivered twice because of a network retry. How should the handler be designed?

exercises.explanation: pending means the content has not been fully verified, so other devices must not treat it as a complete file. Zero-filling would produce a corrupted file. It is not a conflict and does not mean failure; it simply is not verified yet.
options: Assume the upload failed and delete the metadata entry
Download the blocks that have arrived and fill the rest with zeros
Not download it as a complete file yet, and wait until it becomes uploaded
Save it locally as a conflicted copy
exercises.prompt: A phone sees that a file's metadata status is still `pending`. What should it do?

exercises.explanation: Chunking happens on the block server, so the client still sends the whole 1 GB file to it every time. The block server chunks and compares, and writes only the changed blocks to S3. So the chapter's design only saves the block-server-to-S3 hop.
options: The upload from the client to the block server
The traffic of the API server writing to the metadata database
The traffic of the client receiving notifications
The hop from the block server to S3
exercises.prompt: The chapter has the block server chunk, compress, and encrypt files. A user edits one small part of a 1 GB file. With this design, which part of the traffic does delta sync save?

exercises.explanation: Chunking and hashing happen on the client. It sends the block list first and then only the missing blocks, so unchanged blocks never use upstream bandwidth. Dropbox has publicly described this approach (4 MB blocks, SHA-256 hashes).
items: Chunk locally and compute each block's hash
Submit the block list to the server
The server replies which blocks are missing
The client uploads only the missing blocks
exercises.prompt: To save client upload bandwidth, real sync clients upload like this. Put the steps in order

exercises.explanation: Delta sync pays off when a file is large and only a small part changed: only the few changed blocks are sent, which saves most of the traffic. For a brand-new or fully rewritten file, every block is new and there is nothing to save.
options: Uploading a newly recorded video
Rewriting a file's entire content
Creating a new 500 KB document
A few blocks changed in a 10 GB VM image
exercises.prompt: In which scenario does delta sync save the most bandwidth?

exercises.explanation: Compressing already-compressed videos or images again usually gains little: it wastes computation without saving much traffic. That is why the chapter picks the compression algorithm by file type instead of recompressing everything.
exercises.prompt: Compressing already-compressed videos and images again before sync usually brings little benefit.

lessons.title: Download & Storage
lessons.summary: Catch-up, dedup cleanup, versions, failover

exercises.explanation: The notification only says “something changed”. The metadata tells the client which blocks make up the new version, so it downloads the changed blocks and assembles the file in order.
items: The notification service signals a change
The client fetches the latest metadata
Download the changed blocks
Rebuild the file in block order
exercises.prompt: Another device edited a file. Put the steps by which this device gets the update in order

exercises.explanation: While a client is offline, its change information is saved (the architecture calls this the offline backup queue), and the client pulls the latest changes after coming online. Only when the offline record has outlived its retention period is a full reconciliation needed.
options: The phone pushes the files directly to the laptop over P2P
The laptop must download the entire drive again
The notification service keeps resending until the laptop powers on
Changes made while offline are stored first, and the laptop pulls them once online
exercises.prompt: A laptop was off for three days, and 20 files were edited on a phone in the meantime. How does the laptop get those changes when it comes back online?

exercises.explanation: Notifications can be lost, duplicated, or reordered. The client must remember which version or cursor it has synced to: after a missed notification it can re-pull a snapshot or the delta from its cursor, and duplicate notifications are ignored by version number.
exercises.prompt: A client can simply pull changes whenever it receives a notification, with no need to track a version number or change cursor.

exercises.explanation: Offline records have a retention period. Once it passes, the delta is gone, so the only option is to compare local state against a server snapshot in full. Assuming nothing changed would miss updates, and notifications are not kept forever.
options: Run a full reconciliation with the server
Assume nothing changed in the meantime
Wait for the notification service to resend all historical notifications
Ask the user to re-upload all local files
exercises.prompt: A client was offline so long that the offline changes the server kept for it were purged after the retention period. What should it do when it comes back online?

exercises.explanation: Equal block hashes mean equal content, so multiple files or versions can reference the same block. Because blocks are shared, deletion must check whether any references remain and cannot simply remove the block along with one version.
exercises.prompt: Deduplication identifies duplicate content by block hash within an account, so identical blocks in the same account are stored only once.

exercises.explanation: Deduplication lets several versions share blocks. Only blocks with no live reference and past the retention or rollback window may be reclaimed. Otherwise deleting an old version would corrupt the current file.
options: Move them to cold storage and remove v3's references to them
Keep them; reclaim only unreferenced blocks past retention
Have v3 re-upload those blocks, then delete them
Delete them immediately along with v1 to save space
exercises.prompt: A user deletes the old version v1, but some of v1's blocks are also referenced by the current version v3. What is the right way to handle those blocks?

exercises.explanation: If every edit of a frequently modified file leaves a version, history grows without bound. The chapter's policy is to cap the number of versions and prefer recent ones. Keeping only the first version would drop the functional requirement to retain revisions.
options: Keep only the first version to save space
Keep every version so you can go back to any moment
Cap the number of versions and prefer the recent ones
Copy the whole file as a new version on every edit
exercises.prompt: A file is autosaved hundreds of times a day. Following the chapter's version policy, how should versions be kept?

exercises.explanation: The three target duplicate content, ever-growing history, and cold data. Delta sync saves transfer bandwidth, not storage space.
exercises.prompt: Complete the three storage optimizations
exercises.text: Use [[deduplication]] by block hash, cap the [[number of versions]] you keep, and move files that are rarely accessed to [[cold storage]] such as S3 Glacier.

exercises.explanation: Every component has redundancy: a standby LB, replaceable block servers, primary-replica failover, cross-region replicas, and reconnectable notification nodes. To close out, also confirm how much data loss is acceptable (RPO) and how fast recovery must be (RTO).
pairs: A standby load balancer takes over
Pending tasks go to other servers
exercises.prompt: Match each failure with its handling

chapters.title: Proximity Service
keyPoints: Nearby search has two steps: a spatial index recalls a few candidates, then real spherical distance filters and ranks them. Never guess from cells.
Business locations rarely change and reads dominate. The LBS is stateless and read-only, replicas scale reads, and updates can apply in a daily batch.
A longer geohash prefix means a smaller cell, but nearby points may not share one. Query the home cell and neighbors; expand if the circle isn’t covered.
A quadtree splits cells by density (here, at most 100 businesses per leaf). It suits k-NN, but takes minutes to build at startup and is hard to update.
