Use the geohash, not GPS coordinates, as the cache key. A cell caches business IDs and business_id caches details, so same-cell users share candidates.
S2 numbers spherical cells along a Hilbert curve. Multi-level cells can cover any region, which suits geofencing.

labs.title: Geohash Nearby Search: Pick Precision, Query Nine Cells, Filter Exactly
Quadtree: Split Cells by Density, Then Find the Nearest k

lessons.title: Needs and Design
lessons.summary: Estimation, read-heavy load, service roles

exercises.explanation: 100 million × 5 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 5,787, which the chapter rounds roughly to 5,000. This is an all-day average. Peaks in popular areas need a separate estimate and can’t be used for capacity directly.
options: About 580
About 58,000
About 5,800
About 1,200
exercises.prompt: With 100 million DAU, each searching 5 times a day, what is the average search QPS?

exercises.explanation: 5,000 is the all-day average (about 5,787 exactly). The non-functional requirements call for surviving peak traffic in popular areas, so the peak needs its own estimate and some headroom.
exercises.prompt: The estimate of about 5,000 QPS already includes peak traffic in popular areas, so provisioning capacity for it is enough.

exercises.explanation: A business address barely moves and updates needn’t be real time, yet users search all day. In the nearby-friends case, locations keep changing, so writes and pushes dominate. The LBS is read-only. Creates, updates, and deletes belong to the business service.
options: Business search must be strongly consistent, so reads go to the primary
Business locations rarely change and reads far outnumber writes, so write load is light
There are more businesses (200 million) than users (100 million)
The LBS also handles creating, updating, and deleting businesses
exercises.prompt: Nearby businesses and nearby friends both look things up by location. Why does this chapter focus on scaling reads?

exercises.explanation: Structured data, transactions, and mature indexes with replication together make the case. Being read-heavy doesn’t by itself point to MySQL, and nearby search still depends on the spatial index covered later.
options: Business data is structured
The system is read-heavy, so a relational database is required
It has mature indexing and primary-replica replication
Business updates need transactions
An ordinary relational index can handle nearby search efficiently
exercises.prompt: The chapter stores business data in a relational database such as MySQL. Which of these are sound reasons?

exercises.explanation: In the service tier, the LBS is read-only and stateless, while the business service handles creates, updates, deletes, and details. In the data tier, writes land on the primary and replicate out, and the LBS reads from replicas. Replica lag is acceptable because business changes needn’t take effect in real time.
pairs: Routes requests to the right service
Copies the primary, may lag slightly
exercises.prompt: Match each role in the high-level architecture with its responsibility

exercises.explanation: The functional requirements say business creates, updates, and deletes needn’t take effect in real time, so a briefly stale replica is fine. Reading from the primary or replicating synchronously would give up read scalability, and the LBS never handles write requests.
options: No, the LBS must switch to reading from the primary
Yes, because the LBS writes the new address back to the replica
No, replication to all replicas should be synchronous
Yes, business updates don’t have to take effect in real time
exercises.prompt: A business just changed its address on the primary, but the LBS still reads the old address from a replica. Under this chapter’s requirements, is that acceptable?

exercises.explanation: The LBS holds no session or write state that would need migrating. Any instance can answer any query, so the load balancer can route freely and you simply add machines at peak. Write requests all go to the business service.
exercises.prompt: The LBS only handles location queries and no writes, so it can be stateless and add or remove instances with traffic.

exercises.explanation: radius is the search radius, 5,000 meters by default. In the final flow’s example the user sets it to 500 meters, and the LBS picks a longer geohash accordingly.
exercises.prompt: Complete the parameters of the nearby-search API
exercises.text: `GET /v1/search/nearby` takes the user’s latitude, longitude, and [[radius]], which defaults to [[5,000 meters]].

lessons.title: Geohash
lessons.summary: 2D search, grids, and geohash boundaries

exercises.explanation: The latitude condition matches a whole horizontal band and the longitude condition a whole vertical band. Each contains many businesses, and only their intersection is the small patch you want. An ordinary one-dimensional index can’t restrict both dimensions efficiently, which is the problem spatial indexes solve.
options: SQL doesn’t allow BETWEEN on two columns in one query
Coordinates are decimals, so the database can’t index them
Each index covers one dimension, and two large result sets must still be intersected
The business table is too small, so indexes only slow queries down
exercises.prompt: You index longitude and latitude separately, then query nearby businesses with two `BETWEEN` conditions. Why is this still slow?
exercises.refAnchor: d16/方案一二维搜索朴素方案

exercises.explanation: The rectangle only recalls candidates. Its four corners lie outside the circle, and the distance covered by one degree of longitude varies with latitude. After fetching candidates you must still filter out businesses beyond the radius by spherical distance.
exercises.prompt: Once the radius is correctly converted to degrees of latitude and longitude, the `BETWEEN` rectangle results can be returned to the user directly.
exercises.refAnchor: d16/方案一二维搜索朴素方案

exercises.explanation: Fixed cells can’t suit both dense cities and sparse countryside. With large cells, downtown packs businesses into one cell. With small cells, the suburbs are full of empty ones. This is also why quadtrees split cells by density.
options: A limited number of cells can’t encode the whole world
You can’t work out which fixed cells are neighbors
Each cell needs its own database table
Businesses are unevenly spread: city cells are packed, rural cells nearly empty
exercises.prompt: What is the main problem with indexing the world as fixed-size cells?

exercises.explanation: A shorter geohash means larger cells. In the chapter’s example, 500 meters uses length 6. With a bigger radius and still-fine cells, the home cell plus its neighbors can’t cover the circle. Use the radius reference table to pick a length that covers the query area.
options: No change, geohash length is unrelated to radius
Longer, using finer cells for more precision
Shorter, using larger cells to cover a larger area
Jump straight to the maximum precision of 12
exercises.prompt: The user raises the search radius from 500 meters to 5 km. How should the geohash length the LBS uses change?

exercises.explanation: The relationship runs one way. A long shared prefix means both are in the same small cell, but being close doesn’t guarantee a shared prefix. Two points only a few meters apart on opposite sides of the equator may share no prefix at all.
exercises.prompt: If two places share no geohash prefix at all, they must be far apart.

exercises.explanation: A geohash is a hierarchical grid: each extra character subdivides the previous cell. So the longer the shared prefix, the smaller the cell both locations fall in. The reverse doesn’t hold, so don’t treat it as a distance formula.
exercises.prompt: The longer the prefix two geohashes share, the smaller the grid area they both fall in.

exercises.explanation: Cell boundaries are arbitrary. A user standing at an edge may have a restaurant a few dozen meters away in the next cell. Querying the home cell plus 8 neighbors covers an area centered on the user, then you filter by real distance.
options: Near a cell edge, closer businesses may sit in a neighboring cell
Businesses in neighboring cells usually have higher ratings
Querying more cells improves the Redis cache hit rate
Geohash encoding has errors that multi-cell voting corrects
exercises.prompt: After computing the user’s geohash cell, the LBS also queries the 8 surrounding cells. What is the main reason?

exercises.explanation: The boundary problem comes from the grid itself. A longer encoding only makes cells finer, and the boundaries remain. The fix is to query adjacent cells too, then filter precisely. Geohash is still a common choice for nearby search.
options: Choosing a 12-character encoding eliminates the boundary problem
The boundary problem means geohash can’t be used for nearby search
Queries must include the adjacent cells
Two points with a long shared prefix can still fall in different fine cells
Two close points on opposite sides of the equator may share no prefix
exercises.prompt: Which statements about the geohash boundary problem are correct?

exercises.explanation: The nine cells do the recall, and distance makes the final call. Cells only say a business may be nearby, and the corners of the combined square stick out past the query circle. Filter by real distance rather than guessing from prefix length.
exercises.prompt: Complete the two steps of geohash nearby search
exercises.text: First take the businesses in the home cell and its [[8]] neighbors as candidates, then filter out those beyond the radius by [[spherical distance]] and sort.

lessons.title: Quadtree and S2
lessons.summary: Density splits, k-NN, operations, choosing

exercises.explanation: The build starts at the root and subdivides recursively. Every internal node has exactly four children, and splitting stops once each leaf holds at most the threshold x (100 here). The denser the businesses, the deeper the tree and the smaller the cells.
options: It keeps splitting into four quadrants until each leaf has at most 100
It stays one leaf and is only flagged as a hotspot
The extra 350 are moved into neighboring leaves
That region switches to its own geohash index
exercises.prompt: A quadtree’s leaf threshold is 100. What happens to a region with 450 businesses?

exercises.explanation: A cell splits only when its business count exceeds the threshold, so dense areas are cut fine and sparse areas get one big cell. That is how it adapts to density differences better than fixed-precision geohash.
exercises.prompt: Quadtree cell sizes vary with business density: leaf areas are small downtown and large in the suburbs.

exercises.explanation: k-nearest neighbors asks for the closest k, and the distance isn’t known up front. A quadtree splits by density, so you can search outward from the user’s region until you have k. A fixed-precision nine-cell query may find none in the suburbs.
options: One-dimensional indexes on the table’s latitude and longitude
A quadtree, searching outward from the user’s region for the nearest k
Fixed-precision geohash, querying only nine cells
An even grid, since fixed cells are easy to compute
exercises.prompt: A user wants the 3 nearest gas stations with no radius limit, and in the suburbs they may be far away. Which index fits best?

exercises.explanation: A server can’t take traffic until the build finishes. Restarting all of them at once leaves most LBS instances unable to serve for several minutes. So roll out new versions in batches and always keep enough instances available.
options: They can’t take traffic while building, so many servers are unavailable at once
The old and new quadtrees conflict and corrupt data
Only the first query is slightly slower
The quadtree is copied from other servers, so the impact is small
exercises.prompt: Each LBS server spends several minutes building the quadtree in memory at startup. What happens if you restart every LBS at once to release a new version?

exercises.explanation: Rebuilding is simple but invalidates caches, while in-place changes must handle concurrency and are complex to implement. Business updates aren’t required to be real time here, so a daily batch works. This is also why hard updates count as a quadtree drawback.
options: A quadtree supports no updates at all, so you must switch to geohash
You can modify the tree in place, but that needs locking or similar concurrency control
Under this chapter’s requirements, business updates can be processed in a daily batch
Modifying the tree in place is simpler than rebuilding, so it should be the first choice
The simplest way is to rebuild the tree step by step, invalidating caches
exercises.prompt: Which statements about updating the quadtree after businesses change are correct?

exercises.explanation: An estimate isn’t a guarantee. Memory must also cover IDs, coordinates, node pointers, and language object overhead, and build time depends on tree depth and data distribution. Measure with real data before launch.
exercises.prompt: The chapter estimates the quadtree index at only a few GB, so you can size memory to that number at launch without measuring.

exercises.explanation: S2 can combine cells of different sizes to cover a region of any shape, and lets you set a minimum level, a maximum level, and a maximum cell count, which suits geofencing naturally. Fixed square cells struggle to fit irregular boundaries.
options: A latitude/longitude BETWEEN rectangle query
An even grid, checking fixed cells
S2, using multi-level cells to fit any region
A fixed-precision geohash nine-cell query
exercises.prompt: To build a geofencing feature such as “push a coupon when the user enters a shopping district,” which option fits best?

exercises.explanation: On a Hilbert curve, nearby IDs are usually close in space, but the reverse fails. If two points straddle a high-level cell boundary, the curve may pass one side early and the other much later, so their IDs differ a lot. Don’t use the ID difference as geographic distance.
exercises.prompt: Two points that are close in space can still have S2 cell IDs that are far apart.

exercises.explanation: An even grid has only one cell size. Geohash is a hierarchical grid, and a longer code means finer cells. To choose: nearby search with a fixed radius suits geohash, strong density differences or k-NN suit a quadtree, and complex region coverage or geofencing suits S2.
pairs: String code, longer prefix, smaller cell
Strong at spherical region coverage, geofencing
No levels, one cell size worldwide
Two 1D indexes, slow on large data
exercises.prompt: Match each indexing option with its characteristic

exercises.explanation: A cell keeps splitting only while its business count exceeds the threshold (100 here), so cell size follows density and the search can fan out from near to far to find the nearest k. Fixed precision and fixed radius are geohash traits, and geofencing is S2’s strength.
exercises.prompt: Complete how a quadtree is built
exercises.text: A quadtree splits cells recursively by [[business density]] and stops once a leaf holds no more than the threshold. It excels at [[k-nearest neighbors]] queries.

lessons.title: Scaling and Lookup
lessons.summary: Sharding, replicas, cache keys, a full lookup

exercises.explanation: The premise is that the index table fits on a single machine. It only stores the mapping between geohash and business_id, so there is no technical need to shard it, and its load is reads, which read replicas address most directly. The business table is large, and sharding it by business_id spreads data evenly.
options: The geohash table is the most important data, and sharding risks losing it
The geohash table must sit on the same shard as the business table
Once sharded by geohash, you can’t look up business details
It fits on one machine and the load is reads, so replicas scale it
exercises.prompt: The business table is sharded by `business_id`, but the geohash index table should get read replicas first, not shards. Why?

exercises.explanation: GPS readings are imprecise and change as soon as the user moves, so coordinate keys almost never hit. A geohash maps a whole area to one key, and users in that cell share the business ID list. The final ranking is still computed from each user’s own coordinates.
options: With GPS coordinates as keys you can’t compute neighboring cells
A geohash key can cache the final results already sorted by distance
Redis can’t use decimal coordinates as keys
Coordinates change with every small move, but users in one cell can share a key
exercises.prompt: Why does nearby search use the geohash as the cache key instead of the user’s GPS coordinates?

exercises.explanation: Users in the same cell can share the candidate business ID list, but their coordinates differ, so each business is at a different distance and the ranking differs too. Recompute distances and filter using each user’s own coordinates.
exercises.prompt: Two users in the same geohash cell can directly share the cached final results, already sorted by distance.

exercises.explanation: The first layer answers “who is in this cell,” and the second answers “what does this business look like.” A lookup first fetches the business IDs for the 9 cells from the first layer, then fetches details from the second.
exercises.prompt: Complete the two cache layers
exercises.text: The cache keyed by [[geohash]] stores the business IDs in a cell, and the cache keyed by [[business_id]] stores details such as name, address, and reviews.

exercises.explanation: First settle the cells (in the chapter’s example 500 meters maps to length 6), then fetch candidate IDs for the 9 cells in parallel, and finally fetch details and sort by distance from the user, filtering out candidates beyond the radius.
items: Client sends coordinates and radius to the load balancer
Load balancer forwards to the LBS
LBS picks a geohash length and computes neighbors
Query the geohash Redis in parallel for business IDs
Fetch business details, sort by distance, and return
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a “restaurants within 500 meters” lookup in order

exercises.explanation: The nine cells together form a square larger than the query circle, so businesses in the corners may be over 500 meters away. Filter and sort by real distance. Keeping only the home cell would miss close neighbors just across the boundary.
options: Compute real distances, drop those beyond the radius, then sort
Sort by business ID ascending and return
Keep only businesses in the same cell as the user
Sort by geohash alphabetical order and return directly
exercises.prompt: The LBS queried 9 cells at geohash length 6 and got 120 candidate restaurants. What must it still do before returning them?

exercises.explanation: Actual cell size varies with latitude and precision, so nine cells aren’t guaranteed to suffice. Check that the chosen cells cover the whole query circle, keep expanding neighbors if they don’t, and filter precisely at the end.
options: Switch the cache key back to GPS coordinates and query again
Automatically shrink the user’s radius to the nine-cell area
Return only the businesses in the nine cells and ignore the rest of the circle
Expand neighbors or use a shorter encoding until the circle is covered
exercises.prompt: The encoding length was chosen too long, so the home cell plus 8 neighbors is still smaller than the search circle. What should you do?

exercises.explanation: The chapter lists three key optimizations: parallel Redis calls cut waiting, the geohash index cuts candidates, and caching speeds up ID and detail lookups. Batch updates and primary writes address writes and don’t directly shorten search latency.
options: Caching each cell’s business IDs and the business details
Processing business updates in a daily batch
Calling Redis for the 9 cells in parallel
Sending all business writes through the primary
Using the geohash index to cut the number of candidates
exercises.prompt: In the final architecture, which practices directly shorten nearby-search response time?

exercises.explanation: Although the chapter’s section is titled as handling real-time updates, the actual design processes business updates in a daily batch. The functional requirements also say business creates, updates, and deletes needn’t take effect in real time, so this delay is acceptable.
exercises.prompt: Under this chapter’s design, after a business changes its address, users may not find the new location until the next batch run, and the requirements allow this.

chapters.title: Nearby Friends
keyPoints: People keep moving: online devices report locations over WebSocket and the backend fans out to online friends instead of scanning everyone.
The Redis location cache holds only current locations with a TTL; expiry means inactive. History goes to a write-heavy store like Cassandra.
One Pub/Sub channel per user: you publish to your own channel, friends’ servers subscribe, and distance filtering happens on the subscriber side.
10 million ÷ 30 seconds ≈ 333,000 updates/s (the chapter rounds to 334,000); a fan-out of about 40 gives about 14 million pushes/s.
Pub/Sub finds channels via service discovery and consistent hashing; migrating a channel forces resubscribes and missed points, so do it off-peak.
Nearby strangers use per-geohash-cell channels plus neighboring cells; Erlang can replace Redis Pub/Sub, but talent is hard to find.

labs.title: Nearby friends: one channel per user, filtered by distance on the subscriber

lessons.title: Scope & Estimates
lessons.summary: Scoping Q&A, update QPS, and push volume

exercises.explanation: The 5-mile straight-line distance decides how you filter, the 10-minute disappearance maps to the location cache’s TTL, and keeping history calls for a separate history database. The scope explicitly uses straight-line distance; GDPR is set aside to keep the interview simple, but a real product can’t ignore privacy.
options: Distance must account for actual roads and rivers
Location history must be kept for analytics such as machine learning
Inactive friends can drop off the list after 10 minutes
“Nearby” means a straight-line distance within 5 miles, configurable
GDPR data-deletion requests must be handled in real time
exercises.prompt: Which assumptions agreed during the opening scope Q&A directly affect the design?
exercises.refAnchor: d17/第一步理解问题并确定范围
exercises.refTitle: Step 1: Understand the Problem and Establish Design Scope

exercises.explanation: Periodic reporting only happens while the app is open. Of 100 million daily users, 10% online at once gives 10 million, the number that keeps generating updates. The 10% of friends online comes in later, for fan-out; don’t mix the two up.
options: Only 10% of the 100 million have any friends
Only users online at the same time report locations periodically
Redis can store at most 10 million keys
Only 10% of each person’s friends use the feature
exercises.prompt: When estimating location-update QPS, why use 10 million rather than 100 million daily active users?

exercises.explanation: 10 million ÷ 30 ≈ 333,000 per second; the chapter rounds this to 334,000 and carries it through the later estimates. 14 million is the push volume after multiplying by a fan-out of about 40, so don’t confuse reports with pushes.
options: About 33,000 per second
About 330,000 per second
About 3.3 million per second
About 14 million per second
exercises.prompt: With 10 million users online at once, each reporting every 30 seconds, roughly what is the location-update QPS?

exercises.explanation: 400 × 10% = 40, and 334,000 × 40 ≈ 13.36 million, which the chapter rounds to about 14 million. This push volume, not memory capacity, determines how many Redis Pub/Sub servers you need.
exercises.prompt: Complete the push-volume estimate
exercises.text: With an average of 400 friends, [[10%]] of them online, one update fans out to about [[40]] messages; multiplied by about 334,000 updates per second, that gives about [[14 million]] pushes per second.

exercises.explanation: Update QPS = online users ÷ interval, so shrinking the interval to 1 second multiplies the load by 30. People walk slowly, and a position that is a few dozen seconds old barely affects a “within 5 miles” check, so it isn’t worth multiplying the cost.
options: Redis TTLs can’t be set shorter than 30 seconds
People move slowly, so reporting more often gains little while multiplying the load
A phone’s GPS chip can only get one fix every 30 seconds
A WebSocket connection can only send one message every 30 seconds
exercises.prompt: The chapter sets the location refresh interval at 30 seconds, not 1 second. What is the main reason?

exercises.explanation: Update QPS becomes 10 million ÷ 10 = 1 million per second, and each update still fans out to about 40 messages, so pushes reach about 40 million per second, 3 times the original. At about 100,000 per second per server, the Pub/Sub cluster would need about 400 servers.
options: About 40 million, 3 times the original
Still about 14 million, because push volume depends only on friend count
About 140 million, 10 times the original
About 4.7 million, one third of the original
exercises.prompt: If the refresh interval drops from 30 seconds to 10 seconds with all other assumptions unchanged, roughly how many Pub/Sub pushes per second result?

exercises.explanation: The non-functional requirements say an occasional lost point is acceptable as long as the system stays generally available. Locations refresh every 30 seconds, so one lost point is quickly overwritten by the next. This is also why a few missed points during a Pub/Sub migration are tolerable.
exercises.prompt: Nearby friends can tolerate the occasional lost location point, because the next periodic update brings a fresh position soon.

exercises.explanation: The requirements call only for eventual consistency: a few seconds of lag between replicas is acceptable. Locations update only every 30 seconds and carry a timestamp, so a few seconds of lag barely affects whether a friend is “within 5 miles.”
exercises.prompt: Location store replicas must be strongly consistent with each other, or friends will see wrong distances.

exercises.explanation: Each requirement lands on a component: long connections keep updates timely, a TTL makes inactive users drop off on their own, and the history store is kept separate from the current-location cache. Tolerating lost points and eventual consistency relax the constraints and make the system easier to scale.
pairs: A few missed points tolerated in migration
A few seconds of cache replica lag is fine
exercises.prompt: Match each requirement with its design choice
exercises.refAnchor: d17/第一步理解问题并确定范围
exercises.refTitle: Step 1: Understand the Problem and Establish Design Scope

lessons.title: Push Architecture
lessons.summary: Connections, location cache, a channel per user

exercises.explanation: Each person would need a connection to dozens of online friends, but mobile networks come and go and batteries are limited, so P2P is impractical. Phones can do both encryption and distance filtering, so those aren’t the issue. The backend handles fan-out, and a phone needs only one long connection to a server.
options: Mobile networks are flaky and drain batteries, so P2P links are hard to keep up
P2P takes more hops, so latency is always higher than going through a server
Phones have no way to filter friends by a 5-mile range
P2P communication has no way to encrypt location data
exercises.prompt: Why not have friends’ phones exchange locations directly, peer to peer (P2P)?

exercises.explanation: The server must push friends’ locations to clients at any time, which needs a bidirectional long connection; adding a friend or editing a profile is an ordinary request-response call. Note that WebSocket servers are stateful, so scaling them is actually harder.
options: WebSocket servers are stateless, so they scale more easily
Locations need server-initiated pushes; auxiliary features are plain request-response
REST endpoints can’t carry decimals such as latitude and longitude
WebSocket encrypts more strongly, which suits sensitive locations
exercises.prompt: Location updates use WebSocket, while friend management and profile edits use REST. Why split them this way?

exercises.explanation: A channel belongs to the person being followed: A publishes their location to A’s own channel, and the server hosting A’s friend B subscribes to A’s channel. One server can share a single subscription on behalf of many of its local clients.
exercises.prompt: Each user subscribes only to their own channel, and friends’ location updates are written into that channel.

exercises.explanation: The publisher just publishes to its own channel and doesn’t need to know which server each friend is on; Redis Pub/Sub delivers to all subscribers; S2 computes the distance using B’s coordinates in memory and pushes only if it is within 5 miles.
options: B’s client queries Redis for A’s location every 30 seconds
S1 publishes to A’s channel, and subscriber S2 filters and pushes it to B
S1 finds that B is on S2 and sends the location straight to S2
S1 publishes to B’s channel, and B subscribes to their own channel
exercises.prompt: A and B are friends, both online, connected to servers S1 and S2. After A reports a new location, how does B receive it?

exercises.explanation: A publisher always publishes to its own channel and doesn’t know where each friend is. Filtering happens on the subscribing server, which holds its local users’ coordinates and drops the update when the distance exceeds the threshold.
options: It is pushed to B as usual, and B’s client hides it
C’s server never publishes the update in the first place
The server computes a distance over 5 miles and doesn’t push it to B
Redis intercepts it before delivery
exercises.prompt: Friend C is 30 miles away. What happens after C’s location update reaches the server hosting B?

exercises.explanation: The cache only cares about where someone is now; the TTL lets people who stop reporting disappear on their own, and initialization reads friends’ locations from here. Full trajectories go to the history store, and the requirements call only for eventual consistency.
options: Clients load friends’ current locations from it at initialization
It must keep full trajectories for machine-learning analysis
Entries carry a TTL; expiry means the user is inactive
Replicas must replicate with strong consistency
It stores only each active user’s latest location
exercises.prompt: Which statements about the Redis location cache are correct?

exercises.explanation: The history store records trajectories for analysis and has a different retention policy. Showing nearby friends needs only each person’s current location, read straight from the TTL cache. The two have different jobs.
exercises.prompt: The nearby friends list reads from the location cache; the location history database is not on this read path.

exercises.explanation: TTL expiry means the user is inactive and the cache entry is deleted, which matches “inactive friends can disappear after 10 minutes.” The history database isn’t on the read path, and channel names are agreed in advance, so no channel is deleted.
options: Their last known location, shown indefinitely
The system fills in the last location from the history database
Their channel is deleted and you must add them as a friend again
They disappear from the nearby friends list, treated as inactive
exercises.prompt: A friend closes the app and stops reporting, and their location cache entry is deleted when its TTL expires. What do other people see?

exercises.explanation: The WebSocket servers are stateful and hold the device connections. Redis plays two roles: a location cache with TTLs and a lightweight Pub/Sub bus. For the history, choose a write-heavy store such as Cassandra.
pairs: Current location per user, with a TTL
Message bus with one channel per user
exercises.prompt: Match each component with its role

lessons.title: Update Flow
lessons.summary: Reporting, init, subscriptions, and data model

exercises.explanation: This leaves out two steps: writing to the history database and updating the location cache. The key point is that the publisher does no distance check and only publishes to its own channel; filtering happens on the subscribing servers.
items: Phone sends its location to a WebSocket server
Server publishes to that user’s own Redis channel
Redis delivers it to servers subscribed to that channel
Subscribing server computes distances to local friends
Only updates within 5 miles are pushed to clients
exercises.prompt: Put one location update in order, from the phone to the friend’s screen

exercises.explanation: A subscribing server must decide whether a friend is within 5 miles, which requires its local user’s latest coordinates; keeping them in memory avoids a Redis lookup for every friend update. It is not a durable backup.
options: As the only backup of locations in case Redis fails
As a write buffer for batching inserts into the history database
To decide which Redis server should host that user’s own channel
To compute distances from local coordinates when a friend’s update arrives
exercises.prompt: While updating the location cache, the WebSocket server also keeps the user’s coordinates in memory. Why?

exercises.explanation: Client initialization: fetch the friend list, subscribe to each friend’s channel, pull current locations from the location cache, then send them to the client. Otherwise a newly online user could wait up to 30 seconds to see the first nearby friends.
exercises.prompt: When a client first connects, the server fetches friends’ current locations from the location cache and sends them right away, without waiting for the friends’ next report.

exercises.explanation: When a friendship changes, the server hosting the affected user subscribes to the new friend’s channel; this is the “subscribe to a new friend” operation in the API. Channel names are agreed in advance, so none needs to be created on the fly, and the history database isn’t on this path.
options: Forward B’s channel to D
Create a new channel for D
Subscribe to D’s channel
Pull D’s entire trajectory from the history database
exercises.prompt: B has just become friends with D, and both are online. What must B’s WebSocket server do before B starts receiving D’s location?

exercises.explanation: A’s channel still has other friends subscribed and A’s server keeps publishing as usual, so only B’s side unsubscribes. Deleting the channel or clearing the cache would hide A from A’s other friends too.
options: B’s server unsubscribes from A’s channel
Clear A’s entry in the location cache
Delete A’s channel
Tell A’s server to stop publishing
exercises.prompt: B removes friend A. What should happen so that B no longer receives A’s location?

exercises.explanation: User IDs are not secret, so you can’t protect locations by assuming others don’t know them. The server must verify the real friendship and the location-sharing permission before subscribing on the client’s behalf.
exercises.prompt: When a client asks to subscribe to a user’s channel, the server can simply comply, since only friends know each other’s user ID.

exercises.explanation: Location reporting, receiving updates, client initialization, and subscribing or unsubscribing to friends all happen on the long connection. Auxiliary features such as editing a profile or maintaining friendships use traditional HTTP request/response.
options: Adding a friendship record to the friends table
Reporting your own location periodically
The server sending down which friends to subscribe or unsubscribe
Receiving friends’ location updates
Editing your profile
exercises.prompt: Which of these operations go over WebSocket rather than the regular HTTP API?

exercises.explanation: Add a sequence number to each report or compare event times: if the cache already holds the 12:00:30 location, a late 12:00:00 one is discarded. Overwriting in arrival order is exactly what causes the bug.
options: Average the two locations and write the result to the cache
Shorten the TTL so old locations expire sooner
Overwrite in the order the server received them
Attach a sequence number or event time and accept only newer locations
exercises.prompt: Because of network jitter, A’s 12:00:30 location reaches the server later than A’s 12:00:00 location. How do you keep the older location from overwriting the newer one?

exercises.explanation: The timestamp tells users how long ago a location was updated. A current location with a TTL is Redis’s strength; the history is a constant stream of heavy writes, which Cassandra handles well. ZooKeeper is what records how Pub/Sub channels are distributed.
exercises.prompt: Complete the data model
exercises.text: The location cache stores `user_id → (latitude, longitude, [[timestamp]])`. It only cares about the current location and needs a TTL, so it uses [[Redis]]; the write-heavy history table uses [[Cassandra]].

lessons.title: Scaling & Variants
lessons.summary: Pub/Sub cluster, scaling in and out, nearby strangers

exercises.explanation: A WebSocket server is stateful and holds a large number of long connections. Mark it as draining so it stops accepting new connections, then take it out of the pool, which avoids dropping a big batch of users at once.
options: Copy its connection info to Redis, then shut the machine down immediately
Wait until the machine’s CPU usage drops to 0, then shut it down
Shut it down right away; clients will reconnect to other servers on their own
Mark it as draining so it takes no new connections, then remove it from the pool
exercises.prompt: What is the right way to scale in (remove) a WebSocket server?

exercises.explanation: Memory and throughput are separate budgets: at about 100,000 pushes per second per server, 14 million ÷ 100,000 = 140 servers, so CPU is the real bottleneck. These are estimates; message size, subscription count, and Redis version all change the result, so load test before launch.
options: The memory estimate is wrong; about 14 TB is really needed
Every channel must be replicated 70 times for reliability
The bottleneck is about 14 million pushes per second, not memory
Each Redis server can create at most 1 million channels
exercises.prompt: The chapter’s estimate puts the channels at about 200 GB of memory, which two 100 GB Redis servers could hold. Why does it end up needing about 140 servers?

exercises.explanation: A channel with no subscribers doesn’t need to retain messages the way a durable queue does. That suits nearby friends: an offline person doesn’t need old locations, and on coming online gets the current location from the location cache.
exercises.prompt: A Redis Pub/Sub channel with no subscribers keeps its messages like a durable queue and replays them when subscribers come online.

exercises.explanation: A channel name can be derived directly from the user ID, so publishers and subscribers both know where to look; a channel nobody subscribes to doesn’t need to retain messages, so agreeing on names in advance adds no coordination step.
exercises.prompt: You can agree on all users’ channel names in advance, so no extra coordination is needed to create a channel when a user comes online.

exercises.explanation: The TTL limits how much data is held at once, but the write load of about 334,000 location updates per second remains. The chapter’s answer is to add Redis nodes and shard.
exercises.prompt: Because the location cache has a TTL and bounded data size, a single Redis server can handle all the location writes.

exercises.explanation: A service discovery component such as ZooKeeper or etcd records the live nodes and channel distribution, and each WebSocket server caches the hash ring in memory and computes a channel’s location directly from its name. Querying every server is too expensive, and one primary Redis can’t carry the push volume.
options: Broadcast a query to every Redis server, one by one
The client reports which server its channel is on
Get channel distribution from service discovery, then use a local hash ring
Keep all channels on one primary Redis
exercises.prompt: After Pub/Sub grows to several Redis servers, how does a WebSocket server know which machine holds a user’s channel?

exercises.explanation: Channels carry subscriptions, so moving one forces its subscribers to resubscribe, and points may be missed meanwhile. A few lost points are tolerable, but schedule it off-peak anyway. Consistent hashing means a node change affects only a small share of channels. The location cache is separate and unaffected.
options: Consistent hashing reduces the number of channels that must move
It triggers many resubscribe requests
The migration wipes the data in the location cache
Pub/Sub nodes are stateless and can be added or removed at any time
Some location points may be missed during migration
exercises.prompt: When you scale out the Redis Pub/Sub cluster and move channels, which statements are correct?

exercises.explanation: The chapter cites Facebook’s 5,000-friend limit as an example: cap friend counts first. The WebSocket server hosting a super user carries more load, but their friends are spread across a large number of servers, so the total pressure is spread out.
options: Deploy a dedicated Redis cluster just for them
Have all their friends poll for their location every second
Stop fanning out their updates and only write them to the history database
Cap the number of friends and let the many servers spread out the rest of the load
exercises.prompt: A “super user” has 5,000 friends. How does the chapter view the load such users create?

exercises.explanation: Strangers have no friend relationship, so you can’t use “subscribe to a friend’s channel.” Instead, everyone in the same geohash area shares one channel, and you also subscribe to adjacent cells so nearby people just across a cell border aren’t missed.
options: Every user subscribes to the location channels of all users
Have strangers become friends first, then subscribe to each other’s channels
Scan the whole table every 30 seconds to find people nearby
Create channels per geohash cell and subscribe to neighboring cells too
exercises.prompt: The interviewer adds a requirement: “occasionally show nearby strangers on the map.” What does the chapter suggest?

exercises.explanation: Strangers have no friendship, so channels are built per area; super users first get a friend cap; migration uses consistent hashing to move fewer channels; stateful WebSocket servers must be drained before going down. Erlang handles connections and channels with lightweight processes, but it is niche and hard to hire for.
pairs: Channel per geohash cell, subscribe to neighbors
Consistent hashing to move fewer channels
Powerful lightweight processes, hard to hire
exercises.prompt: Match each scaling problem with its approach

chapters.title: Google Maps
keyPoints: A map splits into three paths: batched location reports, static tiles via a CDN, and routing over layered routing tiles, each sized to its own load.
Reporting QPS depends on the batch interval: 5 billion navigation minutes a day is about 200,000 QPS, peaking near 1 million. Size each path separately.
Location data is write-heavy and stales fast: Cassandra favors availability, the partition key adds a time bucket, and Kafka feeds traffic and ETA.
Each zoom level multiplies tiles by 4, yet a screen needs only ten or so. Static tiles are pre-generated and served by a CDN; vector tiles save bandwidth.
Image tiles are for seeing, routing tiles for computing. Long trips use high-level tiles; aim for accurate, reasonably fast routes, not global shortest.
To reroute around an incident, filter candidates with coarse tiles, then check the actual path. Use WebSocket for continuous traffic pushes.

labs.title: Map Tiles: Each Zoom Level Multiplies the Tiles by 4
Routing Tiles: Load Only the Subgraph a Route Needs

lessons.title: Scope and Maps
lessons.summary: Scope, projections, geocoding, and the road graph

exercises.explanation: The scope explicitly includes real-time traffic, because ETAs are inaccurate without it. Multi-stop routes are only a possible extension mentioned in the wrap-up, and business places and photos are excluded. Nearby restaurant search depends on business place data, so it is out of scope too.
options: Showing photos and reviews of business places
Planning a ride-hailing route through several stops in order
Estimating ETA with real-time traffic
Searching for restaurants near the user
exercises.prompt: The interviewer asks whether business places, photos, and multi-stop routes are in scope. Given the scope this chapter sets, which of these **still needs** to be designed?
exercises.refAnchor: d18/第一步理解问题并确定范围
exercises.refTitle: Step 1: Understand the Problem and Establish Design Scope

exercises.explanation: Projections almost always distort area and distance, and Mercator-style projections magnify more the closer you get to the poles. Compute exact distances from latitude and longitude with a suitable geographic algorithm, not by subtracting screen pixels.
exercises.prompt: On a Web Mercator map, two points 1 cm apart on screen are the same real-world distance apart, whether near the equator or at high latitudes.

exercises.explanation: Users type addresses, but routing algorithms need coordinates, so you geocode before navigating. Showing a location fix as a street address takes reverse geocoding. Both can use a GIS mapping between streets and coordinates, then interpolate to estimate where an address falls.
exercises.prompt: Complete the two opposite conversions
exercises.text: [[geocoding]] converts an address to latitude and longitude, and [[reverse geocoding]] converts latitude and longitude to an address.

exercises.explanation: The world’s tiles are estimated at about 70 PB, which a client can neither store nor should download; like a mosaic, it fetches only the few pieces on screen. Tiling does not change projection distortion, image tiles are only for “seeing”, and per-request real-time rendering is exactly what the chapter’s design did not choose.
options: Tiles carry the road graph, so the client can route offline
The full map is petabytes, so the client fetches only the few tiles in view
Tiles let the server render each request in real time
Tiling removes projection distortion, so distances are more accurate
exercises.prompt: Why does a map client split the world into tiles and download them on demand instead of downloading the whole map at once?

exercises.explanation: The road network is modeled as a graph: intersections are nodes and roads are edges. Image tiles are for “seeing” and routing tiles are for “computing”, so they are different things. A projection turns three-dimensional coordinates into a flat plane and almost always distorts some geometric properties.
pairs: A node in the road graph
An edge in the road graph
Pixels or vectors shown to the user
Intersections, roads, and rules for routing
Turns spherical coordinates into a flat plane
exercises.prompt: Match each concept with its meaning in a map system
exercises.refAnchor: d18/将道路数据处理为导航图
exercises.refTitle: Processing Road Data into a Routing Graph

exercises.explanation: The algorithms can handle large graphs; the problem is scale. Searching global roads for every request would exhaust memory and bandwidth, so the graph is split into routing tiles and only the subgraph for the route is loaded. Cycles do not stop Dijkstra from terminating, and one-way streets are just directed edges.
options: Search cost grows with graph size, so loading the whole graph each time is too expensive
One-way streets are directed edges, which Dijkstra cannot handle
The global road graph contains cycles, so the algorithm never terminates
Dijkstra and A* can only handle a graph within one city
exercises.prompt: Why doesn’t the navigation service run Dijkstra or A* directly on the complete global road graph?
exercises.refAnchor: d18/将道路数据处理为导航图
exercises.refTitle: Processing Road Data into a Routing Graph

exercises.explanation: That is exactly how routing tiles are used. Instead of preloading the whole graph, you stitch together the tiles you need along the search direction, loading only data relevant to the route and cutting memory and bandwidth.
exercises.prompt: Routing tiles store references to adjacent tiles, so a search can start from the tile containing the origin and load and stitch together neighboring tiles on demand.
exercises.refAnchor: d18/将道路数据处理为导航图
exercises.refTitle: Processing Road Data into a Routing Graph

exercises.explanation: Stitching many fine tiles over a long route is expensive, so routing tiles are prepared at several levels of detail and chosen by distance. It is like taking the highway first and expanding local roads only near the start and destination. Loading the full national road graph is exactly what routing tiles exist to avoid.
options: Fine tiles get directions wrong; compute routes from image tiles instead
Fine tiles cannot span provinces; load the full national road graph
Fine tiles lack highway data; compare geohashes directly
Too many fine tiles is costly; pick coarser routing tile levels by distance
exercises.prompt: You drive from Shanghai to Beijing. What goes wrong if the whole trip stitches together the finest-grained routing tiles, and how does the chapter’s design handle it?
exercises.refAnchor: d18/将道路数据处理为导航图
exercises.refTitle: Processing Road Data into a Routing Graph

exercises.explanation: Image tiles hold only pixels or vector graphics for display. Routing needs intersections, road connections, and traffic rules, which live in routing tiles. The names are similar but the jobs differ: one is for “seeing”, the other for “computing”.
exercises.prompt: During navigation, you can compute routes directly from the image tiles the client has already downloaded, with no separate routing tiles.
exercises.refAnchor: d18/将道路数据处理为导航图
exercises.refTitle: Processing Road Data into a Routing Graph

exercises.explanation: The non-functional requirements are accuracy, smooth rendering, and saving data and battery, plus ordinary availability and scalability. Navigation only needs routes that are “reasonably fast”, not a guaranteed global shortest. Location data goes stale quickly, so the chapter picks availability over strong consistency.
options: Save mobile data and battery wherever possible
Strong consistency for all location data
Accuracy: never give the user wrong directions
Guarantee every route is the mathematically global shortest
Smooth map rendering
exercises.prompt: Which of these are non-functional requirements in this chapter?

lessons.title: Location Reporting
lessons.summary: Estimation, batch uploads, and Cassandra modeling

exercises.explanation: 1 billion × 35 minutes ÷ 7 days = 5 billion minutes per day. 35 billion is the weekly total, from forgetting to divide by 7; 500 million is off by a factor of 10. This number is the starting point for estimating the reporting QPS later.
options: About 3.5 billion minutes
About 5 billion minutes
About 35 billion minutes
About 500 million minutes
exercises.prompt: With 1 billion DAU, each person uses navigation 35 minutes per week. How many minutes of navigation do all users accumulate per day?

exercises.explanation: That is 4 batches per minute, so 5 billion × 4 = 20 billion per day; ÷ 100,000 seconds ≈ 200,000 QPS, matching the chapter’s estimate. Uploading every second would give 5 billion × 60 ÷ 100,000 = 3 million QPS, and once a minute about 50,000, so the batch interval directly sets the QPS.
options: About 200,000
About 50,000
About 3 million
exercises.prompt: A map service logs about 5 billion minutes of navigation per day. If clients upload their locations in one batch every 15 seconds, and you approximate a day as 100,000 seconds, what is the average write QPS?

exercises.explanation: With the same usage time, uploading every second versus every 15 seconds changes the request count 15-fold. QPS depends on the batch interval and the number of points per batch, and the chapter’s estimate skips that derivation.
exercises.prompt: Location reporting QPS is determined only by DAU and usage time, regardless of how often clients submit a batch.

exercises.explanation: The three request types differ in frequency, payload, and the component that serves them: GPS reports go to the location service, tiles come from the CDN, and navigation requests need route computation. Lumping them together distorts capacity planning. The chapter’s peak is about 5 times the average, not a fixed 10 times.
options: Estimate navigation requests, GPS reports, and tile downloads separately
Estimate only tile downloads; GPS volume can be ignored
Always take the peak as 10 times the average, with no need to split
Merge the three request types into one total QPS for planning
exercises.prompt: The chapter’s estimate files GPS reporting under “navigation requests” and arrives at about 200,000 QPS, with a peak of about 1 million. What is the more rigorous approach?

exercises.explanation: The chapter gives just two reasons: location data is write-heavy and goes stale quickly, so a NoSQL store that excels at high write throughput and favors availability fits. Looking up coordinates by address and read-heavy access are traits of the Redis-backed geocoding database. Cross-table transactions are not needed here.
options: Locations go stale fast, so availability matters more than strong consistency
It supports cross-table transactions, so writes are absolutely accurate
It can look up latitude and longitude directly from an address
Write volume is huge, and Cassandra excels at high write throughput
Reads dominate writes, which suits a hot cache
exercises.prompt: Why is Cassandra a reasonable choice for storing user locations?

exercises.explanation: The API takes an array of (latitude, longitude, timestamp) tuples. The client accumulates points for a while before uploading, so receipt time is later than capture time. Event time and receive time must be kept apart, or trajectories and traffic analysis get out of sync.
exercises.prompt: In a batch upload, every location point must carry its own timestamp, because the time the server receives the batch is not the time each point was captured.

exercises.explanation: The partition key keeps one user’s data together and the clustering key orders it by time, so fetching one user’s trail over a time range is the most efficient query. Finding users by segment or tile needs a separate index or stream processing, and address lookup belongs to the geocoding database.
options: All users on a given road segment at one moment
Reading one user’s location trail in time order
Looking up latitude and longitude by address
Counting the vehicles currently in each tile
exercises.prompt: The Cassandra location table uses `user_id` as the partition key and `timestamp` as the clustering key. Which query does this design support most directly?

exercises.explanation: With the partition key unchanged, one user’s data keeps growing over the years into a huge partition. Adding a daily time bucket caps each partition’s size. Using only timestamp as the partition key would pile writes from the same moment into hot partitions, and reading one user’s trail would span many partitions.
options: Too many partitions keep Kafka from consuming; use a single partition
The clustering key makes writes fail out of order; drop timestamp
Old users’ trails pile up into huge partitions; use a (user_id, day) time bucket
One user’s points scatter across nodes; use timestamp as the partition key
exercises.prompt: If the location table uses only `user_id` as the partition key, what problem appears after several years, and what fix works?

exercises.explanation: Batching cuts request overhead and battery use, Cassandra absorbs the high write rate, and Kafka fans the same location stream out to downstream services such as traffic and ETA. In this chapter Redis serves the read-heavy geocoding data, and the CDN distributes tiles.
exercises.prompt: Complete the key components of the location reporting path
exercises.text: Clients upload location points [[in batches]] to cut request overhead; the server writes to [[Cassandra]], which excels at high write throughput, and streams locations downstream through [[Kafka]] for analysis.

exercises.explanation: The client first accumulates points, then calls POST /v1/locations with a batch. Besides persisting to Cassandra, the location service writes the data to Kafka, where the traffic update and ETA services each consume it to monitor road conditions and detect closures.
items: The client accumulates several GPS points locally
One request uploads the batch to the location service
The location service writes the location stream to Kafka
Traffic, ETA, and other services consume the stream
exercises.prompt: Put the flow of location data, from the phone to downstream analysis, in order

lessons.title: Map Tiles
lessons.summary: Tile counts, on-demand fetching, and CDN delivery

exercises.explanation: Each level up splits the map in half horizontally and vertically, so one tile becomes four: 4 times, not 2 times. That also shows why the tile count at high levels is enormous and tiles must be fetched on demand.
exercises.prompt: Complete the two basic tile numbers
exercises.text: At the lowest zoom level, a single [[256×256]] tile covers the whole world; each zoom level up, the total number of tiles becomes [[4 times]] what it was.

exercises.explanation: Each level multiplies by 4: level 0 has 1 tile, level 1 has 4, level 2 has 16, and level 3 has 64, which is 4^3. 12 treats the exponential growth as 4 × 3, and 16 counts one level too few.
options: 64 tiles
12 tiles
256 tiles
16 tiles
exercises.prompt: Call the lowest zoom level level 0, where one tile covers the whole world. How many tiles are there at level 3?

exercises.explanation: The tile total covers the whole world, while the screen covers only a small piece of it, so any level needs just ten or so tiles. Every tile is 256×256, so tiles at higher levels are not smaller, just covering less ground. Preinstalling all tiles is impractical, since the total is petabytes.
options: Tiles at higher zoom levels have lower resolution and are smaller
The client downloads only the ten or so tiles the current view and level need
The CDN merges high-level tiles into one before sending
The client ships with tiles for every level preinstalled
exercises.prompt: The total number of tiles in the world grows 4 times per zoom level. Why doesn’t client traffic explode along with it?

exercises.explanation: Tiles are fetched on demand by position and zoom level. Zooming changes the level, and panning or moving along the route changes the position, so both need new tiles. GPS reporting goes to the location service and route ranking happens inside the navigation service; neither triggers a tile download.
options: The client reports a batch of GPS locations
The server re-ranks candidate routes
Navigation enters a new tile area
The user pans the map
The user zooms the map
exercises.prompt: Which actions make the client fetch new map tiles?

exercises.explanation: The same tile is requested by huge numbers of users. Pre-generated and cached on the CDN, it is served from a nearby edge node (POP). Dynamic rendering burns server time on every request and is hard to cache. Static tiles do not reflect traffic automatically, and they require a tile identifier to be computed first.
options: Static tiles can be cached and reused by the CDN, avoiding repeated rendering
Static tiles update automatically with live traffic, so data is fresher
Dynamically generated images distort the projection more, so are less precise
Static tiles spare the client from computing any tile identifiers
exercises.prompt: Why did the chapter’s design choose pre-generated static tiles over generating map images dynamically for each request?

exercises.explanation: Tiles are pre-generated static files served from nearby CDN edge nodes, and when you pan back to an area you just viewed, the client may even use its local cache. Only dynamic generation would need to render every time.
exercises.prompt: When the user pans the map back and forth, every tile to be displayed must go back to the origin server to be regenerated.

exercises.explanation: Having the server compute URLs costs one extra request, but a rule change takes effect on the server alone. A built-in client algorithm saves a request, but old app versions linger, so the numbering rules must stay compatible forever. Real-time rendering and downloading a whole level are approaches already ruled out.
options: The client downloads every tile of that zoom level
A server API computes the tile URLs and returns them to the client
The client embeds the numbering algorithm; new rules ship in new versions
The server renders the whole map image on each request
exercises.prompt: The team expects to change the tile numbering scheme later but cannot force every user to upgrade the app. Which way of determining tile URLs fits better?

exercises.explanation: A geohash is an alphanumeric string from recursive quadrant splitting, while common tiles are numbered by z (zoom), x, and y, so the two are not equivalent. What matters is that client and server share one numbering system; CDN tiles are stored under one scheme, so a client choosing its own would fetch the wrong tiles.
options: With geohash you no longer need to distinguish zoom levels
Geohash and z/x/y are fully equivalent and interchangeable
Common web tiles are numbered z/x/y; what matters is that both ends agree
Once tiles are on the CDN, each client version can choose its own numbering
exercises.prompt: The chapter loosely calls tile identifiers “geohash”. Which understanding is correct?

exercises.explanation: Dynamic rendering burns server time and is hard to cache. Static tiles are pre-rendered images fetched by identifier. The CDN serves them from a nearby POP. Vector tiles send paths and polygons for the client to draw instead of whole images, saving significant bandwidth.
pairs: Rendered per request; high load, hard to cache
Serve tiles from nearby, cutting latency
Send paths and polygons; client renders
exercises.prompt: Match each tile delivery approach with its characteristic

exercises.explanation: When estimating the world’s tiles, the chapter takes into account that tiles like deserts compress to very small sizes, arriving at about 70 PB. Metadata is comparatively tiny and can be ignored. Even compressed it is petabytes, so tiles stay on the server and are delivered on demand.
exercises.prompt: Large areas of similar tiles, such as deserts, compress very well, and the chapter’s estimate of about 70 PB of tile storage already accounts for this.

lessons.title: Navigation and ETA
lessons.summary: Route services, dynamic ETA, and push updates

exercises.explanation: Routing algorithms need coordinates, so geocoding comes first. Next, spatial identifiers locate the origin and destination tiles. An A* variant traverses from the origin tile until it finds a good enough route to the destination tile. The route planner then calls the ETA service, which uses traffic and machine learning.
items: Geocode the origin and destination addresses
Find the routing tiles for origin and destination
Load neighboring tiles on demand while searching
The ETA service times candidate routes with traffic
exercises.prompt: Put the server-side steps of one navigation request in order

exercises.explanation: If the heuristic never overestimates, A* will not miss the truly optimal route by pricing a path too high; underestimating only expands more nodes. Traffic weights or hierarchical approximation usually lose this guarantee, so the chapter promises only routes that are “accurate and drivable, reasonably fast”.
options: It must be computed from screen pixel distance
It must never overestimate the remaining cost to the destination
It must include live traffic
It must never underestimate the remaining cost to the destination
exercises.prompt: For classic A* to guarantee an optimal route, what condition must the heuristic function (the estimate of remaining cost) satisfy?

exercises.explanation: The chapter tolerates a little latency, and routes need not be absolutely fastest, but directions and traffic rules must be accurate. Hierarchical routing tiles and weights that change with traffic are approximations, so the goal is stated as “accurate and drivable, reasonably fast”.
exercises.prompt: This chapter’s navigation service promises to always return the mathematically globally shortest route.

exercises.explanation: The route planner is the coordinator. It gets coordinates from geocoding, calls the shortest path service for candidate routes, asks the ETA service for times, and has the ranking service order routes by user criteria. The updater service refreshes important data asynchronously in the background.
pairs: Runs an A* variant on routing tiles
Estimates time from traffic and machine learning
Ranks routes by preferences like avoiding tolls
exercises.prompt: Match each service in the navigation subsystem with its responsibility

exercises.explanation: Routing tiles are generated periodically and read whole, needing no database transactions or queries, so object storage like S3 plus caching fits best. Cassandra takes the write-heavy location data, and Redis serves the read-heavy geocoding.
exercises.prompt: Complete how routing tiles are produced and stored
exercises.text: Routing tiles are generated periodically by an [[offline pipeline]] from multiple road data sources, compressed into binary files, and stored in [[object storage]] with aggressive caching.

exercises.explanation: A key-value mapping suits exact lookups of “which coordinates does this address have”. Real users misspell, use aliases, and hit duplicate address names, and reverse spatial queries exist too, all of which need text indexing, aliases, and disambiguation. Read-heavy is exactly where Redis fits, and it supports persistence.
options: Redis is a poor fit for read-heavy workloads
Key-value mapping oversimplifies; real lookups need text indexing and disambiguation
Redis cannot persist, so all mappings are lost on restart
Geocoding has heavy writes, so it must use Cassandra instead
exercises.prompt: The geocoding database is read-heavy with few writes, and the chapter uses Redis to speed up reads. What is the limit of this choice?

exercises.explanation: A large parent tile containing the accident only means the user may be affected; the route may not pass through it. Pushing without verifying would make many unaffected users reroute constantly. After confirming who is affected, notify the user if a faster candidate route exists.
options: Nothing; a parent tile hit means the route avoids the accident
Mark the user as a candidate, then check whether the actual route passes the accident
Immediately push a reroute to the user
Clear the user’s cached routing tiles
exercises.prompt: A tile has an accident. For each navigating user, the system stores the origin tile and its successive parent tiles, up to one that covers the destination. A user’s final covering tile contains the accident tile. What should happen next?

exercises.explanation: A route may cross many fine tiles, while a few levels of parent tiles cover the destination, so storage is far smaller. The cost is coarseness: a hit only means possibly affected, and the actual path must still be checked. A tile → active routes inverted index can also reduce scanning.
exercises.prompt: Storing only the origin tile and its successive parent tiles takes less storage than storing every tile the route passes through.

exercises.explanation: Mobile push payloads are limited and unsuited to continuous navigation data, long polling repeatedly sets up requests at higher overhead, and SSE only pushes one way. WebSocket wins because its two-way channel can also support extensions such as last-mile delivery.
options: WebSocket: lower overhead than repeated long polling, and two-way for extensions
Long polling: simplest to implement and lowest server overhead
SSE: one-way push is enough, and simpler than WebSocket
Mobile push notifications: system-level delivery for frequent navigation data
exercises.prompt: During navigation the server must keep pushing traffic changes and reroute suggestions to clients. Which channel does this chapter favor?

exercises.explanation: The location stream from the location service can improve ETA, monitor traffic, and detect closures; Kafka feeds it to downstream services such as traffic. Many users’ speeds are the traffic signal, linking the location path to the navigation path. Address aliases, tile logs, and cached image tiles say nothing about speed.
options: Map image tiles cached on clients
Tile access logs on CDN edge nodes
The location stream continuously reported by navigating users
Address aliases in the geocoding database
exercises.prompt: Dynamic ETA and rerouting need to know where traffic is building up. Where does this real-time traffic information mainly come from?

chapters.title: Distributed Message Queue
keyPoints: Topics split by business, partitions split parallelism, brokers store data, consumer groups track progress. Order holds only within a partition.
In a group, a partition belongs to one consumer at a time, so active consumers never exceed partitions. Groups share the log but keep separate offsets.
An append-only segmented log, sequential I/O, and batching give high throughput. Expiry reclaims whole segments; batch size trades latency for throughput.
A message is committed once all ISR replicas have it. A stricter ACK is slower and safer; ACK=all also needs a minimum in-sync replica count.
Committing the offset after processing is at-least-once; use event IDs or unique constraints for idempotency. Exactly-once needs transactions too.
A rebalance is a shift handover, and the old consumer must stop. Adding partitions changes key mapping, so ordering for the same key needs a transition.

labs.title: Consumer Groups: Assignment, Rebalancing, and Offset Commits
Replicas, ISR, and ACK: Is Data Lost When the Leader Dies?

lessons.title: Queue Model
lessons.summary: Topics, partitions, groups, ordering

exercises.explanation: A queue brings performance (no waiting on downstream), scalability (each side scales independently), availability (one side can fail while the other still uses the queue), and decoupling. Global order is not free: it holds only within one partition. At-least-once delivery can duplicate messages, so handlers must be idempotent.
options: Producers and consumers scale independently with their own traffic
Duplicate messages are automatically processed only once
Producers do not wait for consumers to finish processing
All messages automatically get a global order
Producers can keep writing while consumers are briefly down
exercises.prompt: What benefits does a message queue bring when placed between two services?

exercises.explanation: In point-to-point, one consumer processes each message and it is deleted once acknowledged, so acknowledged data is not retained. It does allow competing consumers, and messages wait while consumers are offline. This scenario needs long retention and replay, so it uses publish/subscribe with consumer-group offsets.
options: A message is deleted once acknowledged, so it cannot be replayed
Point-to-point does not allow competing consumers
Point-to-point cannot persist messages to disk
Point-to-point needs consumers online, or messages are lost
exercises.prompt: A scenario requires keeping messages for two weeks and letting different consumers read them repeatedly. Why can’t the classic point-to-point model do this?

exercises.explanation: “Each group reads the full stream” is a logical statement: the data log is shared, and only the read position (offset) is independent per group. So a slow order group does not affect the statistics group, and storage does not double.
exercises.prompt: When an order group and a statistics group subscribe to the same topic, the broker physically copies the message log for each consumer group.

exercises.explanation: Within one group, a partition goes to only one consumer at a time; otherwise ordering within the partition cannot be guaranteed. So active consumers max out at the partition count, and the extra 2 stand by to take over if another fails. To raise parallelism, add partitions.
options: 4, and the other 2 sit idle
6, with two partitions each read by two consumers at once
6, with partitions split and shared
2, each responsible for 2 partitions
exercises.prompt: A topic has 4 partitions, and a consumer group starts 6 consumers. Once things settle, how many are actually consuming?

exercises.explanation: Order is guaranteed only within a single partition. Sending the same key to the same partition keeps the parallelism of many partitions while preserving each user’s order. Re-sorting across partitions after round-robin writes is hard and unreliable, and concurrent threads scramble the completion order within a partition.
options: Let one consumer process a partition’s messages with multiple threads
Use user_id as the partition key so a user lands in one partition
Give messages a global increasing ID and write to random partitions
Write round-robin to partitions and re-sort by timestamp when consuming
exercises.prompt: Events for the same user must be processed in the order they happened, and the topic needs several partitions for throughput. What is the most reasonable approach?

exercises.explanation: Each partition is an independent FIFO log, and there is no inherent ordering between partitions. Messages that need an order should go to the same partition through the partition key. Order holds only within a single partition.
exercises.prompt: After a topic is split into several partitions, consumers still see messages in a global order across partitions.

exercises.explanation: Mnemonic: topics split by business, partitions split parallelism, brokers store data, consumer groups track progress. An offset is a message’s position in a partition, a replica is a partition copy for fault tolerance, and a segment is a file chunk cut from the partition log.
exercises.prompt: Complete the core queue concepts
exercises.text: A [[topic]] splits messages by business, [[partitions]] set the parallelism, and a [[broker]] is a server hosting partitions.

exercises.explanation: Messages land in data storage. Consumption progress goes in state storage, so consumers resume from it after a failure. Topic config lives in metadata storage. The coordination service handles service discovery, keeps the list of live brokers, elects leaders, and helps with partition assignment.
pairs: Service discovery, live brokers, leader election
exercises.prompt: Match each high-level architecture component with its job

exercises.explanation: The queue guarantees only in-order delivery within a partition; what happens after delivery is up to the application. Concurrent processing scrambles the order in which business effects complete, for example a “cancel order” taking effect before “create order”. The application has to cooperate to preserve order.
options: The processing order of messages within the same partition
The offsets of other consumer groups
Replica consistency across brokers
The producer’s mapping from partition key to partition
exercises.prompt: A consumer fetches a batch of messages from one partition and hands them to a thread pool to process concurrently. What is this most likely to break?

exercises.explanation: The same key always goes to the same partition. If one key is especially hot, say one large customer produces half the events, its partition becomes a hotspot, and adding more partitions cannot split a single key.
exercises.prompt: The partition key decides which partition a message goes to, but whether data is spread evenly across partitions depends on how the keys themselves are distributed.

lessons.title: Logs and Producing
lessons.summary: Segmented log, message format, batching

exercises.explanation: Messages are immutable and accessed in order, so a database’s indexes, transactions, and random access add cost without helping. An append-only log makes writes sequential and uses the page cache well. Logs are poor at content queries and secondary indexes, and general-purpose databases can replicate across nodes.
options: A general-purpose database cannot replicate across nodes
Messages are often queried by content, which logs handle better
An append-only log can build secondary indexes on any field
Messages are never updated or deleted singly, and mostly accessed sequentially
exercises.prompt: Why does a message queue store messages in an append-only log (WAL) instead of a general-purpose database?

exercises.explanation: HDDs are slow at random seeks, but sequential throughput is much better, and an append-only log is exactly sequential access. The OS page cache also reduces actual disk reads. As long as access stays sequential, a hard disk is up to the job.
exercises.prompt: Hard disks are slow at random seeks, so they are unsuitable for storing a message queue’s logs.

exercises.explanation: Old segments are read-only and ordered by time, so a whole segment expires together, and deleting the file reclaims the space without any per-message deletes. Segmenting also keeps any single file from growing too large.
options: Reclaim whole expired old segment files directly
Move unexpired messages to a new segment, then delete the old file
Run delete on each message, then compact the file
Mark each message deleted and skip it on reads
exercises.prompt: A partition log is cut into segments, and only the newest one is writable. When retention expires, what is the simplest way to delete messages older than two weeks?

exercises.explanation: A message key is not a primary key as in a KV database. Its job is to choose the partition, so messages from the same user should share a key. A message is located by the (topic, partition, offset) triple, not by its key.
options: Both are valid: the key picks the partition and may repeat or be empty
Keys must be unique, and a duplicate overwrites the old message
The broker drops messages with an empty key
Two messages with the same key are merged into one
exercises.prompt: One message has an empty key, and another has the same key as an earlier message. Which statement is correct?

exercises.explanation: The key is hashed and taken modulo the partition count to pick the partition, and a producer can override the default strategy; the value is the payload. The CRC detects corruption in transit or storage. The offset is only known after the write lands in a partition, so it cannot choose the partition.
exercises.prompt: Complete the roles of two fields in the message structure
exercises.text: By default the partition is chosen by hash([[key]]) % numPartitions, and the [[CRC]] field verifies message integrity.

exercises.explanation: A large batch moves more data per network round trip and writes more sequentially, so throughput is high, but it waits to fill up. A small batch is sent sooner, so latency is low but throughput suffers. Adding partitions spreads disk load and raises throughput, but it cannot remove the batching delay.
options: Small batches for logs, to limit loss per batch
Large batches for logs, small batches for payment notifications
