Small batches for both, and make up the throughput with multithreaded consumers
Large batches for both, and remove the latency by adding partitions
exercises.prompt: One queue runs both log aggregation (throughput first) and payment notifications (low latency required). How should batch size be tuned?

exercises.explanation: At low traffic, a batch may take very long to fill. In practice you set both a size threshold and a maximum wait, and send when either is met: large batches build up at peak, and nothing waits forever in the troughs.
exercises.prompt: If a producer only sends once “1,000 messages are collected”, messages in low-traffic periods may wait a long time to be sent.

exercises.explanation: The routing layer reads and caches the replica plan from metadata beforehand, so when a message arrives it knows which leader to forward to. Writes always go to the leader first, and followers pull to replicate. Only after enough replication acknowledgements does it commit and reply to the producer.
items: The routing layer caches the replica plan in advance
The producer sends the message to the routing layer
The routing layer forwards it to the partition’s leader
Followers pull the new message from the leader
Enough replicas sync, then the leader commits and replies
exercises.prompt: With a separate routing layer, put the path of a message from send to commit in order

exercises.explanation: Client-side routing saves a network hop: the producer decides which partition to target and accumulates a batch in memory before sending it at once. A separate routing layer can batch too, but it adds state and coordination complexity. This is an engineering trade-off.
options: One less network hop; the producer picks the partition and batches more
The producer no longer needs to know where the partition leader is
A separate routing layer cannot batch at all and can only forward one by one
Replication can be skipped and acknowledged directly
exercises.prompt: The chapter finally puts routing logic inside the producer instead of keeping a separate routing layer. What is the main benefit?

exercises.explanation: Sequential access, immutable messages, and batched writes are the chapter’s three choices. Indexing every message would turn sequential writes into many random writes. Deleting on consumption defeats long retention and repeated consumption; history should be reclaimed by whole segment.
options: Immutable messages, which reduce copying
A B+ tree index on every message
A structure suited to sequential disk access and the page cache
Deleting each message in place right after consumption
Batched writes, which reduce small I/Os
exercises.prompt: To support high throughput and long retention, what storage choices does this chapter make?

lessons.title: Groups and State
lessons.summary: Pull, rebalance, offsets, metadata

exercises.explanation: With push, the broker sends as soon as a message arrives, so a slow consumer is overwhelmed. Push can batch too, so throughput is not the issue. With pull, consumers fetch at their own pace, a slow one can scale out to catch up, and big batches fit naturally. Its costs, latency and empty polls, are softened by long polling.
options: Consumers pull at their own pace, so a slow one is not overwhelmed
Pull never produces empty polls, so no wasted requests
Push cannot send in batches, so throughput stays low
Pull has the lowest latency, delivering as soon as a message arrives
exercises.prompt: Consumers vary in processing power, and sometimes fall far behind the production rate. The chapter picks the pull model. What is the key reason?

exercises.explanation: With long polling, a request with no data waits on the broker and returns when a message arrives or a timeout hits. This reduces idle requests and also shortens the wait for new messages.
exercises.prompt: The pull model sends empty requests when there are no new messages, and long polling can reduce this waste.

exercises.explanation: The group coordinator is a role played by one broker, chosen by hashing the group name, so all members of a group necessarily connect to the same broker. It is not the global coordination service that ZooKeeper provides; in the chapter’s design, ZooKeeper handles metadata and leader election.
options: Connect to any broker, which broadcasts to all members
Connect to ZooKeeper, where the global coordination service assigns partitions directly
Hash the group name to find one broker, and all group members connect to it
Connect to the leader of the topic’s partition with the largest offset
exercises.prompt: A new consumer wants to join Group 1. How does it find the group coordinator for that group?

exercises.explanation: A learns of the rebalance through its heartbeat response. After all members rejoin, the coordinator picks a group leader. The group leader computes the assignment and the coordinator broadcasts it, while the other members wait. Finally each consumes its new partitions.
items: B asks the coordinator to join
The coordinator signals a rebalance via heartbeats
Members rejoin, and the coordinator picks a group leader
Group leader computes the plan; coordinator broadcasts it
All members start consuming under the new assignment
exercises.prompt: Consumer B joins a group that only had A. Put the rebalance steps in order

exercises.explanation: A rebalance decides who owns which partition, so members joining, leaving, or timing out on heartbeats, or partitions being added or removed, all change the assignment. Scaling out producers does not affect partition ownership, and a single failed message is a retry issue that does not reassign partitions.
options: The topic gains new partitions
A single message fails to process
A new consumer joins
The producer adds an instance
A consumer sends no heartbeat for a long time
exercises.prompt: Which events trigger a consumer-group rebalance?

exercises.explanation: A rebalance is like a shift handover: the old consumer must stop processing partitions it no longer owns, or old and new instances write at the same time. B continues from the committed offset, not from 0, and the coordinator does not roll back business results.
options: The coordinator automatically rolls back A’s results
A and B may both write business results, causing duplicates or conflicts
The broker deletes the messages of partition 3
B re-consumes all history from offset 0
exercises.prompt: A rebalance hands partition 3 from consumer A to B, but A, stalled, is still processing partition 3 messages. What goes wrong?

exercises.explanation: The committed value is defined as “the next position to read”, so everything before 6 has been processed, and it resumes at 6. Starting at 7 would skip message 6, and starting from 0 or from the latest would re-read or skip large amounts of messages, respectively.
options: From offset 6
From the partition’s latest message
From offset 0 again
From offset 7
exercises.prompt: Group 1 committed offset 6 on a partition (meaning the next position to read). After a consumer crashes and restarts, where should it read from?

exercises.explanation: The chapter’s design uses ZooKeeper to store metadata and consumption state and to help elect leaders, but other consensus or coordination implementations can do the same, and systems with built-in consensus-based metadata need not deploy it. What to remember is the responsibilities: who stores metadata, and who elects leaders.
exercises.prompt: ZooKeeper is an irreplaceable component of this design; without it, metadata cannot be stored and leaders cannot be elected.

exercises.explanation: Offsets are tiny, updated constantly, accessed randomly by group and partition, and need consistency: a wrong value means missed or repeated messages. Append-only sequential reads fit the message log; rare changes fit metadata. The chapter’s design uses a ZooKeeper-like store, but Kafka keeps offsets in an internal topic.
options: Small data, frequent reads and writes, random access, consistency matters
Written once and read many times, suitable for caching on a CDN
Rarely changes, small data, eventual consistency is acceptable
Large data, append-only writes, sequential batch reads
exercises.prompt: State storage holds each group’s consumption offsets. What is its access pattern?

exercises.explanation: The group coordinator is a broker that organizes the process and broadcasts the result. The group leader is one of the consumers in the group and computes the assignment. The partition leader is a replication concept and has nothing to do with consumer-group assignment.
exercises.prompt: Complete the two roles in a rebalance
exercises.text: All group members connect to the same [[group coordinator]]; when membership changes, it picks a [[group leader]], which computes the partition assignment.

lessons.title: Replicas, Delivery
lessons.summary: ISR, ACK, scaling, delivery semantics

exercises.explanation: A message is committed once it is synced to all replicas in the ISR. Replica 4 has left the ISR and no longer holds up commits; that is the ISR’s trade-off between performance and durability. Acknowledging once the leader writes locally is the ACK=1 behavior and does not mean the message is committed.
options: No, they must wait for replica 4 to catch up
No, they must wait for every broker in the cluster to acknowledge
Yes, a write to the leader’s local disk counts as committed
Yes, only the replicas in the ISR must all be in sync
exercises.prompt: Replica 4 fell too far behind and was removed from the ISR. Replicas 2 and 3 have copied the leader’s two new messages. Are those two messages committed?

exercises.explanation: The stricter the ACK, the slower it is and the less likely data is lost. ACK=all has a loophole: when the ISR shrinks to just the leader, it can still acknowledge. So pair it with a minimum in-sync replica count that rejects writes when replicas are too few, accepting brief unavailability rather than pretending to be safe.
pairs: No wait for ack: fastest, failures go unseen
Leader-only ack; loses data if it crashes first
Waits for all ISR replicas: slower, more durable
Rejects writes when too few replicas in sync
exercises.prompt: Match each acknowledgement setting with its trade-off

exercises.explanation: ACK=all waits for all replicas in the ISR, and when the ISR shrinks to just the leader, it waits only for itself. To truly prevent loss, combine it with a minimum in-sync replica count and forbid unsafe leader election.
exercises.prompt: Even with ACK=all, if the ISR has only the leader left, a message may be acknowledged with just one copy stored.

exercises.explanation: The coordination service keeps the live-broker list, so it detects the failure first. A new leader is then elected at once from the remaining in-sync replicas so the partition keeps serving. The missing replica is rebuilt on another broker as a follower pulling from the new leader, and joins the ISR only once caught up.
items: The coordination service notices the broker is lost
A new leader is chosen from the remaining ISR replicas
Another broker rebuilds the replica and catches up
The new replica joins the ISR once caught up
exercises.prompt: The broker hosting a partition’s leader goes down. Put the partition’s recovery steps in order

exercises.explanation: Once N changes, the same key may map to a new partition while its old messages remain in the old one, so there is no ordering guarantee across them. New partitions receive only new messages, and old data is not moved. Producers must be told, and a consumer-group rebalance assigns the new partitions.
options: Nothing for producers: the partition count only matters on the broker
Nothing for consumer groups: new partitions can go unconsumed for now
A key’s old and new messages may split across partitions, so ordering needs a transition
History in old partitions must be moved to new partitions immediately
exercises.prompt: A topic for orders is partitioned by `hash(key) % N` and grows from 4 to 6 partitions. What most needs extra handling?

exercises.explanation: For example, a task that checks payment status after 30 minutes is stored in a temporary topic, timed with a delay queue or hierarchical timing wheel, and moved to the target partition when due. If the move succeeds but its acknowledgement fails, the message may be delivered twice, so consumers must still be idempotent.
exercises.prompt: A delayed message can first go into temporary broker storage (such as a dedicated topic) and be moved into the target partition for consumers to read once it is due.

exercises.explanation: The offset has already moved past this message, so after the restart reading begins at the next one and this message is lost. That is at-most-once. Committing only after successful processing would make a crash cause a re-read: at-least-once. A retry topic needs the application to route there; it is not automatic.
options: The broker redelivers it automatically, exactly once
It is read and processed again (at-least-once)
It is never processed again, effectively lost (at-most-once)
It automatically goes to a retry topic to be tried later
exercises.prompt: A consumer fetches a message, commits the offset immediately, and crashes while processing it. What happens to the message after the restart?

exercises.explanation: At-least-once means a crash after processing but before the commit causes a re-read, so handlers must be idempotent: use event IDs, unique constraints, or transactional records to recognize processed messages. Committing first becomes at-most-once and may skip a charge. ACK affects only write durability, not duplicates.
options: Add a unique constraint on charge records
Commit the offset before charging
Record processed messages in a transaction
Change the producer ACK from all to 1
Check idempotency by event ID
exercises.prompt: A payment service consumes at-least-once. To avoid double charges without losing messages, which approaches work?

exercises.explanation: That combination gives at-least-once: a crash after processing but before the commit still causes duplicates, and producer retries can write duplicates too. Queue transactions can make a read-process-write cycle commit exactly once, but an external database or payment API still needs transactional coordination or idempotency.
exercises.prompt: Committing the offset after processing and having producers retry on failure is enough to achieve end-to-end exactly-once.

exercises.explanation: A topic per subset duplicates storage and wastes resources, and forces producers to change whenever consumer needs change. Better to tag messages, let consumers declare the tags they subscribe to, and have the server filter. Filtering on the payload can run into encryption or serialization that is hard to parse.
options: A consumer cannot subscribe to multiple topics at once
After splitting topics, ordering within each topic’s partitions is lost too
The data is stored more than once, and producers must change with consumer needs
A queue supports only a few dozen topics, which is not enough
exercises.prompt: A consumer cares only about “refund” messages in a partition. Someone proposes a separate topic for each message type. What is the main problem?

chapters.title: Metrics, Monitoring, and Alerting
chapters.fullTitle: Chapter 20: Metrics Monitoring and Alerting System
keyPoints: Clarify scope: internal metrics and alerts only, no logs or tracing. 10 million series sampled every 10 seconds is about 1 million points per second.
A series is metric name plus labels; the count depends on combinations that occur. Keep high-cardinality values like request_id or user ID out of labels.
Pull eases debugging and shows failures directly; push suits short jobs and network boundaries. Kafka after the collectors rides out database outages.
Aggregating earlier saves writes but costs flexibility; pre-aggregate by keeping sum and count, since averages and P95s cannot simply be averaged again.
Time-series databases compress with delta encoding and downsample by data age; downsampling erases spikes, so store the maximum too when it matters.
Alerts use a threshold plus a for-duration to avoid flapping; retries give at-least-once delivery, so receivers deduplicate. No data is not healthy.

labs.title: Alert Rules: Threshold Plus For-Duration
Downsampling and Tiered Retention: What You Save, What You Lose

lessons.title: Scope and Scale
lessons.summary: Scope, components, write rate, tiered retention

exercises.explanation: This is operational metrics monitoring for a large company’s internal use: CPU, memory, disk, requests per second, plus alerting. Log monitoring (commonly ELK) and distributed tracing are explicitly excluded, and so are business metrics. Clarifying scope keeps you from designing a log search system by mistake.
options: Tracing one request across multiple services end to end
Collecting CPU, memory, and requests per second, and alerting on them
Reporting business metrics such as daily order value and conversion rate
Collecting and full-text searching each service’s error logs
exercises.prompt: An interviewer says, “Design a monitoring system for us.” After the scoping questions in this chapter, which of the following is within the design scope?
exercises.refAnchor: d20/第一步理解问题并确定范围
exercises.refTitle: Step 1: Understand the Problem and Establish Design Scope

exercises.explanation: Collection gets metrics from application servers, databases, queues, and other sources. Transmission moves them into the system, with a queue as a buffer at scale. Storage keeps them as time series. Alerting detects anomalies and notifies people. Visualization shows trends. Order: collect → transmit → store → alert → display.
pairs: Move metrics into the monitoring system
exercises.prompt: Match each of the five monitoring system components with its job

exercises.explanation: The non-functional requirements are scalability, low latency, reliability, and flexibility. Reliability applies to critical alerts; occasionally losing a metric point is acceptable, and collectors can send on a best-effort basis (fire and forget). This is an internal company system, not a SaaS product for external customers.
options: Low query latency for dashboards and alerts
Multi-tenant billing for external customers
Not missing critical alerts
Keep adding more metrics and alerts
Not a single metric point is ever lost
exercises.prompt: Which of the following are non-functional requirements in this chapter?

exercises.explanation: 1,000 × 100 × 100 = 10 million series. Each series produces one point every 10 seconds, so 10 million ÷ 10 = 1 million points per second. 10 million points per second mistakes the number of series for the write rate.
options: About 100,000 points per second
About 100 million points per second
About 10 million points per second
About 1 million points per second
exercises.prompt: 1,000 server pools × 100 servers per pool × about 100 metrics per server. If each series records one point every 10 seconds, what is the write rate?

exercises.explanation: The series count only says how many timelines there are; the write rate also depends on the sampling interval. One point every 10 seconds is about 1 million points per second. Change the interval to 1 minute and the write volume drops to about one-sixth.
exercises.prompt: “10 million metric series” means the system must write 10 million data points per second.

exercises.explanation: Older data is queried less and only needs to show trends, so precision drops tier by tier to save storage. Writing the tiers as age ranges avoids the overlap between “7 days” and “30 days” in the chapter’s wording.
exercises.prompt: Complete the rule for tiered retention by data age
exercises.text: Keep [[raw resolution]] for 0–7 days, downsample to [[1-minute]] resolution for 7–30 days, and to [[1-hour]] resolution for 30 days to 1 year.

exercises.explanation: One day has 86,400 seconds ÷ 10 = 8,640 points. At 1-hour resolution a day has only 24 points, about 360 times fewer. 1,440 is the points per day at 1-minute resolution. Downsampling is what keeps a year of retention affordable.
exercises.prompt: One series records a point every 10 seconds. After downsampling to 1-hour resolution, how does the number of points per day change?

exercises.explanation: 3 months is past 30 days, so only 1-hour resolution remains, and a 20-second spike gets averaged with the other points in that hour, making it hard to see. Data is kept for a year, not deleted. This is also why you should store the maximum alongside the average when downsampling.
options: Only hourly aggregates; a spike is likely averaged away
The raw 10-second data, fully intact
Nothing, because only 30 days are kept
Data at 1-minute resolution
exercises.prompt: You investigate a 20-second CPU spike from 3 months ago. Under this chapter’s retention policy, what will you see?

lessons.title: Data Model
lessons.summary: Time series, label cardinality, time-series databases

exercises.explanation: A series is identified by the metric name plus the label set, for example CPU.load with host and region. The timestamp and value belong to one data point on that series. Change the host label and you have a different series.
options: The label set and the value
The metric name and the timestamp
The metric name and the label set
The timestamp and the value
exercises.prompt: In `CPU.load host=webserver01,region=us-west 1613707265 50`, which parts together identify “which time series this is”?

exercises.explanation: The number of series is set by the label combinations that actually occur. request_id is different for every request, so each new request creates a new series and the index and memory balloon. method, region, and status_code have limited values, so their combinations stay manageable.
options: method (GET, POST, and so on)
request_id (unique per request)
region (a handful of regions)
status_code (a limited set of codes)
exercises.prompt: You add labels to an HTTP request-count metric. Which one is most likely to make the series count explode?

exercises.explanation: The series count is roughly the number of label-value combinations that actually occur, so what matters is the values, not how many label names there are. If just one of the 3 labels is user_id or request_id, the combinations can reach hundreds of millions. Evaluate before putting user IDs or raw URL parameters into labels.
exercises.prompt: As long as each metric has no more than 3 label names, the series count cannot get out of control.

exercises.explanation: A direct average assumes every point has equal weight. A machine sampled more densely gets counted more, and more samples do not cancel that bias; machines with different core counts may need weights too. A shared timestamp is the book’s example problem: duplicates may be overwritten, and one timestamp cannot show 10 minutes.
options: The series are sampled at even intervals, so every sample has the same weight
There are so many samples that weight differences are negligible
There are no more than 100 servers
All data points share the same timestamp
exercises.prompt: To compute the average CPU load across all us-west web servers over the past 10 minutes, you average the values of all data points directly. What must hold for this to be valid?

exercises.explanation: Every machine reports on a schedule without pause, so writes are steady and heavy. Normally only dashboards and alert rules read; during an incident everyone looks at the data at once and read traffic spikes. The storage design has to handle both loads.
exercises.prompt: A metrics system’s access pattern is heavy, continuous writes and light reads most of the time, with sudden bursts of queries during incidents.

exercises.explanation: The book does not say a general-purpose database cannot do it: with expert tuning it can reach the scale, just with more effort. A time-series database offers ready-made interfaces for filtering by label and aggregating by time, plus compression. Any database can store timestamps, and metrics need no cross-table transactions.
options: A time-series database supports cross-table transactions, so metrics are never lost
A time-series database has built-in aggregation by label and time, saving tuning
A general-purpose relational database cannot handle this scale however you tune it
Only a time-series database can store timestamped numbers
exercises.prompt: Why does this chapter lean toward a dedicated time-series database for metrics rather than a general-purpose relational database?

exercises.explanation: Each candidate has a cost: a relational database is costly to tune, NoSQL makes you design the time-series model yourself, and OpenTSDB needs Hadoop/HBase first. Over 250,000 writes per second on 8 cores and 32 GB is a benchmark under specific conditions; this chapter needs about 1 million points per second, so load-test it.
pairs: Can scale, but needs expert tuning
You must build time-series storage yourself
Figure for one setup, not a capacity guarantee
exercises.prompt: Match each storage candidate or figure with the caution that goes with it

exercises.explanation: With the same metric name, labels, and timestamp, these are the same series at the same instant, and the time-series database may keep only one value. That makes a 10-minute average impossible to compute, and it shows the example is only an illustration of the row format, not real data.
options: Data from two different hosts is merged into one series
The same timestamp doubles the label cardinality
Same-series duplicates at one instant may be overwritten or deduplicated
The time-series database rejects the whole batch
exercises.prompt: In the book’s example, two `host=webserver01` rows use the same timestamp with different values. What problem does this cause?

exercises.explanation: Aggregating by labels such as region and host relies on the label index. Every new label combination adds a series and an index entry, so high-cardinality labels make the index and memory grow with them.
exercises.prompt: Complete the key to aggregation queries in a time-series database
exercises.text: A time-series database builds an [[index]] on labels to aggregate efficiently, so you must limit label [[cardinality]]; otherwise the series count gets out of control.

lessons.title: Collection
lessons.summary: Push vs. pull, Kafka buffering, where to aggregate

exercises.explanation: Consistent hashing gives every target exactly one responsible collector, and adding or removing collectors moves only a few targets. Scraping everything and deduplicating later multiplies the wasted resources; having targets push to collectors turns it into the push model.
options: Have each target server pick a random collector to push to
Have every collector scrape all targets, then deduplicate at ingestion
Have all collectors take turns scraping the same target to share the load
Use consistent hashing to assign each target to exactly one collector
exercises.prompt: In the pull model with multiple collectors, how do you keep the same target server from being collected twice?

exercises.explanation: Pull can only scrape targets that are still alive at scrape time, so a short job may never get scraped. A Push Gateway lets the job push its metrics there first, and the collector then pulls from it. It also shows that push fits short-lived jobs better.
options: No problem: service discovery will collect it after the job ends
The job ends before the next scrape; bridge the gap with a Push Gateway
Scraping is so frequent it overwhelms the job; change the interval to 10 minutes
Pull requests interrupt the job; switch to UDP pulling
exercises.prompt: A batch job runs for only 20 seconds, and the pull collector scrapes every 60 seconds. What is the most likely problem, and how do you fix it?

exercises.explanation: A pull collector can hit /metrics at any time, which helps debugging. A short job may not live until the next scrape, so push fits better. Across data centers, sending to a reachable load balancer entry is simpler than letting collectors reach every target. But any client can push, so you need an allowlist or authentication.
pairs: Push fits better: send before exiting
Push is easier: send to a reachable entry
Push needs an allowlist or authentication
exercises.prompt: Following the book’s push vs. pull comparison, match each scenario with its conclusion

exercises.explanation: Missing reports could mean the service is down, but also a network failure or a problem on the sender, and the push model cannot tell these apart directly. A failed pull is a more direct signal, but it too has to distinguish network failures from service failures.
exercises.prompt: In the push model, if you have not received data from a machine for a long time, you can conclude that the machine is down.

exercises.explanation: The book’s table gives TCP pull and UDP push as examples, but they are only examples, not the essential difference between push and pull. TCP connection overhead may also be small relative to the payload, so there is no need to force UDP just to save overhead.
exercises.prompt: Push or pull does not determine the transport protocol; push can also send over HTTP/TCP.

exercises.explanation: Collectors can scale automatically, but if the time-series database goes down, data is lost. Kafka is reliable and scalable: it holds the data first, and consumers or stream processors such as Flink write it once downstream recovers. The cost is one more system to operate.
options: Guarantees every alert is delivered exactly once
Removes the need for compression encoding and downsampling in the time-series database
Holds data while the time-series database is down, decoupling collection from processing
Removes the need for service discovery and configuration in collectors
exercises.prompt: You add Kafka between the collectors and the time-series database. What is the main problem it solves?

exercises.explanation: Data for one metric goes to one partition, so aggregating it downstream needs no cross-partition merge. If a single metric is too large, split it by label; you can also classify by importance to handle critical data first. “One partition per metric” is only an illustration: with many metrics, map them onto fewer partitions.
exercises.prompt: Complete Kafka’s partitioning strategy
exercises.text: The book suggests partitioning Kafka by [[metric name]], which makes aggregating the same metric easier; at larger scale, shard further by [[label]].

exercises.explanation: The earlier you aggregate, the lower the write volume and the flexibility: the agent does simple aggregation, pipeline aggregation cuts writes but loses raw detail, and query-time aggregation keeps all raw data. Averages smooth peaks away for good; query-time aggregation writes every raw point, so its write volume is largest.
options: Aggregating before ingestion cuts writes, but not storing raw values loses detail
After pre-ingestion aggregation, you can still recover raw peaks from the averages
Aggregating at query time is most flexible, but processes more data and may be slower
Aggregating at query time has the smallest write volume
The collection agent suits simple aggregation, such as counting over 1 minute
exercises.prompt: Which statements about “where to aggregate” are correct?

exercises.explanation: Percentiles cannot be added and averaged: the cluster P95 depends on the combined distribution of all requests. Averaging the per-machine P95s, weighting them, or taking the maximum all fail to produce it. Either keep the raw samples, or store distribution data that can be merged and recompute from it.
options: Take a weighted average of the P95s by each machine’s request count
Take the plain average of the machines’ P95s
Recompute from the raw samples or their distribution
Take the maximum of the machines’ P95s
exercises.prompt: Each machine reports its own P95 latency. To get the P95 for the whole cluster, which approach is correct?

exercises.explanation: Overall average = (10×1 + 40×3) ÷ 4 = 130 ÷ 4 = 32.5. Simply averaging the two averages gives 25, which ignores the sample counts. That is why pre-aggregation should keep sum and count, not just the average.
exercises.prompt: Work it out: why pre-aggregation should keep the sample count
exercises.text: Machine A has an average of 10 (1 sample) and machine B has an average of 40 (3 samples), so the overall average of the two machines should be [[32.5]].

lessons.title: Storage and Alerts
lessons.summary: Compression, downsampling, alert rules, delivery

exercises.explanation: [00,30) holds 10, 16, 20: 46÷3 ≈ 15.33. [30,60) holds 30, 20, 30: 80÷3 ≈ 26.67. 19 and 25 come from an arithmetic error in the book’s table; 22 and 25 come from wrongly using (00,30] and (30,60]; 19 and about 26.67 puts the point at second 30 into the first window.
options: About 15.33 and 26.67
19 and 25
19 and about 26.67
22 and 25
exercises.prompt: CPU values sampled every 10 seconds from 19:00:00 are 10, 16, 20, 30, 20, 30. Averaged over 30-second windows [00,30) and [30,60), what are the results?

exercises.explanation: Once raw points are dropped, an average cannot recover a brief peak; interpolation and back-calculation are only guesses. Storing the maximum alongside the average when downsampling preserves spike information in long-term data. A median is even less sensitive to spikes.
options: Also store the maximum when downsampling
Back out the peak proportionally from the hourly average
Store the median instead of the average
Re-interpolate the hourly data back to 10-second resolution
exercises.prompt: After downsampling keeps only averages, a 10-second CPU spike disappears from the hourly data. What should you do?

exercises.explanation: With a steady sampling interval, the delta is always 10 and the delta of the deltas is all 0, which takes very few bits to encode. This is why delta and delta-of-delta encoding can compress timestamps so well, and good time-series databases usually build it in.
exercises.prompt: Work through second-order delta encoding of timestamps
exercises.text: Timestamps 1000, 1010, 1020, 1030: storing the deltas gives a constant [[10]], and storing the delta of the deltas gives all [[0]]; smaller numbers compress more easily.

exercises.explanation: The book cites a Facebook study: about 85% of operational queries target the past 26 hours. Keep recent data in a fast storage tier, and downsample old data and move it to cold storage, which keeps queries fast and costs under control.
exercises.prompt: Most operational queries target data from roughly the last day, so storage should focus on optimizing recent hot data, and old data that is rarely accessed can move to cold storage.

exercises.explanation: A query layer decouples components, eases swapping databases, and allows a cache. But many visualization and alerting tools have mature plugins, so skip it if the database interface is good enough. Alert rules query time-series data periodically instead of reading Kafka; delivery relies on retries and durable acknowledgements.
options: No: the tools have mature plugins, so skip it if the interface and cache suffice
Yes: without a query service you cannot guarantee alert delivery
Yes: Grafana can only read the interface of a self-built query service
No: alerts can consume the raw metrics in Kafka directly
exercises.prompt: A team uses Grafana and an off-the-shelf alerting tool, and the time-series database’s own query interface and cache are good enough. Do they still need to build a query service?

exercises.explanation: “No data” does not mean “healthy”: a host that has gone silent is exactly the one that needs attention. Missing metrics need an explicit rule, such as a separate alert on missing data; otherwise the alert would wrongly “resolve” while the host is down.
exercises.prompt: When a host goes silent and stops reporting, a threshold alert rule finds no value over the threshold, so the system can be considered healthy again.

exercises.explanation: Rule configs are loaded into the cache first. The alert manager queries data periodically, creates an alert event when a condition is met, and filters, merges, and deduplicates repeated triggers. After the event is written to Kafka, notification consumers send it through each channel.
items: The alert manager reads alert rules from the cache
It calls the query service periodically to fetch data
When a rule is met, an alert is created and deduplicated
The alert event is written to Kafka
Notification consumers send email, PagerDuty, and so on
exercises.prompt: Put the steps from rule evaluation to notification for one alert in order

exercises.explanation: for: 5m requires the condition to hold for 5 minutes before the alert actually fires. Until then it is only pending, and if the condition clears it returns to normal. This filters out false alarms from brief flapping, at the cost of reporting a real failure a few minutes late.
options: No alert: the condition must hold for 5 minutes to fire
An alert fires immediately and resolves itself after 2 minutes
An alert is sent 5 minutes later
An alert fires once at the 2-minute mark
exercises.prompt: A rule has `expr: up == 0` and `for: 5m`. An instance is unreachable for 2 minutes because of network flapping, then recovers. What happens?

exercises.explanation: Repeated triggers from the same instance should produce only one event, alert rules need access control, and retries guarantee at-least-once delivery. Dashboards belong to a visualization system such as Grafana, and downsampling is the storage layer’s job.
options: Downsampling historical data
Rendering dashboard charts
Controlling who may change alert rules
Filtering, merging, and deduplicating repeated triggers
Retrying failed sends to guarantee at-least-once delivery
exercises.prompt: Besides evaluating rules, what else should the alert manager be responsible for?

exercises.explanation: Retries prevent missed sends, but if a send succeeds and the acknowledgement is lost, it is sent again. Storing only alert state does not guarantee delivery by itself; you also need recoverable tasks, durable acknowledgements, and handling of downstream responses.
exercises.prompt: Alert notifications are retried at-least-once, so the same alert may be delivered more than once, and the receiving side needs to deduplicate.

chapters.title: Ad Click Aggregation
keyPoints: Keep raw clicks and serve queries from aggregates: the former can be recomputed and reconciled, the latter is small and fast, so store both.
Decouple stages with Kafka: Map routes, Aggregate counts, Reduce merges. Gather each ad on one node before choosing Top N.
Billing needs accuracy: use event time and fire when the watermark passes the window end. Longer waits are more accurate but slower; reconcile stragglers.
Exactly-once means each event is counted once: commit offset, state, and output atomically, or write downstream idempotently by version.
Split hot ads into local counts, then merge. A snapshot must match its offset, or recovery misses or recounts events.
Reconcile daily by recomputing from raw data on the same rules. Following Kappa, recomputation reuses the streaming logic and writes back with versions.

labs.title: Event Time, Windows, and Watermarks
Aggregation Node Crash: Duplicated or Lost Results

lessons.title: Scoping and Data
lessons.summary: Requirements, traffic estimates, and two data sets

exercises.explanation: 1 billion ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11,574; rounded to an average of 10,000 QPS, times 5 gives a peak of about 50,000. 11,574 is just the exact average, before the peak factor is applied. 5,000 and 500,000 are each off by an order of magnitude.
options: About 5,000 QPS
About 50,000 QPS
About 500,000 QPS
About 11,574 QPS
exercises.prompt: Each day brings 1 billion ad clicks, and peak traffic is estimated at 5 times the average QPS. Roughly what is the peak write rate?

exercises.explanation: 1 billion × 0.1 KB = 100 million KB ≈ 100 GB per day; times 30 days is about 3 TB. This figure leaves out replicas, indexes, and extra fields, so real capacity planning has to add headroom on top.
exercises.prompt: Complete the storage estimate for raw clicks
exercises.text: At 0.1 KB per event, 1 billion clicks take about [[100 GB]] per day and about [[3 TB]] per month, before replicas and indexes.

exercises.explanation: RTB usually has to finish within one second, while click aggregation serves billing and reports and can accept a few minutes of delay. They are different requirements on different paths, so do not merge them into one latency target.
exercises.prompt: Click aggregation tolerates a few minutes of end-to-end delay, so real-time bidding (RTB) can relax to minutes as well.
exercises.refAnchor: d21/第一步理解问题并确定范围
exercises.refTitle: Step 1: Understand the Problem and Establish Scope

exercises.explanation: Aggregates are small and fast but have already lost detail. When the aggregation logic is wrong or the filter rules change, only the raw events let you recompute. Raw data is the large, slow-to-query side, which is exactly why it can go to cold storage instead of serving the dashboard.
options: After an aggregation bug is fixed, you can re-filter, recompute, and reconcile
Raw data takes less storage space than aggregated data
Raw data is faster to query than the aggregate table, so it suits the dashboard
The aggregate table cannot store counts at per-minute granularity
exercises.prompt: The dashboard only queries the aggregate table. Why does the system still keep the raw click events?

exercises.explanation: Boundaries are part of the API: whether the interval is open or closed, the time zone, and whether late events can still revise a result all change the numbers each side computes. The Top N algorithm and the choice of threads or processes are server-side details that callers do not need to agree on.
options: Which time zone times are interpreted in
Whether the aggregation service uses threads or processes
Whether a returned result can still be revised by late events
Whether the time range is half-open `[from,to)`
Whether aggregation nodes use a heap or a sort for Top N
exercises.prompt: Besides parameter names such as `from`, `to`, and `filter`, what semantics should the query API settle up front?

exercises.explanation: Raw clicks are a classic write-heavy, read-light workload. A relational database could work, but scaling its writes is hard, so a store that scales writes easily is the better pick. Append-only clicks need no cross-row transactions or JOINs, and Cassandra does not automatically fit ad hoc OLAP, so that is no reason to choose it.
options: The workload is write-heavy and read-light, so it needs writes that scale out easily
Analysis needs frequent multi-table JOINs with the advertiser table
Billing settlement needs cross-row ACID transactions
Troubleshooting needs ad hoc OLAP analysis on any field
exercises.prompt: Raw clicks arrive at 10,000 QPS on average and 50,000 at peak, and are rarely looked at except when troubleshooting. Why does the design pick Cassandra for them?

exercises.explanation: Raw data is faithful but large; the aggregate table stores counts by (ad_id, click_minute, filter_id), which is small and fast. The most_clicked_ads table precomputes the Top N ad IDs per window. filter_id encodes a combination of region, IP, and user_id as one ID, and `*` means that dimension is not filtered.
pairs: Full fidelity, but large and slow to query
Counts by ad, minute, and filter
Precomputed hot ad IDs per window
One ID standing for a set of filters
exercises.prompt: Match each table to its role in the system

exercises.explanation: Raw data exists to debug and repair aggregation errors and is rarely read, so cold storage fits. Fast queries are served by the aggregate data, so moving raw data to a cheaper tier does not hurt dashboard performance.
exercises.prompt: Raw click data is mostly used for troubleshooting and recomputation, so it can move to cold storage to save cost.

exercises.explanation: Cassandra does not automatically fit arbitrary OLAP. Tables and partition keys must still be designed around the queries you actually run: by ad, by minute, by filter. Picking a database is only the start; the data model decides whether queries are efficient.
exercises.prompt: Since Cassandra stores the aggregates, it can directly and efficiently support any dimensional OLAP query.

lessons.title: Pipeline Design
lessons.summary: Queue decoupling, MapReduce, and Top N

exercises.explanation: Input and output are both unbounded event streams, so with synchronous writes, one failing consumer stalls the upstream. Decoupling stages with Kafka lets each one scale and recover independently. RTB is a separate sub-second path, and neither grouping nor time semantics depend on sync versus async.
options: It slows real-time bidding past its one-second limit
Synchronous calls rewrite event time into processing time
Any slow or failing downstream stage blocks the whole chain
Synchronous calls cannot group by ad_id
exercises.prompt: If the click ingestion service calls the aggregation service synchronously and then writes to the database synchronously, what is the main risk?

exercises.explanation: The first queue carries raw fields such as ad_id, timestamp, user_id, ip, and country. The aggregation service computes per-minute counts and Top N, writes them to the second queue, and from there they go to the database. Offset snapshots belong to fault tolerance and do not travel through the queues.
exercises.prompt: Complete what each of the two queues stores
exercises.text: The first queue holds [[raw click events]]; the second queue holds the per-minute [[aggregated counts]] and Top N, used for end-to-end atomic commit.

exercises.explanation: An extra queue does not automatically give exactly-once. Input progress and output results must sit in the same transaction or recoverable checkpoint, and the final database write must be idempotent or transactional. Otherwise a crash and replay still duplicates or loses counts.
exercises.prompt: Putting one more Kafka queue between the aggregation service and the database automatically gives exactly-once counts.

exercises.explanation: Map reads, filters, transforms, and routes events by ad_id. When you cannot control upstream partitioning and one ad’s clicks are scattered across partitions, it gathers them onto the same aggregation node, and it is a convenient place to clean data. Merging lists is Reduce’s job; per-minute counting is Aggregate’s.
options: It accumulates click counts per minute in memory
It commits the final offset to Kafka
It cleans events and re-routes by ad_id when upstream partitions are uncontrolled
It merges the local Top N lists from the aggregation nodes
exercises.prompt: If upstream can write each ad_id to the same Kafka partition and aggregation nodes consume it directly, why might you still need a separate Map node?

exercises.explanation: Map, Aggregate, and Reduce form a DAG: route first, count locally, then merge. The second queue decouples aggregated results from the downstream database write and is one link in the end-to-end atomic commit. The raw database takes no part in real-time computation; it is kept for lookup and recomputation.
pairs: Counts clicks per minute in memory
Merges node results into the final value
exercises.prompt: Match each component in the aggregation pipeline to its job

exercises.explanation: The remainder depends only on ad_id, so one ad always gets the same remainder and its count accumulates on a single node. This is what makes merging local Top N lists valid later. The cost is that a popular ad turns its node into a hotspot.
exercises.prompt: Map routes clicks to 3 aggregation nodes by `ad_id % 3`, so all clicks for one ad land on the same node.

exercises.explanation: If an ad’s clicks are spread across 3 nodes, each holds only part of the count and the ad may miss every local Top 3, so the merge drops a true global winner. Load balancing, commit timing, and using a heap cannot fix counts that were never combined.
options: Each ad’s count is fully accumulated on a single node
All nodes commit their local results at the same moment
The nodes process roughly equal numbers of events
The Reduce node also merges with a heap
exercises.prompt: Each of 3 aggregation nodes picks a local Top 3, and Reduce merges them into a global Top 3. What must hold for the result to be correct?

exercises.explanation: An ad may rank N+1 in every minute, never entering a per-minute list, yet make the top N once M minutes are summed. Storing only per-minute lists discards those counts, so a sliding-window ranking cannot be recovered exactly. You need to keep each ad’s per-minute counts.
exercises.prompt: If you store the Top N for every single minute, you can compute the exact Top N for any last M minutes.

exercises.explanation: Route by ad first so each ad is counted on one node only. Local Top 100 can be picked only after counting is done. Reduce merges the candidates into the global result, and finally it goes through the second queue into the aggregate database for the dashboard to read.
items: Map routes clicks to aggregation nodes by ad_id
Aggregation nodes count each ad’s clicks this minute
Each aggregation node picks a local Top 100 with a heap
Reduce merges node candidates into the global list
The result goes to the second queue, then the database
exercises.prompt: Put the data flow for “the 100 most-clicked ads in the past 1 minute” in order

exercises.explanation: Pre-aggregating by dimension makes filters fast and reuses the same aggregation service. The downside is that more conditions mean more buckets. ip and user_id take huge numbers of values, so the combinations multiply and storage explodes; you cannot precompute for arbitrary conditions. Slower queries is backwards.
options: Filtered queries get slower and must rescan raw data
Top N results become inaccurate
Dimension combinations multiply, so buckets and records explode
The aggregation service cannot be reused and must be rewritten
exercises.prompt: To support filtering by country, the system pre-aggregates by (ad_id, minute, country). If ip and user_id are added as dimensions too and every combination is precomputed, what is the main cost?

lessons.title: Time and Windows
lessons.summary: Stream vs. batch, event time, watermarks, windows

exercises.explanation: Online services reply to users at once; batch processing works on bounded datasets and values throughput; stream processing handles unbounded streams. Lambda runs both paths, with two codebases. Kappa keeps only stream processing and replays history through the same logic, as this chapter’s recomputation does.
pairs: Answers users; needs availability, low latency
Batch and stream paths, two codebases
One stream engine; replay uses the same logic
exercises.prompt: Match each processing style to its characteristic

exercises.explanation: Kappa replays historical data through the same aggregation code. Separate instances avoid competing with real-time processing for resources, and results update the database through the second queue. A separate SQL job means two sets of logic, pausing real-time hurts production, and proportional adjustment has no basis.
options: Pause the real-time aggregation instances and let them replay last week’s data first
Recompute from raw storage on separate instances running the same logic
Adjust the affected counts in the aggregate table proportionally
Write a separate batch SQL job to recompute and overwrite the streaming results
exercises.prompt: You fixed a serious aggregation bug and need to backfill last week’s results. Following this chapter’s Kappa approach, what is the best way?

exercises.explanation: Recomputation and real-time aggregation may write the same window one after the other. With versions, the downstream accepts only newer ones, so a late old batch cannot wash out the correct result. Reusing the same code does not mean results can be overwritten freely.
exercises.prompt: When recomputed results are written back, they should carry a batch or version number so an old recompute cannot overwrite a newer, more complete result.

exercises.explanation: Processing time is when the server handles the event, so a 30-second delay puts this click in the next minute. Billing values accuracy, so this design uses event time, at the cost of handling late events explicitly.
options: It is dropped for being late and never counted
It is counted in the 12:01 minute, the wrong window
It is counted in the 12:00 minute, the right window
It is counted in both the 12:00 and 12:01 windows
exercises.prompt: A click happens at 12:00:50, but network and queue delays mean the aggregation service only processes it at 12:01:20. What happens if you aggregate by minute using processing time?

exercises.explanation: Event time makes results match when the click really happened, but it comes from the client clock, which can be wrong or tampered with. Processing time uses the server clock, which is easier to control but does not reflect when the click happened. The design still uses event time, with fraud controls and reconciliation.
exercises.prompt: One cost of aggregating by event time is that the timestamp comes from the client, which may be inaccurate or even maliciously forged.

exercises.explanation: A watermark estimates event-time progress in the stream; it is not the extra stretch that lengthens a window. The window stays fixed, such as [12:00,12:01), and fires once the watermark passes 12:01. It is only an estimate and does not guarantee that all events have arrived, so you also need allowed lateness and corrections.
options: It guarantees all events for the window have arrived when it fires
It estimates how far event time has advanced; windows fire once it passes their end
It is the extra waiting time added to extend a window
It is the largest committed offset in Kafka
exercises.prompt: Which statement about a watermark is accurate?

exercises.explanation: A larger tolerance makes the watermark advance more conservatively and delays window firing. Late events are more likely to make it in, so accuracy improves but output slows, and fewer events go to the side output. However long you wait, very late events can still arrive, so zero misses is never guaranteed.
options: No late event will ever be missed again
Fewer late clicks are missed, but results come out more slowly
Firing time stays the same, but more events go to the side output
Results come out faster and fewer late clicks are missed
exercises.prompt: What is the most likely effect of raising out-of-order tolerance from 15 seconds to 2 minutes?

exercises.explanation: The window itself is fixed; the watermark decides when it is computed. Allowed lateness lets a window keep accepting late events for a while after it fires and correct its result. Later events are not silently discarded but go to the side output, for recomputation and reconciliation.
exercises.prompt: Complete window firing and late-event handling
exercises.text: A window [[fires]] only once the watermark passes its end; events later than the [[allowed lateness]] go to a side output or are recomputed.

exercises.explanation: This chapter counts per minute with tumbling windows, uses sliding windows for the Top N of the last M minutes, and session windows split by activity gaps. Frameworks name hopping and sliding windows differently, so in an interview the safest approach is to state the window length and slide step directly.
pairs: No overlap; a separate ledger per minute
Looks at the last M minutes by step; can overlap
Closes after a gap with no activity
exercises.prompt: Match each window concept to its meaning

exercises.explanation: A bounded wait only lowers the chance of missing events. Something later can always arrive, and waiting too long slows results. You still need a correction mechanism: events past the limit go to the side output or are recomputed, and daily reconciliation fixes billing results.
exercises.prompt: As long as the watermark waits long enough, every late click is guaranteed to be counted, so billing no longer needs reconciliation.

lessons.title: Fault Tolerance
lessons.summary: Exactly-once, hotspots, snapshots, reconciliation

exercises.explanation: Upstream got no acknowledgement, so it assumes the batch was not finished. After recovery it redoes the batch from the old offset and sends it again, and a downstream that applies +count will double count. Kafka does not detect business-level duplicate results for you.
options: This batch’s result is lost for good; downstream never receives it
Kafka automatically detects and drops the duplicate result
Processing restarts from the old progress and the result is sent again
Downstream is guaranteed to record it only once, unaffected
exercises.prompt: An aggregation node has sent the result for offset 100 downstream, then crashes before it can get an acknowledgement and commit the offset. What most likely happens after recovery?

exercises.explanation: Progress already says “offset 100 processed”, but the result never went out. Recovery resumes at 101, so those counts are never produced. Send-then-record duplicates and record-then-send loses, so saving progress and committing the result must happen atomically.
options: After recovery it starts from the new progress, and the batch’s result is never sent
After recovery it redoes the batch from the old progress, and the result is sent twice
Downstream times out and pulls the batch’s result itself
Progress is already durable, so the result is unaffected
exercises.prompt: To prevent duplicates, the node first saves the processed offset to HDFS/S3 and then sends the result downstream. If it crashes between the two steps, what happens?

exercises.explanation: Exactly-once is about result semantics: duplicate transport is allowed, and atomic commits, idempotent writes of absolute results by a unique key, and exact dedup by event_id make each event count once. Merging by IP wrongly merges different users behind a shared egress IP, and network retries cannot be avoided.
options: Exact dedup at input using a stable event_id
Count only one click per IP per minute
Downstream writes absolute values keyed by (ad, window, filter, version)
Make saving the offset and committing the result downstream one atomic step
Require the network to deliver each message only once
exercises.prompt: Which practices help ensure each real click contributes exactly one count?

exercises.explanation: A Bloom filter has false positives: it can wrongly report a click it has never seen as “seen”. Using it for billing dedup would drop real clicks and undercharge advertisers. Billing needs exact dedup based on a stable event_id.
exercises.prompt: A Bloom filter saves memory and checks for duplicates quickly, so it can be used on its own to dedup billable clicks.

exercises.explanation: Within a consumer group, one partition goes to one consumer, so extra consumers sit idle when partitions run short; reserve enough partitions. Separate consumer groups would each receive every message and process it twice. The number of producers has nothing to do with consumption parallelism.
options: The total Kafka log size is trimmed small enough first
Producer instances are scaled to 200 as well
The topic has enough partitions, at least 200
Each consumer is put in a different consumer group
exercises.prompt: To grow the aggregation consumers in one consumer group from 50 to 200, what must you ensure beforehand?

exercises.explanation: Kafka is a durable commit log: messages are kept for the retention period even after consumption, so growth in total size is normal. To tell whether consumers keep up, watch consumer lag such as `records-lag`. Only when lag jumps do you diagnose the cause and add aggregation resources if needed.
exercises.prompt: If the total log size in Kafka keeps growing, the aggregation consumers must be falling behind.

exercises.explanation: In the example, the node asks the resource manager for more resources, splits 300 events into three groups of 100 to process in parallel, then merges the partial results. Dropping clicks undercharges, a longer watermark only delays output, and a bigger machine does not solve the single-hotspot scaling problem.
options: Move all ads onto one bigger machine to aggregate
Split its events across several nodes for local counts, then merge
Lengthen the watermark wait so the node can work through it slowly
Drop clicks on that ad above a threshold to protect the node
exercises.prompt: One ad suddenly goes viral and the aggregation node responsible for it is overloaded. What does this chapter suggest?

exercises.explanation: Counts from each shard simply add up, but the same user may appear in several shards, so distinct-user counts cannot just be summed. When splitting, also keep the source shard and window identifiers so a retried merge does not add the same part twice.
exercises.prompt: After splitting a hotspot, metrics like count and sum merge easily, while a metric like distinct users is more complex to merge.

exercises.explanation: The snapshot only has counts through 100, so resuming at 120 skips 101–119. Resuming from 80 would instead recount 80–100. A checkpoint must keep state, input position, and committed output consistent with each other; you cannot stitch together the “latest” value of each.
options: Events 101–119 are missed
Events 101–119 are counted twice
No effect; the snapshot already holds all the state
Events 80–100 are counted twice
exercises.prompt: The latest snapshot’s window state covers up to offset 100, but the takeover node resumes consuming from offset 120. What is the result?

exercises.explanation: Reconciliation is an independent recomputation from raw data, compared against the streaming result. Both sides must share time zone, filter rules, lateness range, dedup, and version, or the differences mean nothing. Once differences are found, there must be a review and a correction record, not just an alert.
items: A batch job reads the day’s events from raw storage
Recompute with the same time zone, filter, dedup rules
Compare with the aggregate database item by item
Record reviewed differences and correct billing results
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of daily reconciliation in order

chapters.title: Hotel Reservation System
keyPoints: The inventory unit is hotel × room type × stay date, and stays are half-open; all nights commit in one transaction or the whole booking rolls back.
Same-order retries need an idempotency key and unique constraint; competing orders need row locks, version checks, or conditional updates.
Optimistic locking uses WHERE version = the version you read and checks affected rows; fine at low contention, heavy retries at high contention.
10% overselling becomes an integer cap floor(1.1N) that reservations must not exceed; it does not mean forbidding all overselling.
The cache is for display only; the database decides sales. Write a time-limited hold before payment, and never hold a lock while waiting for payment.
Microservices lose same-database atomicity: 2PC can block, Saga needs compensation; keep tightly linked inventory and booking in one database.

labs.title: Two Guests, One Last Room
Multi-Night Transactions, Idempotent Retries, and Cache Delay

lessons.title: Needs & Estimation
lessons.summary: Scale estimates, service split, and API semantics

exercises.explanation: About 1 million × 70% = 700,000 room nights are occupied per day. Each reservation takes 3 nights on average, so in steady state about 700,000 ÷ 3 ≈ 233,000 new reservations arrive per day, which rounds to about 240,000. 700,000 forgets to divide by 3, and 2.1 million multiplies instead of dividing.
options: About 700,000
About 2.1 million
About 240,000
About 30,000
exercises.prompt: With 1 million rooms, 70% occupancy, and an average stay of 3 nights, about how many new reservations are made per day?

exercises.explanation: 240,000 ÷ 100,000 = 2.4, rounded to about 3 TPS. Working back up the funnel, 3 bookings per second means 30 booking-page views and 300 room-detail views per second. 30 is the booking-page volume; 3,000 divides by the conversion rate once too often. Writes are low, reads two orders of magnitude higher.
exercises.prompt: Complete the estimate of booking write traffic and page QPS
exercises.text: About 240,000 reservations a day over roughly 100,000 seconds is about [[3]] TPS. With 10% conversion at each step (detail page → booking page → booked), the detail page gets about [[300]] QPS.

exercises.explanation: A low average does not mean there are no hotspots: in peak season, the last few rooms of a popular hotel on a given date can still be fought over by many people at once. Concurrency control protects the invariant of each inventory row and has nothing to do with site-wide average traffic.
exercises.prompt: Average site-wide booking TPS is only in the single digits, so you don’t need to worry about two people grabbing the same room at once.

exercises.explanation: Overselling means a hotel deliberately sells more rooms than it has, expecting cancellations; the cap should be configurable, with a plan for guests when it bites. Overselling from a concurrency error goes past that cap. One is a rule and the other is a bug, so keep them apart.
exercises.prompt: The 10% overselling the problem allows is a business strategy, not extra sales caused by database concurrency errors.

exercises.explanation: `reservationID` is the idempotency key that prevents duplicate orders: a double click or a timeout retry carries the same ID, so the backend recognizes it and returns the existing result. An inventory row is identified by (hotel, room type, date), shards by hotel_id, and the room number is usually assigned later.
options: The primary key of each row in the inventory table
The specific room number the guest will stay in
An idempotency key that detects duplicate submissions
Decides which database shard the booking is written to
exercises.prompt: The booking request body carries a `reservationID`. What is its main purpose?

exercises.explanation: The most direct reason is atomic commit, unique constraints, and invariant checks, which is exactly what preventing double-deducted rooms requires. ACID covers only this one database and does not automatically solve consistency with a payment provider; scaling writes and flexible schemas are not relational strengths either.
options: Inventory and bookings need atomic commit, unique constraints, and invariant checks
ACID automatically guarantees consistency with the payment provider
The data shape keeps changing, so a flexible schema helps
Relational databases scale writes horizontally more easily than NoSQL
exercises.prompt: This design uses a relational database. What is the strongest justification?

exercises.explanation: Hotel and room info is fairly static, so cache it aggressively; rates can change daily and belong to pricing; the reservation service maintains inventory on booking and cancellation; booking status advances only after payment succeeds; the gateway handles cross-cutting concerns such as auth and rate limiting.
pairs: Hotel and room info; cache aggressively
Charges payment; updates booking on success
Single entry point for auth and rate limiting
exercises.prompt: Match each service to its responsibility

exercises.explanation: The endpoint name is only illustrative: cancellation is usually a status change (for example to “canceled”) that keeps an audit record and releases the matching inventory. Physical deletion would lose the history needed for refunds, reconciliation, and dispute handling.
exercises.prompt: The cancel endpoint is `DELETE /v1/reservations/{id}`, so the implementation should physically delete the reservation record.

lessons.title: Inventory Model
lessons.summary: Room type × date rows, multi-night, oversell cap

exercises.explanation: Booking specific rooms is more like Airbnb; hotel guests choose a type such as “king room,” and the room number comes later. So the API changes roomID to roomTypeID and adds roomCount to book several rooms at once. Data volume, pricing, and cancellation are not reasons to change the model.
options: Prices vary by room number, so they are hard to compute
There are too many rooms for the database to store
Booking specific rooms cannot support cancellation
Guests book a room type; the room number is assigned later
exercises.prompt: The first data model booked specific room numbers. Why do hotels manage inventory by room type instead?

exercises.explanation: The stay is the half-open interval [check_in, check_out): you stay the nights of the 28th and 29th, and the checkout day, the 30th, no longer uses a room night. Deducting three rows would needlessly sell one room fewer on the 30th; deducting only one row would miss the 29th.
options: Three rows: the 28th, 29th, and 30th
Only one row: the 28th
Two rows: the 29th and 30th
Two rows: the 28th and 29th
exercises.prompt: Check-in is 4/28 and check-out is 4/30. Which inventory rows does this booking occupy?

exercises.explanation: BETWEEN includes both ends, so it counts the checkout day too. A real implementation should use `date >= startDate AND date < endDate`, consistent with the half-open stay interval.
exercises.prompt: The original SQL queries inventory with `date BETWEEN startDate AND endDate`, which covers exactly the nights of the stay.

exercises.explanation: A missing row means some day’s inventory record does not exist (for example, it was not pre-generated), and that cannot be treated as “rooms available.” Verify that the returned row count equals the number of nights; otherwise a missed day would still let the booking succeed.
exercises.prompt: If a date-range query returns fewer inventory rows than there are nights, the booking should be rejected even when every returned row has rooms available.

exercises.explanation: 5,000 × 20 × 2 × 365 = 73 million. 36.5 million counts only one year, and 146 million counts double. A single database can hold this much, but you should still judge it against row width, indexes, and real measurements.
options: About 7.3 million rows
About 146 million rows
About 36.5 million rows
About 73 million rows
exercises.prompt: With 5,000 hotels of 20 room types each and inventory rows pre-generated for the next two years, about how many rows are there?

exercises.explanation: The tightest night decides: min(2,0,4)=0. A consecutive stay is one ticket that cannot be split, and if any night fails within the same transaction, everything rolls back. If the product allows splitting the booking or switching room types, that must be shown to the user explicitly and never substituted silently.
options: Book nights 1 and 3, and tell the user to deal with night 2 themselves
Confirm the order first, then fill night 2 if someone cancels
Fail the whole booking and roll back the nights already deducted
Average 2 rooms left over the three nights, so treat it as bookable
exercises.prompt: A user books 1 room for 3 consecutive nights, and the remaining sellable counts for those nights are 2, 0, and 4. What is the correct handling?

exercises.explanation: The limit is floor(1.1 × N): 15 × 1.1 = 16.5, rounded down to 16. 9 × 1.1 = 9.9; rounding up to 10 would oversell by 1 room, which is 1/9 ≈ 11.1% and exceeds 10%, so only 9 can be sold.
exercises.prompt: Compute the integer sellable limit for “at most 10% overselling”
exercises.text: 100 physical rooms can sell [[110]] rooms, 15 rooms can sell [[16]], and 9 rooms can sell [[9]].

exercises.explanation: That constraint forbids any overselling, which contradicts the 10% the problem allows. Store an integer `sellable_limit`, constrain `total_reserved <= sellable_limit`, and on each order use a conditional update that checks `total_reserved + q <= sellable_limit`.
exercises.prompt: When 10% overselling is allowed, the database constraint should be written as `total_inventory - total_reserved >= 0`.

exercises.explanation: This is an inventory gap that operations must resolve: stop selling first, then arrange fulfillment, relocation, or compensation under policy, with a full audit trail. Quietly canceling orders hurts users, ignoring the outage keeps overselling, and waiting until check-in day leaves no time to handle it well.
options: Automatically cancel the 3 most recent bookings
Ignore the outage and keep the limit at 110
Stop new sales and let operations arrange fulfillment or relocation
Do nothing and see whether anyone cancels by check-in day
exercises.prompt: On one date, a room is temporarily taken out of service, so the sellable limit drops from 110 to 105 while 108 valid bookings already exist. What should you do?

lessons.title: Concurrency
lessons.summary: Idempotent retries, locks, and version numbers

exercises.explanation: Disabling the button only improves the experience: disabled scripts, timeout retries, and direct API calls all bypass it. The reliable approach is an idempotent API: the same order always carries the same reservation_id, with a database unique constraint as the backstop.
exercises.prompt: Disabling the button on the front end after the user clicks submit reliably prevents duplicate orders from the same user.

exercises.explanation: The key is that the ID is generated before submission, so repeated submissions carry the same ID; if each submission generated a new one, the server could not recognize duplicates. The database unique constraint is the last line of defense, and on spotting a duplicate it should return the existing order.
items: Generate a globally unique reservation_id
Submit the booking with that ID attached
The user clicks again; the same ID is sent again
Unique constraint blocks it; original result returns
exercises.prompt: Put the idempotent ordering flow in order

exercises.explanation: Idempotency governs how many times one thing is done: R7 was already done, so return the original result. An error makes the user think it failed and reorder under a new ID, creating a duplicate; a new ID also bypasses idempotency. The server should store a request digest and reject the same ID with changed dates or room type.
options: Return R7’s existing order or status, and don’t deduct again
Report a unique-constraint error and ask the user to re-enter the order
Deduct inventory again, then merge the two orders afterward
Place the order again under a new ID to make sure it succeeds
exercises.prompt: The server already deducted the room for R7 and created the order; only the response was lost. The client retries with the same R7. What is the correct handling?

exercises.explanation: R7 and R8 have different idempotency keys and are both valid new orders, so a unique constraint cannot stop them. You must atomically check `reserved + 1 <= sellable_limit` and update; one succeeds and the other gets sold out. Idempotency keys and inventory control are two different gates.
options: A conditional update or lock on the inventory row
A unique constraint on reservation_id
Disabling the button on the front end after submit
The remaining count in the Redis cache
exercises.prompt: 1 room is left, and two different orders, R7 and R8, are submitted at the same time. What guarantees that only one succeeds?

exercises.explanation: If you deduct inventory first and then insert the order, and the insert is rejected as a duplicate without a rollback, inventory drops by one room with no matching order. The unique constraint and the inventory update must commit together: either both succeed or both roll back.
exercises.prompt: Inserting the order (protected by a unique constraint) must commit in the same transaction as the inventory deduction; otherwise, when a duplicate request is blocked, inventory may already have been wrongly deducted.

exercises.explanation: Both transactions passed the check on a stale read, and each then added one to the current value, so 109 became 111. “Check, then update” has no concurrency protection by itself; you need pessimistic locking, optimistic locking, or a database constraint to close the gap.
options: Booked becomes 111, exceeding the limit
The database rolls back both transactions
The later transaction automatically rereads and gives up
Booked becomes 110 and the later committer is rejected automatically
exercises.prompt: The limit is 110 and 109 are booked, under read committed isolation (not serializable). Two transactions both read 109 and judge the room bookable, then each runs `total_reserved = total_reserved + 1` and commits. What is the result?

exercises.explanation: Put “the version I read” in the WHERE clause: if someone else changed the row first, 0 rows are affected, and you roll back and reread. If the database computes version+1, the new version is always larger, so two stale reads would both pass; local clocks are unreliable; and reading then updating still leaves a race window.
options: Compare each server’s local timestamp and let the later one win
Read the version once more before committing, and update if unchanged
`WHERE version = v_read`, then check the affected row count
`SET version = version + 1`, and pass if the new version is larger
exercises.prompt: When updating an inventory row with optimistic locking, which approach actually detects a concurrent conflict?

exercises.explanation: A pessimistic lock (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) serializes conflicts; an optimistic lock verifies the version at update time; a CHECK constraint makes the database reject bad data. The first three guard against different orders competing for stock; the idempotency key (with a unique constraint) guards against the same order done twice.
pairs: Lock the row first, hold it until commit
Verify the version on update; retry on conflict
Reject writes that break the stock invariant
Make retries of one order take effect once
exercises.prompt: Match each protection to how it works

exercises.explanation: Optimistic locking is cheap when conflicts are rare, but under high contention most requests find the version changed and roll back to retry, wasting resources and adding latency. Queued reads are what pessimistic locking looks like; deadlock is a pessimistic-locking risk; a correct optimistic lock does not oversell.
options: Many requests hit version conflicts and keep rolling back and retrying
Every read blocks, queuing behind the previous transaction’s commit
Two transactions wait on each other and deadlock
Several transactions succeed at once, causing overselling
exercises.prompt: During a promotion, the same inventory row of a popular hotel sees extreme contention. If you still use optimistic locking, what is the most prominent problem?

exercises.explanation: A hot inventory row needs some form of serialization anyway, so pessimistic locking is not always unscalable. The real risks are long transactions and out-of-order locking: the first blocks everyone behind it, the second causes deadlocks. Payment can take seconds, so never wait on it while holding an inventory row lock.
exercises.prompt: Pessimistic locking remains usable under high contention if you keep transactions short, lock in a fixed order, and never hold the lock while waiting for third-party payment.

lessons.title: Scale, Consistency
lessons.summary: Sharding, caching, holds, cross-service transactions

exercises.explanation: Queries specify a hotel, so with hash(hotel_id) sharding, an ordinary multi-night booking’s inventory rows sit on one shard and a local transaction covers them (the transaction is still needed).
