One hotel lives on one shard, so a popular hotel’s traffic is not spread out; the distribution is not perfectly uniform.
options: hotel_id is perfectly uniform and never creates hotspots
After sharding by hotel_id, transactions are no longer needed
Almost every query specifies a hotel, so an ordinary booking lands on one shard
It spreads a popular hotel’s traffic across several shards
exercises.prompt: Traffic grows to 1,000 times the original, so the database needs sharding. Why choose `hotel_id` as the shard key?

exercises.explanation: 1,875 is only an average. A popular hotel’s traffic concentrates on its one shard, so the assumption of an even split fails; how much each shard can take must still be verified by load testing with real SQL, indexes, and hardware.
exercises.prompt: Splitting 30,000 QPS across 16 shards by hotel_id gives about 1,875 QPS per shard on average, so no shard will be overloaded.

exercises.explanation: CDC updates the cache asynchronously, so there is a brief delay: the database already shows 0 while the cache shows 1. The database is authoritative at submit time, so the rejection is correct, not a bug. A same-ID double click returns the original order; an ID collision gives a different error.
options: A database transaction bug misjudged an available room as sold out
Someone else just booked it, and CDC hasn’t synced the new inventory to the cache
The user double-clicked, and the first request already took that room
The reservation_id collided with another order and was rejected
exercises.prompt: The page shows 1 room left for a room type, but the user is told it is sold out on submit. What is the most likely cause?

exercises.explanation: Even when reading the database directly, a user who sees 1 room and hesitates for 10 seconds can still lose it to someone else. There is an inherent race window between viewing and ordering that removing the cache cannot close; the only fix is an atomic check on the authoritative inventory at submit time.
exercises.prompt: Dropping the cache and querying the database directly every time completely eliminates “saw a room, order failed.”

exercises.explanation: Only a hold that is actually deducted from the authoritative allocated count and carries an expiry time counts as a reservation. A front-end countdown is just an animation, a cache number is an observation that goes stale, and reaching the payment page does not mean the inventory has been taken.
options: A time-limited hold has been written to the authoritative inventory
The cache still shows more than 0 rooms of that type
The page has started showing a 15-minute countdown
The user has reached the payment page and filled in their details
exercises.prompt: Under what condition can the system promise the user “this room is held for you for 15 minutes”?

exercises.explanation: CDC (such as Debezium) reads database changes and applies them to Redis, so the cache and database can briefly disagree. The cache therefore only displays; the final booking must check the authoritative inventory. A CDC pipeline must also handle duplicates, reordering, and backlog.
exercises.prompt: Complete how the inventory cache is updated and what it is for
exercises.text: Database changes sync asynchronously to Redis through [[CDC]]; the cache is used only for [[display]], and the database decides whether a sale goes through.

exercises.explanation: Payment connects through a state machine: time-limited hold → payment → confirm or release. Holding a lock while waiting for external payment blocks everyone; a timeout is not a failure, since the money may be charged and must be verified. A database rollback cannot undo a bank charge; retry the confirmation or refund.
options: Write a time-limited inventory hold first, then take payment
If payment succeeds but confirmation fails, verify, then retry confirmation or refund
Release held inventory accurately when a hold expires or an order is canceled
Keep the database lock on the inventory row for the whole payment
Treat a payment API timeout as failure and release inventory right away
exercises.prompt: When connecting payment to the booking flow, which approaches are reasonable?

exercises.explanation: Keeping booking and inventory in one service and database lets local ACID guarantee atomicity. After splitting databases you can use 2PC (costly waiting and locking; a coordinator failure can block) or Saga (eventually consistent, relying on compensation). CDC only synchronizes and gives no transactional atomicity.
pairs: Local transaction in one DB, atomic by nature
Atomic commit across nodes; may block
Async sync of database changes to the cache
exercises.prompt: Match each consistency approach to its characteristic

exercises.explanation: Compensation is not time travel: a sent email cannot be recalled, only corrected, and a payment needs a separate refund transaction. A Saga needs durable state, retryable forward and compensating actions, and a path for manual handling; it is an eventually consistent flow, not a strongly consistent one.
options: One catch at the outermost level is enough to roll everything back
Compensation makes completed steps look as if they never happened
Each step needs a retryable compensation; an email gets a correction notice
A Saga guarantees strong consistency between its steps at all times
exercises.prompt: A Saga chains “deduct inventory → take payment → send confirmation email,” and after the email goes out, the whole booking must be undone. Which understanding of compensation is correct?

exercises.explanation: A pragmatic hybrid puts booking and inventory in one service and relies on same-database ACID for atomicity. Cross-microservice consistency adds the complexity of compensation, retries, and state management, so first judge whether splitting is worth it.
exercises.prompt: Keeping inventory deduction and booking records in the same service and database is often simpler and more reliable than splitting them into two services coordinated by a Saga.

chapters.title: Distributed Email Service
keyPoints: SMTP moves mail between servers; HTTP and IMAP let users read it. Accepted, accepted remotely, in the inbox, and read are different successes.
Persist before replying “accepted”; reject or quarantine invalid mail. Retry outbound 4xx with backoff, record 5xx as failed; diagnose any backlog.
Partition metadata by user_id and sort by timeuuid. Attachment bytes go in object storage; the database keeps only the reference, size, and checksum.
Read/unread query tables make reads simple, but every state change must then update several views, idempotently and tolerating out-of-order events.
The search index is a rebuildable async view. If new mail isn’t searchable, check the index queue watermark; a drained queue isn’t proof.
Deliverability relies on IP warm-up, traffic separation, and SPF/DKIM, but none guarantees the inbox. Replication is not a backup.

labs.title: An Email’s Journey and Queue Watermarks

lessons.title: Needs & Protocols
lessons.summary: Scale estimates and what each protocol does

exercises.explanation: 10 billion emails a day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 116,000 per second, so the order of magnitude is about 100,000. 10,000 is one order of magnitude too low, and 1 million is one too high.
options: About 10,000
About 1,000
About 100,000
About 1 million
exercises.prompt: With 1 billion users each sending 10 emails a day, roughly how many emails are sent per second on average?

exercises.explanation: 40 billion emails a day × 50 KB = 2 PB a day, about 730 PB a year. Attachments: 40 billion × 20% × 500 KB = 4 PB a day, about 1,460 PB a year. Together that is about 2,190 PB, before replicas, indexes, and encoding overhead.
exercises.prompt: Complete the yearly storage estimate (1 billion users, each receiving 40 emails a day)
exercises.text: Each email has 50 KB of metadata, about [[730 PB]] a year; 20% of emails carry a 500 KB average attachment, about [[1,460 PB]] a year.

exercises.explanation: Here “metadata” includes the body, unlike the few hundred bytes a header alone takes. So the metadata DB holds the subject, body, sender, recipients, and so on, and only attachments go to object storage.
exercises.prompt: In this chapter’s estimate, the 50 KB of “metadata” per email actually includes the message body, not just a few hundred bytes of headers.

exercises.explanation: SMTP carries mail between servers. POP and IMAP are for users fetching mail; IMAP treats the server as the source of truth, so it suits multiple devices. Here, web clients call an API over HTTP. A sender looks up the target domain’s MX record to learn which server to hand the mail to.
pairs: Downloads remote mail to the local device
Mail stays on the server, synced across devices
Web clients call the mailbox service API
Tells senders a domain’s receiving server
exercises.prompt: Match each protocol or record with its role in an email system

exercises.explanation: HTTP replaces only the “user reads mail” interface. Servers still use SMTP between themselves, especially when exchanging mail with other providers, and native clients can still use IMAP or POP.
exercises.prompt: The requirements say clients access mailboxes over HTTP, so mail exchange with external email systems should switch to HTTP too.

exercises.explanation: POP is often described as deleting server mail after download, but that is not mandatory: the client’s actions and settings decide. IMAP, however, naturally treats the server as the source of truth, which suits multi-device sync better.
exercises.prompt: After fetching mail over POP, whether the server keeps or deletes the messages depends on the client’s actions and settings.

exercises.explanation: Base64 turns every 3 bytes into 4 characters, so size grows to about 4/3: 3 MB becomes about 4 MB, plus MIME headers and line breaks. So don’t compare the uploaded file size directly with a provider’s attachment limit as if it were the email size.
options: About 6 MB; encoding doubles the size
About 4 MB, plus MIME headers and line breaks
Still 3 MB; encoding doesn’t change the size
About 2.25 MB; encoding compresses the data
exercises.prompt: A user uploads a 3 MB attachment, which is Base64-encoded into the email. About how large is it on the wire?

exercises.explanation: The sender first hands the mail to her own mail server. That server looks up the target domain’s MX record to find the receiving server, then relays the mail over SMTP. The recipient finally fetches it from his own server over IMAP/POP.
items: Alice hands the mail to her sender’s server over SMTP
The sender’s server looks up gmail.com’s MX
The sender’s server relays it to Gmail over SMTP
Bob fetches it from Gmail over IMAP/POP
exercises.prompt: Alice sends an email from Outlook to Bob on Gmail. Put the traditional flow in order

exercises.explanation: Single-machine storage works for a few users. As it grows, disk I/O can’t keep up, and a disk failure or outage hurts reliability and availability, which a distributed design solves. SMTP isn’t the bottleneck (servers still use it), directories already separate users, and one machine can serve IMAP.
options: A single server can only offer POP, not IMAP
SMTP itself can’t carry that many users
Local directories can’t separate users’ mail
Disk I/O becomes a bottleneck and single failures hurt
exercises.prompt: A traditional single mail server stores each email as a file in a local directory. As the user base grows, which problem shows up first?

lessons.title: Send & Receive
lessons.summary: Outbound queue, inbound storage, success semantics

exercises.explanation: The entry point first blocks abusive sending, and web servers run basic checks such as size. Valid mail goes into the outbound queue (attachments are passed as object storage references) and failures go to an error queue. Outbound workers pull asynchronously, check spam and viruses, then deliver to the target server.
items: The load balancer entry point limits excessive sending
Web servers run basic checks such as size
Mail that passes goes into the outbound queue
An outbound SMTP worker checks spam and viruses, delivers
exercises.prompt: Put the distributed email service’s sending flow in order

exercises.explanation: The cause of a backlog decides the action. If the other side is rate limiting, more workers just send harder and get limited harder, so retry with exponential backoff; scaling out helps only when consumers are short. Dropping mail breaks “never lose an email,” and servers don’t switch to HTTP between themselves.
options: Retry with exponential backoff; don’t blindly add workers
Double the outbound workers right away
Switch to pushing directly to their server over HTTP
Drop the backlogged emails to avoid overloading the system
exercises.prompt: The outbound queue keeps backing up, and you find the destination mail server is rate limiting you. What is the better action?

exercises.explanation: Same-domain delivery can skip external SMTP and save a hop, but spam must still be checked first: spam and phishing can come from accounts in your own domain too.
exercises.prompt: When the recipient is in the same domain as the sender, the mail takes a short internal path and can skip the spam check.

exercises.explanation: A 250 depends on the stage it comes in. After RCPT TO, a 250 only accepts that recipient. A 354 after DATA merely permits the body to be sent. Only the success reply after the complete DATA ends means the other side has taken over responsibility for delivery. Inbox placement and reading come even later.
options: The email is already in the recipient’s inbox
The full email has been received and the server owns delivery
The recipient has already opened the email
This one recipient is accepted; the body hasn’t been sent yet
exercises.prompt: In an SMTP session, the server replies 250 after `RCPT TO`. What does that mean?

exercises.explanation: A 250 after complete DATA means the server has taken over delivery. Under RFC 5321 it must not drop the mail casually; it should retry or generate a bounce. It doesn’t prove the mail reached the inbox, let alone was read: the destination system can still file it as spam or quarantine it after accepting.
options: The relay has taken over responsibility for further delivery or hand-off
The other side won’t classify it as spam
On a later temporary failure, it should retry or send a failure notice
The recipient has read the email
The email is already in the recipient’s inbox
exercises.prompt: A relay SMTP server replies 250 after the complete DATA ends. Which conclusions can you draw?

exercises.explanation: 4xx means a temporary problem (the other side is busy or rate limiting), so a later attempt may succeed. 5xx is a permanent rejection (for example, the recipient doesn’t exist), so retrying is pointless; produce a traceable failure result. With several recipients, some may succeed and others fail, so track each separately.
exercises.prompt: Complete how outbound delivery handles the two kinds of failure replies
exercises.text: On a temporary [[4xx]] reply, retry with backoff; on a permanent [[5xx]] reply, record the rejection reason and stop, without resending forever.

exercises.explanation: Replying success means taking on the duty not to lose the email, so it must already be persisted before you promise; if it’s only in memory, a crash loses it. Real-time notification and search indexing are later asynchronous views that may fail for a while and must not block the acknowledgement.
options: After the email has a durable copy that meets the reliability target
After the real-time notification has been pushed to the user’s client
Right after the email is placed in this machine’s in-memory queue
After the email has been written to the search index
exercises.prompt: When may the receiving SMTP server reply “accepted” to the sender?

exercises.explanation: The WebSocket push is just a notification channel that speeds up “seeing the new email.” The email is already stored durably, so an offline user, or one whose push failed, can still read it through the API after coming online. A failed notification must never lose mail.
exercises.prompt: If the real-time push service fails temporarily, users should still be able to read the new email from the durable mailbox through the HTTP API.

exercises.explanation: Rejecting and accepting-then-discarding are different things. Replying “accepted” takes on responsibility for delivery, and silently discarding afterward makes the sender think it was delivered. Invalid mail should be rejected outright under SMTP semantics, or put in quarantine.
exercises.prompt: For a malformed email that can’t be processed, the SMTP server may reply “accepted” first and then quietly discard it in the background.

lessons.title: Metadata Storage
lessons.summary: Partition key, attachment split, read/unread tables

exercises.explanation: The properties: a single column holding a few MB, strong consistency, less disk I/O, high availability, and easy incremental backup. This design favors consistency: in a partition, better to make affected users unavailable than accept conflicting writes. Queries stay within one user, so no cross-user JOIN.
options: A single column can hold a few MB of data
Keeps accepting writes during a network partition, favoring availability
Strong consistency
Supports JOINs between any two users’ mailboxes
Easy incremental backup
exercises.prompt: In an interview you don’t need to design a new database on the spot, but which properties should you say the metadata store needs?

exercises.explanation: Mailbox operations are almost always scoped to one user, so partitioning by user_id puts a user’s data on one shard and queries needn’t cross shards. Time ordering within a partition comes from the clustering key timeuuid. When one email goes to many people, each person’s read and folder state is independent.
options: Fetching, marking as read, and searching mostly involve a single user
user_id keeps emails sorted by time within a partition
user_id guarantees perfectly even data with no hotspots
One mass-mailed email is stored once for all recipients
exercises.prompt: The metadata DB uses `user_id` as its partition key. What is the main reason?

exercises.explanation: Primary key = partition key + clustering key. Using user_id as the partition key keeps a user’s data together; using a timeuuid email_id as the clustering key orders emails within the partition by creation time, which makes paging through lists easy.
exercises.prompt: Complete the division of labor between the two parts of the primary key
exercises.text: The [[partition key]] decides which shard the data goes to; the [[clustering key]] decides the order within a shard, for example arranging emails by timeuuid.

exercises.explanation: Two emails can both carry `report.pdf`, so file names will collide. The real key must include the user, email, and attachment ID; the display file name is stored as an ordinary field.
exercises.prompt: The attachments table can use the file name directly as an attachment’s globally unique key.

exercises.explanation: Metadata totals 1,000 × 50 KB = 50 MB. Attachments are 200 × 500 KB = 100 MB, which is 100/150 ≈ 2/3. Attachments appear in only a fifth of emails yet make up most of the bytes, which is a key reason to split them off into object storage.
options: About half
About one tenth
About one fifth
About two thirds
exercises.prompt: Take 1,000 emails under this chapter’s assumptions: 50 KB of body/metadata each, 20% carrying a 500 KB average attachment. About what share of total bytes are attachments?

exercises.explanation: Attachments are large, rarely modified, and read whole; email lists need small fields queried often. Splitting them lets capacity, queries, and lifecycle be optimized separately, and listing an inbox doesn’t move multi-MB attachments. Object storage still costs requests and traffic, and downloads need a permission check.
options: Object storage automatically verifies mailbox access permissions
Once in object storage, downloads cost nothing
Large, whole-read attachments no longer slow down frequent small-field queries
Attachments no longer need extra backup and redundancy
exercises.prompt: Attachment bytes go in object storage, and the database keeps only the attachment ID, object key, size, and checksum. What is the main benefit?

exercises.explanation: Cassandra isn’t suited to unbounded filtering on non-key fields, and fetching a whole folder to filter it is infeasible at scale. Model tables by query: read and unread tables, looked up by key. The cost is keeping them in sync on every state change. A cache holds only hot data; object storage can’t serve such queries.
options: Query unread emails only from the Redis cache
Fetch the whole folder and filter in memory
Denormalize into separate read and unread query tables
Store the read state in object storage instead
exercises.prompt: In Cassandra you need to list a folder’s unread emails, but is_read is not a key. What does this chapter do?

exercises.explanation: Denormalization turns one complex query into a set of writes on every state change: remove from unread, add to read, update counters and search filter fields, all idempotently. A frontend shuffling its list is only temporary display and can’t replace server-side maintenance; rebuilding every index is disproportionate.
options: Remove it from the unread view and write it to the read view
Update dependent data such as unread counters
Change only is_read on the main record and let the frontend adjust the views
Make sure a duplicate event doesn’t decrement the unread count again
Clear and rebuild all of this user’s search indexes
exercises.prompt: Email M changes from unread to read. With read/unread query tables, which writes does the server still have to own?

exercises.explanation: Projection consumers must handle out-of-order events: record the applied version or event ID and drop older versions when they arrive, or defer to the authoritative state. Otherwise a late event would “resurrect” a deleted or moved email in the wrong view.
exercises.prompt: Version 9 has already moved the email to the trash, so a late version 8 “read” event must not put it back in the read inbox.

exercises.explanation: Don’t assume cross-table or cross-partition updates are automatically atomic just because you use NoSQL. Either maintain them in one transaction where supported, or atomically save the authoritative state plus a pending event and let a retryable projection consumer update the views, with reconciliation to repair partial updates.
exercises.prompt: Because the metadata lives in a NoSQL store like Cassandra, updating the main record and the read/unread query tables is automatically atomic.

lessons.title: Delivery & Search
lessons.summary: Sender reputation, search index, multi-DC

exercises.explanation: Anti-spam systems distrust new servers, so warm up IPs gradually, separate marketing from transactional traffic, and use SPF/DKIM against spoofing. Spamming accounts must be banned quickly or they drag down the whole sending reputation; full volume from a new IP on day one is the surest way to be flagged as spam.
options: Configure sender authentication such as SPF and DKIM
Don’t ban spamming accounts yet, to avoid hurting normal users
Warm up a new IP gradually, ramping volume slowly
Send marketing and important transactional email separately
Send full volume from a new IP on day one to build reputation
exercises.prompt: Which practices help improve deliverability for a self-hosted sending server?

exercises.explanation: A dedicated IP and warm-up only help build reputation, and there’s no fixed time that guarantees results. Landing in the inbox also depends on domain reputation, unsubscribe and bounce handling, DMARC alignment, and the receiving platform’s own rules.
exercises.prompt: Using a dedicated sending IP and warming it up guarantees that email reaches the recipient’s inbox.

exercises.explanation: Mailbox search has a small scope, sorts by time, and needs freshness, unlike internet search. Elasticsearch works out of the box but is an extra service to run. A custom engine can be tuned for mailboxes and integrated with storage, but costs heavy engineering; the hard part is write-heavy optimization, which LSM trees target.
pairs: Whole web, usually ranked by relevance
Own mailbox only, often sorted by time
Ready to use, but a separate service to run
Integrates with metadata storage, but costly
Favors sequential writes; merges level by level
exercises.prompt: Match each search-related item with its characteristic

exercises.explanation: The email has already arrived, so the problem is on the asynchronous indexing path “email change → Kafka indexing task → Elasticsearch.” Check consumption progress using the partition and offset of that email’s event. The outbound queue, MX records, and push are not on the path of this search failure.
options: The outbound queue length, and scale out SMTP workers
Whether the sender domain’s MX record is correct
The consumption progress of this email’s event in the index update queue
The number of WebSocket connections on the real-time push service
exercises.prompt: A user reports that an email they just received can’t be found by search. You’ve confirmed the original is in the authoritative mailbox store. What should you check first?

exercises.explanation: 4280 < 4312 ≤ 4315, so the event has been emitted but not yet consumed. Check this partition’s backlog growth, consumer errors, retries and dead letters, and hotspots. Compare watermarks per partition; one partition’s numbers can’t tell you about the whole system.
options: The producer never emitted this event
Consumption is behind by 35 on every partition
The event is already indexed; the problem is in the query conditions
The event is still queued; check backlog, consumer errors, and hotspots
exercises.prompt: The email’s index event is at offset 4312 in partition P, P’s log end is at 4315, and the index consumer has only processed up to 4280. What does this show?

exercises.explanation: “Fetched and committed progress,” “written to ES,” and “searchable after refresh” are different watermarks: a bulk request can partially fail, and committing the offset too early hides missed indexing; after an ES write, a refresh is usually needed before it is visible. Then check routing, aliases, and query conditions.
exercises.prompt: Even if the index consumer has committed offset 4312, you still can’t conclude that the email is searchable.

exercises.explanation: Data isn’t first persisted only when memory fills up. The write goes to the WAL first, so data not yet flushed survives a crash. Flushed files are merged level by level: this favors sequential writes but causes write amplification, and a read may have to merge several levels.
exercises.prompt: Complete the LSM tree’s write path
exercises.text: A write is first appended to the [[WAL]] for crash recovery, then applied to the memtable; once the memtable reaches a threshold it is [[flushed to disk]] and merged level by level.

exercises.explanation: An LSM tree is a write-heavy storage organization that answers “how do we write to disk efficiently.” Full-text search must go from a term to the documents containing it, which is what an inverted index does. The two can be combined, but an LSM tree is not a full-text search algorithm by itself.
exercises.prompt: Organizing an on-disk index as an LSM tree doesn’t replace the inverted index; full-text search still needs an inverted structure.

exercises.explanation: Choosing consistency means writes affected by the partition wait or are rejected: better temporarily unavailable than producing conflicting data. But this affects only the relevant users, not the whole system. Accepting writes and merging conflicts later is the availability-first approach.
options: Every query for every user must stop
Sync and updates for affected users may be temporarily unavailable
Automatically fall back to eventual consistency to keep accepting writes
Keep accepting writes and merge conflicts afterward
exercises.prompt: This design favors consistency. During a failover or network partition, which behavior best matches that trade-off?

exercises.explanation: Replication is not a backup: an accidental delete is replicated to every copy too. A backup must restore to the state before the deletion, and restores must be verified. Strong consistency and replication don’t automatically mean nothing is lost; you still need durable storage and backups.
exercises.prompt: Emails are replicated across data centers, so accidentally deleted mail can always be recovered from a replica, and no separate backup is needed.

chapters.title: S3-like Object Storage
keyPoints: Metadata and data are separate: the name finds metadata and an object ID, the ID finds a data node, and the node’s index finds the file offset.
Persist the bytes first, then publish metadata: a failure leaves at most a reclaimable orphan; the reverse exposes unreadable broken references.
Synchronous replication keeps acknowledged writes safe but isn’t linearizability: write order, read path, election, and caches need their own rules.
8+4 erasure coding uses 1.5 times the space (50% extra), half of three replicas, at the cost of encoding, decoding, and cross-node reads.
Durability comes from failure-domain placement, checksums, and scrubbing; a checksum only detects damage, so repair needs healthy copies or enough shards.
Sharding by hash(bucket name, object name) favors point lookups; prefix listing fans out and merges. Deletes write a marker first; GC reclaims later.

labs.title: Fault Tolerance and Space: 8+4 Erasure Coding vs 3 Replicas
Orphan Objects, GC, and a Stale Metadata Cache

lessons.title: Storage Types
lessons.summary: Tell storage types apart and estimate object counts

exercises.explanation: This object storage supports only whole-object writes, replacement, and versioning, not in-place partial edits. Workloads that often change bytes in the middle suit block or file storage better; object storage is strongest at write once, read many times.
options: Send a PUT with an offset and rewrite only those few KB
Rewrite the matching disk blocks on the data node directly
Upload a complete new object over the same key, or create a new version
Mount the bucket as a directory and edit through the file interface
exercises.prompt: An application often modifies a few KB in the middle of a 5 GB file. If the file lives in this chapter’s object storage, what is the only way to update it each time?

exercises.explanation: Object storage is built for massive scale, high durability, and low cost, storing and fetching unstructured data whole by key through a RESTful API. VM disks and database files need in-place random rewrites, which suits block storage; a directory mounted by many machines is the classic use of file storage.
options: Huge volumes of user photos and backups, stored and read whole by key
A shared directory mounted by many servers and rewritten often
Database data files that need in-place updates of data pages
A virtual machine’s system disk with low-latency random reads and writes
exercises.prompt: Which kind of data fits object storage best?

exercises.explanation: A bucket is the logical container for objects, and an object is data plus metadata; versioning lets one key keep several versions in a bucket. An SLA is a contractual commitment, which is not the same thing as design goals such as durability and availability.
pairs: Logical container; name assumed globally unique
The data itself plus its metadata
Keeps several versions of an object in a bucket
The provider’s service commitment to customers
exercises.prompt: Match each term with its meaning

exercises.explanation: A bucket has no directory hierarchy in the filesystem sense. The `/` is usually just a prefix convention used to simulate paths and list by prefix. Treating it as a POSIX directory leads you to expect whole-directory renames or locks that don’t exist.
exercises.prompt: An object key like `photos/2021/a.jpg` means the bucket contains a real directory named photos.

exercises.explanation: Durability asks whether data is lost over the long run; availability asks whether it can be accessed right now. When a node is down, the data may be intact but unreadable for a while, and a service being online does not mean data was never corrupted. Design and measure the two separately.
exercises.prompt: Six nines of durability and four nines of availability are different goals: data can be intact yet temporarily unreadable.

exercises.explanation: Weight by share: `0.2×0.5 + 0.6×32 + 0.2×200 = 59.3 MB`. 77.5 MB is the plain average of the three representative values, which ignores that 60% of the objects fall in the 32 MB band.
options: 32 MB
40 MB
exercises.prompt: By count, 20% of objects are under 1 MB, 60% are 1–64 MB, and 20% are over 64 MB, with representative sizes of 0.5, 32, and 200 MB. What is the average object size, roughly?

exercises.explanation: `10^11 MB / 59.3 MB ≈ 1.69×10^9`, about 1.7 billion. The 40% is an assumption about used capacity; if the 100 PB is already actual data, you should not multiply by 0.4 again. The 270 million figure applies 40% a second time to 680 million.
options: About 270 million
About 4.2 billion
About 680 million
About 1.7 billion
exercises.prompt: An estimate assumes 100 PB of capacity with 40% used, which gives about 680 million objects. If the 100 PB is entirely actual data instead, about how many objects are there?

exercises.explanation: `680 million × 1 KB ≈ 680 billion bytes ≈ 0.68 TB`. Next to 100 PB of data, the metadata is tiny, but it has a huge number of entries and is queried often, so the object table still needs sharding and the bucket table needs more read throughput.
exercises.prompt: Complete the metadata size estimate
exercises.text: At 40% used capacity there are about [[680 million]] objects; at 1 KB of metadata each, the total metadata is about [[0.68 TB]].

exercises.explanation: Object storage can be limited by capacity or by IOPS. The number of random seeks decides how many small random I/Os a disk completes per second, and with huge numbers of small objects it often becomes the bottleneck before capacity does. Sequential I/O doesn’t seek repeatedly, so you can’t derive throughput from this number.
options: A disk’s annual failure rate
The throughput ceiling for large sequential reads and writes
The IOPS ceiling for small-object random reads and writes
The total disk capacity the whole cluster needs
exercises.prompt: A 7200 rpm SATA disk can do roughly 100–150 random seeks per second. What is this number best used to estimate?

exercises.explanation: The features from requirements clarification are: create buckets, upload/download, versioning, and listing the objects in a bucket. Partial in-place modification is out of scope, since an object can only be replaced whole; POSIX mounting is a file storage capability.
options: Mount a bucket as a POSIX file system
Modify part of an object’s bytes in place
List the objects in a bucket
Create a bucket
Object versioning
exercises.prompt: Which of these features does this problem’s object storage need to support?
exercises.refAnchor: d24/第-1-步理解问题并确定范围
exercises.refTitle: Step 1: Understand the Problem and Establish Scope

lessons.title: Read/Write Path
lessons.summary: How a PUT/GET flows and how bytes get replicated

exercises.explanation: Metadata is small and queried often; content is large and mostly read or written whole. Separating them lets each side scale against its own bottleneck. The cost: a read needs an extra hop to metadata, and a write spans two systems with no shared transaction, hence orphan objects.
options: Reading an object touches only one system, saving a network round trip
Metadata and bytes fit in one transaction, so they are consistent by nature
Objects can therefore be modified partially in place
The two have different access patterns, so each scales and is tuned independently
exercises.prompt: Object storage keeps metadata and object content in two separate stores. What is the main benefit?

exercises.explanation: The API service holds no state: it calls IAM for auth first, then talks to the metadata store and the data store. The data store knows only UUIDs, not bucket or object names; the mapping from name to ID lives in the metadata store.
pairs: Spreads API requests across service replicas
Stores and fetches real bytes by object UUID
Records buckets, object names, and object IDs
exercises.prompt: Match each high-level component with its responsibility

exercises.explanation: Authenticate first, then write the bytes. Once the bytes are durable and a UUID comes back, publish the metadata, and only then reply with success. Writing bytes before publishing metadata means a failure leaves at most a reclaimable orphan, never an object users can see but cannot read.
items: The client sends a PUT request to the API service
IAM verifies the identity and write permission
The data store persists the body and returns a UUID
The metadata store records object ID, bucket ID, and name
Success is returned to the client
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of uploading the object `script.txt` in order (the bucket already exists)

exercises.explanation: The path is bucket/key, then the metadata store returns the object UUID, then the data store fetches the bytes by UUID. File names and offsets belong to the data node’s internal local index, which global metadata doesn’t track; read permission is checked by IAM.
options: The object’s UUID, used to fetch the bytes from the data store
The full byte content of the object
The object’s file name and offset on the data node
Whether the caller has read permission
exercises.prompt: When handling `GET /bucket-to-share/script.txt`, what key piece of information does the API service get back from the metadata store?

exercises.explanation: If the bytes are written but the metadata commit fails, you are left with an unreferenced orphan that can be reclaimed later. If the metadata is published before the bytes are durable, users see a broken reference that can’t be read. Better an extra box with no waybill than a waybill with no box.
exercises.prompt: In an upload, making the metadata visible first and persisting the bytes afterward is more dangerous than writing the bytes first and committing the metadata afterward.

exercises.explanation: A timeout doesn’t mean the commit failed: it may have succeeded with only the response lost. Check with a stable upload/request ID, then retry idempotently. Deleting O9 might destroy a legitimate object; a new ID leaves an extra copy; reporting success outright may be false and the object unreadable.
options: Assume the commit succeeded and return success to the client
Generate a new object ID and write the data again
Check the commit status first, then retry idempotently if it did not commit
Delete O9 immediately and make the client upload from scratch
exercises.prompt: The three replicas of object O9 are written. While committing the metadata `photo.jpg → O9`, the connection drops and the client gets a timeout. What is the safest next step?

exercises.explanation: Consensus requires a surviving majority: with 5 nodes at least 3 must be healthy, so at most 2 can fail; with 7 nodes at least 4 must be healthy, so at most 3 can fail. The placement service holds the virtual cluster map and is a critical component, so it is replicated with consensus.
options: 3 nodes
2 nodes
1 node
4 nodes
exercises.prompt: The placement service is replicated with Raft, with 5 or 7 replicas recommended. If you deploy 5 replicas, how many node failures can it tolerate at most while a majority can still communicate?

exercises.explanation: The routing service first picks the replica group, then hands the data to the primary. The primary replies only after both replicas have copied the data, so getting a UUID back means several copies are on disk. Waiting for replication adds write latency: you trade latency for durability.
items: The API service passes the object to the routing service
The routing service sends it to the group’s primary
The primary copies it to two replicas and waits
The data store returns the object UUID to the API service
exercises.prompt: Put the flow of writing object bytes into the data store in order

exercises.explanation: The replica count only answers how many copies of the data exist. Which version of history a read sees depends on write ordering, the read path, and election rules, and a cache must not bypass them. Adding replicas or switching to erasure coding changes only durability and space; it can’t fix reading a stale version.
options: Switch to 8+4 erasure coding
A single order and commit point for concurrent writes to the same key
A read path that returns only a committed, sufficiently recent version
Fencing off the old primary with a term during failover
Raise the replica count from 3 to 5
exercises.prompt: For “a read after a successful write always sees the new value” to hold, what must be specified besides writing synchronously to three replicas?

exercises.explanation: A heartbeat timeout means only a suspected failure: it may be network flapping, a stalled process, or a partition, and the data on disk may be intact. Handle it using the timeout, the node’s identity or term, and a rejoin procedure, so you don’t re-create replicas while the old primary keeps accepting writes.
exercises.prompt: When the placement service sees a data node’s heartbeat time out, that proves the data on the node is permanently lost.

lessons.title: Node Durability
lessons.summary: Storing small objects; replication vs erasure coding

exercises.explanation: Filesystems allocate in blocks, so a 1 KB object still takes a typical 4 KB block, and hundreds of millions of small files also mean hundreds of millions of inodes. Appending to large files cuts both space and management overhead, at the cost that deletion doesn’t free space at once and compaction is needed to reclaim it.
options: Large files naturally support listing by key prefix
It reduces wasted block space and inode overhead
Deleting an object frees its disk space immediately
Large files allow partial in-place modification of objects
exercises.prompt: Why don’t data nodes store one file per object, and instead append small objects into files of several GB?

exercises.explanation: The bottleneck is that appends to one file must be serial. Giving each core its own file removes the lock contention. Raising the rollover threshold doesn’t change the contention; a global lock is the serialization itself; one file per object returns to the small-file problem.
options: Raise the file rollover threshold above a few GB
Go back to one file per object
Take a global lock before every append
Let different cores append to different files
exercises.prompt: Many CPU cores append objects to the same data file at once, so writes must be serialized and throughput stalls. What improvement does this chapter give?

exercises.explanation: The name finds metadata and an object ID, the ID locates a data node, and the node then looks up the file offset. The local index records `object_id`, `filename`, `file_offset`, and `object_size`; it covers only this node’s objects and is not global metadata.
exercises.prompt: Complete the two-level mapping used to locate an object
exercises.text: Global metadata maps the bucket name and object name to the [[object ID]]; the data node’s local index then maps it to the [[file and offset]], from which the bytes are read.

exercises.explanation: A shared remote database would have to serve the whole cluster’s queries, with an extra network round trip on every read. A local index covers only this node’s objects, so an embedded database is enough. Whether to pick SQLite or RocksDB should be settled by measuring concurrency, recovery, and persistence cost.
exercises.prompt: Each data node only looks up the objects it stores, so it can embed SQLite for its local index instead of having every node share one remote mapping database.

exercises.explanation: A file append and a database insert live in two different systems and are not a transaction by themselves: the file may be written without the index entry, or the index may commit before the file reaches disk. Recovery after a restart relies on logs, flush ordering, object boundaries, and checksums.
exercises.prompt: A data node appends an object to `/data/c`, then inserts a record into the mapping table. These two steps naturally form an atomic transaction, so nothing is inconsistent after a crash.

exercises.explanation: Multiplying the three probabilities requires failures to be uncorrelated. If all three replicas sit in one rack, one power outage loses them all, which is why you spread them across failure domains such as racks and data centers. Repair windows, silent corruption, and operator error also push real risk above the formula.
options: Every disk is read and written sequentially
Metadata and data are stored separately
Data is written to the primary first and then replicated
The failures of the three replicas are independent
exercises.prompt: The chapter takes an HDD annual failure rate of 0.81% and concludes that three replicas reach about six nines, estimating the loss probability as `0.0081³`. Which assumption does this calculation depend on most?

exercises.explanation: Cut into 8 shards of 100 MB each, then generate 4 parity shards of the same size: 12 shards, 1,200 MB in total, which is 1.5 times the original and 50% extra. 2,400 MB is what three replicas take, so 8+4 uses only half the space of three replicas.
exercises.prompt: An 800 MB object is stored with 8+4 erasure coding. How much space does it take in total? (Ignore metadata and alignment padding.)

exercises.explanation: Erasure coding trades computation and cross-node access for space: reads fetch shards from several nodes and may decode; repairs pull many shards. It uses 1.5 times the space, versus 3 times for three replicas. 8+4 tolerates any 4 missing shards while three replicas can lose only 2 copies, so its fault tolerance is not worse.
options: Extra computation for encoding, decoding, and checksums
A larger total storage footprint
Higher implementation complexity
Reads and repairs must touch shards on multiple nodes
Fewer simultaneous node failures tolerated than three replicas
exercises.prompt: Compared with three replicas, what does 8+4 erasure coding cost you?

exercises.explanation: A replica can serve a whole object from one node, so latency is low but it takes 3 times the space. Erasure coding saves space, but reads and repairs span nodes and need computation. So latency-sensitive workloads lean toward replication, and cost-sensitive large-scale storage leans toward erasure coding.
options: Both use three replicas
A uses replicas, B uses erasure coding
A uses erasure coding, B uses replicas
Both use erasure coding
exercises.prompt: Service A has little data but needs very low read latency; service B is a petabyte-scale archive that is rarely read. According to this chapter, which redundancy scheme does each lean toward?

exercises.explanation: Recomputing and comparing the checksum on read only tells you the data is bad. Repair relies on another intact replica, or on rebuilding from at least 8 valid shards in 8+4. Periodic scrubbing finds problems before a second failure; data that fails verification is quarantined first, never deleted if it is the only copy left.
exercises.prompt: A checksum can detect silent corruption, but repairing it still requires a healthy replica or enough valid shards.

lessons.title: Metadata & GC
lessons.summary: Sharding, listing, versions, multipart upload, and GC

exercises.explanation: Sharding by bucket puts all objects of a bucket in one shard, so a huge bucket becomes a hotspot. Its upside is exactly that single-bucket point lookups and listings hit just one shard. Buckets are usually limited in number, so the bucket table fits in one database; it is the object table that needs sharding.
options: Objects in one bucket cannot be listed by prefix
The bucket table grows too large for a single database
Looking up one object by bucket name and object name queries every shard
One huge bucket with billions of objects overwhelms its shard
exercises.prompt: If the object table is sharded by `bucket_id`, what problem is most likely?

exercises.explanation: Point lookups, inserts, and deletes all carry the bucket and object name, so the hash sends them straight to one shard. But objects in the same bucket with the same prefix are scattered over all shards, so listing must query each shard and merge in memory. This is the trade-off between balanced point lookups and range locality.
options: Deleting one object by bucket name and object name
Listing the objects in a bucket whose key prefix is `abc/`
Finding one object by bucket name and object name
Uploading a new object and writing its metadata
exercises.prompt: The object table is finally sharded by `hash(bucket_name, object_name)`. Which operation becomes slower as a result?

exercises.explanation: Two paths work: accept fan-out and merge, or build a separate listing table partitioned by bucket. In pagination each shard returns a different number of rows, so a sorted cursor that remembers each shard’s position beats a large offset. Querying one shard misses data; bucket sharding brings back the big-bucket hotspot.
options: Go back to sharding by bucket_id and ignore hotspots
Query every shard and merge in memory, accepting slower listing
Use sorted cursors and per-shard positions instead of large offsets
Build a separate denormalized listing table partitioned by bucket
Query only one shard and return the full result
exercises.prompt: After hash sharding, which approaches deal with listing a bucket’s objects becoming slow or hard to paginate?

exercises.explanation: Deleting just inserts a special delete marker as the newest version, so a default GET sees it and returns 404. The old version bytes remain and may still be read by version number; space is freed only by lifecycle cleanup and GC. It also does not “restore” the previous version as the current one.
options: Mark all versions of the object read-only
Roll the current version back to the previous version
Physically delete the bytes of all versions at once
Insert a delete marker as the newest version
exercises.prompt: A bucket has versioning on, and a user deletes the object `report.pdf`. What does the system do by default?

exercises.explanation: Client clocks can drift or even be tampered with, so they can’t decide version order. `object_version` uses a TIMEUUID so versions sort by time, but the order of concurrent versions of one key should be decided by server-side rules, so that every reader sees the same “latest version.”
exercises.prompt: Two clients upload new versions of the same key at almost the same moment. The system can use each client’s local clock to decide which version is newer.

exercises.explanation: Parts travel independently, and a failure retransmits only that part. The commit must carry every part number and ETag, so each part must have returned its ETag first. The full object becomes visible only after the commit, and uncommitted temporary parts are cleaned up by garbage collection.
items: The client sends an initiation request
The server returns a unique upload_id
The client uploads each part with the upload_id
The server returns an ETag for each successful part
The client commits the upload_id, part numbers, and ETags
The server assembles the object and returns success
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a multipart upload of a large file in order

exercises.explanation: An ETag is an identifier defined by the service. For multipart uploads and some encryption modes it is not the MD5 of the full bytes (it often has a part-count suffix), so a mismatch doesn’t show corruption. To verify integrity, use a declared checksum algorithm and check whether it covers the whole object or combines parts.
options: The ETag of a multipart upload is not an MD5 of the whole file in the first place
The local file was modified during the upload
The server missed the last part when computing the MD5
One part was corrupted in transit; delete the object and re-upload
exercises.prompt: A client uploads a file in two parts, then compares `md5(local file)` with the returned ETag and finds they differ. What is the most reasonable conclusion?

exercises.explanation: The point of multipart upload is that parts transfer and retry independently, and parts that already succeeded are kept. Once all parts are in, you commit the part list, and the object becomes visible only after the server has assembled it, so readers never see half a file.
exercises.prompt: If one part fails during a multipart upload, you only need to resend that part with the same upload_id instead of uploading the whole file again.

exercises.explanation: GC reclaims deferred deletions, orphans from failed uploads, and corrupted replicas that can be replaced. A new upload by design writes bytes before publishing metadata, so having no reference at this instant isn’t proof of garbage, and an old file must wait for in-flight reads. Reclamation lags behind visibility.
options: Space held by objects whose deletion was deferred
Orphaned data left by failed uploads and confirmed to have no references
A new upload whose bytes were just written but whose metadata isn’t published yet
An old file whose mapping was switched but is still used by in-flight reads
Corrupted replicas confirmed to be replaceable
exercises.prompt: What space can the garbage collector reclaim?

exercises.explanation: First copy the valid objects, and switch the mapping only after the new file is durable, so readers can always find the data. Switch the mapping in one transaction so nothing is half old, half new. An old file may still be being read, so it can’t be deleted at the instant of the switch.
items: Pick old files that reach the compaction threshold
Copy still-valid objects from the old files to a new file
Point object_mapping to the new location in a transaction
Free the old files after in-flight reads finish
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of one compaction (merging and cleaning up files) in order

chapters.title: Real-Time Gaming Leaderboard
keyPoints: Only a trusted game server may submit scores, after verifying the match and with a unique event ID for dedup; HTTPS and login don't prove a score is real.
A Redis sorted set uses a hash table to look up scores by member and a skip list for score order; adding points and finding a position are both O(log N).
ZREVRANK returns a zero-based position and doesn't tie equal scores; competition rank = the number of players with a strictly higher score + 1.
Redis Cluster assigns slots by key and never splits a big ZSET; split the key in the application, and don't share a hash tag across shards.
Hash sharding: each shard's top K merge into the global top K, but a personal rank needs a fan-out count. Range sharding must handle cross-range moves.
Replicas and persistence can still lose points; rebuild by idempotently replaying durable match events. Percentiles need product's approval.

labs.title: Sorted Set Leaderboard: Position, Rank, and Ties
After Sharding: Top K Merge, Cross-Shard Rank, and Hot Keys

lessons.title: Needs & Scoring
lessons.summary: Estimate update volume; who may add points

exercises.explanation: Arrivals are about `5,000,000 / 100,000 = 50/s`; at 10 games per player, average updates are `50×10 = 500 QPS`. 2,500 is the peak (5 times the average); 50 is only the arrival rate.
exercises.prompt: With 5 million DAU, about `10^5` seconds in a day, and an average of 10 games per player, what is the average update QPS, using the simplified upper bound that each game may trigger one update?

exercises.explanation: Peak is `50×5 = 250/s`, and peak updates are `250×10 = 2,500 QPS`; 500 QPS is the average update rate, not the peak. With one top-ten view per player per day, average reads equal the arrival rate, 50 QPS. At this order of magnitude, a single Redis instance can handle the load.
exercises.prompt: Complete the leaderboard's peak and read estimates
exercises.text: Average arrivals are about 50/s; a peak at 5 times that is [[250/s]]; with 10 games per player, peak updates are about [[2,500 QPS]]; one top-ten view per player per day gives average reads of about [[50 QPS]].

exercises.explanation: DAU divided by seconds gives an arrival or activity rate, not online concurrency. Concurrency also depends on session length: if each player plays 30 minutes straight, far more than 50 are online at the same time.
exercises.prompt: 5 million DAU divided by the seconds in a day is about 50/s, so roughly 50 players are online at any moment.

exercises.explanation: The requirements are the top ten, a given user's rank, and, if time allows, the four players above and below. The board restarts every month and old boards are archived, so no cross-season total is required; a friends board is an extension beyond the requirements.
options: Show an all-time total leaderboard across every past season
Filter the leaderboard by friend relationships
Show the rank of a given user
Show the top ten players
Show the players four positions above and below that user
exercises.prompt: Which of the following are functional requirements of this leaderboard (optional ones included)?

exercises.explanation: HTTPS only protects data in transit from eavesdropping and tampering; it cannot stop the sender from making things up. Players control their own clients and can send `score: 999999` over a perfectly encrypted connection. The score must be computed by an authoritative game server from the match result.
exercises.prompt: Even if HTTPS is used all the way from client to server, it cannot stop a player from submitting a forged high score.

exercises.explanation: Login proves who is submitting, not how the score was earned; a signing key shipped with the client can be extracted, or the signing logic called directly. Only a game server that has verified the match result should call the scoring endpoint.
options: Any client connected over HTTPS
Any logged-in player client
Only trusted game servers
Any client that signs requests with a built-in key
exercises.prompt: `POST /v1/scores` adds points to a player. Who should be allowed to call it?

exercises.explanation: The key step is the game service verifying the win: only verified wins reach the leaderboard, and a client's claim of victory doesn't count. If the server runs the game logic authoritatively, it already knows the outcome, so the client notification step can be dropped.
items: The client tells the game service that the player won
The game service verifies the win is valid
The game service calls the leaderboard service
The leaderboard service updates the score in storage
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a player's win becoming a leaderboard score in order

exercises.explanation: `ZINCRBY` is not idempotent: each replay adds again. Give each match result a unique event ID and check whether it was already processed before applying it. A message queue can also redeliver, so it can't replace dedup; HTTPS and persistence are unrelated to duplicates.
options: Give events a unique ID and deduplicate by it
Put a message queue in between
Enable Redis AOF persistence
Send the scoring request over HTTPS instead
exercises.prompt: A win's scoring event was resent three times after a timeout. To make sure the player gets only 1 point, what is the key practice?

exercises.explanation: A queue's value is letting several downstream consumers (analytics, push) consume the same match result without coupling. This design has no such need, so the first version can connect directly. A queue doesn't handle ordering and doesn't deduplicate; it can even redeliver.
options: No, a queue would scramble the score ordering
Yes, or retries will add points twice
Yes, or scores can't update in real time
Optional at first; add it once other services need the events
exercises.prompt: Should there be a message queue between the game service and the leaderboard service? Following this chapter's approach, which answer fits best?

exercises.explanation: With keys like `leaderboard_feb_2021`, a new month starts from an empty board and the old board is archived as a whole. Sharing one key means clearing tens of millions of members at month start and losing history. The API and database unique keys should also include the month or season.
options: Encode the month into the high bits of the score
Create a new Redis instance every month
Share one key across all months and delete members one by one at month start
Create a new key each month and archive the old month's key to historical storage
exercises.prompt: The requirement is a new contest and a new leaderboard every month. Implemented in Redis, what is the most natural organization?

lessons.title: Sorted Sets
lessons.summary: Top ten, rank, and neighbors with a sorted set

exercises.explanation: The top ten needs only 10 index rows; a middle player's rank is the number of players ahead of them, so counting scans millions of rows and the cost grows linearly with the player count. Indexes are updated with each write and don't become invalid. A Redis sorted set gives a position in `O(log N)`.
options: It must count every row with a higher score, close to a full scan with many players
The score index has to be rebuilt for every query
Frequent score updates invalidate the index, forcing a full table scan
The player table has no primary key, so the player can't be located
exercises.prompt: A relational database has an index on `score`, so `ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10` is fast. Why is finding the rank of a player in the middle of the board still expensive?

exercises.explanation: `>=` counts yourself and everyone tied with you, so both 100-point players get 2. The usual tied competition rank is the number of players with a strictly higher score + 1, which gives 1, 1, 3.
exercises.prompt: Computing rank with `COUNT(*) WHERE score >= my_score`, with scores 100, 100, and 90, both 100-point players get rank 1.

exercises.explanation: With scores 100, 100, 90: 0 players are above the 100s, so both are rank 1; 2 players are above the 90, so it is rank 3. Using “not lower than” would count yourself and the ties. In Redis, `ZCOUNT key (score +inf` counts the players with a strictly higher score.
exercises.prompt: Complete the formula for tied competition rank
exercises.text: Competition rank = the number of players whose score is [[strictly higher than]] mine, [[plus 1]].

exercises.explanation: The two structures split the work: the hash table finds a member's score quickly, while the skip list keeps the order by score and supports range reads and position lookups. Persistence and sharding are not jobs of the sorted set's internal structures.
options: Persisting data to disk
Keeping members ordered by score
Sharding the set across nodes
Looking up a member's score directly
exercises.prompt: For large collections, a Redis sorted set uses both a hash table and a skip list. What is the hash table for?

exercises.explanation: A skip list stacks progressively sparser index layers on a sorted linked list and homes in on the target from the top layer down. In the 64-node example, the linked list walks 62 nodes while the skip list takes about 11; insertion and lookup are typically `O(log N)`.
options: It puts all nodes in an array so binary search works
It adds layers of sparse indexes on top of the list, so many nodes are skipped
It keeps only the top ten, so the data is tiny
It buckets nodes by hash value so they can be located directly
exercises.prompt: Why is a skip list so much faster to search than a plain sorted linked list?

exercises.explanation: Use `ZREVRANGE key 0 9` for the top ten and `ZREVRANK` for a player's own position. To count the members of one shard, use `ZCARD`; `INFO keyspace` is wrong for this because it counts keys, not members.
pairs: Add to a score; a missing player starts at zero
Read by position range, high score to low
Get a player's zero-based position, high to low
Count the members within a score range
Count the total members in the set
exercises.prompt: Match each Redis command with its use in a leaderboard

exercises.explanation: Both ends of the range are inclusive. Only positions 0 and 1 are ahead of this player, so the start is clamped to 0, not -2 (negative indexes count from the end in Redis); the end is `2+4 = 6`. In the chapter's example, position 361 maps to `357 365`.
options: `ZREVRANGE key 0 8`
`ZREVRANGE key -2 6`
`ZREVRANGE key 2 10`
`ZREVRANGE key 0 6`
exercises.prompt: You want to show a player and the four players above and below. If `ZREVRANK` returns 2 (that is, position 3), which command should you run?

exercises.explanation: With equal scores, a sorted set orders members by the lexicographic order of the member string, and `ZREVRANK` returns the zero-based position after sorting, such as 0 and 1. The tied rank the problem asks for has to be computed separately; you can't just add 1 to the position.
exercises.prompt: When A and B both have 100 points, `ZREVRANK` still gives them different positions; it does not treat them as tied automatically.

exercises.explanation: `26 bytes × 25 million ≈ 650 MB`. 65 GB is the figure after scaling up 100 times. Note this is only the payload; actual Redis memory use is much higher.
options: About 65 MB
About 6.5 GB
About 650 MB
About 65 GB
exercises.prompt: Using a payload-only model: 25 million players, each with a 24-byte ID and a 2-byte score, roughly how large is the leaderboard data?

exercises.explanation: Redis scores are double-precision floats, not 2 bytes; member objects, the dictionary, skip list nodes, allocator fragmentation, replicas, and persistence all use memory. Doubling is only a rough margin; run a load test with realistic ID lengths and distributions.
exercises.prompt: 650 MB is only a payload estimate; actual Redis memory must also account for double-precision scores, member objects, skip list nodes, and memory fragmentation.

lessons.title: Scaling & Sharding
lessons.summary: Splitting keys, and merging Top K across shards

exercises.explanation: 5 million to 500 million is 100 times, not 10 times. `2,500 × 100 = 250,000 QPS` and memory `650 MB × 100 = 65 GB`, which match the chapter's figures. 25,000 is the result of wrongly using 10 times.
options: 2.5 million
exercises.prompt: DAU grows from 5 million to 500 million. Using the chapter's model (a current peak of 2,500 updates/s), what is the peak update QPS?

exercises.explanation: Redis Cluster assigns hash slots by key. A key lands in exactly one slot, handled by one primary. Adding nodes only moves whole keys; it never slices a key's members into pieces. Splitting a logical board into several keys is the application's job.
exercises.prompt: After enabling Redis Cluster, a large ZSET with 100 million members is automatically split across multiple nodes.

exercises.explanation: Ordinary keys are located with `CRC16(key) mod 16384`, and the unit of assignment is the whole key. If a logical board is a single key, all its writes and memory concentrate on one primary.
exercises.prompt: Complete Redis Cluster's slot rule
exercises.text: Redis Cluster has [[16,384]] hash slots and computes the slot from the [[key]], so all members of one ZSET live in the same slot.

exercises.explanation: Cluster hashes only the part inside the braces (the hash tag), so sharing `{2026-09}` deliberately sends them all to one slot. Shard keys should not share a tag, e.g. `board:2026-09:s00`; keys share a tag only when they need atomic operations within the same shard.
options: They share a hash tag, so they all land in the same slot
There aren't enough hash slots for 16 keys
16 shards is too few; at least 100 are needed
ZSET keys can't be spread across multiple slots
exercises.prompt: A monthly board is split into 16 keys, `board:{2026-09}:s00` through `s15`. After launch, writes still concentrate on one node. Why?

exercises.explanation: Under range sharding, players in a higher range always rank ahead of those in lower ranges, so read the top shard first and, if it has fewer than ten, continue down the ranges in order. This is one hidden cost of range sharding, but it is still cheaper than fanning out to all shards.
options: Return only those 6 players
Split [900, 1000] finer and reshard
Fetch the top 4 from the next range down to fill up
Show only the top six
exercises.prompt: With range sharding by score, the top range [900, 1000] currently has only 6 players. How do you return the global top ten?

exercises.explanation: Global position = players in higher shards + position within the shard = `1,200 + 3`. The number of players in higher ranges comes from summing `ZCARD` over each shard; the sum needs a consistent snapshot, or you accept a briefly approximate result.
options: 3rd
exercises.prompt: With range sharding by score, a player ranks 3rd (counting from 1) within the [500, 600) shard, high to low, and all higher ranges hold 1,200 players in total. What is the player's global position?

exercises.explanation: Range sharding lets the top ten read only high shards and a personal position count only higher shards, at the cost of cross-range migration, boundary filling, and count consistency. Fanning out to all shards for the top ten is the cost of hash sharding; concentration in one key is the problem of not sharding.
options: Crossing a range boundary means migrating the member and updating routing
Fill from the next shard when the top range has fewer than ten players
Summing higher-range counts needs a consistent snapshot or an approximation
One logical board is still concentrated in a single key
The global top ten must fan out to every shard
exercises.prompt: With range sharding by score, which extra problems must you handle?

exercises.explanation: Suppose someone is in the global top 10 but ranks below 10th in their own shard. Then 10 players in that shard are ahead of them, so they are at best 11th globally, a contradiction. So the global top 10 lies within the union of each shard's top 10. This requires one ordering rule and each player in exactly one shard.
exercises.prompt: With hash sharding, if all shards use the same ordering rule, taking each shard's top 10 and merging them is enough to pick the global top 10 players.

exercises.explanation: A local top 10 only guarantees picking 10 players; it doesn't guarantee including every player tied at the 10th-place boundary. With ties the result may exceed 10 players: find the score at the global 10th position first, then fetch everyone at or above it from each shard.
options: The result is complete; all 12 are returned
Two tied players are missed; widen the fetch using the 10th score
The 12 players are double counted during the merge
Redis automatically returns all 12 tied players
exercises.prompt: 12 players all have 100 points and are in the same shard. Product requires that the top ten include all tied players. What happens if each shard returns only its top 10 and you merge?

exercises.explanation: A relational database returns the top ten fast but must count every row ahead of a middle player; a single ZSET ranks quickly but the whole key sits on one node. After splitting, range sharding must handle players migrating across ranges, while hash sharding must take the top K from every shard and merge.
pairs: Ranking a middle player means counting many rows
Memory and writes limited to one node
Crossing a range means migrating members
Global top K needs a merge across all shards
exercises.prompt: Match each leaderboard storage approach with its main cost

lessons.title: Options & Recovery
lessons.summary: Lambda, DynamoDB, and rebuilding after failure

exercises.explanation: A serverless platform manages servers and scaling, removing hardware and OS operations. But cold starts, concurrency limits, connections from function instances to Redis, network latency, and cost still need planning, and real-time targets must be tested end to end.
options: Manually adding or removing servers with traffic
Function concurrency limits and Redis connection counts
Buying and racking physical servers
Operating system patching
exercises.prompt: After moving the leaderboard to API Gateway + AWS Lambda, what does the team still have to plan?
exercises.refTitle: To Use a Cloud Provider or Not

exercises.explanation: After a snapshot forks a child process, the parent must copy each page it modifies, so the more writes and the longer the snapshot, the more extra memory. Two times is only a rule of thumb; check the write rate and fragmentation, and measure with `redis-benchmark` under a real workload.
options: Primary and replica running on the same machine
Scores doubling in size when changed from integers to doubles
Extra memory from fork copy-on-write when taking a snapshot
Every skip list level holding a full copy of the data
exercises.prompt: The chapter suggests reserving about twice the memory for a write-heavy Redis. What is this mainly meant to cover?

exercises.explanation: Both replication and persistence have timing windows, so a failure may lose the most recent score updates. The reliable approach is to keep match events durably in a database as the source of truth; the Redis board is just a view that can be rebuilt.
exercises.prompt: If Redis has replicas and persistence enabled, it is guaranteed not to lose a single point of score during a failure.

exercises.explanation: Recovery needs a concrete data source: a match-event table plus a processed watermark, replayed idempotently by unique event ID, then totals reconciled. “Replay the MySQL WAL” is too vague: the redo log, binlog, and a match-event table are different things. Having clients resubmit goes back to untrusted input.
options: Idempotent replay by unique event ID, so duplicate events don't add points twice
Having player clients resubmit their own scores
A watermark recording how far processing has reached
Relying only on automatic Redis replica failover
Durably stored match result events
exercises.prompt: After a large-scale Redis failure, what is needed to reliably rebuild the monthly board to the correct state?

exercises.explanation: Write sharding appends a number suffix to the hot partition key, spreading one month's writes across N partitions; a string ID can be hashed first, then taken modulo. The cost is scatter-gather over N shards when querying. Removing the GSI doesn't help: the base table is still partitioned by month.
options: Remove the GSI to reduce writes to the current month's partition
Put the username in the sort key
Append a `user_id % N` suffix to the month key
Make the score the partition key
exercises.prompt: A DynamoDB leaderboard table uses the month as the partition key, so all writes for the current month land on one partition. What fix does this chapter give?

exercises.explanation: The shard count trades write throughput against read fan-out: one more shard spreads writes more evenly but adds one more query to merge when reading the top ten. Choose the count by benchmarking; more is not always better.
exercises.prompt: With DynamoDB write sharding, more shards spread writes more, but also mean more shards to scatter-gather when querying the top ten.

exercises.explanation: The sort key keeps each partition readable in score order; with the score alone, tied players' keys would collide, so the user ID makes them unique. The month is already used in the partition key. Updating a score moves the index entry, and GSI propagation delay must be counted against the real-time target.
exercises.prompt: Complete the key design of a DynamoDB leaderboard
exercises.text: The DynamoDB board uses the month plus a shard suffix as the partition key and [[score]] as the sort key; to keep keys unique on ties, append the [[user ID]].

exercises.explanation: A percentile changes the product's meaning: the requirement is a real-time exact rank, and a periodically computed approximate percentile is a different feature. It is fine to discuss switching to percentiles with product, but not to swap it in quietly on the technical side.
exercises.prompt: When the player base is too large to compute exact ranks in real time, you can simply switch to showing a periodically computed score percentile, without checking with product.

exercises.explanation: Dense ranking counts the distinct score levels strictly above: C has only the 100 level above it, so C is rank 2. Competition ranking counts players, giving C rank 3, and the zero-based Redis position plus 1 is also 3. Lexicographic order only decides the display order among ties; it doesn't affect rank.
options: 1st
3rd
Depends on the lexicographic order of member names
2nd
exercises.prompt: Scores are B=100, A=100, C=90. If the product uses dense ranking (ties share a rank, with no skipped numbers), what rank is C?

exercises.explanation: The authoritative server confirms the result first, then the result gets a unique ID; the leaderboard service deduplicates by ID before adding points, and the dedup check and the score update are best done in one atomic script. That way a timeout resend or a queue redelivery adds points only once.
items: The game server confirms the match result is valid
Generate a scoring event with a unique event ID
Leaderboard service checks if the event ID was processed
Run `ZINCRBY` to add to the player's score
exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a reliable score update in order

chapters.title: Payment System
keyPoints: At 1 million payments a day (about 12 TPS), the hard part isn’t throughput but moving money correctly exactly once.
Record the payment intent before calling the PSP. A timeout only means the result is unknown: query or retry with the original idempotency key.
The payment order, wallet, and ledger each answer one question: how far the charge got, what the balance is, and where the balance came from.
A browser redirect is not proof of payment; post the result from a signature-verified webhook or an active PSP query.
Exactly-once = at-least-once (retries) + at-most-once (idempotency); a consumer group alone doesn’t make business logic run once.
Reconciliation uses PSP settlement files as the safety net; fix differences with new correcting records, never by overwriting history.

labs.title: Retries, Idempotency Keys, and Reconciliation After a Payment Timeout

lessons.title: Pay-In Basics
lessons.summary: Estimate scale, trace pay-in, and keep three records

exercises.explanation: `1,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 11.6 TPS`; the chapter rounds it to about 10. That is no strain for a database. The hard part is moving money correctly exactly once, so failure handling, idempotency, and reconciliation all stay. Peak load needs a separate estimate.
options: About 1,200 TPS; the focus is sharding the database
About 12 TPS, so retries and reconciliation can be skipped
About 120 TPS; the focus is adding a cache
About 12 TPS; the focus is correctness, not throughput
exercises.prompt: At 1 million payments a day, about how many TPS is that on average, and what does it mean for the design focus?

exercises.explanation: The requirements rule out storing card data directly, for compliance reasons. A hosted payment page has the PSP collect and store the card details; the system keeps only a token that references the payment, so far less card data is exposed.
